Feiglin: There was 'terrible betrayal dismantling IDF' before Oct. 7 massacre, forgives Smotrich

Zehut party chairman Moshe Feiglin said that he fully forgave Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich for the harsh comments made against him in the past, while discussing their parties' joint run in the upcoming election with 103FM on Thursday.
“I think what you do not understand is that it is possible to forgive as well,” Feiglin explained. “We are in the month of mercy and forgiveness. The fact that I truly forgive is not just lip service. You probably have not experienced the pressure of political campaigns, during which he said those things. I have experienced it, and I can understand how a person gets to that point. I forgot about it, and now you are reminding me.”
Feiglin went on to clarify the planned political arrangement, explaining that the Zehut party and the Religious Zionist Party were running as a technical bloc. “We are a completely separate party from the Religious Zionist Party. We respect it, but we will run a separate campaign and operate separately afterward. After the elections, each party will go its own way, without a doubt. I believe we are going to bring five Knesset seats in the upcoming elections, and the connection with Smotrich will bring a double digit number of mandates, ‘read my lips.’”
One of Feiglin’s demands is the Defense Ministry portfolio. When asked, “How can a person who is irresponsible and megalomaniacal be defense minister?” Feiglin chuckled and responded, “With all due respect, the person who has been fighting Oslo for 30 years and the processes that led to the massacre, I was your loyal servant. The line represented by the Zehut party is a line that knew how to predict this massacre better than all the generals.”
The discussion later turned to security issues and the Israel-Hamas War. Feiglin strongly criticized the handling of the campaign and explained why he opposed hostage release deals.
“I think this deal will lead to the next kidnappings. I did oppose it, and I still oppose it,” he said emphatically. “The hostages could have been brought back after two weeks simply by shutting off Gaza’s water supply, a real siege. Anyone who wanted a cup of water would have left the tunnels with a hostage. That is why it took two years and has not ended. The first decision should have been that Gaza must be defeated immediately, and that this problem must be eliminated rather than leaving future generations with another round of kidnappings and massacres.”
October 7 was fault of both right and left, Feiglin claims
Regarding responsibility for the October 7 failure, Feiglin refused to point a finger at the political leadership.
“Responsibility for the massacre is divided equally between both sides, between the left and the right,” he claimed. “Although the left, through Oslo, brought the terrorists to the doorstep of the kindergartens of Kibbutz Be’eri and directly caused the terrible massacre, the right, which came to power in 1996 and did not cancel Oslo, cannot avoid responsibility. Netanyahu, when he did this thing of transferring funds to Hamas, did something terrible, without a doubt. But when the left was in the transition period into power, Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid also continued it and were proud of it.”
Asked whether there was a "betrayal from within" that led to the massacre, Feiglin responded cautiously. “I truly do not know if we will ever be able to know, because everything is hidden and concealed. But one thing I do know: shortly before October 7, there was a terrible betrayal here by those who did everything they could to openly dismantle the army, especially with foreign state money.”
Regarding the establishment of a state commission of inquiry, Feiglin expressed reservations about the involvement of the judiciary, saying that while he believed a commission of inquiry must be established, "at the same time, the High Court of Justice is a political party. On this specific issue, I completely agree with the Likud.”
Feiglin accuses LGBT community of 'progressive coercion'
At the end of the interview, the Identity chairman addressed the controversy surrounding his comments about the LGBT community.
“I am not against the rights of anyone, on the contrary. The Zehut party brings uncompromising personal freedom for every citizen of Israel,” he said. “Not long ago there was Pride Month. Everywhere I go, pride flags are flying over every mountain and hill. Imagine if I declared a Temple Month and the entire country mobilized budgets to put Temple flags throughout Israel. What would people shout? Religious coercion. So when there is progressive coercion, that is acceptable? Straight people also deserve rights.”

Middle Israel: Why is Sara Netanyahu going to war against Yair Golan? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:12:05 UTC
19:12:05 KST

Having survived his ship’s bombardment and emerged bewildered from the Mediterranean into which he was thrown, Menachem Begin resolved to turn military defeat into moral victory.
The consequent twisting of the confrontation’s events, from who provoked the Altalena war to who waged it, was discussed here last week. Yet Begin twisted another fact, concerning the size and significance of the cargo on the arms ship he led to Tel Aviv in June 1948.
Emerging that evening on the Irgun’s radio station, Begin delivered his famous address in which he ordered his men not to join a prospective civil war. While at it, he claimed that his crippled vessel had carried “10,000 aerial bombs.” Had those bombs joined the Independence War along with the cargo’s rifles and machine guns, “we might have been standing today on the Jordan, and maybe even beyond it,” Begin asserted.
In fact, that number was far-fetched, and so was the strategic claim attached to it – a sequel to Begin’s earlier suggestion that “the ship of salvation” would “decide the fate of the war.” (Avi Shilon, Begin: 1913-1992, Am Oved 2007, pp. 127, 135).
In fact, Begin’s cargo was but a fraction of what David Ben-Gurion had already secured half a year earlier, through an extensive arms deal with Czechoslovakia that included 50,000 rifles, 6,000 machine guns, and 20 fighter planes. This was besides 14,000 submachine guns and mortars that the Hagana had obtained and manufactured before 1948.
Begin’s twisting of the facts came to mind this week as Sara Netanyahu – whom this column has generally refrained from discussing – made an even more preposterous quip about one of her husband’s rivals, the Democrats’s Yair Golan.
'I don't want to talk'
“YOU CLAIM you fought on October 7,” she said on Channel 14, referring to Golan, suggesting he did not fight. “Early in the morning,” she continued, “you were already there, dressed and ready at a very early hour, while others, like the prime minister, didn’t know.” Asked whether there was treason that day, she didn’t say “God forbid,” or “let’s not get carried away,” or “are you out of your mind?” Rather, “I don’t want to talk.”
Yet talk she did, and her insinuation was as transparent as it was flabbergasting. Golan, according to this “conspiracism,” had advance information of the enemy’s invasion, and was part of it.
Golan is no political genius. He made some outrageous statements and seems clueless about his party’s domestic agenda, as well as its history as the engine of Zionist pioneering. That is why most voters don’t consider him a suitable candidate for prime minister. But this does not mean he is a villain, let alone a traitor. In fact, Golan is a major-league patriot.
In contrast to Sara Netanyahu’s hallucination, Golan rushed to the western Negev once news of Hamas’s massacre broke out. There are testimonies of people he personally saved and of others who fought alongside him, like Oz Davidian of Moshav Patish, who said he and Golan jointly rescued people from the Supernova music festival’s bloodbath.
No one can rob Golan of these heroic credentials. And so, the question arises: why did Sara Netanyahu utter the libel that Golan did not deserve, and which the swing vote will not reward? And the answer is that she twisted the facts of 2023 for the same reason Menachem Begin twisted the facts of 1948.
 
LIBELS ARE invented when the facts are impossible to refute, and their results are impossible to bear. 
Begin could not justify his reckless refusal to unconditionally hand the Altalena’s arms to the sovereign Jewish state. He therefore tried to shift the blame from those who made the provocation to those who responded to it. Similarly, the lie that his unsolicited arms shipment could have changed the course of the war was meant to change the subject, from his reckless misjudgment, to the war’s results.
Now Sara Netanyahu and the rest of the October 7 conspiracists cannot bear Benjamin Netanyahu’s misjudgments en route to that catastrophe. That is why they, and the entire ruling party, twist the facts and invent libels.
Likud’s denialism did not start with Begin’s lies in 1948.
Disastrous moves or fateful mistakes?
BEGIN’S MENTOR, Ze’ev Jabotinsky, made two disastrous moves that his followers would never admit were fateful mistakes. First, in 1923, he resigned from the Zionist Organization’s executive; second, in 1935, he made his Revisionist party secede from the Zionist Organization to establish a competing outfit, the New Zionist Organization.
It was a separatist mindset that culminated in the creation of a separate militia that challenged the Jewish Agency and its military arm, the Hagana. Jabotinsky thus condemned himself and his followers to history’s margins, where they remained for 37 years after his death.
Admitting that their irrelevance was their leader’s fault was mentally impossible for his followers. He was infallible. Begin never admitted that his mentor’s legacy of going it alone was catastrophic to himself, his followers, and the Zionist cause. Now that same spirit of “we can’t be wrong” and “it’s us or them” is governing the Netanyahu couple’s treatment of the past three years’ events.
That is why Sara Netanyahu, her husband, and the ruling party refuse to assume responsibility for what happened on October 7: not Benjamin Netanyahu’s funding of Hamas, not his rejection of pleas to attack Hamas, and not his 2004 vote for the unilateral withdrawal from Gaza – an idea that was conceived and executed not by Golan or any other lefty, but by a government led by the Likud.
Repenting for any of this does not cross their minds. Like Begin before them, they will finger anyone but themselves. Yet Begin had a good excuse for his denialism and lies: his Jewish enemies had aimed a cannon at him, and fired. What’s your excuse, Sara?
The writer, a Hartman Institute fellow, is the author of the bestseller, The Jewish March of Folly (Yedioth Books 2026), now available in English on Amazon.

Israel cannot prevent another October 7 if Netanyahu keeps rewriting the first one - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:11:57 UTC
19:11:57 KST

“We are getting dangerously close to a violent, multifront confrontation. According to reports from the security establishment, the number of warnings in Judea and Samaria is unprecedented.
“The ones who will pay the price are our children, who will once again have to enter the Jenin refugee camp, once again go into Gaza, and perhaps once again into Lebanon. The ones who will pay the price are our parents, who will once again have to sit in their safe rooms.”
These words sound like something that could have been said yesterday. They were, however, spoken by Yair Lapid, the head of the opposition, three years ago this month, on September 20, 2023 – just a couple of weeks before the Hamas invasion on October 7.
Lapid later explained that he decided to go before the cameras with such a stark, dire warning after receiving one of the regular monthly security briefings given to the opposition leader by the prime minister and his military secretary. During that meeting, Lapid said, he was shown some of the most sensitive and classified intelligence collected by Israel’s security establishment.
The message, as he understood it, was clear: Israel’s enemies were watching the deep divisions tearing through Israeli society over the government’s judicial overhaul. They saw weakness and vulnerability. And they believed there might be an opportunity to strike.
That was why, on the eve of Yom Kippur in 2023, Lapid issued his warning. He could hardly have been more prophetic. Two-and-a-half weeks later, Hamas invaded Israel. Our children were sent to fight in Gaza, Jenin, and eventually Lebanon. Our parents – and the rest of us – were sent running to bomb shelters and safe rooms.
October 7 to play a role in next election
From the moment elections were called for the end of October, it was obvious that October 7 would play a central role in every political party’s campaign. What was less obvious was the extent to which the disaster would become the subject of manipulation, distortion, and outright fabrication, particularly by members of the governing coalition determined to deflect criticism and wash their hands of responsibility for the greatest catastrophe to befall the Jewish people since the Holocaust, a catastrophe that happened on their watch.
That is how we need to look at the interview that Sara Netanyahu gave this week to Channel 14 in which she attempted to tarnish the reputation of Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats Party, who famously put on his uniform on the morning of October 7, drove south, and helped rescue Israelis from the killing fields around the Supernova music festival.
Like so many heroic Israelis who saw their fellow citizens in mortal danger that morning, Golan did not wait for orders. A former deputy IDF chief of staff, he took his sidearm and headed toward the fighting, repeatedly entering an area crawling with terrorists to rescue people and bring them to safety.
Yet Sara Netanyahu insinuated that Golan must somehow have had advance knowledge that something was about to happen, because he put on his uniform that morning – while her husband, the prime minister, had not been woken by the heads of the security establishment.
It was a disgusting accusation. It not only suggested some sort of conspiracy against Benjamin Netanyahu, but cast suspicion on a man who risked his own life to save others. To question the integrity, courage, and motives of Israelis who voluntarily entered a combat zone that morning is appalling.
While her comments were rightly condemned across the political spectrum, Sara Netanyahu is not really the story. She is the prime minister’s wife, not an elected official, and her comments should not consume too much of our attention.
The more important story is the coalition itself, which continues to do all it can to evade responsibility.
While Sara was in the headlines, Netanyahu was also pushing his new claim – had he been woken at 4 or 5 a.m. on October 7, he would have made decisions that could have prevented the Hamas invasion. Why wasn’t he woken? Because, he suggested, the security chiefs knew that he would force them to act, and they did not want him to.
There are several problems with this argument. The first is that it is highly unlikely Netanyahu would have done what he now claims.
Had he been woken, he would have heard from IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) director Ronen Bar, and Military Intelligence chief Aharon Haliva. All three would have given him essentially the same assessment they themselves mistakenly believed as they analyzed the little intelligence that was coming in that night: Hamas was probably not preparing for a major attack, and if something was going to happen, it would be limited in scope.
With every senior security official presenting essentially the same assessment, does anyone seriously believe Netanyahu would have ordered Israel to launch a war against Hamas at 4 or 5 in the morning?
Far more likely, he would have instructed them to remain vigilant, continue monitoring the situation, and reconvene a few hours later.
That, essentially, was the catastrophic mistake that Amir Bohbot and I describe in our book While Israel Slept. The warning signs were there, but they were interpreted through an intelligence framework that assumed Hamas did not want a major war.
But Netanyahu’s political objective now is to portray October 7 as exclusively their failure, a tactical intelligence breakdown that had nothing to do with him, his policies, or the strategy he pursued toward Hamas for years.
That strategy included containing Hamas, allowing Qatari money to flow into Gaza, and repeatedly deciding against using the IDF to remove Hamas from power.
Keeping the national debate focused narrowly on the intelligence and operational failures of the night of October 6 and the early hours of October 7 serves Netanyahu politically. It keeps attention away from the much larger question of strategy: how Israel reached a point where Hamas was able to build an army on the other side of the border, prepare an invasion for years, and convince Israeli leaders that it had no intention of using it.
The second problem with Netanyahu’s argument is even more fundamental.
It is a wrong illustration of leadership. Leadership is supposed to mean understanding that subordinates will sometimes make mistakes – even catastrophic ones – and that ultimate responsibility rests with the person at the top.
Sometimes I wonder what would have happened politically had Netanyahu chosen a different path after October 7. What if he had gone to the funerals of those murdered and visited their families during shiva? What if he had stood before the families and heard their yells and criticism, had appeared before the Israeli public and said something simple: I failed. What if he had publicly grieved for the 1,200 people massacred on his watch and accepted even a measure of responsibility for what happened?
Perhaps it would even have helped him politically. Perhaps showing compassion, humility, and accountability would have won back some of the Israelis who turned away from him after October 7.
It is an interesting thought experiment, but that is all it is. Because Netanyahu’s political doctrine has long been clear: never accept responsibility, never admit failure, and, above all, never say sorry.
The tragedy is that nearly three years after October 7, Israel is not only still fighting over who was responsible for the failures of that day. It is heading into an election in which those failures are being rewritten in real time.
And a country that cannot honestly confront how it reached October 7 will have a much harder time ensuring that another one can never happen.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD Forum, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His latest book (with Amir Bohbot), While Israel Slept, is a bestseller in the United States.

European states criticize Israel, but keep relying on its defense technology - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:11:44 UTC
19:11:44 KST

The gap between Israel’s diplomatic relations with several European countries and the security ties they continue to maintain with Jerusalem is widening. Even countries that have escalated their rhetoric, imposed sanctions, and limited political ties with Israel are not rushing to abandon Israeli weapons systems, technology, and defense equipment.
“Most countries maintain a certain degree of duality,” political officials familiar with the issue say.
Spain is the most prominent example. In September 2025, Madrid adopted a law intended to establish a broad embargo on weapons and defense equipment involving Israel, including restrictions on exports to Israel and imports from Israel. Israeli officials say that in practice, the embargo is not airtight, in part because the law allows the government to approve exceptions when it determines that the national interest requires it.
“There is nothing airtight, and they are not following it either,” Israeli officials say.
According to political officials, defense deals with Spain continued even after the law took effect, including activities permitted under the exemption mechanism.
The Spanish law includes an exception allowing the government to approve deals that would otherwise be prohibited if fully implementing the restrictions would harm “general national interests.” In some cases, therefore, defense activity is not taking place in violation of the embargo, but under the exemption clause that Madrid itself included in the legislation.
The Spanish government has already used the exception to allow Airbus to continue using Israeli technology in strategic projects after determining that completely halting its use could harm production capabilities, jobs and defense projects for which there is no immediate alternative.
Discussions held in Spain also highlighted the country’s continued dependence on Israeli technology, licenses and technical support for several defense systems. Fully replacing these components and systems is not possible in the immediate term and would entail high costs and the development of local or European alternatives.
Madrid has canceled deals with Israel, and Jerusalem does not claim that the embargo exists only on paper. Spain has halted certain purchases and projects and is working to reduce its defense dependence on Israel. However, the exemptions included in the law allow the Spanish government to continue defense cooperation with Israel when it determines that national interests require it.
The Netherlands is also advancing measures against trade with settlements
The Netherlands, for example, is advancing measures against trade with settlements, while its Defense Ministry continues to purchase Israeli systems when no available alternative exists. The Dutch government has publicly stated that, in certain fields, Israeli companies provide essential systems or components for which there is currently no suitable, available Dutch or European replacement.
In Finland, as public and political debate surrounding Israel intensified, Helsinki quietly extended its defense cooperation agreement with Israel until 2034. The agreement, which covers research and development and defense procurement, was renewed in 2024, after the war in Gaza had already begun.
The renewal was initiated by Finland and extended the agreement for 10 years, compared with five years under previous arrangements. The Finnish Defense Ministry did not announce the decision at the time.
The relationship with Israeli defense industries plays a significant role in Finnish defense procurement. Israel is Finland’s second-largest foreign defense supplier and provides systems such as the David’s Sling and Gabriel missiles. Finland has explained that maintaining the relationship is necessary to carry out existing deals, maintenance, and long-term cooperation.
In Germany, expanded defense cooperation with Israel continues even as Berlin has voiced criticism of Israeli policy on issues including E1 and settlements. The Arrow 3 deal and its expansion have made Germany one of the main customers of Israel’s defense industry and were among the factors that helped drive Israeli defense exports to a new record.
In Greece, another major deal with Israel was recorded on Monday, during a period in which criticism of the Gaza war has also been heard in Athens. The two countries signed the “Achilles Shield” deal worth approximately 3 billion euros, the largest defense export deal in the history of Israel-Greece relations and one of the largest in Israel’s history.
In the Baltic states, Jerusalem has identified an “upward trend” in demand for Israeli systems due to growing concerns over Russia. According to Israeli political officials, the Baltic states view themselves as being “on the front line” and fear they could be next if the Russian threat expands.
The war in Ukraine and the Russian threat have changed defense priorities across Europe. European countries are rapidly increasing their defense budgets and seeking systems that have already demonstrated operational capabilities. In several areas, there is no available European replacement for Israeli technology.
Finland, for example, has made it clear that the war in Ukraine has demonstrated the critical importance of air defense capabilities.
Defense exports at a record high
In Jerusalem, officials are seeking to separate, as much as possible, political disputes with European governments from security ties with them. Israel is not rushing to halt defense deals in response to political criticism.
“We are pragmatic,” political officials say.
From Israel’s perspective, stopping deals could harm domestic defense industries, hand market share to competitors, led by France, and reduce the influence created through long-standing ties between Israeli industries and European defense establishments.
The Israeli interest is also reflected in the numbers. In 2025, Israeli defense exports reached a record $19.2 billion, a jump of nearly 30% in one year and more than double the figure from five years earlier.
The Defense Ministry views expanding defense exports as a tool for strengthening industries, financing security needs and advancing diplomatic objectives.
Even in Israel, there is no complete separation between political and security considerations. A deal may be halted if there is concern about technology leakage, the transfer of a system to a hostile actor, or other security risks.
Political officials do not rule out the possibility that political considerations could affect a deal under certain circumstances. The diplomatic tensions with several European governments have not, for now, halted security cooperation.
European countries are increasing defense budgets and confronting the Russian threat, and in areas where no available alternative exists, they are finding it difficult to give up Israeli systems.
Spain is perhaps the most prominent example: even after enshrining a broad embargo on Israel into law, it left room for exceptions when its security needs and national interests require it.

Can technology optimize companionship? A novelist imagines the extreme answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:08:15 UTC
19:08:15 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
I’m just old enough to remember a time when using websites and apps to go on dates was the exception, not the rule. When I fired up OkCupid circa 2012, it wasn’t because you had to use an app to meet someone; I just felt like all of its profile questions and filtering tools felt like they made it easier. By the time I sunsetted my profile for the last time in 2017, things had shifted dramatically to favor not just online dating in general but Tinder-style, swipe-based profile browsing. And by then, it definitely didn’t feel like all those algorithms were making it easier to find love or even like. By selling us the idea that finding companionship could be as easy as swiping right, dating apps had also programmed us to believe that we could find a perfect partner if we just kept on scrolling. That was convenient for their business models but not so great for encouraging people to form lasting relationships.
That golden era of the dating app and all the downsides that came with it helped inspire today’s guest, Sarah Pierce. Her debut novel For Human Use imagines a future where efforts to optimize human connection reach an absurd and macabre conclusion: an app that matches users to dead bodies. It’s a darkly funny tech thriller that makes some fascinating observations about the mismatch between our desire for companionship and what supposedly social apps actually sell us instead.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Sarah recently sat down to chat with SciAm’s books and culture lead Bri Kane. Here’s their conversation.
Kane: I’m so excited to talk to you about your book For Human Use. There’s a really wild core concept in this book, so I wanted to ask for your top-line summary and how you came up with this core concept.
Pierce: All this time, I’m still really bad at the top-line summary. And it’s changed a little, but it’s basically, it’s about a tech founder who convinces the world to use a dating app, except when you swipe right, the person’s dead body shows up, and you live with it. And it’s about that tech founder and the finance guy who’s kinda trying to stop him.
Kane: Yeah, and so this book, I really liked how it spun out from this core concept because you see that on the cover, “Oh, you’re dating a dead body. What does that even mean?” And it turns into this really wild, twisty thriller. So I wanted to ask you: What trends on dating apps do you see that inspired your interest in these larger cultural fads and how they spin out to not just a trend on a dating app anymore?
Pierce: It’s funny, when the book first came out, [it] was like, you know, you were dating in “the golden age of dating apps,” which is just such a funny phrase because it certainly didn’t feel that way. But, you know, there was a period in New York, let’s call it 2015 to 2017, where dating apps were huge. People were using them in the way they were intended to be used.
And so, at that same time, there was a finance trend going on in New York, which is like, all these tech guys were getting pretty far in finance with, sort of, these bullshit California tech ideas. They were just getting really far in New York culture. And for New York, which has generally and historically been dominated by finance, there was a big period where it felt like tech was really big in New York. And it was like, “Is this the sunset of the Wall Street archetype in New York, and we’re gonna be ruled on both coasts by the Californian tech founder?”
And so I was really drawn into that idea of these two archetypal men: Silicon Valley tech founder, Wall Street guy. And, you know, “Who do you hate more?” is sort of one question of the book.
Kane: Yeah, I mean, it seemed like a very, you know, pretty pointed critique of how these apps, these, like, start-up culture apps, are often financed before they’re truly understood. And in the book, we really see the ramifications of that lack of understanding that still has billions of dollars on the line.
Pierce: Yeah, ’cause, like, meeting people was something that was extremely hard to commodify. You know, you could commodify it indirectly, I suppose, in clubs and in entertainment culture is a thing. But I thought it was really funny that the, sort of, meat market of human dating was so commodified with, you know, Bumble and Tinder and Hinge and The League. It was like they all happened at once in this explosion. And it’s funny, looking back on it, for as much as I didn’t enjoy it while it was happening, I didn’t appreciate that, like, people were using the apps as they were intended to be used. So when you swiped right on someone, and you both connected, yes, there was always someone who didn’t message you or, like, just wanted to message and not meet up. That’s always been there. But it seems, talking to people who are still active on these apps, that seems to have become the dominant thing, is that people now will swipe, and then there’s no conversation. They’re having trouble making that last step into meeting in real life, which is funny, ’cause it’s like, “Then what are you doing? Do you log on to this app just to talk to random people?” And the answer is, like, for a lot of people, it seems to be that’s what they’re using it for.
Kane: Yeah, and so this book also tackles teens using this app, which I thought was a really interesting twist. It’s one thing to think about teens using Instagram or even dating apps and how the lines of appropriate behavior there need to be investigated, they need to be understood. I don’t wanna spoil too much about your book in this interview, but all this discussion about teen safety online, what you’ve been thinking about it, marinating in these thoughts, given your work, and what inspired you to involve teens in this story of this dating app with the dead that you created?
Pierce: Everything cool has to have some large connection to youth culture. That’s sort of the nature of what cool is. The book is really more about everybody’s reaction to this app being used and observation. And so it’s funny, a lot of the younger readers will pick up the book, and they’re like, “I wanted to read about dating a dead body.” And it’s like, “I know you did,” like, “I wrote this book about you.” And older readers, you know, I’ve tried with different people to sort of pinpoint the age of the reader that’s really perfect for this book, and the best thing I can come up with age-wise: If you were old enough to watch the news on September 11th, I have a more than decent chance of entertaining you with this book. If you were not old enough to watch the news on September 11th, I think some of it is just, the humor isn’t gonna land with the person in the same way, if that makes sense. And I think that’s a roundabout way of saying: If you have sort of two feet in your adolescence having grown up without all this stuff, you have a different experience watching Gen Z interact with these trends than if you’re on the borderline or if you are Gen Z.
Kane: Yeah, I mean, there’s a real generational divide in our understanding of dating apps and their purpose, and the years that you’re on it, as you’re saying, have really changed what your experience on those apps is—which also makes me think about the changing understandings that we’ve had around death and our relationship with death and our cultural institutions’ relationship with death. So I wanted to ask you about some of your inspiration behind these cultural traditional relationships with death and what you found so interesting about, kind of, poking at them and bringing them to the modern world and how disturbing that can be.
Pierce: Yeah. You know, it’s funny, the book is about dead bodies, but I wouldn’t necessarily think that it’s about death but death as this sort of last sacred, intense thing. You know, we have so many things that have become less sacred in our culture—premarital sex, like, people living much of their lives unmarried, or they spend a good chunk of their lives in these dating periods. A person is likely to date for 10 or 12 years, which is just so different than past generations. But when you have these—around death, there is a sort of forced reverence, which I was drawn to.
Just also completely unrelated, but as a, you know, practical matter, the idea came to me in a dream. You know, I met my husband on a dating app. When he was just my boyfriend, we moved in together. And, you know, very early on after moving in, I had a dream, and I’m a big lucid dreamer. I woke up from our bed, and I went to our front door of the apartment that we had just moved into. I opened it, and there was a dead body there. And my first thought was like, “I don’t need this because I have a boyfriend.” And so in the way that dreams sort of bring things together that are not connected, I think at that period where I was truly, I was falling in love with my husband, and I knew that I was never gonna be dating again, there was some part of my brain decided to deliver that in the form of a, a corpse that got dropped at the doorstep. And at the same time, I was taking a creative writing class, and the rest is history.
Kane: Yeah, I don’t want to psychoanalyze your dreams too much on the podcast, Sarah, but that is fascinating to me because the book really does seem to be dealing with the much larger question about human connection and that we are all driven to connect in some capacity. But “our modern world and modern dating apps have made it harder to have a genuine connection with people, to the point that, to find something that feels genuine, people are willing to connect with a corpse” seems to be what I took away as a message from the text. So I wanted to ask you how you connect with the dead. Do you have some sort of death doula practice that inspired any of this, or are you freaked out by dead bodies as much as I am?
Pierce: I am just as freaked out. And you know, it’s funny, on day one of the book, people should know, the protagonist of the book thinks this is crazy.
Kane: It helped me get through the book as well. [Laughs.]
Pierce: He’s like, “What is going on?” And I think that feeling I’m very familiar with. I think the strangest part about getting older—I’m 39 now—is, you know, the things that have happened in the last five or 10 years, it’s just, if you had told me in high school, like, “This will be happening,” I would’ve been like, “You’re crazy.” And I think that a lot of people are experiencing that on a political level, on a cultural level, that we’ve really lost a lot. We all seek a frictionless existence, when it’s like: What is the benefit of that? And I think in love, it’s, there’s a huge drawback to it. The book goes after a lot of online affirmation culture about how it’s, like, always the other person—all this therapyspeak that’s everywhere, and we’ve sort of just forgotten, like, the first rule of human interaction: to just be there with another person and talk and have back-and-forth. And we’ve added just too much information to these, what should be, sort of, natural interactions. And I think a lot of people feel sort of paralyzed, and there’s something attractive about this, sort of, organic but inanimate stand-in.
Kane: Yeah, I think that’s an interesting twist on the book overall. It’s a book that’s interested in the psychology of “Who would interact with this, and how would they interact with it? Why are they drawn to it, why are they repulsed by it, and what do those feelings cause them to do?”
So to close this out today, I have to ask you, “Do you have any advice to us still on the apps? Should we just not settle for the dead ones?” or anything else that you can give me. [Laughs.]
Pierce: I mean, I tell everyone, like, keep going. Dating sucks. It does. And I think it’s really tough that there are so many people out there with this expectation that it should improve or be something meaningful, when in reality, that’s a feature, not a bug. It’s meant to suck because that makes it all the more obvious when you find the right person. And so I think people getting out there and just accepting that’s the nature of it. It’s supposed to be hard; it’s supposed to be demoralizing. There’s all these terrible experiences that you have, some of them really serious, and it’s so tempting to not wanna have them. But there’s a pretty big drawback to not having it, and that’s when you make yourself safe from those terrible experiences, you also cut off everything good, too.
Kane: Exactly. Maybe you get a great listener in a dead body but not a great conversationalist.
Pierce: Correct.
Kane: Well, awesome. Thank you so much for talking with me today. I loved For Human Use, Sarah. I cannot stop recommending it to people. I think it’s a really fun and twisty horror book for this year, so thank you so much for talking with me about it.
Pierce: Thanks so much for having me.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. We’ll be off on Monday for Labor Day, but we’re back next Wednesday with another story about our universal need for companionship—no corpses in this one, though. I promise. The cost of living isn't killing joy - it’s just making us surgical about it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:03:07 UTC
19:03:07 KST

Nearly half - about 46% - of all money spent by EU households goes to three basic things: food, housing and energy, and transport. You need them to live, to get to work, and to keep the lights on.
For millions of families across Europe, the monthly budget is tight.
Essential goods like food, housing, energy, and transport consume roughly 46% of every euro spent by EU households, forming the non-negotiable baseline required to cover daily survival, commuting, and utilities.
With eurozone inflation sitting at a three-year high of 3.3% and energy costs jumping 14.3%, fresh Eurostat numbers show a strange counter-trend. Instead of shutting their wallets completely, people are quietly shaving pennies off their daily routines so they can still afford a normal and enjoyable life.
While those heavy bills still consume the most household cash, consumers are quietly trimming fat elsewhere — and redirecting funds toward culture, dining, and well-being.
The heavy anchors
Housing and utilities remain the biggest drain on wallets — a lingering hangover from past energy spikes, with geopolitical tensions continuing to push fuel and utility costs upward. Food prices have also settled at painfully high levels, forcing shoppers to relentlessly rethink their carts.
Then there is transport. Fuel, transit passes, and car upkeep absorb a massive chunk of structural spending.
Eurostat notes that these exact categories drove the worst of recent price hikes, underlining just how much they dictate the broader rise in consumer prices. When utilities, rent, and groceries dictate where the paycheque goes, everything else becomes a zero-sum game.
Where the money is moving
Instead of cutting back across the board, consumers directed a larger share of their budgets toward a few unexpected areas between January 2025 and January 2026, according to Eurostat.
Recreation, sport and culture saw the biggest jump, rising by 1.2 percentage points. Restaurants and accommodation services ticked up by 0.3 percentage points, while education edged up by 0.1 percentage points.
It's a clear sign of consumer resilience—people are still finding cash for a concert ticket or a meal out, even if they're pulling back at the grocery store.
Where households pulled back
To balance the books, shoppers tightened up on other expenses. Transport budget shares dipped by 0.4 percentage points over the year.
While it remains a massive chunk of total spending, this shift highlights how households are dynamically reprioritising their wallets — optimising transit costs where possible to free up cash for personal well-being.
Simultaneously, information and communication spending fell by 0.3 percentage points, reflecting how households optimise fixed connectivity overhead when inflation pinches disposable income.
According to Eurostat’s HICP (harmonised index of consumer prices) monitoring frameworks and category weightings, this spending split isn't felt equally. Lower-income households are largely forced to absorb higher utility and food costs without room to pivot, meaning the cash flowing into recreation and dining is driven primarily by middle- and higher-income consumers protecting their quality of life.
These shifting decimal points reveal a deeper economic reality about post-inflation consumer behaviour in Europe.
Rather than reacting to the crisis with cutbacks, households are making careful trade-offs. Because essentials like rent and groceries consume 46% of every budget and refuse to shrink, every extra euro requires a choice.
People are quietly cutting back on transit and phone plans to defend personal well-being. Modern economic resilience isn’t about spending less across the board – it’s about protecting what matters most.

Farmers face livestock cuts as nitrogen plan falls short

Farmers face livestock cuts as nitrogen plan falls short
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch farmers are still facing a compulsory cut in the number of animals they can keep as livestock, after the government’s environmental assessment agency found the cabinet’s nitrogen plan would fall just short of its own 2035 target.
The agency, PBL, assessed the €20 billion nitrogen plan at the cabinet’s request and called it an important step that could bring the farming emissions target within reach.
But it found the measures worked out so far leave a gap, and that an across-the-board cut of 5% to 10% in farmers’ livestock rights, the permits that cap how many animals a farm may hold, is still needed.
The coalition has always said that a blanket cut is a last resort, to be used only if the targets are missed in 2035. Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen called it an “emergency brake” on Friday and “a no-go for the cabinet.”
Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035, against 2019 levels, under the package agreed in June. PBL expects the herd to shrink further regardless as farms adapt to those rules, with some businesses forced to close.
The agency was more positive about the plan’s benefits for the environment, but warned the nitrogen problem will not just disappear. On more than half the area of the most sensitive protected sites, deposition is still expected to breach the critical threshold in 2035.
Nature groups called the plans the minimum needed to start repairing decades of damage. The farmers’ party BBB and the farm lobby LTO said the extra cut was unacceptable, though LTO is staying at the table to negotiate the rest of the package.

IKEAhas installed a series of handcrafted miniature homes across public locations in Melbourne, Chengdu, and Beijing. Created with Stockholm-based artist Christopher Robin Nordström, the detailed 1:12 scale models highlight how domestic environments maintain character within limited footprints. Modern homes are increasingly expected to perform beyond their original layouts, serving as workplaces, creative studios, classrooms, and sanctuaries within unchanged square footage. This spatial pressure often creates friction in daily life.
Addressing this spatial pressure, the ‘Tiny Houses’ public project reflects findings from IKEA’s Store and Organise Report 2026. Surveying over 30,000 respondents across 31 global markets, the study reveals a cultural shift away from sterile minimalism toward meaningful mess, with 59% of people preferring a characterful home over a manicured one. Driven by this shift, the initiative demonstrates how simple layout reconfigurations can unlock usable space without requiring extensive renovations.
IKEA collaborates with Stockholm-based artist Christopher Robin Nordström for ‘Tiny Houses’| all images courtesy of IKEA
INTENTIONAL OWNERSHIP RETHINKS THE IDEAL OF HOME
The miniature installations mark the launch of IKEA open house, a global initiative exploring how adaptable storage creates physical and mental room for daily domestic life. Inside each model, everyday furniture adapts to real living routines, featuring scaled icons such as the BILLY bookcase and METOD kitchen. Reframing storage beyond simple concealment, the Swedish company’s project demonstrates how affordable, intuitive layout adjustments support daily life rather than enforce perfection. This spatial rethinking arrives as the friction between domestic expectations and reality widens, with 82% of people keeping items purely for sentimental reasons, even if they remain out of sight or rarely used.
‘People aren’t chasing a perfect home anymore,’ says Licca Li, Home Furnishing and Retail Design Manager at Ingka Group (IKEA). ‘They want a home that feels like them, holding their stories, their memories, and the things that matter. What we keep says a lot about who we are. It was never just stuff.’
the miniature layouts showcase how intuitive adjustments open physical and mental space for personal history
IKEA FORGEs PURPOSEFUL ORGANIZATION OVER PERFECTION
The public installations examine how spatial constraints shape daily domestic behavior across different cultures. Findings from the report reveal that many inhabitants navigate two distinct environments simultaneously, balancing the actual lived-in interior with the curated version presented to guests. Kitchen countertops emerge as primary points of spatial friction, while concealed nooks absorb the weight of daily organization. Across households globally, 68% maintain a dedicated drawer for misplaced items, cables, and keys. Limited square footage also prompts unconventional storage habits, with 10% of homes worldwide, rising to 21% in South Korea, using ovens as supplementary storage space.
These spatial compromises link directly to emotional retention. Globally, nearly 1 in 5 people keep unwanted gifts simply to avoid hurting the giver’s feelings. At the same time, 26% of inhabitants admit to concealing mementos from past relationships, a behavior 6% more common among men.
kitchen countertops act as primary zones of daily spatial friction
Domestic clutter carries direct social consequences. Globally, 10% of people have canceled plans with friends because their space felt too messy, while 34% shuffle clutter between rooms before guests arrive. Time spent searching for misplaced items also varies by region, taking 15 minutes a day in the UK compared to 80 minutes in India. However, disorganization is not universally negative. Around 15% of people globally view mess as a spark for creativity, a figure that jumps to 31% in China compared to 4% in Japan. Nordström’s miniature homes and the supporting global report demonstrate that functional design should not force artificial perfection, but rather offer flexible solutions that allow people to live comfortably alongside what they treasure.
IKEA’s adaptable systems balance functional storage with room for personal history
While miniature installations introduce the project in public spaces, IKEA open house extends the experience into retail environments from late August through September. Across participating markets, visitors can explore modular storage configurations, spatial setups, and practical design solutions that make home feel calmer, more functional, and better suited to everyday routines.
‘When you build in miniature, you can’t include everything,’ says Nordström. ‘Every object has to earn its place. You quickly realize that a home isn’t defined by how much it contains, but by the things people choose to make room for. Those are the details that tell a human story.’

Regular coffee beats decaf in protecting the brain from chronic stress, mouse study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:00:32 UTC
19:00:32 KST

Regular coffee consumption might do more than just wake you up; it appears to protect the brain against the damaging effects of chronic stress. A new study in mice found that drinking caffeinated coffee prevented stress-induced memory loss and mood deterioration, while decaffeinated coffee offered no such benefits. The findings, published in Neurobiology of Stress, suggest that caffeine is the primary ingredient responsible for coffee’s mood-protecting properties.
For years, researchers have tried to understand the relationship between dietary habits and mental health. Epidemiological evidence frequently points to coffee as a protective beverage. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 indicated that moderate coffee consumption is associated with a lower risk of mood and stress disorders. These population studies raised an interesting question about which specific parts of the complex beverage drive these benefits.
Scientific investigations have built a case for caffeine as the active ingredient. As an example, a 2011 study of women found that drinking regular caffeinated coffee was linked to a lower risk of depression, whereas decaffeinated coffee offered no such protection. Following this, a 2015 study in mice demonstrated that pure caffeine prevents the mood and memory problems normally triggered by long-term stress. Yet, a 2018 analysis showed that decaf coffee still contains nearly all of the same healthy antioxidants as regular coffee, leaving scientists wondering if other nutrients in the beverage also played a role.
To settle whether caffeine is truly the essential ingredient for stress resilience, Ângelo R. Tomé and Rodrigo A. Cunha of the University of Coimbra led a research team to directly compare the effects of regular and decaffeinated coffee. They focused on how these beverages affected mice exposed to chronic unpredictable stress.
Chronic unpredictable stress is a laboratory model used to mimic human depression and anxiety. By exposing animals to mild, changing stressors over a period of several weeks, scientists can observe the resulting emotional and cognitive decline. The research team also wanted to look closely at changes in the brain, specifically measuring long-term potentiation and brain-derived neurotrophic factor.
Long-term potentiation is a process where the connections between neurons strengthen, serving as a cellular foundation for learning and memory. This activity is heavily concentrated in the hippocampus, a brain region dedicated to forming memories. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor is a protein that acts like a fertilizer for the brain, helping neurons grow and survive. The researchers measured this protein in the frontal cortex, an area heavily involved in complex behaviors and emotional regulation.
The research team studied 24 adult mice, dividing them into four groups. One group drank water and experienced no stress. The other three groups underwent three weeks of chronic unpredictable stress. During this time, they experienced random daily stressors, such as damp bedding, a brief cold bath, or having their cage tilted. One of the stressed groups drank regular water, another drank a caffeinated coffee extract, and the final group drank a decaffeinated coffee extract.
The mice received their respective beverages during their active nighttime hours, starting a week before the stress protocol began and continuing throughout the experiment. The amount of coffee the mice voluntarily drank roughly translated to an adult human consuming about 350 milligrams of caffeine a day, or roughly two to three standard cups of coffee.
Following the three weeks of stress, the researchers put the mice through a series of behavioral tests. They used an open field arena to measure spontaneous movement and general anxiety. They also evaluated anxiety by seeing how much time the mice spent in the unprotected open arms of an elevated maze. To assess depressive-like behaviors, the team observed the mice in a forced swimming test, recording how quickly they gave up struggling and simply floated.
The team sprayed a sticky sugar solution on the mice for a splash test, measuring how quickly they cleaned themselves as a sign of motivation and self-care. They also tracked whether the mice lost their natural preference for drinking a sweet sugar water solution. A loss of this preference serves as an indicator of anhedonia, which is the inability to feel pleasure.
Finally, the researchers tested spatial memory. They watched whether the mice could recognize when a familiar object had been moved to a new location in a testing arena. They also tested whether the mice preferred to explore a newly opened arm of a maze they had previously navigated.
The results showed that chronic unpredictable stress took a heavy toll on the mice drinking plain water. Compared to the unstressed controls, these mice lost weight, displayed heightened anxiety, and showed a pronounced lack of self-care. They also exhibited severe anhedonia, drinking much less sugar water than usual. Their spatial memory suffered, as they struggled to notice moved objects or explore new areas of the maze.
However, the mice that drank caffeinated coffee weathered the stress remarkably well. Their behavioral patterns were nearly identical to the control mice that experienced no stress at all. The caffeinated coffee prevented the weight loss, the anxiety, the despair in the swimming test, and the loss of motivation for self-care. It also fully protected their spatial memory.
The decaffeinated coffee failed to provide these robust protections. The stressed mice drinking decaf exhibited almost all the same behavioral deficits as the stressed mice drinking water. They failed to recover their body weight, remained anxious in the open field and maze tests, and showed persistent memory issues. While the decaf group showed very slight improvements in a few areas, these small changes were not statistically meaningful.
The brain tissue analysis provided a biological explanation for the behavioral differences. In the stressed mice drinking water, the magnitude of long-term potentiation in the hippocampus dropped from a roughly 61 percent baseline increase down to just 25 percent, indicating a severe disruption in memory-forming capacity. The levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor in their frontal cortex also plummeted.
Drinking caffeinated coffee completely prevented these neurological declines. The mice in this group maintained normal long-term potentiation and normal levels of the neurotrophic protein, keeping their brain networks highly functional despite the chronic stress. Just as with the behavioral tests, decaffeinated coffee offered no protection for the brain, leaving the mice with diminished synaptic plasticity and depleted protein levels.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that caffeine protects rodents from stress-induced spatial memory deficits and hippocampal impairment. They also align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, which demonstrated that caffeine prevents stress-induced depressive-like behaviors and preserves neurochemical balance in mice.
However, the results are in tension with another study covered by PsyPost in 2024. That study found that non-caffeine compounds in coffee protected against stress-induced cognitive deficits. It is worth noting that the earlier research tested isolated coffee polyphenols during early development, rather than using whole decaffeinated coffee in adult mice exposed to chronic stress, which likely explains the differing outcomes.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study did not measure the exact circulating levels of caffeine or other specific compounds in the blood or tissues of the mice. Because the animals were housed in small groups during the fluid consumption phase to avoid the added stress of isolation, the researchers could not track the precise individual intake for every single mouse.
The testing was also performed on a mixed group of male and female mice without isolating sex as a variable. Past studies suggest there may be discrete differences in how coffee impacts mood in males compared to females, which this study design could not explore. Finally, translating behavioral and brain changes from mice to humans always requires caution, as human diets, stress factors, and brain chemistry are far more complex.
The study, “Regular intake of caffeinated but not decaffeinated coffee attenuates behavioral modifications in mice subject to chronic unpredictable stress,” was authored by Ângelo R. Tomé, Nuno J. Machado, Ana Paula Ardais, Ana Nunes, Henrique B. Silva, Manuella P. Kaster, Paula Agostinho, and Rodrigo A. Cunha.

Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:00:18 BST
19:00:18 KST

Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
- Published
As summer temperatures in Europe smashed records this summer and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war.
Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.
This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target.
A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible".
Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd".
But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.
Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem.
Poland's interior minister is clear.
"There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin Kierwiński said, warning people to be on their guard.
- Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack 
  - Published2 days ago
August campaign across Europe
4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered.
10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a factory of the defence firm EMCO, with initial reports that a truck ignited during a fuel delivery.
13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion.
The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons".
15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators.
25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe.
30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires.
One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out".
An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities".
The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz.
Why is this happening now?
Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store.
The novelty now is the concentration of cases.
"The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says.
She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
"We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territory…They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something."
Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes.
After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid.
There are other theories.
To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses.
"Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank.
He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe.
"They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it."
The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia.
2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland.
One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger.
"That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds.
It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit.
But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible.
Who are the suspected saboteurs?
Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job.
That would be unusual.
The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs".
They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction.
In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers.
The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online.
The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable.
The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted.
So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success.
In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned.
Nato faced with Soviet-style campaign
Russia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way.
The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war.
"I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next."
As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered.
Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident.
What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane?
"I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react."

Chinese armed trainer jets drive away Philippine aircraft over Scarborough Shoal
At least three JL-10s carrying PL-5 missiles were involved in incident at disputed atoll in what could be a more cost-effective tactic
The footage showed the Chinese jet’s electronic systems locking onto three Philippine aircraft, identifying their models as a BN-2A Islander utility aircraft, a C-208 single-engine turboprop and a PA-31T twin-engine turboprop. A green crosshair was also shown tracking one of the aircraft.

China has controlled the area since 2012 and released baselines for the territorial sea around it in 2024. The Philippines – which challenges the Chinese claim with occasional ship and aircraft activities in the area – filed its own territorial sea baselines for the shoal with the United Nations in July.

Why You Shouldn’t Work on Labor Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

It’s Saturday morning and your boss emails you a question that can wait until Monday. What do you do? If you’re like me, you read the message while walking out of your yoga class and respond before lunch.
This work culture makes the U.S. an outlier among high-income economies. Since 2017, countries including France, Belgium, Spain, Portugal, Ireland, Australia, Slovakia, Greece, and Argentina have legislated some form of a right to disconnect. The European Union is working on a policy that could take effect as soon as 2028. In Australia, employees have the right not to read or respond to employers outside of work hours. In Portugal, mid-size employers risk fines of over $10,000 for contacting employees when they’re off the clock.
As we think about the employment landscape in the U.S. this Labor Day, we should consider a similar approach that protects the right of employees to not work when they’re not officially working. This could solve a lot of problems for families and communities while actually improving job performance. Since the pandemic, the boundaries between work and home have all but collapsed. With many workers still doing a lot of remote work, many of us send our first email early in the morning and our last late at night, creating what Microsoft calls the “infinite workday.” We squeeze in a load of laundry, parent-teacher conference, and family dinner somewhere in between.
Being pulled in so many directions at the same time is awful for our health and the quality of our work, for a simple reason: The human brain can’t multitask.
“Each time we are exposed to a new stimulus and engage in the sequential process of disconnecting and reallocating our attention, we are expending valuable metabolic energy,” University of California, Santa Barbara technology management professor Paul Leonardi writes in Digital Exhaustion: Simple Rules for Reclaiming Your Life. “Our attention is fragmented. We lose focus and become easily distracted. We can’t get things done as quickly or as easily as we should be able to, and often quality suffers.”
Humans just didn’t evolve to keep switching between tasks as quickly and regularly as we do today, Leonardi warns. This explains why so many of us are exhausted and burned out. It also explains why we spend so much time working: We aren’t as efficient as we could be.
When I don’t work on the weekend, I unquestionably show up as a better employee on Monday morning. That’s because spending time with friends and family, exercising, getting outdoors, and volunteering in my community leave me refreshed and energized. What’s more, when I get my kids’ permission slips filled out and the fruit and veggies chopped on the weekend, thoughts of unfinished business aren’t floating through my head while I’m working. That means I can achieve a state of what the psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi famously termed “flow,” getting completely absorbed in my work and reaching peak performance.
Allowing workers to disconnect would therefore make them better employees. It could also solve several public policy problems. Our children need present caregivers. It only takes seconds for a child to fall or drown while we’re distracted by a manager’s latest missive. When parents spend more time on screens, their children also develop poorer language skills. And, of course, children are unlikely to open up about their problems while we’re distracted on our phones.
Plus, if workers disconnected during their off-hours, they’d also have more time to nurture the offline connections that our country desperately needs. I would agree that we’re experiencing what psychologist Marisa Franco calls a “friendship famine.” Since 1990, the percentage of American adults who say they have no close friends has quadrupled, according to last year’s American Perspectives Survey. That is crushing. The quality of our friendships and social connections is one of the strongest predictors of our health, happiness, and how long we’ll live, according to the Harvard Study of Adult Development. It’s more important than things like our cholesterol, genes, and salaries. And being lonely is as toxic for our health as alcoholism or smoking.
Of course, as Americans know one another less, we help one another less. This can explain why volunteerism has also been declining. That’s particularly sad because banding together has long been a central part of our national character, as Alexis de Tocqueville famously wrote in Democracy in America. It’s especially important in a country like ours where people can’t rely on a strong social safety net when they hit hard times.
Labor Day is an obvious prompt for U.S. lawmakers to consider a right to disconnect. In the meantime, we can change our behavior and our workplaces. Employers should take the lead. Even without a national law, they should develop their own policies about disconnecting and publish them prominently on their websites so prospective employees can consider them even before accepting job offers. Volkswagen pioneered this approach in Germany in 2012 when it stopped sending emails to employees who weren’t senior managers 30 minutes after their shifts ended and resumed 30 minutes before their next shifts began.
A series of studies published in 2021 found that when people receive non-urgent work emails outside of work hours, we tend to think we need to respond faster than the senders believe is necessary. Receiving these types of emails also increases our stress and decreases our wellbeing, but senders underestimate the degree to which their messages stress us out. Indicating in the email that a response wasn’t expected right away reduced the pressure on recipients. An even better strategy could be schedule-sending emails so colleagues receive them when they return to work.
Another thing we can combat individually is the urge to check our messages every time we have a spare minute. Pulling out our phones is often a convenient way to avoid negative emotions or awkward encounters. Yet all this task switching leaves us distracted and depleted, and I can’t realistically handle any of the issues in the emails I read in the 30 seconds it takes to walk from my yoga class to my car.
It stands to reason that our brains would be less foggy if we used those small slices of our lives to take a deep breath, notice our surroundings, and have short, pleasant interactions with the people around us. When we returned to our desks, we’d think more clearly, work more efficiently, and send better responses.
This Labor Day, there’s a way for workers to be healthier, happier, more productive, and solve a lot of our public policy problems, too. We need to stop working when we’re not working.
