Press review: Germany, France and UK boost missile ties as China challenges US in Mideast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 4. /TASS/. Russia warns Ukraine’s terrorism may spiral beyond Western control; Germany boosts cooperation on long-range missiles with the UK and France; and China moves to challenge US influence across the Middle East. These stories topped Friday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Ukraine’s terrorism may spiral out of Western control
Ukraine’s Western allies are becoming accomplices in international terrorism by remaining silent on Kiev’s actions, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Eastern Economic Forum. Notably, no one can guarantee that Ukrainian terrorism will not target citizens in Western countries, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told Izvestia.
St. Petersburg State University Professor Natalya Yeryomina pointed out that Ukrainian connections had repeatedly emerged in connection with terrorist attacks in Europe. Kiev’s intelligence agencies sought to assassinate businessman Vadim Yermolayev in Monaco in June. In August, German prosecutors announced the detention of a Ukrainian national in Croatia on suspicion of involvement in the 2022 bombing of the Nord Stream gas pipelines. Ukraine’s role is also being investigated in a recent drone incident in Leipzig, Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service said. The threat of new acts of terrorism is particularly high in countries with large Ukrainian communities, including Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic, Yeryomina said.
According to Putin, Russian and Ukrainian intelligence officials remain in contact. Such communication makes it possible to discuss sensitive issues that are difficult to raise through official channels, said Vladimir Shapovalov, deputy director of the Institute of History and Politics at Moscow State Pedagogical University. In his opinion, this could help pave the way for a resumption of public dialogue.
The latest round of Russia-Ukraine talks, which also involved the United States, took place in Geneva in February. The parties have not held official meetings since then but have maintained humanitarian contact. No date has been set for the next round of talks, although discussions on a new meeting have gained momentum in recent weeks. Media reports said that US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff and businessman Jared Kushner planned to intensify their mediation efforts. US President Donald Trump stated on September 2 that he was ready to meet with Russian leader Vladimir Putin after a Ukraine peace deal was agreed on.
Media: Germany steps up cooperation on long-range missiles with UK, France
Germany has begun work with its European allies on developing long-range weapons. Experts interviewed by Izvestia believe that Moscow will respond by expanding its long-range weapons arsenal further and strengthening the defense of critical facilities.
Europe is stepping up its militarization efforts. Germany is working together with the United Kingdom and France to create long-range capabilities, a spokesperson for the Russian Embassy in Berlin told Izvestia. If the German military initiatives are implemented, Russia will view them as an immediate threat, the diplomat emphasized.
Germany seeks to diversify its sources of missile technology and missile systems as widely as possible, Dmitry Stefanovich, researcher with the Center for International Security at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, said. The expert noted that in response, Moscow was likely to continue developing its layered air and space defense system and further expand its own long-range weapons capabilities.
The missile program is only part of Berlin's efforts to build up its military strength. Germany is also involved in a French nuclear initiative, with the two countries planning to hold joint exercises in this field in the fall. What complicates the situation is Berlin's increasing military assistance to Ukraine. Notably, Germany’s focus is on supplying long-range drones, which the Ukrainian army uses to target civilian facilities in Russia.
Meanwhile, the United States appears to have deployed its new launcher for short-and medium-range missiles to a second European country, Norway, Kommersant writes. Alexander Yermakov, researcher with the Center for International Security at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, expects that the Russian leadership will view such moves by Norway and its allies as part of the "militarization of the Arctic," an issue Moscow has repeatedly criticized. "In practical terms, it will be seen as carrying out measures to block Russia’s Northern Fleet… while the Americans could be no less concerned about the Chinese navy," the expert pointed out.
Media: China moves to challenge US influence in Middle East
Chinese President Xi Jinping has paid a state visit to Egypt. During the visit, he emphasized Beijing’s call for a new security architecture in the Middle East that would not be linked to the United States, Nezavisimaya Gazeta reports.
The Chinese leader’s trip to the Middle East, the first in four years, came as the US war against Iran disrupted normal economic ties across the region and forced US partners to reconsider their strategies, with their trust in America as a mighty power that maintains regional order beginning to decline. Arab countries, from Egypt to Gulf nations, did not want US President Donald Trump to launch the war with Iran, but the White House was unwilling to heed their requests and warnings. As a result, the once-prosperous oil-producing nations are now having to cope with Iranian missile strikes. That said, it’s quite natural for countries such as Egypt to seek to strengthen their ties with China, Shanghai International Studies University Professor Ding Long said. Relying solely on the US is risky, while wise politicians would never place all their bets on one option, he noted.
However, Ding pointed out that in late September, the Chinese president was expected to visit Washington for talks with Trump. This is why Beijing is likely to avoid risky moves for the time being, as relations with the US are crucial not only to China’s exports but also to strategic stability in the Asia-Pacific region.
At first glance, Xi’s visit to Egypt offered an opportunity for the two countries to further strengthen their economic and diplomatic ties. Still, Western observers are more inclined to view the trip as an attempt to expand China’s influence in a region where the United States has for decades been a dominant military power, Kommersant notes.
Ahead of his upcoming visit to Washington, Xi can be expected to spare no effort to demonstrate China’s growing global influence at the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12-13. The Chinese leader’s attendance has not been confirmed yet but since the normalization of relations between Beijing and New Delhi is progressing well, his participation appears highly likely.
Vedomosti: Americans’ perception of government corruption hits new high
The share of US citizens who believe their government is corrupt has climbed from 59% in 2006 to 89% in 2026, Vedomosti reports, citing a Gallup survey.
The survey shows that the share of people who believe in government corruption increased particularly sharply in 2025-2026, while the United States is the only country among the 38 members of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) where perceptions of government corruption continue to rise rapidly.
According to US President Donald Trump's annual financial disclosure report, he conducted more than 20,000 stock market transactions in 2025, more than any other president in the country’s history. Trump’s family members began taking advantage of their close ties to the president to advance their own business interests during his first time in office (2017-2021). In particular, while his daughter Ivanka served as a presidential advisor, her company obtained several licenses to manufacture women’s shoes in China in 2017. An investment company owned by the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner continues to receive funds from foreign governments, including hundreds of millions of dollars from Saudi Arabia and other Gulf monarchies. The president himself has made no secret of his alleged insider trading.
It is worth noting that politicians, including members of both the Republican and Democratic parties in Congress, regularly take advantage of their proximity to power.
Both parties use such surveys in their information campaigns, Pavel Koshkin, senior researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for US and Canadian Studies, said. Even though these polls are reputable, their representativeness "raises questions," he pointed out.
The expert emphasized that Democrats had promoted the same narrative during Trump’s first term and the 2024 election campaign but had failed to significantly undermine him. This time, it is also unlikely to have much impact, given that the Democratic Party’s reputation in the eyes of voters is far from being spotless, Koshkin concluded.
Izvestia: Analysts expect Russia’s Central Bank to pause key rate cuts
Russia’s Central Bank will take a break from reducing the key rate, keeping it at 14% at the Board of Directors meeting scheduled for September 11, according to consensus estimates by experts interviewed by Izvestia. The scope continues to narrow for the regulator to quickly soften its policy as the inflation rate remains at about 6% compared to the target goal of 4%, the ruble has weakened, and price increase expectations are high. Additional risks are stemming from the fuel situation and a potential increase in budget spending.
The main argument for a pause is the persistence of inflation risks. Gasoline prices have started rising again over the past month, the ruble has weakened by 8%, and inflation expectations remain high. Budget spending could add further pressure, Olga Belenkaya, head of macroeconomic analysis at Finam, noted.
The fuel market situation remains one of the most important factors for the Central Bank to consider, Sovcombank Chief Analyst Mikhail Vasilyev believes. Gasoline supply disruptions are driving up not only prices but also logistics costs.
Overall prices are also being affected by problems faced by e-commerce companies due to drone strikes on their infrastructure, Belenkaya added. The companies are facing additional costs, which could ultimately be passed on to consumers.
Besides, the Central Bank must also consider the state of the economy, Vasilyev pointed out. On the one hand, the regulator needs to curb inflation, while on the other, excessively high rates could further weaken demand and business activity.
The majority of experts believe that a September pause in key rate cuts would not mark the start of a prolonged period of tight policy. Under the base-case scenario, the Central Bank could resume easing later in the fall. However, the regulator is unlikely to take risks and soften its policy until it has a clearer understanding of how next year’s budget parameters will affect the Russian economy. Still, a pause would not signal a tightening of monetary policy but would instead show that the Central Bank has taken time to make a balanced decision.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

EU blasts Serbia over ‘Butcher of Bosnia’ funeral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:57:23 UTC
18:57:23 KST

Ratko Mladić meets his lawyers as he appears for the pronouncement of the Trial Judgement for the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague on Nov. 22, 2017. | Michel Porro/Getty Images
DUBLIN — Serbia’s public commemorations for convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić risk undermining the country’s relationship with the EU, the bloc has warned ahead of the funeral of the man dubbed the “Butcher of Bosnia.”
The former commander of the Bosnian Serb Army during the 1992-1995 Bosnian War died behind bars in The Hague last week, where he was serving a life sentence for crimes against humanity. His coffin was draped in a Serbian flag and flown to Belgrade in a government plane on Thursday, and is due to be buried after a service at the House of the Army on Monday, with thousands expected to attend.
The EU’s enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, told POLITICO that public support for Mladić was incompatible with Serbia’s application to join the EU.
Advertisement
“The glorification of war criminals has no place; it goes really, really strong against European values and has no space, not in the EU member states, but also in our candidates,” she said.
“We are observing the situation very carefully … and we will see what will happen in [the] next days and we also see the actions of the government,” Kos added. “There is for sure a place for Serbia in the EU, but [the EU] demands not just doing the reforms. The strategic alliances or strategic orientation on the field of common security and foreign policy is getting even more and more important.”
A Serbian government official, granted anonymity to speak frankly, insisted the state was not directly involved in Monday’s proceedings. “The commemorative gathering is being organized not by the Ministry of Defense or the General Staff of the Serbian Armed Forces, but by the Association of Retired Generals,” they said, adding that Mladić will not receive the honor of being buried in either the Alley of the Greats or the Alley of Distinguished Citizens.
Under Mladić’s command, the Bosnian Serb Army laid siege to Sarajevo for almost four years, cutting off supplies to the civilian population and turning its streets into sniper lanes in which thousands of civilians were shot. Mladić was found to be responsible by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia for the massacre of more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica, as well as atrocities committed by his troops across the country.
The 2011 capture of Mladić, who had been in hiding for almost a decade, came months before Serbia was awarded EU candidate status, paving the way for significant financial and administrative support from the bloc. The decision to extradite him to face justice in The Hague was controversial in Serbia, with polling at the time showing as many as 40 percent of Serbs viewed him as a hero.
Tributes were held in majority-Serb towns and cities across Bosnia following his death. Prominent Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik said “Mladić was respected by the Serbian people. As a commander he stood to defend Serbs.”
Advertisement
Ireland’s Europe Minister Thomas Byrne, who is chairing a meeting of EU candidate countries in Dublin on Friday, said that while “there’s not actually a state funeral taking place … there may well be senior figures from government memorializing that man, so that’s not acceptable.”
“It is certainly time to bury the past and to work and continue reconciliation in that region,” Byrne added. “What’s happening there, I think, continues to hurt people, particularly in the region, but also in some member states of the European Union in particular.”
Mladić will be buried at Topčider Cemetery in Belgrade on Monday.

Investigation into Air India flight plunge highlights triple hydraulic failure and pilot drug test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:57:08 UTC
18:57:08 KST

India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau said the aircraft detected a triple-hydraulic failure, with the autopilot disengaging and a stall warning triggered for two seconds.
An investigation into an Air India flight that dropped almost 300 feet last month has found that the plane suffered a temporary hydraulics failure.
Flight AI2379 was travelling from Phuket, Thailand to the Indian capital of New Delhi on 4 August when the incident occurred.
The Airbus A320, which had 137 passengers, six cabin crew and two pilots on board at the time, suddenly lost altitude while flying over Indian airspace, leaving 24 people injured.
In a preliminary report published on Friday, India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) said the aircraft detected a triple-hydraulic failure, with the autopilot disengaging and a stall warning triggered for two seconds.
"The aircraft encountered altitude upset. Initially, it gained 372 ft and fell by 292 ft," the report said.
The hydraulic systems then recovered, and the "aircraft operation returned to its normal operating condition."
The report added that both pilots were tested for psycho-active substances following the incident.
"The sample of PIC (pilot in command) was found non-negative. Subsequently, blood samples of both the flight crew were sent to the pathological laboratory for confirmatory test. The confirmatory test report of PIC was found non-negative whereas the sample of the Co-Pilot was found negative in both the tests," it said, adding that the "confirmation of use of psycho-active substance is a serious concern."
Air India has since reportedly ordered one-time drug tests for its pilots.
The investigation remains ongoing and a full report is due to be issued at a later date.

First airline cancels flights to Moscow amid Ukrainian threat to 'close' Russia's skies

The tempo of Ukraine's drone campaign has increased in recent months. Ukraine's Europe minister says non-EU allies need to step up their financial support

Ukraine's Europe minister says non-EU allies need to step up their financial support
It is primarily non-EU countries that need to ramp up financial assistance to Ukraine in 2026 and beyond, said Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Vsevolod Chentsov at an EU meeting of European affairs ministers on Sept. 4 in Wicklow, Ireland.
The meeting, Chentsov's first since he took the position in July, focused on discussing the EU accession status of membership candidate countries, such as Ukraine.
Next to advancing Ukraine's EU membership bid, the main priority for Kyiv vis-a-vis the European bloc is to bridge a looming financial hole of $27 billion by the end of 2026.
"We are talking both to the EU and other partners to cover the gap for this year... frontloading is probably one of the solutions, but it is not a silver bullet," Chentsov told reporters.
The EU in April finalized a 90 billion-euro ($104 billion) support loan for Ukraine to cover two-thirds of Kyiv's total budgetary and defense needs until the end of 2027.
The remaining third was supposed to be covered by other allies of Ukraine, but they have so far failed to do so, prompting President Volodymyr Zelensky to suggest that the EU should frontload the payment of some of the assistance allocated for 2027 already this year.
"We need, first of all, to reach out to countries outside of the EU because the idea was that one third of Ukraine's needs will be covered by other partners," Chentsov said.
Chentsov's remarks mirror those made by Ukraine's incoming ambassador to the EU, Taras Kachka, at an event with the Bruegel think tank in Brussels on Sept. 2.
The two men directly swapped jobs in July as part of a wider government reshuffle.
At the event, Kachka said that Zelensky's call for frontloading was sparked by the "very general promise from other partners who support us to participate in this kind of financing," which remains unfulfilled.
Kachka said he remains optimistic that countries such as the U.K., Canada, and Japan will step up, but explained that without help from others, "it would be natural to ask the EU for some kind of frontloading."
read also
Chentsov also seemed to shift some of the pressure onto other allies for another key pillar of potential EU support for Ukraine: the idea of using some 200 billion euros (around $230 billion) of Russian assets immobilized within the bloc.
"That was a very ambitious proposal last year," Chentsov said, referring to the last time the use of frozen Russian assets was discussed in December 2025.
The minister added that "probably, we need to look into other options, to consider different figures as a first step."
During the discussions last December, the bloc failed to reach an agreement, largely because there were insufficient assurances that the entire EU would share the risks should Belgium, which hosts the assets, be legally challenged.
"Maybe not only the EU but other players can step in and help to answer the concerns of Belgium," Chentsov said.
One of the key demands Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever made in 2025 was that non-EU countries holding frozen Russian assets take a similar step, to spread the risk of Russian countermeasures falling on a single country.
Since then, EU and national diplomats have told the Kyiv Independent that the U.K. was prepared to repurpose frozen Russian assets as well, if needed.
After the EU's estimated 209.2 billion euros ($243.1 billion) in frozen Russian assets, the U.K. ranks third with an estimated 26.6 billion euros ($30.1 billion), according to a December 2025 report from the European Parliament's research service.
That comes after Japan, with 28.1 billion euros ($32.7 billion), and is followed by Canada ($17.7 billion), Switzerland ($7.2 billion), and the U.S. ($5 billion).

Joint Declaration of the Foreign Ministers of the Weimar Triangle Johann…
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:55:47 CEST
18:55:47 KST

Joint Declaration of the Foreign Ministers of the Weimar Triangle Johann Wadephul, Jean-Noël Barrot and Radosław Sikorski on the occasion of the 35th anniversary of the format European Union Joint statement On : September 03rd 2026 "Europe stands at a historical turning point in its history. Its peoples and states have embarked on a path toward new forms of coexistence. We are aware that Poland, Germany, and France bear a decisive responsibility for the success of sustainable structures of European neighbourhood." (Hans-Dietrich Genscher, Roland Dumas, Krzysztof Skubiszewski, Weimar, 29th August 1991 on the occasion of the first meeting of the Weimar Triangle) As the Foreign Ministers of the Weimar Triangle, we are gathered today in Weimar to celebrate the spirit that was born 35 years ago. Over three and a half decades, Germany, France, and Poland have worked for European innovation, integration, prosperity and progress. Jointly we have provided important impulses for a united, strong, and secure Europe. The European Union remains an indispensable framework for the pursuit of freedom, prosperity and security. In the Weimar Triangle we will work together, alongside all EU member states, to make our Union more sovereign, resilient and capable of taking action. As NATO Allies, we are committed to building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO that ensures peace, security and stability in the Euro-Atlantic area. We view the Weimar Triangle as an engine of integration that helps to synchronise different perspectives within the European Union and point to a common, forward-looking direction. By inviting partner countries and key regional stakeholders to join our consultations, we aim to enhance the Triangle’s function as a broader platform to integrate diverse perspectives more efficiently. Today, ministers from all departments of our governments meet regularly, underlining the vital importance of our cooperation. Our civil societies and our scientific and cultural institutions cooperate closely for the benefit of Europe, e.g. as joint guests of honour at the Leipzig Book Fair in 2027. Given current geopolitical developments, the Weimar Triangle emphasises the need to reform the internal set-up of EU external action, to allow for stronger, swifter and more coordinated EU responses. This should comprise the role and the institutional set-up of the relevant EU institutions and bodies, including the High Representative/Vice-President, the European External Action Service, the General Secretariat of the Council and the Commission. Work shall be initiated as soon as possible to reinforce the role and authority of the HR/VP in coordinating the Union’s external action. We also aim to improve EU decision-making by best utilising all options provided within the Treaties. Furthermore, to strengthen cohesion in Europe and demonstrate the Union's capacity to act decisively, we set the following priorities: I. Assuming greater responsibility for our defence Faced with mounting security challenges, our three nations play a key role in advancing Europe’s security. We are united in our determination to strengthen the European pillar of NATO, which remains the foundation for the security and defence of Europe. Our commitment to our Alliance is ironclad. We are assuming greater responsibility for our defence, working together with other Allies and reaffirming the fundamental importance of the transatlantic bond in all its dimensions. We are committed to further strengthening NATO’s deterrence and defence posture. Recognising the immediate threats on NATO and the EU’s eastern flank, we are committed to ensuring the defence of all NATO and EU land, air and maritime borders. Europe must become more sovereign, more responsible for its own defence and better equipped to act and deal autonomously and in a coordinated way with immediate and future challenges and threats, with a 360° approach. We also support the development of a more robust and competitive European defence technological and industrial base, including through EU programmes like SAFE and EDIP and in the next MFF. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has profoundly changed the security of our continent. In light of the long-term threat posed by Russia, we as the Weimar Triangle will continue to address Russia’s broad array of activities, such as hybrid activities, provocations, acts of espionage or sabotage or information manipulation. The recent drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport starkly underlines the need to take further action in light of the evolving hybrid threat we currently face. The Weimar Triangle will continue to impose costs on such activities, both at the national and European levels, such as through the adoption on 13 July of a coordinated European response to the cyber-attacks carried out by Russia against the EU and its member states’ interests, in which the Weimar Triangle played a major role. We will continue to develop robust countermeasures to protect and safeguard our citizens, democratic institutions and critical systems against hybrid interference. II. Achieving a comprehensive, just and lasting peace for Ukraine The Weimar Triangle plays an important role in organizing and consolidating our continued support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders. We are determined to bring about a comprehensive, just and lasting peace for Ukraine, in accordance with international law. We stand ready to contribute to robust and credible security guarantees for Ukraine, including through the Coalition of the Willing and to strengthen Ukraine’s ability to deter and defend itself effectively. We will continue to support Ukraine as long as it takes, with the provision of military support, through the financing and donating of priority equipment, industry procurement, research and development cooperation, co-productions, the ramping up of the European defence industry to ensure swift and long-lasting deliveries, as well as funding for Ukrainian production. At the same time, we will continue to reinforce the pressure on Russia’s war economy through the adoption of targeted and impactful sanctions. We will keep targeting Russian energy revenues and the shadow fleet, the Russian financial sector as well as the Russian military-industrial complex. III. Developing a new European business model Amidst geopolitical tensions and a fragmented global economy, Europe’s only path to prosperity is to bolster its competitiveness and preserve its economic and technological sovereignty. The “One Europe, One Market” Roadmap sets out our way towards enhancing the EU’s long-term competitiveness through strengthening the foundations of the Single Market and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens. We welcome the recent European Technological Sovereignty Package. We will increase the EU’s economic resilience and defend our common rules for fair competition in the digital economy while ensuring a level playing field for European industry by addressing foreign subsidies and market distortions through the appropriate application of existing instruments, and globally, by leading efforts to reform and revitalize the multilateral trading system, advocate for reciprocal market access, and resolve structural imbalances through constructive cooperation. In parallel, we support the European Commission in swiftly strengthening the EU’s trade defence toolbox and economic security, including through new instruments to reduce strategic and supply chain vulnerabilities. Close coordination in the Weimar Triangle addresses these challenges. In parallel, we will make full use of and foster our global partnerships through the conclusion of further ambitious and mutually beneficial trade agreements, to secure new exports markets for EU companies and help diversify value chains. We underline our commitment to fair and rules-based trade. We emphasise the importance of stable and balanced EU-US trade relations, which are beneficial for companies and consumers on both sides of the Atlantic as well as our mutual commitment to uphold the EU-US Turnberry Agreement. We reaffirm the significance of our relations with China and the need to build a more balanced economic relationship with China, based on fair competitive conditions as its non-market policies paired with an undervalued currency threaten to erode our industrial base and turn dependencies into strategic vulnerabilities. We therefore welcome the Commissions’ work on improving and further developing the EU’s geoeconomic toolbox. In order to foster innovation as a key driver of European prosperity, we will promote European research innovation through the Weimar Excellence Initiative, which strengthens trilateral scientific cooperation within the framework of the European University Alliances. Our new growth model includes an ambitious energy and climate policy, which guarantees secure, diversified and affordable energy and a just transition, fully implements international climate agreements, and augments European resilience against extreme weather events, climate change and environmental degradation. IV. Fostering stability in our European neighbourhood The Weimar Triangle helps to advance freedom, stability, and prosperity in our European neighbourhood. The security and stability of our eastern and southern neighbours, including their continued efforts towards closer integration with the European Union, are inextricably linked to our own security. We aim to vigorously advance the opening of negotiation clusters and the merit-based enlargement process with Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, as well as a tailor-made approach to offer immediate and tangible progress to all candidate countries, including the countries of the Western Balkans, in accordance with their respective reform progress. On the way to full membership, gradual steps can inject renewed momentum into candidates’ integration into the European Union while ensuring the integrity and functioning of the EU. The situation in the Middle East remains fragile and continues to be of great concern to us. In the Gulf, we reiterate the importance of reaching an agreement addressing the urgent re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz with unconditional and unrestricted freedom of navigation and ensuring that Iran will have no nuclear weapon and will stop their hostile activities in the region. We reaffirm our commitment to a negotiated two-state solution. We reiterate the urgent need for the full implementation of UNSCR 2803 for Gaza. In this regard, we urgently call on Hamas to finally hand over their weapons and stop their hostilities towards Israel. We reiterate our strong opposition to all illegal settlements and call on the Israeli government to cease all settlement activities. In Lebanon, we stand ready to support the implementation of the framework agreement signed by Lebanon and Israel in Washington, which calls for the disarmament of Hezbollah to enable the IDF to progressively redeploy out of Lebanese territory.. V. Protecting European values and our democratic discourse In a time of increasing polarisation and hybrid threats, we must strengthen social cohesion in Europe and act together against foreign interference and information manipulation as well as attempts to erode European democratic standards. In the Weimar Triangle, we jointly monitor information threats and coordinate our responses, particularly when our democratic standards are targeted. We stand in solidarity in denouncing threats stemming from foreign actors, also by supporting each other’s attack attributions. We must also ensure our reactive and efficient mutual alerting system continues to deliver strong results. By fully implementing the Digital Services Act, our societies are better protected from foreign interference. The Weimar Triangle must be a driving force to bolster and fully implement the DSA, accelerating the regulation of platforms. Through their reliable and independent reporting, Deutsche Welle, France Médias Monde and International Media Centre (Ośrodek Mediów dla Zagranicy TVP) work together to reach audiences beyond our borders and strengthen societies' resilience to disinformation. The Weimar Triangle will support the financing by the EU of this informational shield on a long-term basis. Working together in the EU, NATO and within other multilateral formats, the Weimar Triangle countries actively defend rules-based international order, our European values and democracies. As countries among the most frequently targeted by hostile actions, we share a common threat assessment and focus on building democratic resilience and promoting European principles.

18:55:12 KST

Malaysia declared an emergency in the district of Serian, in Sarawak state, after thick haze caused by forest fires in neighbouring Indonesia pushed air pollution up to hazardous levels on Friday.
Sarawak, on Borneo, has been heavily affected by fires on the Indonesian side of the island, with haze forcing school closures in some parts of the state.
Malaysian authorities categorise Air Pollution Index (API) readings above 300 as hazardous, with a measurement of 500 serving as the threshold for declaring an emergency. The API reached 519 in Serian on Friday, government data showed.
The emergency declaration was issued by Malaysia's king, Sultan Ibrahim, after advice from Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Sarawak premier Abang Johari Openg, Anwar's office said in a statement.
"Sultan Ibrahim has consented to the declaration of a state of emergency throughout the Serian district, Sarawak, following haze conditions that have reached a level of air pollution hazardous to public health and safety," the statement said.
Sarawak disaster management committee chairman Douglas Uggah Embas had earlier told a news conference the state had requested an emergency declaration after API readings breached 500.
The emergency would be confined to the Serian district, covering an area of about 20 kilometres radius, with essential services such as supermarkets, petrol stations, and banks expected to continue operating, Douglas said.
Cloud-seeding operations were also being carried out, he added.
Malaysia is a constitutional monarchy in which the king has a largely ceremonial role, carrying out his duties with advice from the prime minister and cabinet. But the monarch has the power to decide if an emergency should be declared based on grave threats to national security, the economy, or public order.

IFA 2026: What could the home of the future look like?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:54:52 UTC
18:54:52 KST

From AI-powered appliances and smart beds to connected pet gadgets and robot dogs, Euronews went to IFA 2026 in Berlin to see how new technology could reshape life at home.
Artificial intelligence is advancing at a rapid pace, and its growing role in everyday life is on full display at this year's IFA in Berlin, the world's largest consumer electronics and home appliances trade fair.
Under the theme "The Future is Now," the event showcases how emerging technologies are reshaping daily life, from mobility to the increased use of AI in devices and services, with more than 1,900 brands from 49 countries represented at IFA 2026.
Nowhere is this transformation more visible than in the home. The industry is increasingly looking beyond the "smart home" towards what it describes as the "intelligent home" where technology does more than simply respond to commands, learning, adapting to and anticipating people's needs.
With IFA opening its doors to the public today, Euronews took a closer look at some of the innovations on display to explore one key question: What could the home of the future look like?
A simpler everyday life?
For years, one of the main promises of smart home technology and AI has been to make everyday life easier. At IFA 2026, that remains a major focus, with home appliances on display across the exhibition designed to take over tasks that many people would rather not do themselves.
But the next step goes beyond simply doing the work. Manufacturers are increasingly developing appliances that can also help with the planning and decision-making behind everyday household tasks.
One example is a washing machine presented by Haier. Equipped with an integrated camera and AI, the appliance can detect what has been put into the drum and alert users if, for example, a red sock has accidentally ended up among white clothes.
The idea is to remove some of the thinking involved in sorting laundry and potentially save a white shirt from the classic red-sock-turns-it-pink mistake.
For Neil Tunstall, CEO of Haier Europe, cooking is another area where this shift is becoming visible. He points to appliances that can identify what has been placed inside appliances and adjust how food is cooked, reducing the uncertainty for people who may not be confident about choosing the right settings or knowing when a dish is ready.
"The product now will do that for you. And that hopefully means then that we can actually enjoy eating much more at home," Tunstall told Euronews.
_"_We are talking less about products, much more about experiences, we're talking less about consumers trying to think about things and the products and the system itself thinking, making life much, much smarter," he continued.
Helping consumers spend less time thinking about everyday tasks is also a focus for US-based company Cozyla, particularly when it comes to planning and organising a household with several people.
At IFA 2026, the company is demonstrating how AI could be used to coordinate different aspects of everyday life, from family schedules and work to meal planning.
Its stand takes visitors through a simulated day in a connected home. Interactive displays and digital calendars are used to coordinate routines and schedules, while the kitchen setup shows how a recipe can be scanned and used to help plan a meal.
The demonstration then moves into the living room, where the system is used to organise tasks and coordinate plans between family members, before ending with a bedtime routine.
Smarter ways to relax
But the technology does not switch off when everyone goes to bed.
Hong Kong-based BestQi, founded in 2020, is showing how connected technology could extend into the bedroom. Its AMADA Smart Adaptive Sleeping System combines an adjustable bed with a mattress that uses sound and vibrations and can be controlled through an app.
Each side of the bed can be adjusted independently, allowing two people to choose different positions and settings. Users can also control massage functions, vibration intensity and programmes designed for activities such as sleeping, relaxing or reading.
For those looking to take relaxation a step further, South Korean company Bodyfriend is bringing more technology into the traditional massage chair.
Its Quantum Beauty Capsule combines a full-body massage chair with LED modules designed for the face and scalp. Another model, the Davinci AI, incorporates a fingertip PPG sensor that measures biometric data including heart rate, heart rate variability and blood oxygen saturation.
The company says the system uses changes in these measurements to provide users with information about their physical condition, stress and recovery.
Bigger screens, fewer distractions
But relaxing at home is not only about switching off. For many people, it also means entertainment.
Over the past few years, screens have become bigger, picture quality has improved and home sound systems have become more powerful. Now, as with other household technology, the focus is increasingly shifting from individual devices towards a more connected experience.
TCL, one of the major brands exhibiting at IFA 2026, is showing how that could work across different forms of entertainment. Its displays include a gaming setup designed to bring screens, sound and other connected devices together into a single environment.
But alongside making home entertainment bigger and more immersive, TCL is also exploring the opposite idea: using technology to help people disconnect from the constant stream of screens, notifications and other distractions around them.
One example is the company's NextPaper technology, which allows users to switch their phone into a simplified e-reader mode. TCL says the display is designed to reduce blue light and eye strain, while the mode also limits some of the phone's functions.
"When you want to read on a weekend, you don't want to have the disturbance of every app that gives you a notification," Stefan Streit, Chief Marketing Officer TCL Europe, told Euronews.
Smart homes go beyond humans
But the idea of a more connected home does not stop with the people living in it. Even the smallest members of the household have been considered at this year's IFA, with pets also being brought into the increasingly connected home.
Singapore-based Petgugu, for example, is presenting its own ecosystem of connected pet devices. These include a self-cleaning smart cat toilet as well as a robot designed to move around the home, clean up pet hair and interact with animals when their owners are away.
And for those who would rather avoid the need for a cat toilet altogether, there is a more radical option on display at IFA: a robot dog.
One example is the MagicDog Y1, developed by a Chinese robotics company founded in 2024. Unlike the pet-focused devices, however, the four-legged robot is not primarily designed as a companion. It is intended to follow people across different environments, carry equipment and use its integrated cameras and sensors for tasks including monitoring and security.
Could intelligent homes lead to more human connections?
So, what could the home of the future look like?
If the technologies on display at IFA 2026 are any indication, the biggest change may not be a single new device, but how different devices work together.
The key difference from many smart products already on the market is the combination of connectivity and AI. Instead of operating individual devices separately, the aim is to create an ecosystem in which appliances and services communicate, share information and increasingly anticipate what needs to be done.
In that vision, people would spend less time managing individual devices or organising everyday household tasks themselves. Instead, they would become part of a connected system designed to take over some of that work and planning.
Whether that vision becomes reality remains to be seen. But the promise being presented at IFA is clear: technology that requires less attention, with the goal of leaving people more time for family, friends and the things they actually want to do.
IFA lasts until 8 September
Visitors can get a glimpse of what that future could look like until 8 September. Different areas of the exhibition focus on specific aspects of technology and everyday life, including the Beauty Hub, where products can be tried out with experts on hand, and the Creator Stage, which hosts a range of live shows and events.
Another highlight is a dedicated robot show, bringing together humanoid robots and other robotics innovations from around the world.
With so many technologies and ideas on display, IFA offers a look at how everyday life at home could change in the years ahead. Ultimately, however, which of them become part of our homes is a choice everyone will have to make for themselves.

Developers and architects cite staffing shortages as one of main challenges of functioning during wartime
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:54:30 EEST
18:54:30 KST

Staffing shortages, high construction costs, and the slow implementation of reforms and permitting procedures are the main challenges facing developers and architects in Ukraine during the war, construction industry representatives reported during the roundtable discussion dubbed "Building the future: development in wartime."
"There is a significant shortage of construction workers. We all felt this problem this spring. As an owner of the company, I am looking for people to complete projects," said A Development founder and CEO Oleksiy Baranov at the roundtable discussion at Interfax-Ukraine.
Beyond construction-specific professions, the market is also experiencing a shortage of architects, said Yulia Poliukhovych, chief architect of the A Development project.
"During the war, there are many other challenges. For example, there's a significant personnel shortage—there are very few architects now. This is a very serious challenge, because if previously three or four architects worked on a project, now it might be just one," she explained.
At the same time, architects must quickly adjust their designs to account for changes in building codes and standards, particularly those related to safety, the expert noted.
As Vitaly Borul, CEO of CREDO Development, noted, the construction of underground shelters with emergency exits is a significant expense for developers, and therefore the state should cover the cost of their construction.
"It looks cool, it's safe, but it's very expensive. I believe the state should compensate for the underground shelter. The state is responsible for people's safety, so somehow we must reach an agreement with the state, and it should compensate," the expert opined.
Developers have also experienced a significant increase in construction costs. Furthermore, the market reacts to every enemy attack on the city – after such attacks, housing sales fall. Construction insurance is also very expensive, noted Baranov.
"Before the war, the calculation was simple: the cost of materials (concrete or bricklaying) was equal to the cost of labor. Today, the cost of labor exceeds the cost of materials by two to three times," said the founder of A Development.
According to Baranov, significant obstacles are also created by the unfinished process of adopting bylaws by the government and ministries, particularly in the area of cultural heritage protection. Meanwhile, local authorities in Kyiv have not considered the issue of land allocation for a year and a half.
"For example, amendments were made to the law on cultural heritage, but the Ministry of Culture still hasn't approved the regulations. In May 2022, amendments came into force that make it impossible to do anything in the central historical area without zones and regimes. And the regulations were only approved in May of this year—that's four years later. Meanwhile, for example, there's still no regulation regarding monument areas," he noted.
Baranov emphasized that construction in Kyiv's historic center must be meaningful and transparent, but at the same time, overseen by the city.
"Kyiv should be a role model. Construction is very expensive, and you can't erase a construction project with an eraser. We need to adopt an approach that is transparent and quick, while still building something that will be relevant for years to come," the expert said.

Israel says it has cleared Hezbollah fighters from tunnels under key Lebanon ridge

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

Israel says it has cleared Hezbollah fighters from tunnels under key Lebanon ridge
BEIRUT/JERUSALEM, Sept 4 - Israel's military has cleared Hezbollah fighters holed up in tunnels under the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Friday, though the Iran-backed group did not immediately comment.
Israel had said Hezbollah fighters were embedded in tunnels under the ridge, which overlooks a wide area and had become one of the most hotly contested areas in the Israel-Hezbollah war, despite a ceasefire announced in June.
Reuters reported on Thursday that Iran had warned the United States last month that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli assault on its Hezbollah allies' positions within the ridge.
"The mission was completed and the tunnels were cleared of terrorists," Katz said on social media, after a statement by the military late on Thursday saying it had operational control of the ridge.
The military said some Hezbollah fighters had been "eliminated", while others had fled.
Hezbollah did not immediately respond to a request for comment and Reuters was not able to independently verify the status of the ridge.
The Shi'ite Muslim group is believed to have built an underground command centre and weapons stores within the ridge and had said it would resist any Israeli assault.
ISRAEL RELEASES FIVE LEBANESE DETAINEES
Israel has expanded its military presence across swathes of southern Lebanon since launching a new campaign against Hezbollah in March.
On Friday, Israeli authorities transferred four people who had been detained in Israel to Lebanese authorities via the International Committee of the Red Cross.
One Lebanese man had been released earlier on Thursday. The release of the detainees is part of confidence-building measures agreed in U.S.-brokered talks between Lebanon and Israel.
Israel said on Thursday that none of the five had been found to have ties to militant groups.
A Lebanese committee advocating for Lebanese in Israeli custody says Israel has detained dozens of people inside Lebanon over the last six months. Some have been released after days or weeks, others remain in Israeli custody.
The ICRC said on Friday that it had not access to anyone in Israeli detention since October 2023.
"Many families in Lebanon are still waiting for answers about the fate of loved ones who may be detained, deceased or otherwise unaccounted for," it said.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said on Friday that those freed this week were among a "first batch", suggesting more could be coming.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Lebanon would also transfer the remains of Jewish figures killed in Lebanon in the 1980s to Israel, although there were no details of names or any timeframe. REUTERS

Bardella to meet with Farage at Reform party conference in Birmingham, as part of international tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:48:43 UTC
18:48:43 KST

Jordan Bardella and Nigel Farage are set to discuss illegal migration, as well as joint cooperation between the UK and France aimed at tackling small boat crossing at the Reform party conference on Friday.
The far-right National Rally Party's Jordan Bardella is set to host a joint press conference with Reform UK party leader Nigel Farage on Friday afternoon, as the party's annual conference kicks off in Birmingham.
Speaking to Euronews, a National Rally spokesperson said the pair are set to discuss illegal migration, as well as joint cooperation between the UK and France targeting small boat crossings, a day after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron discussed how to "scale up" efforts to tackle illegal crossings and strengthen the UK's relationship with Europe.
The 30-year old firebrand was once seen as the National Rally's most likely candidate for France's 2027 Presidential elections. He is now operating on a joint ticket with Marine Le Pen, campaigning to be her Prime Minister.
Despite this united front, policy disagreements have emerged between Bardella and Le Pen, notably on the topic of pensions and rules related to the hijab in France.
He has described France’s current pension system as “unsustainable", while also attempting to defuse the controversy around Le Pen's proposed hijab ban in public spaces. Bardella told reporters on Monday that the goal was not to "enforce a dress code", emphasising that a referendum would be held on the matter.
The leader of the Patriots group in the European Parliament also appears to be presenting himself as candidate with a more market friendly approach than Le Pen, who has typically backed protectionist measures.
These divides have fuelled speculation about what is going on behind the scenes, as Bardella has been increasingly present on an international level. After his trip to Birmingham, he will travel to Cernobbio in Italy, to take part in the Ambrosetti Forum, an annual economic and geopolitical conference on Saturday.
Farage and Bardella also met in December last year at a private members' club in London. But despite their shared eurosceptic views, Farage has not always had a smooth relationship with the National Rally Party — or with Le Pen.
In 2014, Le Pen accused Farage of "aggression" against her party, after he refused to form an alliance with the National Rally party (which at the time was known as the National Front) in the European Parliament due to their "anti-Semitism and general prejudice."
Since launching her 2027 presidential bid, Le Pen has maintained a strong eurosceptic stance, telling business leaders last week that there was "no reason" for France's contributions to the bloc — which reached nearly €29 billion for 2026 — to exceed €5 billion.
She also favoured getting rid of thousands of European norms, "every time the European Union sets a minimum norm, we go above and beyond — we want to be the top student in the class."
A meeting clouded by a new scandal for Reform
On Friday, hours before Reform's conference was set to begin, Farage's Reform UK was reported to the Metropolitan Police and the Electoral Commission over illegal donations.
This followed an undercover investigation aired by British broadcaster Channel 4 News, in which an investigative group called Verbatim posed as a wealthy American financier and his UK-based son. Under UK law, donations from foreign investors are illegal.
Reform has denied wrongdoing and dismissed the report as "a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors," insisting the party has "a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission".
Nigel Farage has also been seeking to draw a line under a damaging row over a £5 million (€5.8 million) "gift" donation he received from British crypto-currency billionaire Christopher Harborne.
According to Farage, the money — which is being probed by parliament's sleaze watchdog — was for his security. He says it was received before he was elected as an MP and therefore did not need to be declared to parliamentary authorities.
Reform enjoyed significant success in May’s local elections and until late July, the party had led Labour in the polls for more than a year, but has since slipped behind.

Nepal-China flash floods death toll tops 1,300 as search continues for 5,624 missing: Official data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:45:47 UTC
18:45:47 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
- 844 are foreigners among 5,624 missing people on both sides of Himalayan border, according to official data from Nepal, China
The death toll from flash floods and mudslides along the Nepal-China border rose above 1,300 on Friday, while more than 5,600 others remained missing, nine days after the disaster struck the Himalayan region, according to official data from both countries.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 1,287 people were killed, while 5,083 others, including 583 foreigners, remained missing.
The latest data was released after Nepal rescued two people from the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project.
At least six hydropower projects have been hit by flash floods on the Nepalese side of the border, while a search continues for around 900 personnel deployed at the facilities.
Chinese authorities said at least 21 people were killed, while 541 others remained missing in the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.
The combined death toll on both sides of the border reached 1,308, while 5,624 people remained missing.
Of those missing, 844 are foreigners, according to official figures.
The disaster struck Aug. 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).
The fracture triggered an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley.
The disaster also buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang.

Ukraine proposes creating international consortium to manage strategic logistics hubs
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:44:27 EEST
18:44:27 KST

Ukraine could put forward an initiative to create an international consortium to manage logistics hubs important for economic security and geoeconomics, foreign and domestic policy expert Liudmyla Pokrovshchuk said.
"There's a certain proposal… it could be some kind of international consortium for managing these logistics hubs that affect economic security, geoeconomics specifically," Pokrovshchuk said at a press conference titled "Food Security Amid Russian Aggression: Transforming Logistics Chains and Strategic Alternatives" at the Interfax-Ukraine press center on Friday.
Alternative routes need not only to be found but also built up, including on the territory of other countries, so Ukraine can fulfill long-term export contracts and maintain its position on world markets, she said.
Oleksiy Buriachenko, president of the International Institute for Security Studies, stressed the global significance of Ukrainian logistics, saying Ukraine's "solidarity lanes" traditionally supply grain to about 400 million people worldwide, and that Russian strikes on logistics affect not only Ukraine but global prices and food security as well.
"...We need to turn this into tools of global pressure on the Russian Federation, in order to stabilize the Black Sea basin," Buriachenko said.
Yaroslav Zhalilo, doctor of economic sciences and deputy director of the National Institute for Strategic Studies, who also heads its Center for Economic and Social Research, said alternative logistics alone are not enough and a comprehensive state policy is needed.
"It's not enough to just try to build alternative logistics — we need to form what I'd call complementary compensators, that is, at the level of state policies that would support proper adaptation," he said.
Military-political commentator Denys Popovych, meanwhile, said logistics needs to be decentralized to reduce reliance on large warehouses.
"The main tool is decentralization — reforming logistics so it works differently, so instead of concentrating on large warehouses, it's distributed, maybe selling straight off trucks, maybe developing some small enterprise model, where a truck arrives, sells out, and doesn't get concentrated in large warehouses," he said.

Taiwan Cabinet defends use of frozen funds in 2025 budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:43:14 UTC
18:43:14 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) defended Thursday the Cabinet's decision to use NT$500 million (US$15.7 million) in funds frozen in its 2025 budget, stressing that the action was lawful.
During the review of the 2025 budget, opposition lawmakers, angered by then-Cabinet Secretary-General Kung Ming-hsin's (龔明鑫) decision to leave a legislative committee meeting without approval from the meeting's convener, proposed freezing NT$500 million from the Cabinet’s budget, per UDN. While the funds could have been unfrozen if Kung apologized, he never did, and the proposal was approved by the committee.
However, the financial statement for the Cabinet's 2025 budget year revealed it spent nearly all of its NT$1.5 billion budget despite the freeze. When questioned by KMT lawmakers about the situation, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics explained that the Cabinet had decided that the frozen funds, which were not attached to any specific budget item, would be used for personnel expenses, a mandatory spending item.
Lee explained the Cabinet's reasoning, saying that to maintain basic operations and minimize the impact on contractors, the Cabinet had decided to designate the frozen funds as personnel expenses, per CNA. She said civil servants' pay is a mandatory expense under the law, so the Cabinet was required to issue the payments, stressing that its spending had undergone scrutiny by the National Audit Office.
KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chair Chen I-hsin (陳以信) criticized the move, arguing that the frozen funds were for operational expenses rather than personnel expenses, per Z.Media. He noted that under the Budget Act, operational expenses should not be used for personnel expenses, alleging that the Cabinet had bypassed legislative oversight to access the funds.
Chen argued that Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) should be impeached for this. Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) echoed Chen's criticisms, noting that the Cabinet had previously refused to countersign legislation passed by the legislature, per Liberty Times.
TPP Legislative Caucus Convener Chen Ching-lung (陳清龍) noted that the Cabinet had unilaterally decided to use the frozen funds despite not meeting the conditions for unfreezing them. He called on the National Audit Office to review the action immediately.
TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) argued that the audit office should not allow the Cabinet to pass its financial statement review, per FTNN. He also suggested that the legislature should only propose budget cuts in the future, since the Cabinet might seek a workaround to access frozen funds.
DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) defended the action, saying that the situation was the result of political maneuvering by the opposition, per RTI. He said the Cabinet had reasons to justify the move, adding that the legislature should be more precise in its budgetary oversight.

Prevot said the act represents “a step distancing Serbia from EU’s fundamental values of respect for human dignity, human rights and the fight against impunity.”
He warned that it was “going in the opposite direction of what is expected from a EU candidate country.”
Serbia has been an EU candidate country since 2012 and has been engaged in accession negotiations with the bloc since 2014.
Mladic, known as the “Butcher of Bosnia,” was found guilty by the UN tribunal of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, including for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica genocide.
Mladic died on Aug. 27 while serving his sentence in prison in The Hague, the Netherlands.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic offered to organize the burial in Serbia for him.

Oil use and emissions fell in China as Iran war curbed imports. Will it be a lasting change?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:43:06 UTC
18:43:06 KST

This is the first time that reductions in oil consumption – rather than coal – have been responsible for a drop in China's CO2 emissions.
China's carbon dioxide emissions fell in the second quarter of the year, new analysis shows.
The country's emissions have fallen before, but this was the first time it was driven by lower oil consumption – with a "dramatic fall" in China’s demand for oil imports following Middle East shipping disruptions linked to the US-Iran war.
Planet-warming CO2 emissions were down one per cent in the April-June period, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) analysis published by Carbon Brief.
Oil use fell nine per cent overall and 16 percent for transport, based on assessments of Chinese government data.
The situation "has very clearly validated China's energy security strategy and especially the role of electrification as a part of that strategy", says CREA co-founder and lead analyst Lauri Myllyvyrta.
Restricted oil imports have sped up electrification in China
Severe disruption to traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz – which was previously used to transport 20 per cent of the world's oil and gas – has heavily impacted shipments of oil to China, the world's second-largest economy and the top importer of crude.
Now, more than six months into the US-Iran war, China has weathered the complications more smoothly than many experts initially anticipated.
Myllyvirta says that the crisis has accelerated adoption of electric fleets in China across traditionally gas-guzzling industries including construction and mining.
"These kinds of changes are highly likely to prove sticky," he says.
Electric heavy-truck sales rose by about 77 per cent in the second quarter year-on-year, while the number of EVs on the road grew by 33 per cent and charging volumes rose by 60 per cent, indicating increased utilisation of existing EVs.
Previous drops in China's emissions have been driven primarily by lower coal consumption, rather than oil, according to the CREA.
Solar has surpassed coal in the world's biggest emitter
China is the world's biggest emitter, responsible for over 30 per cent of global greenhouse gases.
Its leaders have promised to step up efforts to reduce CO2 and boost the green transition, aiming for carbon neutrality by 2060.
While emissions fell in the second quarter, they rose two per cent in the first, according to the CREA data, leaving levels "up marginally across the first half of the year".
Earlier this week, Chinese authorities said that the country's installed solar energy capacity had surpassed that of coal-fired power for the first time.
China has seen explosive growth in renewable installation, with coal's share in its energy mix edging down in recent years.
Still, emissions from the power sector rose between April-June due to increased coal use, while gas-fired generation fell. This is despite strong growth in wind and solar capacity, with “wasted” power a persistent problem linked to a grid not adapted to increasing shares of variable renewable generation.

Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte faces arrest warrant over threats charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:42:03 UTC
18:42:03 KST

A Philippine court on Friday issued an arrest warrant for Vice President Sara Duterte over an alleged death threat against the country's president, with her defence team saying she would "exercise all her legal remedies".
Duterte was charged last month with "grave threats" stemming from remarks in November 2024 that she had spoken with an assassin and instructed him to kill President Ferdinand Marcos, his wife and his cousin, who at the time was speaker of the Philippine House.
Duterte made the remarks during an online news conference, saying they would be assassinated if she were killed. She has denied threatening them.
The alleged assassination threat also forms a crucial element of her ongoing Senate impeachment trial, where a guilty verdict would see her removed from office and permanently banned from politics.
Under the Philippine legal code, a criminal conviction on the charge would carry a jail term of up to six months.
Justice department spokesperson Polo Martinez confirmed the warrant had been issued, noting that a court in Metro Manila's Quezon City had quashed a motion to defer it.
But the warrant seemed unlikely to result in Duterte being taken into custody.
Duterte appeal options
Paolo Tamase, associate dean at the University of the Philippines College of Law, told AFP that Duterte's lawyers could now be expected to file for bail, perhaps before day's end.
"The easiest thing for VP Sara to do is to file for bail with the regional trial court," Tamase said in a phone interview, noting Duterte would likely not need to be present.
He added that the warrant could yet be challenged at a higher court.
"She can potentially question the issuance of the warrant of arrest, which means she would go up to the Court of Appeals or potentially the Supreme Court," he said.
The vice president's legal team issued a statement saying she had "no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies".
Justice department officials have rejected arguments by the vice president's legal team that she cannot be prosecuted for offences that are also tied to her impeachment.
Duterte was impeached in May by the House of Representatives, the lower chamber of parliament, on charges that also included graft and corruption.
A guilty verdict in the Senate — where her trial recently concluded its ninth week — would spell an end to a planned run for president in 2028. Duterte first announced her candidacy in February.
She is the daughter of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte. She previously served as the co-concurrent Secretary of Education and as the longtime mayor of Davao City before stepping onto the national stage.

"We will examine every aspect of (the indictment) with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process," a Romanian lawyer for the Tates, Eugen Vidineac, said in a statement.
"Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them."
The Tate brothers remain in jail in the U.S. while a judge decides on the request for their extradition to Britain, where they are wanted on rape charges.
The spokesperson for the Romanian anti-organized crime prosecuting unit DIICOT — which is investigating the Tates — said it was not immediately clear whether the unit will seek their extradition from the United States.
The Tates can be tried in absentia in Romania, but the trial will not start immediately. Under Romanian law, the indictment gets sent to a preliminary court chamber, where a judge will inspect the case files to ensure legality.
While the law states that the preliminary chamber judge has 60 days to finalize the report, indictments routinely take significantly longer.
Andrew Tate, a self-described misogynist, previously said he moved to Romania because law enforcement was more lax there.

Parashat Nitzavim: Why we are all responsible for one another
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:36:25 UTC
18:36:25 KST

One of the defining characteristics of the Western world is its preoccupation with personal achievements and the pursuit of phenomenal success. Billions of people move alongside one another, viewing others as competitors for success and as threats to their privacy.
This outlook creates a fundamental social problem. A healthy society is based on mutual assistance, in which it is the strong person’s role to support the weak and help them emerge from their difficult circumstances. It is founded on the understanding that the wheel turns: Today I help you, and tomorrow your child will help my child.
But when every person is preoccupied with themselves, people have neither the time nor the inclination to think about the problems of others. An ideology of supposed indifference develops from this: People should be left to manage on their own; they cannot become a burden on society; and every person is responsible for themselves.
The attitude of “leave me in peace,” in which the main concern is that things should be good for me, is a dangerous one. Ultimately, the problems around us reach us as well and they cannot simply be ignored.
Mutual responsibility
This approach is also evident in spiritual and moral matters. Here, in particular, a taboo sometimes develops according to which one should not interfere in another person’s life, and a person has neither the right nor the authority to tell someone else what is true or what is right for them.
Thus, people live according to the principle of “everyone does what is right in his own eyes,” while moral values gradually erode. The enlightened world sometimes prefers to ignore the consequences as long as things are good for me.
Parashat Nitzavim, which is read in the period leading up to Rosh Hashanah, comes to proclaim loudly that the only way to ensure a good and successful new year and a repaired and improved world is through the concept of mutual responsibility.
This approach, known in the world as “social responsibility,” is based on a popular parable about a group of people sitting aboard a ship. One of the passengers took a drill and began drilling a hole in the floor beneath his seat. The other passengers saw him and exclaimed in panic, “What are you doing?!”
He replied, “Why should you care? I’m drilling underneath my seat, not yours!”
They answered him, “We care about the damage, because the water will rise and sink the entire ship, and we will all drown together with you.”
The understanding that when murky waters are flowing through someone else’s home, they may eventually flood the entire world, is a description of human reality. This is precisely the starting point of the idea of mutual responsibility: There is really no such thing as “only under my seat.” What happens to one person may ultimately affect society as a whole.
Everyone is a partner
THIS CONCEPT is the foundation of the Jewish approach to the values of truth and the shaping of the inner soul. We cannot leave the world without anyone taking responsibility, allowing everyone to behave however is convenient for them. Ultimately, the ship carrying our collective values may sink, and the world may reach the state described in the generation of the Flood, when “the earth was filled with violence.”
To understand the importance of this idea, the parasha opens with the words: “You are standing today, all of you, before the Lord your God: your heads, your tribes, your elders, and your officers – every man of Israel. Your little ones, your wives, and your stranger who is in the midst of your camp, from the woodchopper to the water drawer” (Deuteronomy 29:9-10).
The Torah, which is meticulous about every word and formulation and contains nothing superfluous, nevertheless chooses here to elaborate and enumerate all the different types of people who make up the Jewish people: leaders and ordinary people, men and women, adults and children, native-born and converts. They all stand together.
The message is that the way to build a repaired and improved world cannot rely on individuals alone. Everyone is a partner, everyone is needed, and every person has a place and a role in the collective effort.
This commitment took on even greater significance when the principle of mutual responsibility was established anew among the Jewish people. The parasha describes how Moses, on his final day on Earth, gathers the entire Jewish people and presents them with a new standard of the covenant with God. From that point onward, every member of the Jewish people would also bear responsibility for the actions of others.
In the words of the Talmud: “All Jews are responsible for one another” (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 27b).
Once the principle of mutual responsibility was renewed among the Jewish people, it was no longer a matter of personal opinion. Whoever has the ability to influence those around them and fails to do so bears responsibility for the consequences, as the Talmud teaches:
“Whoever is able to protest against the members of his household but does not, is held accountable for the members of his household; against the people of his city but does not, is held accountable for the people of his city; against the entire world but does not, is held accountable for the entire world” (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 54b).
Anyone who possesses the knowledge, tools, and ability to influence others, both physically and spiritually, is obligated to become involved and offer assistance, particularly to those who are influenced by them.
The entire idea is encapsulated in the wonderful words of Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, former chief rabbi of Britain: “I don’t need you to agree with me; I need you to care about me!” There is no need for everyone to think alike. Nor is there any need for everyone to live in the same way. But it is important that everyone care about the people who are in the same boat with them.
This is the important message that Parashat Nitzavim comes to teach us as we prepare for the new year: not only to care for ourselves but also to see the person beside us – because ultimately, we are all in the same boat. And this is the surest path to a good and sweet new year.■
The writer is rabbi of the Western Wall and Holy Sites.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
