YEREVAN, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The South Caucasus has entered a period of structural and geopolitical adjustments, and the principles of the "Shanghai Spirit" are highly relevant to regional stability and development, Armenian scholar Johnny Melikyan has said.
In a recent written interview with Xinhua, Melikyan, a senior analyst at Armenia's Orbeli Center, said the expansion of cross-regional connectivity, shifting regional balances, and evolving security dynamics require the countries of the South Caucasus, including Armenia, to pursue foreign policies that are highly pragmatic, flexible and multidimensional.
Melikyan said the core principles of the "Shanghai Spirit" -- mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations, and pursuit of common development -- align closely with Armenia's foreign policy priorities. Armenia's institutional engagement with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) should be viewed within the framework of its active efforts to pursue a diversified foreign policy, he added.
Against the backdrop of today's fragmented international landscape, countries in the South Caucasus should play a constructive role in promoting regional connectivity, he said.
He said the SCO has evolved from a primarily security-focused organization into a comprehensive platform for economic and digital cooperation, demonstrating that modern security extends far beyond military might.
"Lasting regional stability requires deep economic interdependence, climate resilience, digital cooperation, and joint disaster-response mechanisms," he said.
Melikyan said the SCO's role as a bridge between civilizational spaces is invaluable as global politics becomes increasingly dominated by narratives of division.
Melikyan said that as the SCO enters its second quarter-century, challenges confronting Eurasia will only grow more complex. He stressed that no single nation or exclusive military-political bloc can resolve these challenges in isolation, adding that the future belongs to flexible, pragmatic networks of inclusive cooperation.
"I hope that the countries of the South Caucasus, with the support of our SCO partners, can transition from a zone of geopolitical competition into a secure, predictable, and prosperous continental hub connecting East and West, North and South," Melikyan said. ■

China's long-term care insurance covers over 320 million people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:31:49 CST
18:31:49 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on advancing the high-quality development of healthcare security to better serve Chinese modernization in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Xiaoyu)
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China's long-term care insurance system now covers more than 320 million people, with the fund's cumulative spending reaching 114.2 billion yuan (16.85 billion U.S. dollars), a health insurance official said on Friday.
More than 4.6 million people have received care services under the program, said Wang Wenjun, deputy head of the National Healthcare Security Administration, at a news conference held by the State Council Information Office.
To date, 22 provincial-level regions have issued implementation plans for the program, Wang said.
The number of localities where the scheme has been established reached 121, and the figure is expected to rise to 247 nationwide by the end of this year, he said.
As an important part of China's social security system, long-term care insurance provides care services or financial support to people who have partially or completely lost the ability to care for themselves. The scheme helps cover their basic daily needs and related medical care, easing the burden on both them and their families.
The program is also a priority under China's five-year plan for improving medical security as the country responds to its rapidly aging population. At the end of 2025, China had 323.38 million people aged 60 or older, accounting for 23 percent of the population. That figure is projected to exceed 400 million by around 2035.
China aims to have the long-term care insurance system in place nationwide by the end of 2028, according to a national plan to implement the program.
Provisions on long-term care insurance were added to the recently adopted law on healthcare security by Chinese lawmakers at a session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress.
The law specifies that a long-term care insurance system should be established and improved. It also stipulates that the relevant authorities under the State Council shall formulate specific measures for the financing, benefits, fund use, and supervision of long-term care insurance. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Chief scientist of China's Tianwen-3 mission says search for signs of life on Mars is top goal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:31:38 CST
18:31:38 KST

HEFEI, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China's Tianwen-3 mission is seeking evidence of whether life has ever existed on Mars, aiming to collect high-value Martian samples and conduct detailed analyses after bringing them to Earth, the mission's chief scientist Hou Zengqian told Xinhua in an interview Thursday.
Searching for potential signs of life on Mars is the top scientific goal of the Tianwen-3 mission, Hou said on the sidelines of the 2026 International Deep Space Exploration Conference, which opened on Thursday in Hefei, capital of east China's Anhui Province.
As a key step in China's planetary exploration program, Tianwen-3, planned for launch around 2028, is expected to become the first Mars sample-return mission in human history. Previously, NASA's Perseverance rover collected shallow surface samples, and will rely on a follow-up mission to return them to Earth. In contrast, Tianwen-3 aims to accomplish both sampling and return in a single mission.
Hou, also an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said China expects to finalize the landing site for the mission by the end of 2026, while Chinese scientists are advancing work on a new-generation geological map of the entire Mars.
Mars is one of the terrestrial planets in the solar system most similar to Earth and is widely considered a celestial body that may have once harbored life beyond Earth. Although Mars has evolved into a cold and arid planet with a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field, its past habitability and the possibility that life once existed there remain among the most important frontier questions in planetary science.
Over the past half-century, 47 Mars exploration missions have been conducted worldwide. However, more challenging endeavors, including sample-return and crewed missions to Mars, have yet to achieve a decisive breakthrough.
"The Tianwen-3 mission will look for microbial traces potentially similar to early forms of life on Earth, while also taking into consideration the possibility of unknown forms of life that may have emerged through Mars' unique evolutionary history, providing crucial evidence to answer this major scientific question," Hou said.
The mission could also deepen scientific understanding of the planet's climate evolution and geological processes and advance research in comparative planetology and the origins of life, the scientist said.
According to Hou, Mars sample return is an extremely complex project, with landing-site selection, planetary protection and contamination control, and the identification of potential signs of life among its key challenges.
Chinese scientists are selecting candidate landing sites for the mission based on factors that include geological age, history of water activity, habitability and the potential for preserving biosignatures.
China will also build the world's first planetary protection laboratory to prevent terrestrial microorganisms from contaminating Mars while ensuring the safe isolation of returned samples, according to Hou.
To address the challenge of detecting potentially tiny amounts of life-related materials in Martian samples, Chinese scientists are conducting dedicated research to establish a high-fidelity methodology covering the entire process for identifying biosignatures in returned samples.
"Regardless of whether signs of life are found, the returned Martian samples will have irreplaceable scientific value," Hou said.
He said analyses of the samples at microscopic, molecular and isotopic scales could deepen understanding of Mars' geology, environment, evolution of habitability and the conditions under which life may originate.
The mission has now entered the stage of developing engineering prototypes, Hou said.
He added that the Mars sample-return mission will not only provide a comprehensive test of China's engineering capabilities, but also serve as a major driver of planetary science.
Chinese scientists are advancing work on a new-generation geological map of the entire Mars by making full use of data from the Tianwen-1 mission and multiple international sources. The project integrates information from imagery, spectroscopy, radar and gravity measurements, and applies artificial intelligence to geological interpretation. Version 1.0 of the 1:5 million scale geological map of the entire Mars is scheduled for completion by the end of 2028.
Tianwen-3 will uphold the principle of open cooperation and work with scientists around the world to explore the mysteries of Mars, contributing China's expertise and solutions to expanding humanity's scientific frontier and advancing planetary science, Hou added. ■

Husband of slain Turkish American activist criticizes lack of US investigation

Ferdi Uzun and Merve Berker
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
The husband of Turkish American activist Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, killed by Israeli soldiers in the occupied West Bank two years ago, criticized Friday the lack of progress in the US legal process over her death.
Speaking to Anadolu at Eygi's graveside in the Didim district of Türkiye’s southwestern Aydin province, Hamid Mazhar Ali said: “The legal process in the US is at exactly the same point as the day she was killed.”
“There has been absolutely no progress,” he said during a memorial ceremony marking the second anniversary of her death.
“Despite our persistent requests over the past two years, no investigation has been launched.”
Ali said the pain of losing his wife remains as intense as it was when she died.
“It is just as difficult now as it was on the day she died,” he said. “It has not become any easier.”
“I think about her all the time. But it is also something a person has to learn to live with over time,” he added.
Ali said he misses hearing her laugh and joking with her.
Describing Eygi as someone who supported struggles for justice in different parts of the world from her youth, Ali said she “passionately advocated for peace and justice not only in Palestine but everywhere in the world.”
“Throughout her youth, she took part in many different struggles for peace and justice,” he added.
Ali said the situation in Palestine had deeply affected her.
“I think she was profoundly affected, especially by the events that began in 2023 and by the genocide,” he said.
“That is why she felt she had to go there. Seeing that all of this is still continuing today after such atrocities would have made her, like all of us, very angry and deeply disappointed.”
'Extremely hypocritical stance' by US
Ali said the family's pursuit of justice in the US has so far produced no results.
“I think this is an extremely hypocritical stance. But it is not surprising. We have seen this for the past 20 years, ever since Rachel Corrie,” he said.
Corrie was an American peace activist killed by an Israeli bulldozer in Gaza in 2003 while trying to prevent the demolition of a Palestinian family's home.
“She was an American, born and raised in the US, and her parents were American too. Yet justice was not delivered for her either,” Ali said.
“This is disappointing and it makes me angry. But when it comes to Israel, this double standard is not surprising,” he added.
“Looking at America's approach toward Israel and its record of not holding it accountable, its talk about justice seems extremely hypocritical.”
Ali said they would continue seeking justice at both the state level in Washington and the federal level.
“We will continue doing this because we know the issue is not only Aysenur. It is everyone who has been unjustly killed around the world, including by Israel,” he said.
Incident
Israeli soldiers opened fire during a peaceful demonstration in the occupied West Bank, seriously wounding Eygi, who had joined the protest in support of Palestinians and also held US citizenship.
Eygi was taken to a Palestinian hospital after being shot in the head and died on Sept. 6, 2024.
She was laid to rest in Didim, Aydin, on Sept. 14.
Eygi was a human rights activist and volunteer with the International Solidarity Movement, which supports Palestinians through peaceful and civilian means against Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories.
The occupied Palestinian territories have periodically witnessed shootings, stabbings and car-ramming attacks targeting Israeli soldiers or occupiers amid Israel’s attacks on the Gaza Strip and occupied West Bank.
Israel has killed more than 73,000 people and injured over 174,000 others in Gaza since Oct. 8, 2023.
Israeli army and settler attacks in the occupied West Bank since the start of the Gaza offensive have killed more than 1,000 Palestinians and injured over 12,000 others, while around 24,000 have been arrested.

Americans evacuated after Mozambique wildlife camp attack, source says
MAPUTO, Sept 4 - At least three Americans were evacuated after suspected insurgents attacked a camp in a wildlife reserve in northern Mozambique, a source familiar with the incident said.
The Mozambican independent English-language digital publication Zitamar News first reported the incident late on Thursday, suggesting there had been some fatalities. Regional analyst Tertius Jacobs said he believed insurgents had abducted a number of civilians. None of the reports could be verified.
Mozambique has been battling an Islamic State-linked insurgency in the gas-rich northern province of Cabo Delgado since 2017, a conflict that has killed thousands of people and displaced hundreds of thousands.
A U.S. State Department spokesperson said the U.S. Embassy in Mozambique was aware of an attack on a hunting lodge close to the Niassa Special Reserve, near Cabo Delgado, but did not confirm whether any Americans were affected.
The source, who declined to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said the camp had been burned but there were no confirmed fatalities. The source said the three Americans had been out hunting when the attack occurred, and that staff had fled and Mozambique's military had responded.
The Mozambican government did not respond to a request for comment.
The State Department had warned its citizens not to travel to Niassa Special Reserve for any reason, adding that terrorists had targeted upscale hunting lodges in and near the area and taken hostages.
Big-game hunting in the reserve, which runs from May to November, often draws hunting parties from the U.S.
Jacobs, an analyst at Focus Group, which monitors the insurgency, said the attack took place near Marangira village in Niassa province, and that insurgents had abducted several civilians and looted supplies before withdrawing towards Cabo Delgado.
He said available information corroborated reports that three Americans had been affected, but that casualty figures and the number of those abducted remained unverified. REUTERS

In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, one person was killed and four others were injured in Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia and settlements in the Zaporizhzhia district. What the Heck? Another Perfect Geometric Shape Has Been Detected on Saturn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

A team of astronomers discovered a strange polygonal atmospheric structure on Saturn near the planet’s south pole. This 10-sided shape, known as a decagon, joins one of the gas giant’s most famous features: a hexagon near the north pole that was first observed 44 years ago. Images of the new decagon were captured by the Hubble Space Telescope, and the discovery was recently published in the journal Science Advances.
The formations at both the north and south poles aren’t solid structures, like a wall or a rock formation. Saturn doesn’t even have a defined solid surface like Earth’s crust. If you were to descend through the atmosphere of the ringed planet, the pressure and density would progressively increase, but you would never reach a “ground” on which to land. Instead, what astronomers have witnessed are patterns formed by clouds, albeit very unusual ones.
Each side of the decagon measures approximately 16,800 kilometers, which is a few thousand miles longer than the diameter of Earth. Near the feature is a jet stream reaching speeds of 116 meters per second, or nearly 260 miles per hour. By way of comparison, a Category 5 hurricane—the most intense storm level possible on Earth—is defined by winds above 157 miles per hour. Interestingly, although the jet stream circulates at tremendous speed, the decagon pattern shifts at a mere 2.5 meters per second—less than 6 miles per hour.
The south pole feature appears to have formed recently. For decades, scientists have been searching for a counterpart to the famous northern hexagon. However, major missions that observed the planet have previously not been able to find an equivalent, long-lasting structure in the south. The search was further complicated because, due to Saturn’s tilt, its southern hemisphere was not clearly visible from Earth for many years.
The first clues of the decagon came from ground-based observations, some by amateur astronomers. As the images accumulated, it became evident that something strange was happening in Saturn’s southern cloud bands. Data from the Hubble Space Telescope made it possible to trace the pattern back to images taken in 2023. Monitoring continued, and by 2025 its 10 vertices had become much more clearly defined, confirming the presence of a new polygonal feature in the ringed planet’s atmosphere. Science, however, hasn’t settled on an explanation for how these structures came to be.
Various hypotheses have been proposed since the discovery of the north polar hexagon. One is that the polygons are the visible manifestations of enormous atmospheric waves confined by powerful jet streams. You can think of these as similar to ocean waves, which are not simply objects traveling across the ocean but rather disturbances propagating through the water.
A wave’s behavior changes depending on the space in which it moves and the boundaries it encounters. On Saturn, waves of atmospheric gases may be encountering jet streams that confine them, in a sense, like the edge of a beach. Except in this case, the “beach” wraps all the way around the planet.
Various other factors, such as Saturn’s rapid rotation, exact wind speeds, and variations in the currents, could all contribute to the distinct geometries of the shapes. A current that coils around the planet six times can form a hexagon; one that does so 10 times, a decagon. This is one of the more likely explanations for how an atmosphere without any solid structure can end up forming something that looks like a gigantic polygon, but there are still many unanswered questions.
We don’t know how deep these geometric figures extend, how long the new decagon might last, whether its appearance is related to Saturn’s seasons, and—most importantly—what sparked its formation in the first place. Researchers hope to find some answers by tracking the decagon’s evolution. To do so, they plan to continue observations with the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes and use more advanced atmospheric models to reconstruct possible conditions that could give rise to such a structure.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Health-tracking smart ring maker Oura to list on US stock market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:29:41 UTC
18:29:41 KST

Fans of Oura are accustomed to using its trendy smart rings to fastidiously monitor their health but now investors are preparing to track a new metric: its share price.
The company’s filing to list imminently on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York was made public on Thursday.
Founded in Finland in 2013 and now headquartered in San Francisco, Oura’s smart rings have become a must-have item among wellbeing enthusiasts, with celebrity fans and ambassadors including Jennifer Aniston, Prince Harry, Kim Kardashian and the Spider-Man actor Tom Holland.
The ring allows users to track metrics including heart rate, temperature and sleep quality.
The rings sell for $349 to $499 (about £258-£360), with subscribers then paying $5.99 a month or $69.99 a year for full access to data on their health. The US filing showed a thriving, high-margin business, which brought in $1.21bn in revenue in the nine months to 30 June, up 74% year on year.
The company said it recently became profitable, making $60.8m in the same nine-month period, compared with $1.6m in that time last year. It is aiming to list on the Nasdaq as soon as later this month with a valuation expected well above the $11bn it was valued at when it raised $900m last year.
Of particular appeal to investors is the after-sales subscription business, which the company said has reached a base of 5 million users, doubling year on year, and which had gross margins of 89% in the nine months to 30 June.
Membership revenue came to $240.5m over the nine months, up 121% year over year and hardware sales accounted for about 80% of revenues. Subscribers opened the app more than 3.5 times a day on average, the company said. The former Friends star Aniston has said publicly she is “addicted” to checking her Oura stats.
Subscribers are skewed towards women, who account for 72%, and 42% of the total base are aged 30 to 45, with 31% under 29.
Oura said it has collected almost 42bn hours of biometric physiological data from users across 50 metrics.
The latest product, Oura Ring 5, went on sale in May at $399 and is 40% smaller than its predecessor. It records heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature and motion, tracking more than 50 metrics involved in sleep, activity, readiness, stress, resilience, heart and women’s health.

Poland's grey market fuel share held at 4 percent in 2025
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:28:55 CEST
18:28:55 KST

Poland's grey market fuel share held at 4 percent in 2025
Illegal fuel trade accounted for 4 percent of the Polish market in 2025, remaining unchanged in yearly terms, the Energy Regulatory Office (URE) reported on Friday.
"This is not a high figure, especially when compared to the estimated scale of this phenomenon at the beginning of the 20th century, when the 'grey market' for liquid fuels in Poland stood at 20–30 percent," URE wrote in a new report on the domestic fuel market.
However, such a rate led to a significant reduction in state budget revenue. From public-law dues on diesel consumption alone, the Polish Treasury lost approximately PLN 2.5 billion (EUR 0.6 bln) in 2025.
The regulator identified the greatest risk of illegal trade in maritime diesel imports, lubricant imports and production, and LPG imports.
Consequently, the URE urged legislative changes aimed to introduce a licensing scheme for the production of lubricating oils and pyrolytic oils, seal the transit of liquid fuels, step up supervision of tax warehouses, and to establish a registration system for plastic fuel tanks used by consumers. Household spending in Latvia reaches record high, nearly doubling in recent years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:28:52 UTC
18:28:52 KST

Household consumption expenditure in Latvia reached an average of 619 euros per person per month in 2025, an increase of 46% compared with 2019, according to data from the Central Statistical Bureau (CSB). However, with inflation expected to return to more moderate levels in the coming years and wages continuing to rise faster than prices, household spending is likely to continue increasing, albeit at a slower pace than in recent years, says Kārlis Purgailis, Chief Economist at Citadele Bank.
Almost a quarter, or 24%, of total household expenditure last year was spent on food and non-alcoholic beverages, while housing costs accounted for 16% and transport for 12%.
Compared with 2019, spending on food increased by 53 euros per person per month, while housing expenditure rose by 39 euros.
“The rapid increase in household spending in recent years has mainly been driven by high inflation. Although expenditure has risen by almost half over six years, the increase in comparable prices has been only around 7%. This means that most of the growth is directly linked to higher prices rather than a significant increase in consumption volumes,” Purgailis said.
He explained that rising energy prices, high food inflation and more expensive services have had the greatest impact on household budgets in recent years. At the same time, average wages and household incomes have also increased, allowing people to spend more not only on everyday necessities but also on leisure, culture and other services.
“Recent data clearly show that basic necessities continue to dominate the spending structure of Latvian households. Food, housing and transport account for more than half of total expenditure. At the same time, CSB data show that the share of several spending categories in household budgets has declined since 2019. The most notable decrease has been in transport expenditure, which fell from 15% to 12%. A smaller share of household budgets is also being spent on personal care and various goods and services, household furnishings and maintenance, clothing and footwear, as well as healthcare,” the economist added.
CSB data also reveal significant regional differences in household consumption expenditure. Residents of the Riga region spent the most, averaging 750 euros per person per month, while the lowest expenditure was recorded in Latgale at 446 euros per month.
The type of place of residence also had a significant impact on spending.
In Riga, average monthly expenditure reached 781 euros per person, compared with 657 euros in other cities and considerably less – 524 euros per month – in rural areas.
According to the economist, household expenditure growth is likely to become more moderate in the coming years as inflation has declined significantly. Inflation this year is forecast to remain moderately elevated at around 4% due to rising global energy prices, but over the following couple of years it is expected to fall to around 2.2–2.3%.
At the same time, wage growth and a resilient labour market are expected to support households’ ability to maintain relatively stable consumption levels. Average wage growth is projected to gradually slow from 7.8% last year to 5.4% in 2028, which would still exceed the projected rate of inflation.
Based on current forecasts, average consumption expenditure could exceed 700 euros per person per month by 2028.

Poland's Zondacrypto exchange might have been insolvent since 2022, media reports
Poland
Unknown Publisher

11:28:33 CEST
18:28:33 KST

Poland's Zondacrypto exchange might have been insolvent since 2022, media reports
Zondacrypto, a major Polish exchange, may have been permanently insolvent as early as the end of 2022, but continued to accept payments and became the main sponsor of the Polish Olympic Committee, the online news outlets Wirtualna Polska and TVN24 reported on Friday.
The media quoted a decision by the Estonian court, which on August 27 ruled on the liquidation of BB Trade Estonia, the operator of the Zondacrypto exchange, and appointed a liquidator to oversee the process.
The bankruptcy proceedings were initiated at the request of an Austrian model who held cryptocurrencies in her wallet on the Zondacrypto exchange.
According to the liquidator, permanent insolvency may have arisen as early as the end of 2022, coinciding with the mysterious disappearance of the exchange's founder, Sylwester Suszek, which led to the company losing access to its cold wallet. The wallet was believed to contain around 4,500 bitcoins, with 1 BTC currently worth approximately EUR 69,433.
The news outlets pointed out that from that moment until April 2026, when the exchange halted withdrawals, it had built a strong market presence in Poland. Between 2023 and 2025, Zondacrypto conducted training courses on cryptocurrencies for the police, the National Tax Administration and prosecutors. In autumn 2025, it ran a major advertising campaign on the largest TV broadcasters. In October 2025, the exchange signed a sponsorship agreement with the Polish Olympic Committee, worth PLN 18.5 million (EUR 4.3 mln).
The Zondacrypto investigation in Poland involves around 30,000 investors who have been unable to access their funds, totalling an estimated PLN 350 million (EUR 81.3 million). The case gained momentum recently after the exchange's CEO, Przemyslaw Kral, began cooperating with prosecutors.
Investigators are also examining whether Zondacrypto funds were used to illicitly finance conservative political figures, foundations and media outlets.
The complex investigation has been merged with the probe into the 2022 disappearance of Suszek (originally the founder of the BitBay platform, which later rebranded as Zondacrypto). Officials are investigating potential ties between his disappearance and Russia's Tambovskaya organised crime syndicate. (PAP)

Putin sees chance for Ukraine peace deal amid intensified fighting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:27:54 UTC
18:27:54 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin has said he sees a chance for a diplomatic settlement to end the war in Ukraine, as Russian and Ukrainian forces continue exchanging strikes and tensions rise on both sides of the conflict.
Speaking on Thursday at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Putin said Russia and Ukraine remained the main parties to the conflict and should reach a consensus before other countries contribute to the process.
“We are grateful to everyone who is trying to contribute to resolving this issue. Are there chances? In my view, yes, there are,” Putin said.
Putin said contacts between Moscow and Washington were continuing, including through intelligence channels, and expressed hope they would lead to a positive result. He also said US President Donald Trump appeared willing to engage in constructive work.
The Russian president separately criticised attacks on civilian vessels and threats against civilian aircraft, calling such actions “state terrorism” and saying they complicated prospects for bilateral peace talks.
Strikes on energy infrastructure
Meanwhile, the conflict between the two countries continues to escalate.
Overnight, Russia attacked energy infrastructure facilities in Ukraine’s southern Odessa region, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said on Friday, warning of possible restrictions on the electricity network.
Odessa Governor Oleh Kiper said one person was killed and at least five others wounded in the attack, which also damaged civilian infrastructure.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Friday that its forces had struck two cargo vessels in the Black Sea that were transporting weapons, ammunition and military equipment for Ukraine. The claim could not be independently verified.
A Ukrainian drone strike, meanwhile, caused a fire at an oil depot in the Russian Black Sea port city of Sochi, authorities in the Krasnodar region said. No casualties were immediately reported.
Tensions inside Ukraine
Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said an investigation would determine how a dispute between two Ukrainian security agencies escalated into a shootout in Kiev that left three members of the Defence Ministry’s HUR Military Intelligence Directorate injured.
The confrontation occurred on Tuesday after the home of a Russian nationalist activist fighting alongside Ukrainian forces was searched. The activist said he had been detained by the SBU Security Service and forced to sign a confession saying he had collaborated with Russian intelligence, a statement he later retracted.
The SBU said its officers had acted to prevent what it described as a Moscow-backed plot to assassinate Russian anti-Kremlin activists in Kiev.
“It is important that the truth come out. And that situations like this do not recur,” Zelenskyy said.
He said the heads of the SBU and HUR would be assessed following an internal investigation, adding that both sides should be held accountable for actions that “should not have happened”.
Two servicemen from the agencies have been issued notices of suspicion in connection with the incident. Zelenskyy also dismissed Oleh Khramov, head of the SBU department responsible for protecting state secrets.
Shooting targets Russian serviceman
In Russia, a serviceman was hospitalised on Thursday after being shot in the city of Engels in Saratov region, according to the regional branch of the Investigative Committee.
Authorities said bullets and shell casings were found at the scene and a criminal investigation was opened on charges of attempted murder and illegal arms trafficking. They did not identify the serviceman or say who carried out the attack.
Last week, a serviceman was killed and his wife injured in a car bombing near St Petersburg, while three weeks earlier a factory director supplying drones to the Russian military was seriously injured and his driver killed when their vehicle exploded near Yekaterinburg.
Kiev has claimed responsibility for some attacks inside Russia. Ukraine’s SBU said in December 2024 that it had organised the killing of Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, who headed Russia’s military nuclear, biological and chemical protection forces. Kirillov was killed by a bomb hidden in a scooter outside his Moscow apartment building.
The latest developments underscore the widening security risks surrounding the conflict, even as Putin says there remains a chance for a diplomatic settlement.

Hezbollah terrorists trapped underground as IDF clears key southern Lebanon ridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:27:00 UTC
18:27:00 KST

The IDF had not planned to disclose its operation on the Ali Taher Ridge in order not to endanger the troops. But a Reuters report saying Iran had threatened to “respond forcefully” to Israeli activity in the area led the military to change its decision. According to security officials, no Iranian advisers or members of the Quds Force were present at the site during the IDF’s weeks-long operation on the ridge.
Special forces from the Yahalom unit were responsible for clearing the Ali Taher Ridge in Lebanon. The troops trapped Hezbollah terrorists inside the compound, identified openings through which they could escape and monitored them, preventing any attempt by the terrorist organization to assist its men from outside. Initially, Hezbollah tried to transfer equipment to them, but as time passed, the effort became increasingly difficult. Security officials said this created pressure within Hezbollah.
During the operation, the forces surrounding the openings engaged in firefights with Hezbollah terrorists attempting to escape and killed dozens of them. The IDF established operational control through offensive operations including ambushes, strikes on shafts using gunfire, grenades, drones and other firepower.
They tried to send food and water by drones
The New York Times also reported that Iran was attempting to present a different picture of what was happening on the ridge. An Iranian official and a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were quoted as saying that capturing the ridge would constitute “crossing a red line” and that Hezbollah had stored critical weapons in the area. Their comments were published in the same article reporting that the IDF had declared the ridge cleared of terrorists.
The Iranian source repeated the claim that Iranian advisers were present at the site along with 70 to 100 Hezbollah terrorists. The source added that the terrorist organization had tried for days to send food and water to the trapped forces by drones, but Israel killed everyone who attempted to reach the supplies.
According to the IRGC member, the compound had three escape routes, two of which were already under IDF control, while the last was on the verge of collapsing. He said Iran and Hezbollah’s priority was to evacuate and save the weapons that had been stored at the site, but that the chances of doing so appeared to be diminishing. It should be noted that despite the reports, Tehran has not officially commented on the developments on the ridge reported by the IDF on Thursday.
Defense Minister Israel Katz, who said Thursday that Iran “likes to attack on Jewish holidays,” issued a statement Friday morning saying that the capture of the Ali Taher Ridge marked the completion of the phase of establishing Israel’s hold on the security zone in southern Lebanon.
“The Ali Taher tunnels served as a command center for attacks against our forces and the Galilee region, while also serving as the last stronghold defending the Nabatieh area — which is extremely important to Hezbollah — and that is why they have strategic importance.
“Now the IDF will complete the neutralization of the tunnels and make the appropriate tactical preparations to hold the ridge and prevent the enemy from re-establishing itself in the area,” Katz said. He added that Israel would not withdraw from the security zone in Lebanon until Hezbollah was disarmed and the threat to residents of the Galilee was removed.
'The clearing is complete'
The IDF announced Thursday that it had completed clearing the underground infrastructure on the Ali Taher Ridge in Lebanon and said it was “working to neutralize it.” Forces from the 36th Division had recently operated to clear two underground routes in the area. The IDF said they had achieved operational control both above and below ground and cleared the area of terrorists. According to the IDF, some of the terrorists were killed while others fled.
“The operation to neutralize the underground infrastructure that was cleared of terrorists is continuing and, once it is complete, the IDF will make renewed defensive preparations,” the military said.
According to the IDF, the underground complex contained command centers, weapons rooms, generator rooms, living quarters, showers and a kitchen, “which enabled the terrorists to conduct fighting and remain there for extended periods. This was a strategic infrastructure project built over two decades, funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime.”
The IDF said that during Operations Northern Arrows and Lion’s Roar, Hezbollah terrorists made continuous use of the ridge. The forces advanced into the area after weakening Hezbollah throughout the war, particularly during those operations.
The military added: “IDF forces continue to operate to clear the security zone in southern Lebanon and will not allow the Hezbollah terrorist organization to advance terrorist operations against them. Any attempt by the Hezbollah terrorist organization to act against IDF forces will be met with force. The IDF remains committed to the ceasefire agreement in Lebanon.”

Guidance for new suppliers
A common way for suppliers to bid for contracts is via online platforms known as frameworks. These are usually set up to help government buy a specific type of product or service, and have standard terms and processes which make it easier to contract with us. Some frameworks are ‘open’, which means they can be joined at any time, while others are only open during certain periods. There also dynamic markets which are similar to frameworks and are always open to join.

Drone targets fuel depot in Libyan capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:25:54 UTC
18:25:54 KST

Drone targets fuel depot in Libyan capital
Libya’s National Oil Corporation (NOC) has reported an attempted drone strike on fuel tanks at a depot in the capital, Tripoli, in the latest attack targeting the conflict-torn country’s energy infrastructure.
The remotely controlled drone targeted the Brega fuel depot on Airport Road on Thursday morning, the NOC said in a statement. It initially reported no damage but raised emergency readiness at all sites and ordered teams to lower fuel levels in the tanks as a precaution.
NOC subsidiary Brega Petroleum Marketing Company later said inspectors had found damage to several pipelines and two tanks. According to the company, a suspected drone entered the depot’s airspace before crashing near one of the storage tanks. No casualties were reported.
NOC described the incident as a “dangerous indication” of attempts to target oil facilities through “acts of sabotage.” It warned that such attacks posed “a direct threat to the supply system and essential services,” including power generation, healthcare, and industry.
No group has claimed responsibility. The incident came less than a month after several drone strikes hit energy and water infrastructure in Zawiya, about 47 km west of Tripoli. The attacks damaged refinery tanks, destroyed a 4.5-million-liter gasoline tank, and struck a desalination plant and power facilities. The state-owned oil company warned that further attacks could force it to halt operations at the refinery. Conflict monitor ACLED linked the violence to intensifying rivalries among local militias, including disputes over territory and fuel smuggling.
The assaults have compounded an electricity crisis that triggered protests across western Libya in July. Demonstrators demanding improved services and the resignation of Tripoli-based Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah stormed the Mellitah energy complex and temporarily shut gas lines supplying power stations.
Libya has remained divided since the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that overthrew Muammar Gaddafi and drove the country into crisis, with Dbeibah’s government controlling the west and an eastern administration backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
On August 30, representatives of the rival camps signed a UN-backed roadmap aimed at holding presidential and parliamentary elections within 24 months under a single executive authority.
Since April, US President Donald Trump’s adviser Massad Boulos has also promoted a power-sharing initiative in an attempt to resolve Libya’s political deadlock. In an RT opinion piece, Libyan academic Mustafa Fetouri argued that the plan could bypass the UN process, keep the rival Dbeibah and Haftar camps in power, and deepen the country’s division.

Iceland’s rejection of accession talks ‘a blow to EU’: Expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:25:25 UTC
18:25:25 KST

Icelanders have rejected reopening accession negotiations with the EU, voting to preserve a relationship that gives them extensive access to the bloc while keeping the country outside it.
In an Aug. 29 referendum, 52.8% voted against restarting the talks, while 47.2% supported the proposal.
Turnout reached 82.5%, the highest since 2009, with 118,040 voting “no” and 105,399 voting “yes.”
The ballot was not a direct vote on EU membership. It asked whether negotiations suspended more than a decade ago should continue. Any resulting accession agreement would have required a second referendum.
“It is a blow to the EU,” Marianne Riddervold, a research professor at the ARENA Centre for European Studies at the University of Oslo, told Anadolu.
“Enlarging to democratically stable and relatively wealthy countries would help balance Eastern enlargement. And the EU has a strong interest in developments in the Arctic,” Riddervold said.
Riddervold said the “no” campaign succeeded in transforming a procedural vote on negotiations into a wider debate over membership.
“The no campaign made this into a discussion about membership more than whether or not to start negotiations,” she said.
“The yes campaign wasn’t really prepared for this, and the no campaign had more resources and support by the main newspaper, which is partly owned by strong fishing interests.”
The final Gallup poll before the referendum showed 51.6% opposing renewed talks and 48.4% supporting them.
However, an earlier survey by Icelandic pollster Maskina had placed the “yes” side narrowly ahead at 51.3%, indicating a shift during the closing stages of the campaign.
Riddervold said the opposition was driven by both economic interests and identity-based concerns.
“The main arguments against were linked to national control over national resources, not least fisheries, and there was a strong ideational component to the opposition, linked to the idea of sovereignty and independence,” she said.
The fishing industry accounts for about 8% of Iceland’s gross domestic product and nearly 40% of exports. A pre-referendum Gallup survey found that 90% of companies connected to the sector opposed EU membership.
“The no campaign had more resources, and support by the main newspaper, which is partly owned by strong fishing interests,” Riddervold said.
Membership would bring Iceland under the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy, although quotas, access and possible exemptions would have been negotiated. Icelanders decided there was no need to open the talks before arguing over how they might end.
The result also exposed an urban-rural divide. Reykjavik North backed negotiations by 57.5%, while Reykjavik South voted 54.5% in favor.
The “no” vote reached 62.9% in the Northwest, 61.2% in the Northeast and 60.5% in the South.
The referendum took place amid Russia’s war on Ukraine, growing strategic competition in the Arctic and uncertainty over the future of transatlantic relations.
Iceland was a founding member of NATO but has no standing armed forces. It relies primarily on the alliance and a bilateral defense agreement signed with the US in 1951.
Despite this dependence, Riddervold said security played a smaller part in the referendum debate than expected.
“Security played less of a role in the debate than I had assumed,” she said.
The country signed a Security and Defence Partnership with the EU on March 18, providing a framework for closer cooperation in areas including maritime security, cyber and hybrid threats, space, crisis management and support for Ukraine.
The partnership is not a collective defense agreement.
Riddervold said Iceland would nevertheless continue trying to deepen practical security cooperation with the bloc.
“This is already an ongoing process. Iceland recently signed a security and defense partnership with the EU, but this is not a binding agreement,” she said.
“Like Norway, it wants to connect more closely in this domain, and I think this cooperation will continue. But like Norway, it is struggling to be included in everything it wants.”
She said the EU could take a pragmatic approach in areas such as Arctic security, while Nordic and Nordic-Baltic defense cooperation would also continue to strengthen.
“European security is a patchwork of different security cooperation agreements,” she said.
Iceland already participates in the EU single market through the European Economic Area (EEA). It is also part of Schengen, the EU Emissions Trading System, and programs including Erasmus and Horizon Europe.
The EU accounts for 53.6% of Iceland’s total trade and receives about 66.5% of its exports, according to European Commission figures.
The EEA largely excludes fisheries and agriculture, conveniently leaving two of Iceland’s most sensitive industries outside the Brussels package.
“I think that the fact that Iceland already is integrated in the single market through the EEA agreement, is part of Schengen and has a lot of other agreements with the EU played a role,” Riddervold said.
“Like in Norway, many people feel that this already gives the country what it needs,” she further added.
Iceland initially applied for EU membership in 2009, after its banking system collapsed during the global financial crisis. Negotiations began in 2010 and were put on hold in 2013 after a change of government. By then, 11 of 35 negotiating chapters had been provisionally closed.
The EU kept a low profile during the campaign, partly because Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir’s government asked it not to interfere in a domestic decision, according to reports.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos gave several interviews to Icelandic media, including public broadcaster RUV, explaining the accession process and what negotiations would involve in practice.
Senior EU officials, however, largely refrained from actively campaigning for a “yes” vote.
After the result, European Council President Antonio Costa said through a spokesperson that the EU “fully respects the democratic choice of the Icelandic people.”
“Iceland remains one of the EU’s closest and most trusted partners,” he added.
Several European lawmakers, however, said on US social media company X that the result should prompt reflection in Brussels.
French Renew Europe lawmaker Sandro Gozi called the vote “a warning for Europe,” saying fears over fishing and emotional arguments had defeated the case for “yes.”
“The EU must change, overcome vetoes and become more effective and sovereign,” he said.
Finnish center-right lawmaker Mika Aaltola said Icelanders had assessed what full membership would add to their current arrangements and concluded it was “not enough.”
“A nation weighed what membership would add to what it already has, and answered: not enough,” said Aaltola, who is also an MEP.
“If we cannot charm a small North Atlantic democracy with Trump in the White House and Putin waging war on our continent, then the conditions for charming will not get better than this,” Aaltola said.
Nicola Procaccini, co-chairman of the European Conservatives and Reformists Group, said Iceland’s decision should not be “dismissed lightly.”
“The fact that the Icelandic people nevertheless chose not to take even that first step should give Brussels pause,” he said.

Claude Peru Luwara, a Congolese refugee in Belgium, is in hospital after undergoing a third violent attack in an attempt to silence him.
Conglese journalist and commentator Claude Peru Luwara has once again been attacked by masked men in Tienen. It is the second attack against the journalist in Tienen, where he lives, and the third against him in Belgium.
Yesterdy evenings, three men wearing hoods and scarves over their faces struck Luwara in the head with a hammer. He was seriously injured and taken to hospital. “They repeatedly struck the man on the head,” said a man who witnessed the attach on the town’s Grote Markt. “He had absolutely no chance of seeing the attack coming. Afterwards, all three of them ran away.”
This was attempted murder. We’re still shaking.
Witness to attack on Luwara
Witnesses to the violent attack tried to stop the bleeding until emergency services arrived. Police and medics arrived quickly on the scene. “It was really shocking to see how violent the attackers were. This was attempted murder. We’re still shaking. You see something like that in a movie, but not right in front of your eyes on the Market Square in Tienen.”
Luwara, 44, has lived in Belgium for several years as a refugee, having fled Congo due to threats against him for his outspoken criticism of president Félix Tshisekedi. Via his YouTube channel and other outlets, such as TV5MONDE, he talks about his home country, which he says has become a dictatorship.
According to reports, the Congolese government has offered €4 million for “information” about Luwara. He was also beaten in the street by masked men in Tienen last summer. In June, four men were convicted, receiving sentences of three to four years in prison.
Talking to VTM News following the court hearing, Luwara revealed that he had also been attacked this year in Louvain-la-Neuve. The judge in the case stated that the perpetrators were motivated by political reasons.
“Exporting regime abroad”
“I am glad that the Belgian justice system recognised that I am not only in danger but that this is about an international operation,” Luwara told VTM. “Today Congo is a dictatorship. President Tshisekedi, who spent most of his life in Belgium, has turned it into a tyranny. Anyone who doesn’t agree with him, who are critical, are fleeing the country. And now he is exporting this dictatorial regime abroad, to here, where we have sought safety.”
The Leuven public prosecutor’s office stated that the victim is in stable condition and that police are seeking the suspects. Security camera footage from in and around the Grote Markt may provide useful leads for the investigation.

New Zealand approves party-drug MDMA for treating patients with PTSD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:24:41 UTC
18:24:41 KST

Two psychiatrists in New Zealand can now prescribe MDMA in controlled clinical settings, built on trial results that have been challenged in the US.
Two New Zealand psychiatrists have won approval to prescribe pharmaceutical-grade MDMA to patients with severe post-traumatic stress disorder, making the country only the second in the world - after Australia in 2023 - to authorise the party drug for clinical use.
New Zealand's medicines regulator, Medsafe, granted the approvals to Wellington's Dr Gary Wynn and Auckland's Dr Tom Paterson, who spent more than a year passing the regulatory process.
"PTSD ruins lives and is difficult to treat," said Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour, who last year backed a similar approval for psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, to treat severe depression.
"MDMA can be very effective at treating it through psychedelic-assisted therapy," he said, adding that New Zealand remains committed to opening access to "innovative treatments."
PTSD develops after a person experiences or is threatened by traumatic events such as combat, sexual assault or sudden death.
Existing pharmaceutical options in most countries are limited to two antidepressants that can take three months to take effect and produce uneven results.
The evidence behind the approval — and why the US said no
The approval draws on evidence from two pivotal international Phase 3 trials, run by the US-based Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS) and sponsored by its public benefit corporation arm Lykos Therapeutics.
In the first, published in 2021, 88% of participants with severe PTSD who received MDMA-assisted therapy showed clinically significant improvement, and 67% no longer met the diagnostic criteria for PTSD.
A second trial in 2023, involving participants with moderate-to-severe PTSD, found 71.2% of those treated with MDMA no longer met PTSD diagnostic criteria by the end of the study.
Despite those results, the US Food and Drug Administration rejected the therapy's approval in 2024, citing insufficient evidence of its safety and effectiveness.
Regulators raised concerns that participants who had taken MDMA before produced an expectancy bias, complicating the trial data.
New Zealand's Ministry of Health said the new treatment would be tightly controlled, combining MDMA with psychotherapy in a clinical setting rather than take-home doses.
"Treatment takes place in a controlled clinical setting under the care of an authorised psychiatrist and forms part of a comprehensive treatment plan," the ministry said, adding that patients must be aged 18 or older.

North African dust hits Portugal and health body urges vulnerable people to stay at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:23:42 UTC
18:23:42 KST

Air quality will worsen in coming days across much of mainland Portugal due to North African dust, especially in central and southern areas; health authorities urge vulnerable people to take extra care.
The Directorate-General of Health (DGS) has issued a warning (source in Portuguese) about poor air quality over the coming days due to an air mass from the deserts of North Africa carrying dust particles suspended in the atmosphere. The Portuguese health authority is advising the most vulnerable members of the population to stay at home whenever possible.
In a statement published on its website, the DGS notes that dust coming from North Africa will affect most of mainland Portugal, especially the Centre and South.
The Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA) also indicates (source in Portuguese) that there will be dust in suspension this Friday and Saturday.
Because of the dust, "a situation of poor air quality is expected to occur on the mainland, with an increase in the concentrations of inhalable particles of natural origin in the air", the DGS says.
According to the health authority, this pollutant (inhalable particles – PM10) affects human health, especially among the most sensitive groups, such as children and older people, whose healthcare needs should be given extra attention while these conditions persist.
Therefore, and for as long as this phenomenon continues, the Directorate-General of Health recommends that the public "avoid prolonged exertion, limit physical activity outdoors and avoid exposure to risk factors, such as tobacco smoke and contact with irritating products".
The DGS specifically advises that children, older people, patients with chronic respiratory problems, particularly asthma, and those with cardiovascular disease should, whenever possible, remain indoors and preferably keep windows closed, "because of their greater vulnerability to the effects of this phenomenon".
In addition, it stresses that "patients with chronic diseases should continue their ongoing medical treatments".
Interior facing maximum rural fire risk
In addition to the dust, eleven municipalities in the districts of Bragança, Guarda, Castelo Branco and Coimbra are on maximum rural fire alert this Friday, on a day when temperatures will remain high, according to IPMA.
Because of the hot weather, IPMA has placed the districts of Bragança, Viseu, Évora, Guarda, Faro, Vila Real, Setúbal, Santarém, Lisbon, Leiria, Beja, Castelo Branco, Coimbra and Portalegre under a yellow warning until 7 p.m. on Saturday.
Although the peak of the heat episode was on Thursday, temperatures are expected to remain above 20 ºC, despite a slight drop this Friday, especially along the coast and in regions south of the Tagus.

Bloomberg: ‘Sanctions from hell’ bill against Russia stalls in U.S. House of Representatives
A bill imposing new sanctions on Russia will likely be pushed back until after the U.S. midterm elections in November, the Bloomberg news agency reported.
The bill, which Republican Senator Lindsey Graham championed during the final year of his life, would give the U.S. president authority to impose 100% tariffs on countries that are major importers of Russian oil.
Bloomberg said the legislation, which would expand President Donald Trump’s tariff authority and risks pushing up fuel prices, is unlikely to come up for a vote ahead of the midterms.
The Senate passed the bill, dubbed the “sanctions bill from hell” bill by American media, in early August. According to Bloomberg, senators voted for it in part in memory of the late Lindsey Graham.
The measure faces less support in the House of Representatives, where Democrats worry Trump could use it as another legal basis for new import tariffs, even as tariffs he has already imposed remain under court challenge.
Big business representatives have also objected, arguing the bill would let tariffs be imposed on countries that are U.S. trade partners and allies, and warning that it “unintended consequences for consumers.”
The bill would impose 100% tariffs on five countries that are the leading buyers of Russian oil and gas. It doesn’t name the countries, but India and China are the largest purchasers of Russian energy.

Ancient traditions come alive at World Nomad Games (VIDEOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:21:11 UTC
18:21:11 KST

Horsemen, wrestlers, and archers are testing their strength and skill against the spectacular backdrop of Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, where the sixth World Nomad Games are in full swing.
Competitors from 90 countries are taking part in 43 disciplines rooted in nomadic traditions, ranging from eagle hunting, horseback wrestling, and archery to tug-of-war and traditional intellectual games.
Horses take center stage in many of the events of the Games, which run through September 6. 
In ‘er enish’ (horseback wrestling), two mounted wrestlers try to drag each other from the saddle, while ‘tyiyn enmei’ (coin picking) requires riders to lean almost to the ground at full gallop to pick up an object.
Another gold for Kyrgyzstan in Er Enish (horseback wrestling) at the World Nomad Games! 🇰🇬🥇 pic.twitter.com/WO5uglfgtX
— Samat (@samat_awa) September 3, 2026
Then there is ‘kok-boru’ (gray wolf), perhaps the games’ most famous spectacle, in which two teams on horseback fight for possession of a goat carcass and attempt to carry it to the opposing side’s goal.
Highlights from Day 1 of the VI World Nomad Games.
The Kyrgyz Kök Börü team defeated Team USA in a very intense game.

Traditional hunting is represented by ‘salbuurun’, featuring golden eagles, other birds of prey, and hunting dogs. Archery, horse racing, and numerous forms of traditional wrestling are also on the program.
Iran’s four-member tug-of-war team finished runner-up at the Nomad Games in Kyrgyzstan. pic.twitter.com/eAe83P3qhV

People coming to the World Nomad Games also get to try traditional Turkic sports themselves.
Like this one.
Two people, one wooden board, one stick. Basically, whoever can’t pull the other guy over loses. pic.twitter.com/cCVvPBNYQl
The games are about more than sport. Yurts, national costumes, crafts, music, and food have transformed the venues into a showcase of nomadic culture.
The event grew out of efforts in Kyrgyzstan in the 2000s to preserve traditional games whose rules risked disappearing as older generations died. The initiative was later recognized by UNESCO as a good practice for safeguarding intangible cultural heritage.
First staged in Kyrgyzstan in 2014, the World Nomad Games have since traveled to Türkiye and Kazakhstan before returning to their birthplace this year. What began as a regional effort to keep old traditions alive has grown into an international celebration of nomadic culture.

52% Back Ukraine Arms, 42% Say Germany Has Gone Too Far, Deutschland Poll Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:19:59 UTC
18:19:59 KST

Most Germans support continuing or even expanding arms deliveries to Ukraine, although opposition to military aid has reached its highest level in recent years, according to a new ARD-DeutschlandTrend poll.
The survey, according to tagesschau.de, was conducted by infratest dimap from Aug. 31 to Sept. 2 for German public broadcaster ARD. It found that 52% of respondents consider arms deliveries to Ukraine appropriate, including 38% who believe they are at the right level and 14% who would increase them.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Meanwhile, 42% said Germany is going too far with its weapons supplies – the highest share recorded in recent years.
Support for military aid is particularly weak in eastern Germany, where a majority of respondents said arms deliveries had gone too far.
The survey comes as concerns over Russia’s threat to Germany remain widespread. Some 56% of Germans said their country’s security is strongly or very strongly threatened by Russia, while 39% disagreed.
Older Germans were significantly more likely to perceive Russia as a major security threat. Among those aged 65 and over, around two-thirds considered the threat very strong or strong, while respondents aged 18 to 34 were more divided.
Russia was viewed as a security threat by majorities of supporters of every party represented in the Bundestag except the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). Over two-thirds of AfD supporters said they considered Germany’s security to be little or not at all threatened by Russia.
Russia Changes Strategy: Non-Stop Alerts in Kyiv
The findings come amid renewed concerns in Germany over Russian hybrid attacks. The German government recently said it believed Russia was responsible for an attempted attack involving a drone found carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport and warned that Germany could face further Russian hybrid attacks.
The ARD-DeutschlandTrend survey questioned 1,319 eligible voters in Germany through a combination of telephone and online interviews. The poll has a margin of error of roughly three percentage points for a result of 50%.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine and Germany are finalizing a bilateral Drone Deal to expand joint drone production and defense cooperation.
Zelensky made the announcement Wednesday after a phone call with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The agreement is expected to cover joint development and production of drones, missiles and related software.
Ukrainian and German leaders discussc mutual Russian threat
Several Ukrainian-German defense projects are already underway.
Germany is financing 50,000 Shrike FPV drones produced by the Ukrainian company SkyFall under a contract worth about €90 million ($104 million), as well as 15,000 STRILA interceptor drones designed to counter Russian Shahed-type UAVs.
Germany will send Ukraine new air defense packages this month as Kyiv faces an intensifying Russian drone campaign, Zelensky said Wednesday.
The announcement comes as Russia has sharply increased its aerial attacks, launching around 1,500 drones against Ukraine over four days in late August, including about 800 jet-powered Shahed drones. The barrage is putting additional pressure on Ukraine’s air defenses ahead of the autumn and winter months, when Russia has repeatedly targeted critical infrastructure.
Zelensky and Merz also discussed Russia’s attempted attack involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig Airport. Merz briefed Zelensky on Germany’s response, while Zelensky offered Ukraine’s expertise in countering Russian drone attacks.
Germany has been one of Ukraine’s key air defense partners since Russia’s full-scale invasion, supplying systems including Patriot and IRIS-T.

Russian occupation authorities sentence abducted Ukrainian journalist Iryna Levchenko to 15 years in prison
Melitopol journalist Iryna Levchenko has been sentenced to 15 years in a penal colony by an occupation court in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Levchenko was unlawfully imprisoned in 2023.
Source: Institute of Mass Information
Details: A statement about the verdict appeared on the occupation court's website and Telegram channel, saying that Ukrainian journalist Iryna Levchenko had been found guilty of alleged "espionage".
The occupation court stated that Iryna Levchenko remained in occupied Melitopol after the start of the full-scale invasion and did not renounce her Ukrainian citizenship.
The occupation authorities claim that "having contacted a resident of territory controlled by Ukraine's armed forces via the Telegram messenger, the woman agreed to assist Ukrainian special services by transmitting data about the locations of office buildings and Russian government officials, movement routes of personnel, military equipment and weapons of Russia's armed forces and other military formations on the territory of Zaporizhzhia Oblast".
According to the occupation authorities, Levchenko allegedly "transmitted information about Russian government ministries and agencies, including those responsible for security and law enforcement, along with their addresses and lists of employees" in February 2023.
"The transmission of said information to the Ukrainian side could have led to strikes on the locations of these strategic facilities," the occupation authorities stated.
In 2023, the occupying forces abducted journalist Iryna Levchenko and her husband in occupied Melitopol and held them in a basement. Levchenko was regularly transported from the Donetsk pre-trial detention centre to occupied Melitopol for investigative actions.
According to RIA Pivden, the journalist's case was completely closed off, and even her lawyer did not have full access to it.
In June 2026, it became known that Iryna Levchenko had been transferred from the Simferopol pre-trial detention centre to the Krasnodar pre-trial detention centre in Russia. According to RIA Pivden, the journalist's husband Oleksandr Levchenko was released in August 2024.
For reference: Iryna Levchenko has been in journalism since 1981. She worked at factory newspapers, the Melitopol district newspaper Novyi Den, and was a local correspondent for oblast and national print publications.

EU to make last-minute decision on Arctic oil and gas drilling ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:16:27 UTC
18:16:27 KST

The European Commission will soon unveil its revised Arctic strategy and whether to maintain or scrap its 2021 position on new oil and gas exploration in the High North. The International Energy Agency and Norway have urged Brussels to reconsider the ban.
The European Union is expected to make a last-minute decision on banning new oil and gas exploration in the Arctic during a weekly meeting of the bloc’s 27 commissioners in October, according to two EU officials who spoke to Euronews on condition of anonymity.
Earlier media reports suggested that the EU is considering dropping its ban on new drilling in the Arctic in its revision of the 2021 Arctic strategy as the bloc is enduring an energy crisis triggered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, where 20% of the world's gas and oil transit.
The Artic has become increasingly contested due to its abundant oil and gas reserves and critical raw materials — essential components for clean technologies and defence systems that are in high demand.
Russia and China have increased activity in the region, including through the “Ice Silk Road,” a regular Arctic shipping route linking eastern ports such as Ningbo with European hubs.
Hard-line rhetoric from the United States seeking to 'acquire' Greenland has also unsettled Europe, prompting the bloc to revise its 2021 Arctic strategy, with greater emphasis on defence and the region's economic potential, even if indigenous people in the Arctic may be sceptical of its outcomes.
Drilling for oil and gas in the Arctic is perhaps one of the biggest sticking points in the upcoming EU strategy, which set a firm stance against it in 2021, declaring a commitment to ensure that "oil, coal, and gas stay in the ground".
Germany, Sweden and Finland broadly backed the Commission's position. Denmark had to thread a delicate balance, supporting the EU's green ambitions while having limited ability to impose them on Greenland, its autonomous region, which controls its own vast mineral resources, including the estimated significant undiscovered oil and gas reserves.
At the time, the Commission proposed developing a multilateral legal obligation to ban new oil and gas exploration in the Arctic and contiguous regions — a proposal backed by Germany — but the strategy has ultimately remained a non-binding political commitment.
Ban or no ban?
The EU’s shift in approach to Arctic drilling was recently echoed by International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol, who urged the bloc to reconsider its ban on new oil and gas exploration projects in the region, citing concerns over security of supply.
Estimates suggest the US-led war against Iran cost the EU an extra €60 billion in imported fossil fuels during the first 100 days of the conflict.
Unlike in 2021, the decision on whether to ban oil and gas drilling in the Arctic is a 'yes-or-no topic' that will be decided by the College of Commissioners, meaning the team of 27 top political leaders who head the Commission, according to one EU official.
Despite the IEA plea and strong lobbying from Norway — which holds vast deposits of oil and gas in the Barents Sea — for the ban to be scrapped, "the most likely is that the EU position remains the same", a second EU official told Euronews.
However, given the strategy's non-binding nature, the decision will ultimately lie with countries alone.
"I can tell you that many member states which are not Arctic countries have been extremely interested in the strategy," the first EU official said.
Paal Frisvold, coordinator at the NGO Alliance to Preserve the Moratorium on Oil Drilling in the Arctic, said that despite the lack of legal instruments, the political weight OF WHAT? will affect other regions’ plans and strategies.
Nonetheless, while the EU wants a bigger geopolitical role in the Arctic, its main tool remains a non-binding strategy, leaving Brussels dependent on persuasion, money and cooperation from countries that actually control the region.
Norway's hard stance
With a looming strategy and mounting fears of gas and oil supply shortages ahead of winter, Norway, a non-EU country and the EU's top supplier of natural gas, said recently that it will continue exploring oil and gas regardless of the EU's position.
"In today's geopolitical and security environment, and given the resource situation, I believe continued activity in the Barents Sea serves both Norwegian and European interests," the Norwegian Energy Minister Terje Aasland recently told Reuters.
Frisvold snubbed Minister Aasland's remarks, saying that EU policies driving the climate and energy transition, like electrification and the shift to domestically produced clean energy, could lead to "stranded assets" if Norway decides to invest in new exploration.
"By 2040, these policies could reduce EU gas demand by around two-thirds. That matters when new discoveries in the northern Barents Sea can take 15–20 years to reach production. Fields discovered today risk coming on stream just as European gas demand is falling sharply, raising an obvious risk of stranded assets," Frisvold told Euronews.
Grunde Almeland, a member of Norway’s parliament, the Storting, declined to speculate on the EU’s final decision but urged the bloc to maintain its opposition to new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic.
"The Arctic is an extremely vulnerable region, and it is already being heavily affected by climate change. We should protect this unique environment, not open up new areas for fossil fuel extraction," Almeland told Euronews.
"Expanding Arctic oil and gas production is also not a sustainable way to address Europe’s long-term energy needs. Norway should help Europe accelerate the transition to clean energy, rather than push for more drilling in the Arctic."
Economic potential vs indigenous people
According to the first EU official, who is involved in the Arctic strategy, the overall idea is to set priorities for the EU’s role in the Arctic and identify potential investments that can be co-financed by the EU budget. Economic and defence elements in the strategy will feature highly, the EU official added.
Mikael Janson, Director of the North Sweden European Office, where he coordinates a network of 14 regions in the European Arctic of northern Sweden, Eastern and Northern Finland, and Northern Norway, expressed concern that the upcoming Arctic talks will "once again lose track" of local and regional perspectives.
"In general, all agree on the competitiveness advantage for the Arctic regions on investments in global green transformation and defence of the area’s integrity in the global power-grabbing we all see," Janson told Euronews.
"It must go hand in hand with societal investments that reach all parts of communities and the interests and potential of small actors. What we lack in EU Arctic policy is a coherent EU response: one part of the EU institutions engages in indigenous dialogue, while another emphasises a “dig it up, babe” approach that ends up in our reality at the local level."

Roosters rest nine, says wild card round could be the answer
Trent Robinson has defended his decision to rest nine players ahead of the NRL finals, but would be in favour of a wildcard weekend to fixture a break for the top teams.
The fourth-placed Sydney Roosters are resting James Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans and seven others from tonight's clash.
Following Sam Walker's injury, Robinson admitted there was a temptation to give new halves combination Cherry-Evans and Hugo Savala a dry run in the last weekend before finals.
"There was some thought around that, but I also trust the way that they both play," he said.
"They've both trained a lot together."
The upheaval on the Roosters' team sheet comes after Penrith memorably rested 16 players for the penultimate round of last season, while finals-bound Cronulla and the Warriors are also resting fit players this weekend.
The situation has reignited suggestions of introducing a pre-finals wildcard round.
That would allow the teams that finish between first and sixth to rest the weekend before finals and therefore play full strength until the end of the regular season.
The teams placed seventh to 10th, meanwhile, would play off to secure one of two finals spots, so would have incentive to name their best teams.
The AFL welcomed 172,769 fans to the two games across their first wildcard weekend last month.
It is understood NRL club chief executive officers were broadly in favour of introducing the concept when quizzed at Wednesday's meeting.
Robinson is also keen on introducing a wildcard weekend, but only once the league expands closer to 20 teams as it aims by the end of the decade.
"I think it makes commercial sense, I think it makes football sense as far as the weekend off and making the finals series at its best as well for those teams," he said.
"I think it's with some foresight not to [use it as we] go to 18 [teams], but probably going towards 20, and I think it's not all four of those teams getting into that finals series, it's only two of them.
"So you're not rewarding four teams, you're rewarding two teams that have to fight their way in."
Rex Bassingthwaighte, Toby Rodwell and Reece Foley all join the Roosters' starting backline with four NRL games of experience between them, while uncapped Hayden Barton, Aston Warwick and Jake Elliott are on the six-man bench.
Robinson insisted he was still taking the clash, between the NRL's two fiercest rivals, seriously.
"History will show that I love this game and respect this game, and I don't think there's any different this weekend, because Daly Cherry-Evans isn't playing and Toby Rodwell is," he said.
"There's a future in what we're going to be playing out there as well."
