Release of Lebanese national detained without charge highlights Israel's admission of arbitrary detentions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:56:13 UTC
17:56:13 KST

Israel held Lebanese national Malik Kamal Razi for nearly 11 months without announcing charges before releasing him after an investigation found no evidence linking him or others to any organization.
Israeli official media had described Razi as a “Hezbollah operative” before his release.
Lebanese lawyer and lawmaker Melhem Khalaf told Anadolu that releasing Razi and other Lebanese nationals abducted by Israel over the past two years does not negate their rights to seek investigations, accountability and reparations for any violations they suffered during their detention.
On Thursday, Israel handed Razi over to the Lebanese army through the International Committee of the Red Cross at the Naqoura crossing, marking the first release since the start of US-brokered negotiations between Beirut and Tel Aviv last April.
The release was part of a decision involving five people detained by Israel in Lebanon.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said an investigation showed they “do not belong to any terrorist organization, have not engaged in terrorism, and there is no justification for their continued detention.”
The statement amounts to an acknowledgment that the Israeli army carried out “arbitrary arrests” in Lebanon and provides evidence that such arrests, which Beirut considers "kidnappings," were conducted before sufficient evidence was available to establish the detainees’ links to any armed activity.
It also highlights the contradiction between Israel’s public broadcaster's description of Razi as a "Hezbollah operative" without providing any evidence, and Netanyahu's office's subsequent announcement that the investigation had not proven the released individuals' affiliation with any organization.
Razi, born in 2005, is from Ain Ata in the Rashaya district of eastern Lebanon.
On Oct. 12, 2025, he left on his motorcycle to exercise in a mountainous area near his hometown before contact with him was lost.
His motorcycle was later found, prompting residents and volunteers to search for him.
It subsequently emerged that Israel was holding him. Israel did not announce charges against him or bring him before a court during nearly 11 months of detention.
A Lebanese official source told Anadolu that Israel was expected to hand over four more detainees, including two Syrians, to the Red Cross at the Naqoura crossing at 11 am local time (0800GMT) Friday.
They would then be transferred to the Lebanese army for medical examinations before being handed over to their families.
Razi’s case is not an isolated one. Lebanon's national human rights commission documented, in a legal document issued on Dec. 15, 2025, the arrest and disappearance of Lebanese citizens during civilian activities.
The document was based on information from families, direct testimonies and corroborated data from national and international bodies, amid a lack of official Israeli information about the detainees’ whereabouts and legal status.
Cases included two nurses detained in Aita al-Shaab in November 2024 and two workers detained while traveling to civilian work in Wadi al-Hujeir on Dec. 19, 2024.
The commission also documented two fishermen detained off Naqoura on Feb. 2 and June 4, 2025.
A shepherd was detained while tending his flock in the Mount Hermon area on June 7, 2025, while others were taken from their homes or while returning to their villages after the ceasefire.
The commission said the documented incidents, particularly those occurring after the ceasefire and during civilian activities, indicated “arbitrary detention” in violation of Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
It also pointed to cases that could amount to “enforced disappearance” and the unlawful transfer of detainees into Israel in violation of Article 76 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, in addition to possible violations involving torture and denial of medical care.
In February 2026, independent research and advocacy organization Legal Agenda documented 22 Lebanese people captured or abducted alive, along with 42 whose fate remained unknown.
In May, it raised the number documented as having been taken alive to at least 30 following renewed Israeli operations.
In December 2025, the "Call for Freedom" campaign was launched to advocate for Lebanese prisoners and abductees.
It organized activities with the participation of their families to demand information about their fate and their release.
Released prisoner and academic Nabih Awada, a specialist in Israeli affairs, told Anadolu that 36 Lebanese prisoners are “alive in Israeli prisons,” citing the Prisoners’ Representatives Committee and relevant Lebanese authorities.
Israel has declared that it is holding 33, Awada said.
Awada told Anadolu that 21 of them were detained after the ceasefire agreement took effect on Nov. 27, 2024, while attempting to return to their villages, and that six detainees faced trials in Israel.
He noted that between seven and 10 detainees are classified by Israel as members of Hezbollah’s “Radwan Force,” meaning that Tel Aviv does not include the remaining detainees in this classification.
Netanyahu's office linked the release to searches for the remains of members of the Jewish community who were kidnapped and killed in Lebanon in the mid-1980s, saying that the decision was made "in light" of field searches conducted by both sides.
Lebanese official sources, however, told Anadolu that the release came amid contacts by Lebanese President Joseph Aoun with Washington to pressure Israel to uphold the ceasefire, release the prisoners and withdraw from Lebanese territory.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam pledged, following Razi’s release, to continue pursuing the issue until all detainees are released and the fate of those missing is determined.
The Lebanese state considers civilians detained by Israel inside Lebanese territory to be abductees rather than prisoners of war involved in a prisoner exchange, particularly since Lebanon does not hold Israelis in return.
 
Lebanese lawyer and MP Melhem Khalaf told Anadolu that when the conditions for prisoner-of-war status are met, a prisoner benefits from the protections provided to prisoners of war under the Third Geneva Convention, while civilian detainees in international armed conflicts are covered by the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Both conventions guarantee humane treatment, protection from torture and ill-treatment, medical care, communication with families and fair-trial safeguards.
Khalaf stressed that the release of a detainee does not extinguish their right to demand an investigation, accountability and reparations for any violations they may have suffered, and that describing a person as a “detainee” or “prisoner” does not legitimize their detention.
The prolonged detention of individuals without charges or trials is not limited to Lebanon.
Human rights organizations have documented the widespread repetition of this pattern against Palestinians from the Gaza Strip.
Israel uses the "Unlawful Combatants Law" of 2002 to detain individuals for renewable periods without indictments.
According to Amnesty International, the law was initially used to detain two Lebanese citizens before being widely applied to detainees from Gaza.
Razi’s release coincided with the incursion of an Israeli force into the southern Lebanese town of Halta on Thursday and the abduction of three people, according to the town’s mukhtar and a local source who spoke to Anadolu.
Since March 2, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed 4,350 people and injured 12,307 others, while displacing more than 1 million people, according to Lebanese authorities.

Bolt drivers in Lithuania protest low fares, ‘unfair’ tax distribution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:56:00 UTC
17:56:00 KST

Some Bolt drivers in Lithuania say falling fares and a tax system they consider unfair are making it increasingly difficult to earn a living, with drivers planning a protest in Vilnius next week.
The drivers plan to hold a demonstration called “Last Trousers” on September 10. The name of the action plays on the Lithuanian expression about taxes and fees forcing one to give up one’s “last trousers”.
The dispute has also affected passengers. One Vilnius resident told LRT that a Bolt driver recently asked him to pay extra because the trip was not financially worthwhile for the driver. When he refused, the passenger was asked to leave the vehicle before reaching his destination.
Vitalis Zigmantas, a longtime Bolt driver, said fares were suddenly reduced in early August.
He said drivers can be left with little profit on longer trips after fuel and other costs. For example, a 10-kilometre trip paying about 4.50 euros could leave a driver with roughly 1.50 euros after basic vehicle costs, he said.
Laimonas Jakštys, Bolt’s head of ride-hailing operations, acknowledged that the company had heard of cases in which drivers asked passengers to cancel rides or pay additional money.
“Any request by a driver for a passenger to cancel a trip or pay extra violates Bolt’s terms,” Jakštys said, urging passengers to report such incidents.
He said fares depend on both the price of individual trips and the number of orders drivers receive. Lower demand at the end of summer can affect prices, while demand typically rises in the autumn, he said.
Drivers are also challenging Bolt’s tax arrangements. Zigmantas said drivers sign contracts with an Estonian company rather than a Lithuanian entity, meaning they are responsible for reverse-charge VAT on Bolt’s commission.
He accused the arrangement of shifting an unfair share of the tax burden onto drivers and said protesters plan to bring a pair of trousers to the parliament, Seimas, as a symbol of their grievances.
Bolt said the arrangement is legal and complies with Lithuanian and European Union tax rules. The company said reverse-charge VAT applies only to its commission, which ranges from 10% to 25% depending on the city, and is paid into Lithuania’s budget.
“We are constantly looking for solutions that benefit passengers, drivers and us as a platform,” Jakštys insisted, adding that Bolt regularly reviews its pricing.
Ignas Jonikas, coordinator of the Lithuanian Platform Workers Union, said platforms should not be allowed to unilaterally determine drivers’ rates.
He called for written service or employment contracts specifying compensation and payment terms, as well as clearer information about the number of platform workers and their earnings.
Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said the issues surrounding Bolt go beyond taxation and require a broader response.
“We should solve these problems comprehensively, rather than addressing only one issue, such as taxes,” Valys said.
He said authorities were aware of broader social problems involving platform workers and that the government was looking for comprehensive solutions.
The planned “Last Trousers” protest is scheduled for September 10.

Chinese radios power Russia’s longer-range drone strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:55:24 UTC
17:55:24 KST

- Russia has extended live drone operator control to 150-175 kilometers using Chinese-made mesh radios, roughly double its 2025 range, according to KI Insights.
- The mesh network technology has let Russia redirect Geran-2 and Gerber drones toward mid-range strikes that have disabled over 250 Ukrainian gas stations.
Russian forces have significantly extended how far they can fly and control attack drones inside Ukraine over the past year by switching many of them to mesh-network radios, according to a report from Kyiv-based analytics firm KI Insights.
The technology, called MIMO mesh radio, lets a drone act as a mobile relay point in a decentralized radio network rather than depending on a single, direct radio link back to its operator. Since 2025, Russia has fitted the system to several of its drone types, including the Geran and Gerbera strike drones, the Orlan and Supercam reconnaissance drones, and the Lancet, Scalpel and Molniya models, according to the report, authored by Etienne Hertz, a radio-frequency specialist based in Ukraine.
Ukrainian military sources told KI Insights that a chain of mesh-linked drones can now maintain live operator control up to 150 to 175 kilometers (93 to 109 miles) from the farthest Russian ground station, roughly double what Russian mesh networks could manage in 2025. Russian pilots have demonstrated real-time control over Geran and Gerbera drones flying near the city of Dnipro, about 100 kilometers (62 miles) from the front line, the report said.
On July 17, a Geran drone operated by Russia’s 50th Separate Operational Brigade of Unmanned Systems Forces, known as Varyag, struck a gas condensate plant near Seleshchyna in Ukraine’s Poltava region while flying 125 kilometers (78 miles) from Russian-held territory and maintaining direct operator control the entire time, according to the report. KI Insights said Varyag has increasingly struck targets in Ukraine’s Sumy and Chernihiv regions rather than its earlier focus further south, a shift the firm said could signal Russian preparation to intensify operations along a northern front.
The mesh radios enabling this reach are not Russian-made. KI Insights traced the hardware to two Chinese manufacturers, Shenzhen Sinosun Technology and Shenzhen Xingkai Technology, with a Saint Petersburg-based company called Ajax Technologies distributing some of the radios inside Russia. The report said Russia remains fully dependent on Chinese components for the underlying mesh radio hardware, even if Russian engineers have contributed to how the systems are integrated into drones.
Mesh radios cost considerably more than the alternative many drone operators use, SpaceX’s Starlink satellite terminals, which run slightly above $400. Russia’s Chinese-made mesh modems cost between $2,000 and $12,000, and their range drops off sharply beyond 100 to 200 kilometers, unlike Starlink’s near-global coverage. Mesh links also carry higher latency, or delay, than Starlink, making them less useful against fast-moving targets, according to the report. Bureau 1440, a Russian satellite company, is expected to extend Russian drone operator range further later this year through a new satellite constellation called Rassvet, KI Insights said.
The report highlighted one specific case: Russian forces in the Zaporizhzhia area have converted the low-cost Molniya 2R drone, which normally costs $800 to $1,200, into an airborne mesh relay node by adding cameras, onboard computer-vision processors and a mesh radio, raising its cost to an estimated $4,000 to $5,000. Because the modified Molniya can both process its own sensor data and forward signals from other drones dozens of kilometers away, it lets Russian forces maintain aerial relay coverage cheaply and repeatedly, without relying on more expensive, harder-to-replace drones like the Orlan.
KI Insights said the range and video quality this technology provides has helped Russia shift many of its piston-engine Geran-2 and Gerber drones away from long-range strikes deep into Ukraine, where Ukrainian air defenses intercept 90 to 95% of incoming drones, and toward mid-range attacks on stationary infrastructure such as passenger trains and gas stations. The firm said this campaign has disabled or damaged more than 250 gas stations across northeastern, eastern, central and southern Ukraine.
KI Insights assessed that Russia’s mesh-drone capability is moving toward technological parity with NATO drone fleets and could pose risks to NATO logistics in a future conflict involving Russia or Belarus, though the firm noted Russian video links still carry higher latency than NATO systems typically tolerate. The report did not specify a timeline for when Russian capabilities might reach that level, or how Ukraine’s own electronic warfare units plan to counter the expanding mesh networks.

Swiss soil underpants study win Ig Nobel Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:51:36 UTC
17:51:36 KST

Swiss soil underpants study win Ig Nobel Prize
A Swiss research project to test soil quality with buried underpants has been awarded an Ig Nobel Prize for entertaining, yet serious, science.
More than a thousand people from all over Switzerland took part in the ‘Underpants as Evidence’ project. Gardeners and farmers buried two standard cotton pairs of underpants in their soil for the experiment.
The research was conducted by the University of Zurich and the Agroscope research institute.
More
Why Swiss kids are burying their underwear
The decomposition of the cotton fabric served as an indicator of soil activity. The principle is remarkably simple: the faster the underpants disappear, the more life there is in the soil. Bacteria, fungi, earthworms and all sorts of other creatures feast on the cotton. A paradise for soil organisms.
“The aim was to make people aware of how important the soil is,” Marcel van der Heijden from the University of Zurich told the Keystone-SDA news agency.
+ US travel visas concerns force Swiss relocation of Ig Nobels ceremony
In theory, the same results could have been achieved using cotton T-shirts. But public interest would probably have been lower.
Health of Swiss soil
The project has now been awarded the Ig Nobel Prize – an award that honours research which first makes people laugh and then makes them think. “A great honour,” the researchers said.
The underpants also yielded some very important results. They showed that organic soils make conventional fields look rather outdated when it comes to the decomposition of underpants.
Whilst the cotton was heavily nibbled away in organically farmed fields, significantly more fabric remained on some conventional plots. The soils in gardens and meadows proved to be particularly vibrant.
The research data is to be incorporated into a map that will, in future, show how healthy Switzerland’s soils are.

France gives farmers €1 billion to recover from record heatwaves
PARIS, Sept 4 - France on Friday announced more than €1 billion ($1.16 billion) in aid for farmers after this summer's record heatwaves and droughts devastated crops, pastures and water supplies.
The support comes as the government is working on a politically perilous budget for next year, with Paris seeking to keep the deficit under control ahead of a 2027 presidential election.
"One billion euros represents a massive effort given the current budgetary context," Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard told reporters.
About half of the package — €520 million — will be sent out as rapid payments to help farmers deal with weather damage, she said.
France's main farmers' union, the FNSEA, said farmers had already suffered at least €10 billion of lost production. The livestock and arable sectors have already estimated their losses at more than €5 billion each.
"The immediate goal is to manage the emergency," Genevard said.
About 30,000 to 35,000 farms were in financial trouble, she said.
The aid plan also creates a €235 million recovery fund to help farms buy seeds, plant and animal feed after droughts left farmland parched. Further measures include land-tax relief, help with social-security payments and a fuel subsidy.
The finance ministry has said this summer's dry and hot weather could shave 0.1 percentage points off France's economic growth this year, mainly due to lost farming revenue.
Another heatwave is expected this week in the European Union's largest agricultural producer. REUTERS

Russian criticism of Finnish President Alexander Stubb reaching new levels, expert says
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:50:06 EEST
17:50:06 KST

Finnish President Alexander Stubb has come under unusually harsh criticism in Russia, with Russian state media and senior officials repeatedly attacking him in recent weeks.
Russian outlets and officials have criticised Stubb in the past, but the tone has now escalated significantly, according to Arkady Moshes, programme director of the Russia, Eastern Europe and Eurasia Research Programme at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.
"Virtually no other Western leader has been insulted as much as Stubb. This exceeds all norms of civilised behaviour," Moshes says.
The criticism intensified after Stubb joined several other European leaders in Kyiv on August 24 to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day. During the visit, he expressed support for Ukrainian attacks on Russian logistics centers.
Russian TV insults Stubb
One of Russia's most popular current affairs programmes claimed on Sunday that the Finnish President's actions have given rise to a new Russian expression, meaning "dumb as Stubb".
Vladimir Chernyshov, host of NTV’s Itogi nedeli programme, also commented on Stubb's appearance, comparing the Finnish president to a character from a 1990s American comedy.
On Rossiya-1, another major state television channel, the presenter claimed that Stubb was seeking territory from Russia.
"Dreams of a Greater Finland reaching the Urals seem to still be alive in Stubb," the Vesti nedeli programme claimed.
Russia has long used state media to portray Finland negatively and rewrite the history of the Winter War. Last year, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov described Finland as one of Adolf Hitler’s most loyal allies.
In a Sunday broadcast, REN TV described Stubb’s comments on Ukrainian attacks on Russian logistics centres as "bloodthirsty".
According to the channel, Stubb’s claim that such attacks make military strategic sense was "no longer even madness or psychopathy, but terrorism".
Russian officials join attacks
Senior Russian officials have also targeted Stubb personally.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, said in an interview last week that Stubb had "degenerated as a statesman, politician and human being".
Former President and current Deputy Chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev called Stubb a "real idiot" and a "moral monster" in a social media post.
Medvedev also accused Stubb and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham of betraying their voters by suggesting that Russia could be defeated.
Stubb has consistently supported Ukraine’s military efforts while also calling for dialogue with Russia.
In an interview with German newspaper Bild published on Saturday, he said Europe should seek to restart political dialogue with Moscow.
"I believe that someone in Europe needs to restart the dialogue with Russia so that we understand what is happening there. We need to talk to each other on a political level," Stubb said.
Finland has become a "traitor" to Putin
According to Moshes, the attacks are partly rooted in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s personal view of Stubb.
Moshes says Putin divides people into three categories: friends, enemies and traitors.
"He may still respect his enemies, but he hates traitors," Moshes says, noting that Putin’s hostility towards Stubb was fuelled by a comment the Finnish president made during his presidential campaign, when he said he would not answer the phone if Putin called.
Moshes describes the remark as a "major diplomatic mistake".
He also argues that Finland’s decision to join Nato has contributed to Putin viewing the country as a "traitor".
Despite the increasingly aggressive rhetoric, Moshes says there is no reason for Finland to panic.
"Finland needs to be vigilant. The worst possible reaction would be to behave as if Finland were at war with Russia," he says.
Moshes points to Finland’s military deterrence, including its strong national defence capabilities and NATO membership, as factors that Russia must take seriously.

Ukraine says it struck a Bastion in Crimea, the launcher Russia pairs Zircon and Oniks missiles on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:46:44 UTC
17:46:44 KST

On 4 September, Ukraine's military intelligence agency HUR published drone footage of an August operation against a Russian coastal missile launcher in occupied Crimea, it said on Telegram. Its special unit Group 13 struck the launcher and hit fuel trucks and a command vehicle on the peninsula in the same operation.
What HUR says its operators hit
The target was a Bastion, the carrier of Zircon and Oniks missiles. Russia uses those missiles for terrorist strikes against Ukraine, HUR said.
Group 13 operators destroyed and struck two fuel trucks and a command-and-staff vehicle belonging to Russian forces, the agency said. It placed the work in August 2026 without giving a date or a place on the peninsula.
The footage shows the view from drone cameras closing on the targets. HUR did not say what kind of drones its operators used, and the unit works with both aerial and naval systems, including naval drones rigged to carry FPV drones.
Designated 3K55, the system defends a shoreline and hits both surface and ground targets, warships among them. It takes up to five minutes to deploy, fires supersonic P-800 Oniks and hypersonic Zircon missiles, and reaches from 300 to 600 km depending on the missile and the mode of use. It doubles as an air defense asset, tracking up to 50 objects along the horizon at up to 250 km with passive radar and 450 km with active radar. Russia has fielded it since 2010 and builds it in a mobile version and a silo-based one.
Other Ukrainian services have hit Bastions before
Ukraine's Navy said its forces struck a Bastion's launch positions and deployment site on the peninsula overnight on 16 August, without naming a unit. Ukrainian forces hit a Bastion launcher in the occupied village of Aktachi in March, and in February they struck the concentration area of the Russian brigade that operates the system in Crimea.
In an operation earlier in the summer, one of Group 13's uncrewed boats launched attack drones at two Russian radars in occupied Crimea without the vessel ever reaching shore.
Strikes on the peninsula continued overnight
Drone attacks on occupied Crimea have been running for weeks, and they continued into 4 September, though what was hit this time is not yet known.
Explosions sounded in Sevastopol and Dzhankoi district, Suspilne reported. Monitoring channels logged blasts and drone flights past 04:00, and satellite imagery showed a fire west of the airfield at Hvardiiske, with the cause unconfirmed. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed 490 drones downed over Crimea, other occupied territories, and Russian regions.

NERDs: The Gen Zers who believe they will never be able to retire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:43:49 UTC
17:43:49 KST

An increasing number of Gen Zers have stopped believing in pensions and are convinced they will never be able to stop working.
We have seen the FIRE (Financially Independent, Retire Early) believers, but we may now be seeing a lot more NERDs: the Never Ever Retiring Demographic.
The term refers to a growing number of Gen Zers and millennials across the UK and Europe who feel they will never be able to retire and who, as a result, believe there is little point saving into a pension plan at all.
A recent study by People's Pension, a leading UK workplace pension provider, found that 47% of Gen Zers aged between 18 and 27 do not engage with their pension.
Despite having decades ahead of them, 12%, or 2.2 million young people, have already stopped saving for retirement altogether, believing they will have to work forever.
This shift stems mainly from the cost-of-living crisis affecting several parts of the world, which has made traditional life milestones such as buying a house, getting married, having children and retiring feel increasingly out of reach for many young people.
Stagnant wages and increasingly frequent rounds of surprise layoffs, particularly in sectors such as tech, have contributed to this instability, alongside geopolitical volatility fuelling inflation.
While socioeconomic and geopolitical factors have driven the rise of NERDs, another significant contributor has been a breakdown in how the financial services sector communicates with young people about these issues.
A widening divide
The survey results point to a stark divide between young people and the financial services sector, with 36% saying it does not properly communicate the advantages of saving for retirement.
Of these, 27% feel firms are mainly concerned with selling their products rather than education or raising awareness, while 16% take issue with the complicated language or jargon used.
Around 20% of these Gen Zers also said financial services providers often make pensions sound irrelevant and boring.
While only 13% of Gen Xers and Baby Boomers felt pension companies do not properly explain why pensions and savings matter for young people, 29% of Gen Zers felt this way.
Some 17% of Gen Zers also believed companies do not use the channels they actually engage with, compared with only 4% of previous generations.
Around 70% of Gen Zers said they would have saved if they had known that starting in their 20s could potentially double their retirement pot, compared with starting in their 30s.
Similarly, 63% said they were motivated by learning that tax relief and employer contributions could significantly boost their savings.
"In a world where financial doom dominates pension conversations, young savers are tuning out. Our research shows they are not disengaged because they don't care, they are disengaged because the messages aren't working. Scare tactics and jargon are alienating the very people we need to reach," said Kirsty Ross, proposition director at People's Pension, said in a release.
"What cuts through is honesty, simplicity and practical advice that shows how small steps today can have a huge impact tomorrow," she added.
What could help?
One of the most popular fixes Gen Zers identified was simple progress bars or goal trackers, cited by 31%.
Around 26% wanted to know they could start with a small amount, while 23% would like more examples of what people their age are doing.
For 22%, clear, bite-sized steps to follow would be useful, while for 19%, light-hearted, relatable stories would make a difference.
Taking this feedback into account, People's Pension has launched a new campaign, Pension Drop, to get more people talking about their pensions, using social media influencers, special events and lifestyle personalities.
"Looking back, I really wish I'd started earlier. Putting something away in your 20s or 30s can make a massive difference later, we're talking tens of thousands of pounds. And I get it, people are really struggling right now, money is tight, and even small luxuries like a takeaway can feel like a big deal," said Iain Stirling, comedian, TV presenter and Pension Drop ambassador, in comments released by People's Pension.
"But the reality is, your pension isn't all on you. Things like employer contributions and tax relief can give you a boost, so even small amounts go further than you think. It doesn't have to mean missing out today, just making smart moves so you don't miss out tomorrow," he added.
Stirling also advised young people to take a few practical steps, such as checking who their pension provider is and finding out if they have more than one.
He also emphasised the importance of matching what an employer is willing to contribute so as not to leave money on the table, as well as topping up pension contributions with every pay rise and every bonus.

Seatbelt sign off, hydraulic failure, pilot tests positive for psychoactive substance: What Air India Phuket probe found
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:43:33 UTC
17:43:33 KST

The finding relates to the Pilot-In-Command of the Air India flight that was operating from Phuket to Delhi on August 4. The aircraft suddenly lost around 300 feet in altitude while flying over Odisha, injuring 20 passengers and four cabin crew members.
NEW DELHI: A preliminary report by the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has provided a detailed account of the August 4 incident involving Air India flight AI-2379 from Phuket to Delhi.The report examines the pilots' post-flight medical tests, a series of hydraulic-system failures, the aircraft's sudden altitude upset, the response of the flight crew, injuries caused inside the cabin and damage to the aircraft.Here are the key points that are covered in the report.
Pilot's psycho-active substance test: Both pilots underwent post-flight medical checks after the aircraft landed in Delhi. Their breath analyser tests were satisfactory. However, a psycho-active substance detection test found the Pilot-In-Command's sample to be non-negative. His blood sample was subsequently sent for confirmatory testing, which was also found to be non-negative. The co-pilot tested negative in both tests.
What triggered the incident: The aircraft was cruising at FL360, or about 36,000 feet, when its flight-control system detected a loss of pressure in the green hydraulic system at 04:02:43 UTC. Four seconds later, it detected the loss of the blue and yellow hydraulic systems too.
Autopilot disengaged: At 04:02:48 UTC, the aircraft's autopilot disengaged, and a continuous repetitive chime sounded. Three seconds later, a stall warning was triggered for two seconds.
Aircraft suddenly moved away from its assigned altitude: The co-pilot, who was the pilot flying, initially responded to the situation. The pilot-in-command then took over the controls. During the altitude upset, the aircraft gained 372 feet and then fell 292 feet from its assigned FL360.
Hydraulic systems recovered: The blue hydraulic system recovered at around 04:02:52 UTC. The yellow and green systems recovered a few seconds later. The recovery restored the flight-control surfaces, and the aircraft returned to normal operating condition.
Why passengers were injured: The aircraft was cruising at FL360 when the altitude upset occurred and, crucially, the seat-belt signs were off. The sudden movement resulted in injuries to passengers and cabin crew. The cabin supervisor informed the cockpit about the injuries.
24 people needed medical attention: On landing in Delhi, the airport medical team treated 20 passengers and four cabin crew members. Twenty were discharged after initial treatment for minor injuries, while four people with serious injuries were hospitalised for further treatment.
Crew chose to continue to Delhi: After assessing the cabin situation, the flight crew decided not to divert to the nearest en-route airport and continued towards Delhi. They later requested medical priority from Delhi ATC. The aircraft landed safely at IGI Airport at 05:30 UTC.
Aircraft suffered cabin damage: The altitude upset also caused damage inside the aircraft. The report records cracked and deformed ceiling panels, dislocated passenger-service-unit panels, broken handrails, damaged emergency-exit hardware and dislodged overhead-bin doors. An overhead-bin divider was cracked, a lavatory commode was uprooted, a crew seat was bent, and panels around the rear crew-door area were severely damaged.
Hydraulic failure being investigated: The A320 has three hydraulic systems, known as green, blue and yellow. The systems provide hydraulic power to major aircraft systems. AAIB has removed relevant hydraulic components and collected hydraulic samples for further analysis.
Warnings recorded after the flight: The aircraft's post flight report recorded a sequence of warnings including "HYD GREEN SYS LO PR", followed by blue and yellow hydraulic warnings. It also recorded "AUTO FLT AP OFF" and an elevator fault.
Aircraft had an existing MEL item: Before departing Phuket, maintenance personnel found no discrepancies other than an already invoked minimum equipment list (MEL) item. The aircraft had been dispatched under MEL item 29-23-01A, relating to the power transfer unit (PTU), which had been invoked on July 28. The crew's walk-around inspection found no discrepancies.
No adverse weather reported: Despite the incident initially being notified as a turbulence encounter, the report says no adverse weather was reported by either the flight crew or ATC during the altitude upset.
Experienced pilot-in-command: The 34-year-old PIC held a valid ATPL and had 5,055 hours of total flying experience, all recorded on the aircraft type. He had flown the type on August 3, the day before the incident. His recorded rest period before the flight was 21 hours and 59 minutes.
Co-pilot was flying when the event began: The 32-year-old co-pilot held a valid CPL and had 1,393 hours of flying experience. The report identifies him as the pilot flying during the incident, while the PIC was the pilot monitoring before taking over the controls.
AAIB calls finding a serious concern: The report says, "The confirmation of use of psycho-active substance is a serious concern, and AAIB recommends appropriate actions by DGCA on priority." It separately recommends that the DGCA take appropriate measures to prevent abuse of psycho-active substances.
Flight recorders are being examined: Both the cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder were recovered. Their downloaded data is now with the investigation team for analysis.
Airbus experts examined the aircraft: Technical experts assigned by France's BEA, including Airbus experts, inspected the aircraft from August 13 to 15. Hydraulic components and samples were subsequently collected for testing.
AAIB says the detailed investigation into the technical and other aspects is still underway. Maintenance and operational records, fuel and oil samples, ATC data and flight-recorder information are among the material being examined.The preliminary report records both the hydraulic-system failures and the PIC's non-negative confirmatory psycho-active substance test, but it does not establish that the substance finding caused the altitude upset. AAIB says the investigation remains in progress and that a final report will be published later.

Frontloading EU loan not a 'silver bullet' for Ukraine, Chentsov says

2026-09-04

17:42:33 KST

Ukraine's Deputy PM Vsevolod Chentsov says frontloading the EU's €90bn loan is not a 'silver bullet' for Kyiv's budget gap, as it seeks help from non-EU partners too.
Frontloading parts of the EU support loan would not be a 'silver bullet' for Ukraine's budgetary needs, Deputy Prime Minister Vsevolod Chentsov said on the margins of a ministerial meeting on Friday.
"We are talking to both the EU and other partners to cover the gap, first of all for our defence needs this year, but also looking at the 2027 financial strategy," Ukraine's Deputy PM for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration told reporters.
The remarks come after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last month that Kyiv is facing a massive €23 billion funding gap, and asked Brussels to bring forward part of the €90 billion support loan, which is due to be delivered in equal instalments across 2026 and 2027.
"We are still working to understand how to cover it, where to get the money from, and what exactly we need for which areas. The EU is our main partner, and the €90 billion loan will help us a lot to cover both defence and civilian needs. Frontloading is probably one of the solutions, but it's not a silver bullet," Chentsov said.
He added that Kyiv first needs to reach out to partners outside the EU, since roughly a third of Ukraine's needs are expected to be covered by others.
Foreign ministers from Norway, the UK, Canada, Iceland and Switzerland joined their EU counterparts for an informal meeting in Ireland earlier this week, though no announcement was made on whether they would top up the EU's loan.
The EU has already disbursed €8.5 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan. Kyiv sent a new payment request earlier this week to reinforce the country's air defences amid a growing wave of Russian airborne attacks, including on the much-needed US-made Patriots.
EU officials have so far shown openness about frontloading parts of the funding that was expected to be disbursed next year earlier, but Brussels has also stressed that the financial plan remains sufficient for the moment.
Chentsov also said Kyiv had again raised the issue of Russia's €210 billion in frozen assets, "to use them in a smart way to generate money and cover the deficit."
Sweden, Poland, the Netherlands and Spain have also brought the issue back to the table last week, as Kyiv's budgetary crunch and the need to sort out Ukraine's financial support ahead of several elections next year made it all the more pressing.
However, Belgium's Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot has reiterated Belgium's opposition to the measure, which risks triggering litigation since most of the assets sit at the Belgian financial institution Euroclear.

Croatia set to buy South Korean Chunmoo rocket launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:42:23 UTC
17:42:23 KST

- Croatia's government is expected to approve buying 18 South Korean K239 Chunmoo rocket launchers for €435.2 million ($506 million) at a Friday cabinet session.
- The system includes rockets ranging from 30 to over 300 kilometers and would replace Croatia's aging Soviet-era Grad and Vulkan launchers by 2028.
Croatia’s government is set to approve the purchase of 18 South Korean K239 Chunmoo multiple rocket launchers for €435.2 million ($506 million), excluding tax, at a cabinet session Friday, Croatian newspaper Jutarnji List reported.
The deal would be Croatia’s largest weapons purchase since its 1990s war for independence, apart from its earlier order of Rafale fighter jets, according to the newspaper. The rockets involved would give Croatia’s military a strike range between 30 and 300-plus kilometers (19 and 186-plus miles), including ballistic rockets that exceed 300 km, intended to serve as a long-range deterrent. Jutarnji List reported that the number of rockets included in the contract has not been disclosed.
About 85% of the system is expected to arrive by 2028, an unusually fast delivery timeline for a major weapons contract. Once the government approves the purchase, Croatian Defense Minister Ivan Anušić is expected to sign the deal with South Korean manufacturer Hanwha Aerospace, along with a separate contract with Polish company WB Group to install a command-and-control system in the launcher vehicles. Payments would run from 2026 through 2029, according to the report.
The Chunmoo system, whose name translates roughly to “heavenly weapon,” would replace Croatia’s existing Soviet-designed Vulkan M92 and 122mm Grad BM-21 launchers. Those systems average more than 30 years old and reach only about 20 km, well short of what Croatian officials say the modern battlefield requires, the newspaper reported.
Croatian and South Korean defense officials began discussing the purchase roughly a year ago during a visit by Anušić to Seoul, according to Jutarnji List. Croatia had earlier signed an agreement with the United States at the end of 2024 for eight HIMARS launchers and 394 rockets with an 80 km range. But the U.S. has since paused exports of 300 km-range rockets to allies to meet its own military’s needs, and it bars foreign sales of the longer 500 km-range variant entirely, pushing Croatia toward South Korea for its extended-range strike capability.
Croatia would follow Poland, Norway and Estonia in ordering the Chunmoo system. Poland’s order covers 288 launchers and 23,000 rockets, along with a rocket factory to be built on Polish territory. Norway ordered 16 launchers and Estonia nine. Both Poland and Estonia also operate HIMARS but turned to Chunmoo for its longer-range rockets.
Hanwha built the Chunmoo to fire multiple rocket types from a single launcher at once, using two separate rocket pods that can each be loaded with a different caliber, without requiring any modification to the launcher itself. A crew can fire, for example, four 280mm rockets from one pod and six guided 239mm rockets from the other, depending on the mission. Loaded with Hanwha’s most powerful ballistic rocket, the 600mm CTM-290 with its 300-plus km range, each pod carries a single rocket. Firing time varies by caliber: the system can launch 12 guided 239mm rockets in under a minute, or around 40 smaller 131mm rockets in several dozen seconds. Three soldiers operate each launcher.
Compared with HIMARS, which fires up to six rockets from a single pod, the twin-pod Chunmoo carries roughly double the rockets per launcher, according to the report. The contract includes logistics support and six weeks of crew training. Operating all 18 launchers would require about 100 soldiers, the same number needed to crew Croatia’s HIMARS systems, Jutarnji List reported. Where the launchers will be based within the Croatian Army has not been disclosed.
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and President Zoran Milanović have both backed the purchase. Milanović alluded to the coming deal two months ago in Ankara following a NATO summit, saying Croatia needed to respond to neighboring Serbia’s acquisition of Israel’s PULS rocket system and its interest in long-range weapons, including China’s CM-400AKG supersonic missile. It remains unclear whether Serbia has obtained 300 km-range rockets for its PULS launchers.
After the rocket system purchase, Croatia still has two other major, and expensive, defense acquisitions pending: a medium-range air defense system estimated at €500 to 600 million ($581 to $697 million), and two corvettes expected to cost roughly €1 billion ($1.16 billion) combined. Jutarnji List reported that officials expect both deals to be finalized within the next year.

Why has the Philippines’ peso plunged to a record low?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:38:34 UTC
17:38:34 KST

Why has the Philippine peso plunged to a record low?
The Southeast Asian country’s currency has plummeted amid the fallout of the Iran war and economic challenges at home.
The Philippine’s peso is hovering at historic lows amid a confluence of economic challenges at home and geopolitical turmoil abroad.
On Friday, the currency hit an all-time low of 62.71 to the United States dollar.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Entertainment over policy? White House arcade games ignite backlash
- list 2 of 4Mladic’s body arrives to full military honours in Serbia
- list 3 of 4Arsenal sell Martinelli to Al-Hilal in post-transfer deadline day deal
- list 4 of 4Argentina’s Milei threatens sanctions over Falklands oil drilling
Here’s everything you need to know about the plunging value of the currency:
What has been happening with the peso?
The peso has been on a downward trajectory since the start of the year, losing about 6 percent of its value against the US dollar since January 1.
The currency has broken several records over the past few months amid rising oil prices and other negative headwinds from the US-Israel war on Iran.
The peso hit a record low of 61.847 to the US dollar on July 24, before falling further to 62.265 last Friday.
The peso has continued its slide this week, closing at 62.565 on Wednesday and sinking to 62.71 on Friday.
Why has the peso fallen so much?
The peso is responding to several negative trends in the Philippine economy and the strength of the US dollar.
Before the war, the Philippines imported almost all its oil from the Gulf. In March, Manila was forced to declare a state of national emergency when Iran’s shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted supplies.
As oil prices have risen, Philippine importers have had to convert more pesos for US dollars to buy dollar-priced crude, driving down the value of the local currency.
At the same time, rising yields of US Treasury Bonds – a type of loan to the US government – have encouraged international investors to trade the currencies of developing economies for safer dollar-dominated assets, pushing the peso lower.
The Philippines’ strained public finances and large trade deficit have exacerbated these downward pressures.
“The weakness in the Philippine peso stems largely from the large twin – fiscal and current account – deficits the economy is running, combined with the elevated inflation that the central bank, the BSP, is trying to tackle,” said Philip McNicholas, Asia sovereign strategist at Robeco Singapore.
“This has left the peso vulnerable to swings in global risk sentiment, which has soured in recent weeks as events in the Middle East have kept oil prices elevated,” McNicholas said.
What is the impact for the Philippines’ economy and Filipinos?
Currency depreciation is not inherently negative, but it typically benefits exporters at the expense of consumers.
A weaker currency means firms can sell their products overseas more cheaply, but also that households pay more for imported goods.
“It can improve competitiveness, support tourism and increase the local-currency value of foreign income,” said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management in Tokyo.
“The problem arises when depreciation becomes too rapid, particularly for energy-importing economies, because it raises import costs and fuels inflation,” Loo said.
The Philippines’ inflation rate stood at 6.1 percent in August, well above regional peers and double the central bank’s target of about 3 percent.
Ashwin Binwani, founder of Alpha Binwani Capital, a private closed-end joint venture fund in Singapore, said the peso could sink past 63.00 to the dollar if oil stays above $90 a barrel.
“The damage becomes materially worse if the currency weakness persists alongside high oil prices and above-target inflation rather than reversing quickly,” Binwani said.
“The peso’s fall does not instantly raise the price of every item in a supermarket. The main transmission is through imported inputs and energy.”
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr’s administration has pledged to improve fiscal discipline and said it expects the central bank to intervene as necessary to stabilise the currency.
One bright spot for the Philippines is the large amount of remittances it receives from the more than two million Filipinos working overseas.
Filipinos sent home a record $35.63bn last year, much of it in dollars, according to the country’s central bank.
“Remittances, which account for roughly 8 to 9 percent of GDP, provide a powerful stabiliser for the peso and help cushion external shocks. However, they are not a complete shield,” Loo said.
Binwani said the peso’s fall will place a significant but “uneven” strain on households.
“It raises the peso cost of essentials that depend on imports – especially fuel, transport, food inputs, and manufactured goods – while offering a partial cushion to families receiving overseas remittances,” he said.

Volkswagen to cut 50,000 more jobs worldwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:38:23 UTC
17:38:23 KST

Volkswagen’s supervisory board unanimously approved a plan on Thursday to cut a further 50,000 jobs worldwide as part of a major restructuring programme through to 2030. The reduction is additional to programmes already running.
Since the end of 2024, Volkswagen had already agreed to reduce its workforce by about 50,000 by the end of the decade. Together, the two rounds would bring planned job cuts to about 100,000.
Chief Executive Oliver Blume called the vote in Wolfsburg “a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group,” saying Future Plan 2030 is “the most strategically profound transformation programme in the Volkswagen Group’s history.”
“We are taking responsibility for our entire workforce, for our partners and for industrial jobs worldwide,” Blume said.
“Over the coming years, we will invest a three-figure billion sum to make our iconic brands even more attractive, stronger and more competitive,” he added.
The company said intensifying global competition, shifting demand and technological change make it essential to align the workforce with “economic reality.”
According to the analysis behind the plan, a further group-wide adjustment of about 50,000 positions, including management jobs, will be necessary beyond existing programmes.
The company employs about 663,000 people worldwide.
Volkswagen said it is targeting annual sales of nine million vehicles, about one million fewer than recent volume plans and three million fewer than before the coronavirus pandemic.
By 2035, the group plans to cut its model portfolio by about 50 percent and reduce product complexity by about 75 percent.
The company said the remaining models should stand out in design and technology while benefiting from higher volumes and lower costs per vehicle.
The board said Volkswagen Group’s European production capacity currently exceeds demand by more than 500,000 vehicles.
It said competitive future production allocations cannot currently be secured for plants in Emden, Zwickau and Hanover, as well as Audi’s site in Neckarsulm, on a staggered basis from 2031 to 2034.
Alternative uses for the four sites are being studied, according to the company.
Volkswagen said a concept for a sustainable and competitive production structure for its European plants is expected to be developed by the end of June 2027.

SWISS cancelled 125 flights during severe storm
A severe storm on August 28 resulted in Swiss International Air Lines cancelling 125 flights.
This affected a total of 15,572 passengers, as a SWISS spokesperson told the AWP news agency. “This figure includes not only flights that were cancelled on Friday itself, but also later flights that we had to cancel as a result of the storm and the resulting disruptions to our flight operations.”
More
When Switzerland launched rockets to fight hail
Such an event quickly leads to a huge “domino effect” in flight operations, said the spokesperson. “If we have to cancel a flight, the aircraft and its crew are no longer where they are needed for the next scheduled flight. At the same time, we have to organise new connections for the passengers affected.”
Furthermore, due to the sometimes significant delays, numerous connecting flights were missed. All of this, in turn, affects further flights and passengers and can have a knock-on effect across the entire flight schedule for several days.
+ How Switzerland is trying to defeat extreme weather events
Teams at the operations centre worked through the night to organise the best possible alternatives for passengers and to stabilise flight operations. “Given the scale of the situation, this was an exceptional situation for us too,” said the spokesperson.
SWISS will cover the resulting support costs for the affected passengers. “Depending on the situation, this includes the cost of a hotel stay, transport to and from the hotel, and meals until the next available connecting flight,” said the spokesperson.
SWISS had already been severely affected by a storm over Zurich airport at the end of June. At the time, the thunderstorm raged over Switzerland’s largest airport for 2.5 hours, leading to operational disruptions.
As a result, 26 aircraft had to divert to other airports. In total, over 10,000 passengers were affected by the thunderstorm on June 30.

Thousands of Lebanese students still displaced by war as school year nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:36:35 UTC
17:36:35 KST

Thousands of Lebanese students still displaced by war as school year nears
TYRE, Lebanon, Sept 4 - The schoolyard in southern Lebanon echoed with the squeals of playing children despite the beating sun and distant booms of Israeli airstrikes. But for most of the youth there, the public school isn't where they learn. It's where they live.
Thousands of children remain displaced from their hometowns in Lebanon's south six months after a new war erupted between Israel's military and armed group Hezbollah. Many still live in schools-turned-shelters, while others are squeezed into rented apartments with their extended families.
As schools gear up for a new academic year beginning on September 15, families who sought shelter in public schools are wondering where they will go — and how their children can pick up schooling amid so much uncertainty.
Najah Ammar, a grandmother of four school-aged children, hails from the coastal village of Mansouri, but fled Israeli strikes to the public school in the city of Tyre, about 10 km (6 miles) north. About 200 other families now live in the school.
Ammar, 62, has two worries: where she'll live if the school reopens, and how her grandchildren can catch up after losing years of schooling during repeated conflicts between Israel and Hezbollah since 2023.
"They’ve been out of school for two years — the last war and this war. My son’s daughter, the poor girl is eight years old. She was a second year and she’s still a second year," said Ammar.
DISPLACED FEAR COSTS OF NEW SCHOOL YEAR
Since March 2, Israeli strikes have killed more than 4,300 people in Lebanon, including more than 250 children, and wounded another 12,000, including 1,000 children, according to Lebanon's health ministry.
At the fighting's peak, more than one million people — nearly a quarter of the population — were displaced. Most have returned home but more than 340,000 remain displaced, because their hometowns are destroyed or fall within territory occupied by Israel's military.
Rula al-Awad, a 27-year-old mother of two also displaced from Mansouri, said she lacked the education to help her daughter through online classes, but brings her pen and paper so she can at least keep writing.
Awad is staying in an apartment but brings her two children to the Tyre school to play and wants to enroll them for the new year. Yet she fears she won't be able to afford schoolbooks or uniforms.
"I hope we can look ahead to a future that is beautiful for the kids – then we can consider having hope, so that when we tell our kids that things are beautiful, they believe us instead of feeling that we're lying to them," she said.
Zeinab Moussa, 56, who lives in tents in the school hall with her sons and grandchildren, says the children can only snatch brief moments of happiness.
"An NGO will come, they play a little bit. The NGO goes away, they despise everything," she said. "I just wish that the children could live their childhoods. But there’s no childhood now."
DOZENS OF LEBANESE SCHOOLS DAMAGED, DESTROYED
Out of nearly 80 public schools still used as shelters as the school year approached, almost half have been emptied and will reopen as schools, Lebanon's education ministry told Reuters. About 30 will partially reopen while continuing to serve as shelters, leaving nine schools still fully used as shelters.
Another 50 Lebanese public schools have been destroyed or severely damaged in the war, and more than 200 others have suffered moderate or minor damage, the ministry said. The United Nations said the impact on schools would jeopardize the new school year for at least 100,000 children.
Last month, the Lebanese army said Israeli troops had blown up a public school and a kindergarten in the southern village of Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Reuters questions on the school.
Lebanon's Education Minister Rima Karami said this week she aimed to ensure as many students as possible from the south could continue their education, whether in their hometowns, if safe, or in displacement.
Save the Children, which is supporting the Tyre school, said only a durable ceasefire could resolve the crisis.
"Children we spoke to over the past few days know what the solution is. It's a political solution. There's no humanitarian solution here," said Danny Glenwright, president of Save the Children Canada. REUTERS

Tesla launches driverless Cybercab service in U.S. Austin
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

17:36:12 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- U.S. electric vehicle maker Tesla on Thursday launched its driverless Cybercab in Austin, Texas, where the vehicle has already begun offering limited ride-hailing services.
In a promotional video released on the day of the launch, Tesla CEO Elon Musk described the Cybercab as "the first car that is specifically built for unsupervised full self-driving."
According to Tesla, the Cybercab is a two-seat vehicle featuring butterfly doors and a large interactive touchscreen. A newly released rider guide shows that the vehicle has no steering wheel, accelerator pedal or brake pedal, relying on camera-based vision and sensors for fully autonomous driving.
For passenger safety, the vehicle is equipped with a stop button. Once pressed, the Cybercab initiates an immediate pull-over when it is safe to do so, and connects the passenger with Tesla Robotaxi Support.
The vehicle's rear trunk can accommodate two standard checked suitcases and two carry-on suitcases.
Tesla's updated webpage noted that the Cybercab is the newest addition to its Robotaxi fleet. When passengers request a ride through the Robotaxi app, the system dispatches either a Cybercab or a Model Y based on vehicle availability and the number of passengers.
Musk did not attend the launch event, Reuters reported, citing attendees.
Tesla executives said at the event that Cybercab rides would use dynamic pricing and promised "a first-class experience at coach price."
Tesla said prospective commercial buyers can submit applications for the Cybercab. However, the official price, delivery dates and a service expansion timeline remain unannounced.
Tesla has yet to disclose the exact number of Cybercabs currently in operation. Tesla had 420 autonomous vehicles registered in the state of Texas, including 45 Cybercabs, as of Wednesday evening.
The U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said Thursday that it is in contact with Tesla and is evaluating the situation.
Tesla first unveiled the Cybercab prototype in October 2024. Production began in 2026, followed by engineering tests of production vehicles on public roads in the second quarter. ■

Economic Watch: Inflation, fiscal risks pressure Europe's sovereign bond markets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:36:09 CST
17:36:09 KST

FRANKFURT, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Government borrowing costs across Europe have climbed to or near multi-decade highs, as persistent inflation concerns, expectations of higher interest rates and mounting worries over public debt weigh on sovereign bond markets.
These pressures, analysts warn, could keep long-term yields elevated, as fiscal strains and geopolitical risks reshape the outlook for Europe's bond markets.
A BROAD-BASED RISE
A global bond sell-off has pushed up borrowing costs across Europe amid concerns over inflation, fiscal deficits and rising public debt.
Germany's 10-year Bund yield climbed to 3.38 percent, its highest level since April 2011, while the two-year yield reached 2.99 percent, its highest since June 2024.
France's five-year and 10-year yields have both risen by around 60 basis points in just over two months, with the 10-year yield briefly exceeding 4.20 percent, its highest level since October 2008.
Italy's 10-year bond yield rose to 4.22 percent, its highest since November 2023, while the 30-year yield reached 4.94 percent.
Poland's benchmark 10-year yield also climbed back above 6 percent after trending higher since July.
Pressure has also spread to traditionally highly rated countries such as the Netherlands. The yield on 10-year Dutch government bonds rose to approximately 3.43 percent on Tuesday, its highest level since May 2011.
The broad-based rise in yields suggests that the pressure is no longer confined to countries with traditionally high debt burdens but has spread across much of Europe's sovereign bond market, according to notes on fixed income strategy from Allianz Global Investors.
FORCES DRIVING YIELDS HIGHER
The recent surge in European government bond yields has been driven partly by a broader global bond sell-off, as renewed increases in oil prices fuel fears of sticky inflation and interest rates remaining higher for longer.
Europe is particularly exposed to such external shocks, including wars, energy disruptions and pressure on critical supplies, which can raise inflation risks and prompt investors to demand higher returns on long-term bonds, according to Christian Odendahl, European economics editor at the British magazine The Economist.
These external inflation shocks are compounding pre-existing domestic challenges.
Kiran Ganesh, managing director and global head of investment communications at UBS Global Wealth Management, said higher energy prices were adding to upward pressure on yields already driven by fiscal concerns.
European governments are also borrowing more to fund defense, the energy transition and to cover the costs of aging populations. The European Central Bank (ECB) projects the eurozone government deficit to rise from 2.9 percent of GDP in 2025 to 3.7 percent in 2027, with debt approaching 90 percent of GDP by 2028.
Fiscal credibility is therefore playing a greater role in bond pricing. France's 10-year yield spread over German Bunds has widened to around 80 basis points (0.8 percent) amid doubts over its ability to rein in deficits. The Bank of France has warned that failing to reduce the deficit to 5 percent of GDP or below could increase the risk of further rating downgrades.
LONG-LASTING PRESSURES
Persistent fiscal deficits, geopolitical tensions and renewed energy shocks could keep European government bond yields elevated even after the latest sell-off subsides.
According to Michiel Tukker, rates strategist at ING, higher structural deficits combined with energy shocks from global conflicts are putting further upward pressure on real yields across Europe.
Frances Cheung, head of FX and rates strategy at OCBC, has also pointed to heightened inflation expectations as an important driver of the recent rise in European borrowing costs.
Higher bond yields could themselves become a significant constraint on the eurozone economy.
ING estimates that a 50-basis-point increase in bond yields could have a slightly greater impact on inflation and economic growth than an equivalent ECB rate hike, suggesting that financial markets are already delivering substantial monetary tightening.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING Research, said the ECB must therefore guard against an excessive tightening of financing conditions, particularly if borrowing costs diverge sharply among member states.
At the same time, the traditional risk gap between countries such as Germany and France, long viewed as safer borrowers, and countries such as Italy and Spain, historically seen as riskier, is becoming less clear.
Massimo Spagnol, fixed-income portfolio manager at Generali Asset Management, noted that stronger growth and more stable debt management in Italy and Spain have encouraged investors to focus more closely on countries' actual fiscal and economic fundamentals rather than past perceptions of risk. ■

More than 2,300 rescuers had been deployed. Multiple rounds of grid and blanket searches have been completed, covering a total area of about 1.59 million square meters.

"Through everyday encounters such as learning each other's language, chatting with classmates and simply spending time side-by-side, members of the post-2000 generation like us get to understand this shared history firsthand and carry forward the Paukphaw friendship," said Liu, an exchange student from Pu'er University, who is currently studying the Myanmar language at Yangon University of Foreign Languages.
The profound youth-driven inheritance of bilateral friendship was highlighted at the China-Myanmar Youth Exchange Event and China-Myanmar Media Tea Party for the third quarter of 2026, jointly hosted by the Chinese Embassy in Myanmar and Yangon University on Thursday.
Young participants stood to gain far more than improved language proficiency and enhanced career prospects. Experts at the event noted that China's advancing technological innovation and in-depth cultural exchange mechanisms have become pivotal platforms for Myanmar's younger generation to access practical development resources and innovative experiences.
Naing Swe Oo, senior advisory board member of the Myanmar Institute of Strategic and International Studies, pointed out that Chinese smart agriculture technologies and new energy solutions have become an indispensable strategic support for Myanmar's national modernization drive. He encouraged Myanmar youth to learn advanced technologies from China and promote their localized application.
Echoing the viewpoint, Thaung Htike, rector of Yangon University, said that national and international cooperation mechanisms, including Lancang-Mekong Cooperation programs, have continuously facilitated in-depth technological exchanges and practical cooperation between young people of the two countries.

By bringing together media workers from these countries, the event stands as one concrete symbol of China-sponsored solidarity among the Global South countries, she said.
"Paukphaw means relatives and we are relatives," Thaung Htike noted. "As kin, we understand and trust each other naturally. We are willing to share resources, deepen pragmatic cooperation, and empower younger generations to jointly drive the common development of both countries."
The event gathered around 300 attendees, including diplomatic officials from the Chinese Embassy in Myanmar and representatives from nearly 40 Chinese and Myanmar media organizations, think tanks and academic institutions. ■

Tanker captain arrested over cargo ship sinking off Istanbul

Tanker captain arrested over cargo ship sinking off Istanbul
Istanbul - The captain of an oil tanker that hit a cargo ship that sank in waters off Istanbul, leaving 10 missing, has been arrested along with his third officer, media reports said on Sept 4.
The pair were formally arrested by a court late on Sept 3, a day after the pre-dawn collision in which the ALSU, an empty oil tanker, struck the Tugberk Imamoglu, a cargo vessel carrying rolled steel, in the Sea of Marmara near Istanbul.
The case is being handled by prosecutors in Silivri on the western outskirts of Istanbul province.
According to the prosecutors’ statement, the Silvri court charged the pair with negligent homicide for failing to fulfil their navigational safety obligations and take the necessary measures to prevent the collision.
It said the captain, identified only as A.E., “failed to fulfil his duty of supervision and oversight of navigational safety” while the other suspect, M.E., “who served as the third captain and watch officer at the time of the incident, failed to take the necessary measures to prevent the collision in a timely and effective manner”.
The court ordered four other suspects be granted conditional release, it said.
Officials said the damaged cargo ship sank “very quickly” in waters about 900m deep, some 18 nautical miles off Silivri, leaving all 10 crew members missing.
Although rescuers have yet to recover the Tugberk Imamoglu’s voyage data recorder (VDR) – its “black box” – an expert report prepared for Silivri prosecutor’s said there had been multiple breaches of safety procedures aboard the tanker.
“The fundamental root cause... resulting in a catastrophe, was the deficiencies and failures on the bridge of the M/T ALSU,” the report said, a copy of which was seen by AFP on Sept 3.
It said an inexperienced third officer was at the helm and there was no lookout on duty, describing it as “serious negligence”.
“No helmsman or lookout was posted on the bridge and the officer, who had only recently joined the vessel and lacked experience, was left alone on watch,” the report said.
It also pointed to shortcomings on the part of the cargo ship.
Search and rescue operations continued on Sept 4.
Prosecutors have started legal proceedings against nine ALSU crew members, excluding the cook, six of whom had appeared in court on Sept 3. AFP

Ukraine is &quot;optimistic&quot; about new U.S. sanctions against Russia, but obstacles remain
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:34:38 EEST
17:34:38 KST

Ukraine is "optimistic" about new U.S. sanctions against Russia, but obstacles remain
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. Senate approved a bill on sanctions against Russia and Iran, but its consideration in the House of Representatives remains uncertain. Vlasiuk said there is broad bipartisan support for increasing pressure on Moscow.
Ukraine's Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk is optimistic about the prospects for the sweeping sanctions bill against Russia in the U.S. Congress, despite growing uncertainty over when the House of Representatives will consider it. UNN reports this, citing RFE/RL.
How the sanctions are progressing
Ukraine's top sanctions official spent this week in Washington, meeting with lawmakers and congressional staff amid hopes of advancing Lindsey Graham's 2026 Sanctions Against Russia and Iran Act.
The legislation was passed by the Senate on August 7 by an overwhelming majority (86-11), reflecting rare bipartisan agreement. The bill would give the U.S. president additional powers to impose "punitive" tariffs on countries that continue to buy Russian fossil fuels. It also contains provisions targeting Iran, which, according to Vlasiuk, cooperates closely with Moscow in the military-industrial sphere.
But the measure will face a more difficult path in the House of Representatives, where some Democrats have raised concerns about provisions that would give U.S. President Donald Trump additional authority to impose tariffs.
In addition, on September 3, Republican leaders announced that the final two weeks of the House session before the November midterm elections had been canceled, significantly shortening the full legislative calendar for September. House members are expected to leave Washington no later than September 17 and return no earlier than mid-November. The House will reconvene for another week of work after next week's Labor Day recess.
The compressed calendar has increased pressure on supporters of the sanctions legislation. Senior Republican aides said the bill remains a Republican priority, provided that Democrats "work it out." Democratic aides, responding to inquiries, expressed cautious optimism about the measure, while emphasizing uncertainty over whether Speaker Mike Johnson will bring it up for consideration.
"A good chance"
Vlasiuk said that during his visit to Washington, he held approximately 20 meetings with lawmakers and congressional staff, including discussions with members of both parties.
He said the Ukrainian delegation encountered broad support for increasing pressure on Russia, and that no lawmaker directly told him they would oppose the legislation.
Everyone agreed that pressure on Russia needed to be increased. No one said that they definitely would not support this bill
He described Ukraine as "quite optimistic" about the level of support for the legislation, particularly among Democrats.
One potentially important avenue could be for the House to consider the bill under a suspension of the rules - an expedited procedure typically used for bills expected to receive broad support. Vlasiuk said this was one of the realistic scenarios for advancing the bill.
I think there is a really good chance that this bill will be brought up for consideration
Vlasiuk had previously identified the week after next as Kyiv's preferred window for a vote in the House. Given the House's compressed calendar, this period could be one of the last opportunities for a vote before lawmakers leave Washington.
Asked whether momentum around the bill still existed, Vlasiuk pointed to what he characterized as continuing bipartisan support for Ukraine.
"There is a great deal of support for Ukraine on the Hill," he said, adding that Kyiv was emphasizing the urgency of passing the bill "very loudly." "At the same time, well, I mean, let's wait and see," Vlasiuk said.
Position on the tariff provisions
Vlasiuk defended the tariff provisions, arguing that they could make the sanctions significantly more effective. "This is a powerful tool that will make it possible to strengthen the effect of the sanctions," he said.
He argued that tariffs and sanctions may have a similar economic impact, but differ in how easily they can be circumvented.
"Sanctions can be adapted, sanctions can be circumvented. Tariffs cannot be adapted or circumvented," Vlasiuk said.
He also dismissed concerns that countries could be arbitrarily targeted by the bill, saying that the legislation establishes criteria based on purchases of Russian fossil fuels.
In particular, he pointed to China and India, which, as the publication writes, "Ukraine considers central to Russia’s continued ability to sell its energy exports."
Vlasiuk said the pressure could become a "huge blow" to Russia’s ability to finance its war against Ukraine.
Ukraine also supports including Iran in the bill, he said, referring to Tehran’s close military cooperation with Moscow.
"Everyone understands how close the cooperation is between the military-industrial complexes of these countries," Vlasiuk said. "Therefore, Iran fully deserves to be recognized as such," he added.
For Kyiv, as noted, the urgency is not merely legislative.
Vlasiuk warned that Ukraine will face another difficult winter after months of Russian missile and drone attacks. He said that 160 people had been killed in missile and drone attacks in recent months.
"We must increase pressure on Russia to force it to change its plans, to force it to truly negotiate," he said.
He argued that passing the sanctions bill now would have two consequences: it could ultimately increase economic pressure on Russia, while immediately sending a political signal both to Ukraine and to the Russian government.
According to him, there is an element of inertia in sanctions policy. Even after the legislation is passed, implementing the measures could take several days, while a significant impact on Russia’s economy could take weeks.
"But at the same time, the very fact of passing this sanctions bill," Vlasiuk said, would send a "strong signal of support to the Ukrainian people" and a "truly strong signal to the Russian government."
