hissy cooling jacket pairs CO₂ cartridges with technical apparel for extreme urban heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:05:30 UTC
15:05:30 KST

Hissy brings a cooling system into lightweight technical apparel
Hissy is a wearable cooling system developed for increasingly high urban temperatures. The garment uses a dedicated CO₂ cartridge in place of the heavy batteries and fan-based ventilation commonly found in portable cooling devices. Once the cartridge is docked, high-pressure liquid carbon dioxide vaporizes within the system, absorbing surrounding heat and producing a cooling airflow of approximately -30°C.
The concept responds to the limitations of conventional cooling technologies in extreme heat. As global temperatures rise and summer outdoor activities become increasingly affected by heat, portable fans become less effective at temperatures above 35°C. Battery-powered cooling devices also become heavier and less efficient, while exposure to high temperatures can further affect battery performance and safety. Hissy addresses these constraints through a lightweight garment-based system that integrates the cooling hardware directly into the apparel.
The garment is organized around an internal tubular Air Path that distributes cooling through the body of the garment. Its pattern and construction are determined by the route of this internal system, with the fabric cut and sewn to accommodate the tubing. The Air Path follows an ergonomic spiral based on the natural curves of the body, helping prevent bending or kinking that could obstruct the high-pressure cooling spray. Micro-perforations along the Air Path direct the airflow toward the body’s major heat-generating areas. Their dimensions and distribution were established through thermal mapping and heat-distribution experiments, allowing the cooling pressure to remain consistent from the hardware connector through to the end of the tube. This localized distribution avoids dispersing airflow indiscriminately while supporting controlled thermal comfort.
Hissy system extends from cooling apparel To lifestyle products
The CO₂ cartridge is integrated into the sleeve through a magnetic docking structure. Instead of screw threads, the system uses magnetic attraction to draw the cartridge into position, where locking protrusions engage with the internal hardware. The connection prevents vertical extraction and keeps the cartridge secured against the recoil generated by the high-pressure cooling spray. Removal follows the same magnetic mechanism. A slight rotation switches the poles of the internal dual-magnetized structure to repulsion. A groove within the hardware guides the cartridge through the required release angle, allowing the empty cartridge to be removed with a simple twist.
Additional details address the garment’s use during outdoor activity. An internal strap and external sleeve zipper secure the hardware according to the wearer’s wrist size and limit movement during use. A dedicated chest pocket provides storage for spare cartridges, keeping replacements accessible while maintaining the garment’s integrated appearance. The cooling system designed by Dongheon Kang, Minseo Jung, Yuha Ko, Juhyeon Jeon, and Woohi Park for Samsung Design Membershipalso incorporates a circular approach to CO₂ use. The carbon dioxide is captured from industrial processes that would otherwise release it into the atmosphere and repurposed as the cooling medium. After use, the cartridges are collected, inspected, refilled, and recirculated. The system is designed to keep both the products and the CO₂ resource in circulation without adding net carbon to the atmosphere.
Hissy’s apparel features a function-driven design, cut and sewn to mirror the optimal path of the cooling airflow
Hissy is conceived as a broader cooling platform beyond the initial garment. Its proposed expansion is structured across three phases. The first extends the CO₂ cooling technology to other wearable formats, including footwear, to distribute thermal management across the body. The second applies the system to lifestyle products such as outdoor can coolers for keeping food and beverages cold. The third moves into industrial applications, positioning the technology as a B2B thermal-management system for machines operating in high-temperature outdoor environments, including delivery robots and drones.
Through this approach, Hissy combines wearable design, airflow engineering, material construction, magnetic interaction, and CO₂ recirculation into a cooling system intended to operate across personal, lifestyle, and industrial applications.

“There is no such thing as a ‘sense of humor’ in the Criminal Code”: Russian stand-up comedians on surviving war and censorship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:03:55 UTC
15:03:55 KST

Russian stand-up comedy has changed dramatically over the past four and a half years of full-scale war. In early 2026, a Russian court sentenced comedian Artemy Ostanin to five years and nine months in prison for a joke about a legless Jesus. Within the stand-up community, the case was seen as a warning: anything said onstage can lead to very real trouble. Venues now ask performers in advance to keep their shows “apolitical,” while comedians themselves remove potentially risky material from acts or hide it behind hints and innuendo. Some comedians left Russia during the mobilization but later returned after finding that they could not afford to remain in exile. The Insider spoke to stand-up comedians who live and perform in Russia. They described what can be joked about today, how fear and self-censorship have changed the scene, and why even audiences are no longer always interested in political humor.
- 1.“Relax. I’ll go to prison, and you’ll be fine.” Stand-up comedian Viktor P.
- 2.“The audience has no idea how many jokes never make it to them.” Stand-up comedian Mikhail Z.
- 3.“Professional comedians are already consulting lawyers.” Stand-up comedian Alexei B.
- 4.“It’s making everyone a little paranoid.” Stand-up comedian Pavel V.
“Relax. I’ll go to prison, and you’ll be fine.” Stand-up comedian Viktor P.
Recently, I hosted a show at a popular bar in central Moscow. The organizers immediately asked us not to do anything political. There used to be times when someone would shout “Russia!” or start singing the national anthem or “Mother Earth” — none of that is allowed now, either.
And this is a bar in central Moscow, where young, modern people go — as modern as people can be these days. There is undoubtedly a demand for something political. You can give a little wink here and there. The kind of wink Ivan Urgant used to give — that’s about as far as you can go now.
For example, at one point my partner says, “I can’t talk about this.” And I say, “The only things we can talk about here are this or apples. Nothing else.” The audience understands that we’re talking about the party, and there’s an immediate, strong reaction. So you flash something for half a second — and that’s it.
There is an internal censorship among bar owners, comedians themselves, and stand-up club owners. The case of Artemy [Ostanin] shows how quickly things can escalate. Even if you didn’t mean anything by it, even if you hardly said anything at all, it’s still better to keep that in mind.
My audience is pretty modern and understands everything. But you still think: someone might record it, send it to someone, and then some activist could pick it up and make a big deal out of it.
I don’t think I’m important enough for anyone to want to put me in prison. But the news scares me — stories about completely unknown people being jailed for something, sometimes just for a repost. And you don’t always even understand what exactly the person did. It’s the same with performing onstage: you think not only about what you said, but also about how it might spread. Like with Nurlan Saburov: someone records something, and then it starts taking on a life of its own, separate from you. So you just become more careful.
The story of Artemy Ostanin, of course, shocked and deeply affected many of my friends and the stand-up community as a whole. When the whole avalanche was just beginning, many people told him to leave. But he treated what was happening as some kind of joke. Then he and his girlfriend tried to leave through Belarus, and they were eventually detained.
In the past, when something happened to comedians, the community reacted differently. Take Idrak Mirzalizade or Sasha Dolgopolov, for example. I clearly remember that when Idrak was having problems, we could end a show by saying, “Idrak is innocent,” or “Idrak should be free.” And we weren’t the only ones doing it. But when it happened to Artemy, nobody spoke out because they were scared. After that, venues became especially insistent: nothing about the “special military operation,” nothing about the war.
But, again, there is still a demand for it. And whenever I feel I can, I try to give a little wink. Sometimes, on the contrary, I take the position that everything is fine. For example, I see that people in the audience have understood, and I say, “America is complete garbage.” Everyone knows it’s post-irony. But technically, those are the words I said. As far as I know, the Criminal Code has no concept of a “sense of humor.”
Sometimes, though, the audience gets tense when political subjects come up. They’ve come to relax, to hear awkward stories about sex or the subway. I even say from time to time, “Relax. I’ll go to prison. You’ll be fine.” I’m not a political comedian. What matters to me is that people have fun.
Once, after a show, a couple of guys came up to me. They said, “That was great, we really loved it. Can we take a photo with you now and send it to a friend? He’s serving at the front right now.” What am I supposed to say to them? Of course, sure. I don’t want to get into a confrontation with them. I don’t want to try to change anyone’s mind or get into a political argument at a stand-up show. I don’t see myself as someone who can do that, and I don’t think it’s my job anyway. At the same time, I’ve been to protests. I was detained. I later emigrated, but I came back. You need money to live in exile, and I’m not a wealthy person.
There are, of course, comedians who describe their stand-up as political. Some joke about sanctions and liberals, perform in Donetsk, and so on. There’s one comedian, for example, who likes to call Vladimir Vladimirovich [Putin] “Uncle Vova” onstage and say, “I’ve got some political material.”
I keep an eye on comedians who have left, but at this point it’s really a matter of taste. I like what Idrak Mirzalizade does, and I like the club they run in Poland. I hardly watch Denis Chuzhoy, for example. Sometimes I feel that some comedians abroad lean too heavily into this “holier-than-thou” attitude. I accept that the problem may be with me. Maybe I just don’t want to admit that I’m also part of what’s happening because I’m still here. They chose to leave, and I didn’t. Well, I did, but then I came back. And when people tell me all this from abroad, sometimes I just don’t find it funny.
Sometimes I feel that some comedians abroad lean too heavily into this “holier-than-thou” attitude
I don’t watch comedians who joke about people who left or about emigration. I don’t even want to make myself angry over this propaganda. I have enough anxiety of my own. I don’t have the energy to sit around hating someone. I have to think about how I’m going to pay the rent.
These days I keep thinking about Ivan Urgant. His first appearance after Evening Urgant was canceled was a broadcast with Ayaz Shabutdinov. Ivan was talking to him about his business and creative work, and they were doing a presentation. The presentation had some blue-and-yellow charts. Ivan said, “Interesting choice of colors by whoever made this presentation.” Or there would be a shot of Dmitry Nazarov — and we know where he stands. Just very subtle things like that. But who finds that funny? I don’t know. It’s not really something for a mass audience anymore.
Do I feel hopeless? No. Probably because I simply don’t want to. I try to stay positive. I didn’t choose the time I was born into. And I still want to be happy. But I guess I’ve stopped expecting hot water to be a given. I’m just trying not to lose heart.
Of course, everything that’s happening gets me down. Sometimes I feel completely drained because I don’t know what else I can do or say. Maybe the only thing I can do is help the audience let off a little steam when I go onstage.
Yes, I don’t have the money to emigrate. But I actually like living in Russia. I’d like to be able to live here and travel at the same time. But I don’t feel like, “That’s it, I can’t make a joke about this subject onstage anymore — what a nightmare, my life is over.” I have no idea what will happen next. Maybe a year from now I’ll look back and think, “Wow, remember when we talked with that journalist? Those were the good old days. Things are nothing like that now!” Or maybe it’ll be the other way around.
“The audience has no idea how many jokes never make it to them.” Stand-up comedian Mikhail Z.
I perform at various venues around the city, and everything there is very chaste. Before a show, the organizer reads through my material and cuts anything that isn’t allowed. I had a pretty innocent joke about women who provide paid call-out services — caregivers. They told me, “Rephrase it so there’s no hint of prostitution.” But how am I supposed to rephrase it? In the end, I said, “A woman with an elevated level of social responsibility.”
Before a show, the organizer reads through my material and cuts anything that isn’t allowed
You can’t joke about VPNs. Crude jokes are off-limits, too — although it’s not clear what counts as crude. I had a joke: “My eyesight is so bad, I vomit farther than I can see.” They even banned the word “vomit.” So someone sits there reading through the material, marking things in red: cut this, absolutely not.
The organizer is about 25, but I understand why he does it: he’s simply afraid. Everything could be checked, someone could come along and jot something down in a notebook, and then there could be trouble. After all the cases of people being detained or punished for things they’ve said at concerts or on air, everyone is now playing it safe.
In fact, it’s even worse than ordinary censorship. Nobody directly orders the organizers to cut a joke about a caregiver or the word “vomit.” Instead, people try to anticipate what they could theoretically be punished for and ban even more — just to be on the safe side.
I don’t perform in clubs, although things are a little easier there. My audience is pretty academic, though: they sit politely, nobody drinks. So I’m grateful for everything. Of course, it’s frustrating when half your material gets cut. But as long as I can still perform, that’s something. Especially since the audience laughs — even if they have no idea how many jokes never made it to them.
“Professional comedians are already consulting lawyers.” Stand-up comedian Alexei B.
I suppose I should start by saying that in March of this year, stand-up comedian Artemy Ostanin was sentenced to prison. And that, of course, sent shockwaves through the stand-up community because it was the first high-profile case of its kind.
Before that, in September of last year, Dima Gavrilov was sentenced to 13 days in jail. At the time [of his alleged offense], he was living either in Armenia or Georgia, and during a performance he said something about the phrase “Russian pigs go home” — he said he liked that they were written there because they made him feel at home. He had a whole monologue about Russophobia, and that ultimately led to him being prosecuted.
But he asked us not to get involved in the case in any way or draw attention to it. He said he would deal with it himself with his lawyer and didn’t want to attract even more public attention. And, in fact, things turned out more or less fine and he was released.
Before Artemy was detained, I even messaged him to ask how things were going and whether he needed any help. He replied that everything was fine and that he would get out of it without a scratch. He didn’t.
A lot of comedians simply don’t know that laws like these exist. After what happened to Ostanin, though, they started getting nervous. Some have sent me their scripts and jokes and asked, “Do you think this could get me prosecuted under this law?” It’s pretty sad, because there’s no real legal awareness among the public.
Sometimes I listen to a monologue and think, Guys, you really can’t do that. And the person simply doesn’t understand that if he jokingly draws a Hitler mustache, sketches a swastika, or makes an ambiguous gesture, that could already be enough to trigger a prosecution. You explain it to him, and he looks at you as if to say, “Are you joking or are you serious?”
It seems to me that changes to the law like these simply don’t generate much public attention. They’re in the news, of course. People have been detained under these laws for years. But many simply don’t pay attention. There’s also this feeling that, “It definitely won’t happen to me. I’m not doing anything like that.” And then one day they could come knocking with a search warrant.
There are several factors at play. First, people are unaware of the law. Second, there’s a sense that things aren’t really that bad, that liberal media outlets are exaggerating it all and stoking panic. It’s like living under a dome: this hasn’t affected me so far, so it won’t affect me in the future, either.
We have a big chat for comedians with almost 3,000 people. Basically anyone who wants to perform can join, not just professional comedians. And after what happened to Artemy, there was a huge discussion there. But time passes, and everything quiets down again. I’ve been going to open mics lately, and I’m hearing jokes about Jesus, Hitler, terrorism, and 9/11 all over again. Almost nobody touches the “special military operation.” But the other subjects are coming back.
I’ve been going to open mics lately, and I’m hearing jokes about Jesus, Hitler, terrorism and 9/11 all over again
A novice comedian comes onstage and says, “I’m going to tell this joke now!” Sometimes it’s pure luck that nobody who matters happens to hear him. People regularly say some pretty controversial things from the stage. Sometimes the whole room even falls a little quiet and gets wary — okay, what’s he going to say next?
I joke a lot about the place where I was born and raised, the post-Soviet space, unrecognized territories, and all that. And I’ve noticed that people always get a little tense when those subjects come up. They’re waiting to see what I’ll say and what position I’ll take — whether I’m for or against. In other words, people want to establish my position first and only then follow me further into the subject.
And if I sense the audience isn’t ready, I usually steer things elsewhere. Because there’s also a sense that it isn’t safe. For example, people have started showing up at our shows whom we privately take to be employees of the “E Center.” They’re hilariously bad at disguising themselves. It’s like a cartoon where a bumbling supervillain’s sidekick is practically announcing, “Boss, I’ve hidden the bomb perfectly.” Someone shows up in plain clothes, but the jeans and the fanny pack… They just don’t fit the atmosphere. That obviously affects how you behave onstage.
I’ve had situations where I was finishing a joke and realized halfway through that it might not be safe.
When you’re writing material, you’re not sitting there with the Criminal Code in front of you. Then you go onstage, deliver the joke, and suddenly think: Okay, could that fall under some law? I’ve even said directly to the audience, “Come on, laugh a little louder, so that if anything happens, I won’t be the only one being taken to a pretrial detention center.”
If I’m performing with other comedians, I try to arrive at the very beginning of the show and listen to the host interact with the audience so I can get a sense of who’s in the room that night. For example, the host asks a man where he works, and he says he’d rather not say. We immediately suspect he works in the security services. And you subconsciously start going through your material in your head.
I know which of my jokes come close to the line. Some I cut; others I simply don’t dare tell. Sometimes I deliberately restructure my set. If I feel I’ve ventured into sensitive social territory and the audience reacts worse than usual, I quickly switch to safer subjects. I feel this constant juggling of topics because I’m a fairly anxious person and I keep a close eye on the news.
Professional comedians I know are already consulting lawyers: they send them their material and revise their jokes with the legal risks in mind. But a beginner who has simply come along to try stand-up may have no idea that he’s running afoul of some law. Especially since some of the wording is extremely vague — “insulting the feelings of believers,” and so on. At this point, you don’t even know what might be considered offensive, or to whom.
There’s a comedian who is writing material about marriage. Even he consults lawyers. There’s now this whole discourse around traditional values, family, and “traditional foundations.” He’s simply joking about not understanding the institution of marriage. We talk about love, about the higher feelings between two people, and then those two people go on Gosuslugi and click a button. It’s a completely everyday joke. But even here, he thinks: "Is this really safe?" Because you just don’t know anymore what might become a problem, or when.
Women tend to talk more about the battle of the sexes, sexism, and relationships. And sometimes that gives them a relatively safe way to talk about the war in general. For example, a woman comes onstage and says, “There seem to be fewer men around. I’m on dating apps, and it’s getting harder to meet anyone.”
Technically, she hasn’t said anything political at all. But everyone understands why there might be fewer men. It’s a form of Aesopian language. The comedian may not have intended any political message, but the audience reads one into it.
Feminist themes are complicated, too. At the same time, there’s now a major women’s stand-up scene, or fem-stand-up. There are women-only open mics. At one point, it even felt as though women’s stand-up had become stronger than men’s. It was as if the girls had really embraced that girl power.
Even if someone in the audience shouts something at a woman, she’s still in a stronger position. She’s onstage. She has the spotlights on her. She’s holding the device that amplifies her voice — a microphone. If some heckler shouts something, she can easily outplay him.
As for comedians who have left, I don’t think there’s any widespread resentment toward them within the Russian stand-up scene. Almost everyone has a friend who lives abroad. Everyone understands how hard it is to live in a foreign country — without your native language, your friends, your home, the culture you’re used to, and even the basic things of everyday life.
You can go to a place where there is freedom of speech and self-expression, but when that means abandoning everything you’ve built here — your work, your connections, your audience, your home — many people choose to stay.
When one side of the scales holds freedom of speech and the other means abandoning everything you’ve built, many people choose to stay
I currently live and work in Moscow. And for me, choosing between leaving behind everything I’ve built here and having the freedom to say everything that’s been weighing on me isn’t so simple. Just two years ago, I swore I would never set foot in another country. Now I realize that if things become too uncomfortable for me, I’ll leave. Of course, it’s frightening to think that I’d have to start my career almost from scratch. I’ve built relationships with organizers here, earned their trust, and developed my own audience.
I started thinking about emigration this year primarily because of something very personal: I started thinking about having a family and children. And at some point, I asked myself: "do I want my children to grow up in this country?" The answer was no longer clear-cut.
I’d say I still choose Russia about 90% of the time. But that 10% of doubt is there. It has to do, among other things, with my political views and with how I feel about what’s happening around me. The war has also started to feel physically closer. There are more reports of drone attacks and of things happening in Moscow and other regions. Every day you read the news: something is happening in Kursk, Belgorod, the Urals, the North.
You come across economic forecasts and new laws, and you inevitably start wondering how much longer this can go on. You ask yourself: "am I ready to get used to this new normal?" And, more importantly, "am I ready for my children to grow up accustomed to it?"
When my friends and I talk about politics, we generally understand each other. We’re mostly centrists; we don’t like radicalism, and we’re against the war. At the same time, we understand that there’s a vast political system in which different people make money and make decisions.
I watch Varlamov, Katz, various news sources, Sobchak, and others, and somehow piece together a reality I can live in. Then I visit my parents in another country and see that they watch all kinds of different channels: Russian, Ukrainian, and local.
I start watching all of it with them. You turn on Russian television, and some of the things I see there are physically hard for me to watch. Then you switch to Ukrainian news, sometimes in Ukrainian, and see what they’re saying there. Then you watch international news.
After trips like that, I usually return to Russia feeling more liberal, because I’ve had a chance to look at it from the outside, even if only a little. My parents lived through an armed conflict themselves in the 1990s. My father took part in it. They understand very well that war is horrible. But they also understand something else: these kinds of decisions aren’t made by ordinary people. Not by the public. They’re made by people at the top who have the power to make them. And everyone else is then left to find a way to live with the consequences.
“It’s making everyone a little paranoid.” Stand-up comedian Pavel V.
There’s a children’s show on STS Kids, one of the few TV programs featuring stand-up. The kids perform themselves, and everything is geared toward a young audience. Some of the participants are already 14 or 15, and those limits are starting to feel restrictive. They want to joke about teenage subjects, about things that are actually bothering them. But they perform alongside nine-year-olds for whom those topics are still taboo. And because it all airs on a children’s channel, there are pretty strict limits on what they can talk about.
At the same time, teenagers are quite happy to make political jokes among themselves. While they’re still young, they can get away with a lot because nobody takes them seriously. But once they turn 18 and start saying the same things into a microphone, the consequences can be very different.
Some of them understand this, while others aren’t thinking about it at all yet. They’re kids; they don’t think that far ahead: "Will I still be doing this in the future? Where will I be five years from now?" I started performing at around their age, when I was about 14. And if you compare what it was like then with what’s happening now, a huge amount has changed.
Even in early 2022, you could still say certain things onstage. People just made sure nothing was recorded and that no video got out. Now that thought barely even occurs to anyone. Self-censorship has changed dramatically. And it’s not just the comedians — the audience has changed too. If you suddenly start saying something like that out loud, it makes everyone a little paranoid. It’s as if one thought immediately hangs in the air: “This isn’t being recorded, is it?”
I remember that feeling well, when someone would still try to slip in a little joke or hint. People in the audience would literally sit up straight. Not necessarily because they disagreed, but because they were struck by the fact that someone had just said it out loud from the stage at a public event. It was as if everyone immediately thought: “If anything happens, I wasn’t laughing.” It’s not outright terror, more a constant sense of tension. There’s already too much of that around us as it is.
A lot of comedians have also reconsidered why they go onstage in the first place. Sometimes a beginner wants to make a statement, to say something important. But an experienced comedian understands that your primary job is to entertain people, make them laugh, and give them a good time. And some subjects are now such that people are more likely to tense up than to laugh.
Some topics have become off-limits not because anyone has officially handed you a list, but because people are intimidated. The atmosphere has changed. And I don’t sense much of a demand for political humor anymore. It seems to me that a large share of those who had a strong appetite for it have left. What remains are mostly people to whom it wasn’t that important to begin with. And, frankly, people are simply scared now. Sometimes you want to add a comparison to an everyday joke, then realize that it vaguely touches on politics — and that’s it. Better not.
Some topics have simply become off-limits, not because anyone has officially handed you a list, but because people are intimidated
Overall, there’s been more everyday comedy: observations about relationships, family, and things everyone can relate to. It’s safe. But you still don’t feel free. Probably because there are simply too many things you can’t talk about.
Of course I’ve thought about emigrating. In fact, I did leave. When the mobilization was announced, I was one of those Russians who left. And I got a taste of what it was like to have freedom in my material. At some point, the mere possibility of discussing something openly with people really hits you. You think, “Wow, so you can actually just say this out loud.” My situation is also somewhat complicated because, in a way, I’m avoiding military service. So even unnecessary interactions at the border are frightening.
Here, by contrast, there are things you simply don’t discuss publicly. In that sense, I really like what’s happening in Poland, for example. And it makes me sad that even just traveling there is quite difficult for me now. In general, it’s become harder for Russians to travel anywhere. But I find the Polish comedy scene fascinating because several languages are mixed together at once.
I lived in Armenia and spent time in Georgia and Uzbekistan. The industry is smaller in Uzbekistan. In Armenia, a stand-up club can operate in two languages, and both Armenians and Russians attend shows in either language. Everyone makes an effort to understand one another. Poland is even more interesting: there are Poles, Ukrainians, Belarusians, and Russians. A single stand-up club can host shows in three languages. That’s really cool.
In Russia, there are some pretty strange things happening around the English language these days. I performed at an English-language open mic in Moscow. The organizers are foreigners — British and American. And they were trying to figure out how to label an English-language open mic in Russian so that people searching for an event in English would still understand what they were going to. A foreigner living in Moscow who wants to attend an English-language event first has to see the event listing in Russian. It’s pretty strange.
In general, there’s this sense of a kind of legalized lawlessness in the air. There are brief moments when you think, “Oh, maybe things are going to get a little freer?” During the whole Yabloko episode, for example, there were literally a couple of weeks when it felt like, “Wait, what? Are we a liberal society again?”
One comedian had a joke about presidential experience. The idea was that if you’re an ordinary professional and you’ve gained a lot of experience at one job, you can take that experience to another job. It’s considered an advantage. But if you’ve been president of Russia for many years, you can’t take that presidential experience and get a job as president somewhere else. There’s no criticism in the joke. Nothing at all. It’s simply a name used for comparison. But the comedian says “Putin,” and the audience immediately goes, “Mmm.” Like Voldemort: a name that’s better left unspoken.
“Putin” is like Voldemort: a name that’s better left unspoken
The story of Artemy Ostanin has had a profound impact on everyone, of course. It’s horrifying, but also revealing. And what I find important is that people are waiting for Ostanin. That’s probably the best thing about the whole situation. He wasn’t some superstar comedian with a huge audience. By the standards of the broader comedy world, he was practically a nobody. And yet people haven’t forgotten him. So much has happened since then that any other news story could easily have been pushed out of people’s minds by the next one. But this story is still there.
Of course, there are stupid comedians, idiotic comedians, and fucking assholes who think it’s his own fault: “He shouldn’t have touched those subjects in the first place.” No. It’s not his fault. What the fuck? They simply took what he said, interpreted it in a certain way, and that was it. It doesn’t even matter that much whether the joke itself was good. You can listen to it a hundred times and say, “Well, it’s not the funniest joke in the world.” But destroying people over their words is horrifying.
And this case also made something else very clear: if you still want to talk about things like that, you now have to do it much more subtly. In terms of censorship, we’ve come very close to the Soviet satirists. If you want to say something, you have to speak in Aesopian language. You can’t simply state the point outright.
If you have a joke like that, people have to get it from the hint. You can only hint at it. If you want to talk about something, you have to really contort yourself. You can’t just say something about Putin or the authorities directly anymore. It has to be all half-hints.
As for pro-government, or what you might call "Z-humor," it certainly exists. There are venues where this kind of comedy is performed. Some projects even feature military personnel doing stand-up. There are comedians who joke about people who have left, about other countries, and so on. But I don’t think it’s becoming a genuinely popular genre. I simply try not to perform at those kinds of venues, so I don’t encounter much of it in my circle. And I don’t think audiences are particularly interested in it, either.
People are already tired of all this. Politics is more likely to trigger people than make them laugh. They go to stand-up to switch off. I can easily imagine someone living on the outskirts of Moscow. At night, he hears several drones being shot down. In the morning, he goes to work. He works all day. In the evening, he decides to go to a stand-up show in the city center, just to take his mind off things for a while. And then you start talking to him from the stage about drones. He still has to go home afterward — back to the place where those drones are. Why the hell would he want that?
It also seems to me that demand for stand-up itself has declined somewhat. Maybe people simply have less money. A ticket costing 1,000 or 2,000 rubles is already a significant expense for some. It’s entertainment, after all, and the price of everything has gone up. Even television stand-up projects, from what I can see, have started buying less material. Maybe that’s because viewership has fallen. And if demand is down, why buy something people aren’t watching?
Still, I want to believe this isn’t forever. I just want to be fucking blown away one day when I suddenly discover: “Wait, we can do this now?” Because I know exactly what that feeling will be like. I already experienced that high when I was living in Yerevan. You suddenly realize you can actually just talk about this subject — not in a whisper, not in hints, not checking whether someone is filming you on their phone. You can just say it. And I really want to feel that way here one day.

Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs in biggest ever industry shake-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:03:07 UTC
15:03:07 KST

German car giant Volkswagen said that management and unions had agreed to cut a further 50,000 jobs by the end of the decade, bringing total job losses to 100,000.
Volkswagen is about to shed one in seven of its workers.
The German car giant said on Thursday that management and unions had agreed to cut a further 50,000 jobs by the end of the decade, on top of 50,000 already planned, bringing total losses to 100,000.
"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," the 10-brand group said in a statement.
The firm had approved a plan involving "the reduction of around 50,000 jobs" on top of another 50,000 already agreed, it added.
Hit by US tariffs, patchy demand for electric cars and, above all, fierce competition in and from China, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble.
The group, which apart from its namesake brand also includes Audi and Porsche, had already agreed to cut about 50,000 jobs worldwide.
The total 100,000 cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry, amounting to about 15% of the carmaker's staff worldwide.
The cuts eclipse the auto industry's previous record-holders. General Motors cut 74,000 jobs and closed 21 plants in 1991 as it lost ground to Japanese rivals, and cut a further 47,000 jobs globally in 2009 during its financial crisis restructuring.
Ford cut 35,000 jobs and closed five plants in 2002, then targeted tens of thousands more under its "Way Forward" plan later that decade. Volkswagen's 100,000 is now the largest total on record.
Volkswagen further said that management and unions agreed the future of four German plants — in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be assured into the 2030s.
Their closure would mark the first time Volkswagen has shuttered full-scale factories in its home country.
The adoption of the plans by Volkswagen's supervisory board, made up of both labour and shareholder representatives, marks progress in delicate negotiations between the two sides.
"The supervisory board has unanimously approved the executive board's future plan presented today," CEO Oliver Blume said. "This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group."
Alongside its namesake marque, the group's stable spans Škoda, SEAT and Cupra at the mass-market end, Audi, Bentley, Lamborghini and Ducati at the premium and luxury end, and Porsche as a standalone sports brand.

Video: Heavy rain overwhelms Pärnu sewer system, causes street flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:03:00 UTC
15:03:00 KST

Video: Heavy rain overwhelms Pärnu sewer system, causes street flooding
During the past night, parts of Estonia saw heavy rainfall — in Pärnu County 95 mm of rain had fallen by 8 a.m. The intense downpour overloaded Pärnu's sewer system and has caused flooding.
The Pärnu city government wrote around 8:30 a.m. that the very large amount of rain in recent hours has heavily strained the sewer system, which is operating at full capacity.
"Unfortunately, both stormwater drainage and sewer services are disrupted, and in many places roads are difficult to pass due to water accumulation," the city noted.
The city government asks drivers to be cautious and avoid flooded road sections. The city and service providers are working to resolve the situation.
"The situation is indeed difficult," the city's post said.
The Weather Service reported that on Friday morning, more than 80 mm of rain had been measured in Pärnu and its surrounding areas in some places.
Meteorologist Kairo Kiitsak reported that as of 9:20 a.m., an exceptionally large amount of rain had fallen in Pärnu and its surrounding areas. Rainfall totals exceeded 100 mm, and in some places passed the 120 mm mark.
Heavy rainfall will continue during the day, especially in southwestern, central and eastern Estonia.
Rääma school sends students home
Pärnu's Rääma school announced on Friday morning that classes would not take place due to heavy rainfall.
"Drainage and toilets aren't working, and the entire ground floor is covered with water," said school director Elmo Joa, adding that students were being sent home.
Joa said that they are currently waiting for a pump to remove water from the basement level.
"Everything is fine for us right now. Children were arriving at school. A large number of younger ones who came with their parents were already turned back at the door, because rubber boots would have been the only suitable indoor shoes. So they went home nicely. They were very sad, because outside it was raining and inside it wasn't — it was exciting here," Joa said.
Deputy mayor: We are declaring an emergency
Pärnu Deputy Mayor Sander Kilk said that after the crisis committee convened, the city decided to declare an emergency.
"Since this water likely won't recede for several hours, property damage is possible. Another problem is manhole covers that have come off. The sewer system cannot handle the water, meaning these spots are dangerous for people driving cars, bicycles, or walking," Kilk said.
According to Kilk, a rainwater‑driven flood of this scale is unprecedented in Pärnu. It also became clear that the city had not been prepared for such a crisis.
"The first goal now is to calmly resolve today's situation and then look ahead. It turned out that no previous city government has put together a crisis manual. We will definitely create one — not only for this type of crisis but for all possible incidents. A task force has been assembled, department heads are working on it, and so are we," Kilk said.
For now, the deputy mayor said, they must wait for the rainfall to ease or stop. After that, pumping water out of people's basements can begin.
The Estonian Rescue Union is also assisting Pärnu.

Concerns have also been raised over the structural risks associated with excessive withdrawals from salt caverns, including pressure changes, salt-wall stability, well integrity and potential damage to long-term storage capacity.
Some oil traders have interpreted Bessent’s signals as an indication that US efforts could push futures prices lower. Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Aussie's EPL teen dream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Lucas Herrington's EPL teen dream
Lucas Herrington has gone to number one with a bullet in 2026, at a speed so dizzying it would leave many teenagers' heads spinning.
Turning 19 this weekend, he is fresh off a breakthrough World Cup, has a multi-million-dollar contract in the best football league in the world, and has fans fawning over him.
But true to his persona on the pitch, the central defender is calm, level-headed and capable of tackling any challenge.
"My parents have always instilled that factor of humility in my life and having that humbleness to stay grounded and just to keep working hard," he told Australian media on a call from Hull.
"I'm always trying to get better. So I think it's always having that positive mindset that I've still got a lot of things to work on. And I'm not the finished product."
Herrington made his bolt-from-the-blue Socceroos debut in March, which turned into a maiden World Cup appearance a few months later.
His impressive efforts in North America captured interest from some of the biggest clubs in the world including Barcelona and Liverpool.
But he settled on Hull City, newly promoted in the English Premier League, and a five-year deal for a transfer fee reportedly worth $33 million with add-ons, to become the most expensive Australian player ever.
Alessandro Circati recently joined that rich list with his transfer from Parma to Benfica.
The money is astronomical for an Australian footballer, and despite his down-to-earth nature, even Herrington was lured in by the EPL stereotype of fancy, fast cars.
"It's a nice car park. I do have a car right now; it's nice. I'm enjoying it," he laughed, almost sheepishly.
But when he speaks about his off-field highlights in his few weeks in England, the teenager goes back to keeping it real.
"Mum's here at the moment. She leaves soon, so I've just been exploring around with her," he said.
"So that's been really nice, some great quality time with her."
Advice from a legend
Herrington made his debut for the Tigers off the bench in their upset win over Manchester United.
"It was only a week and a couple of days from when I landed to that game against Man United," he said.
"Great moment for the city and for me personally, with my mum and my agent in the stands, it was a super proud moment for me.
"And it was a great match, very grateful for the opportunity to be there."
He was again used as a substitute in a win over Coventry, while he started the EFL Cup penalty shootout win against Stoke.
A strong show of confidence for the youngster, who is the only Australian in England's top flight.
"It's probably the best league in the world. So to be here at 18 is super special," he said.
"I've always wanted to play in the Premier League, so I'm very grateful for the opportunity from the coaching staff and the club to do so. And I've loved my first three or so weeks here.
"It's a league with the best players in the world, so to be up against them every week is really special and a great challenge for me as a young defender.
"It's just about trying to learn as much as possible from the older boys in the team and just try and take every game as a lesson."
And don't mistake his modesty for meekness; he knows he belongs.
A message reinforced by former Sweden international Zlatan Ibrahimović, who publicly supported Herrington after missing a penalty in the Socceroos' World Cup round of 32 shootout loss to Egypt.
“This is just the beginning of your career," Ibrahimović said on Fox Sports USA's post-game analysis.
"You stepping up there, you show a lot of courage. Not everybody would do that. My friend, you're the best. Don't listen to the rest. Listen, Herrington, if you want to reach out, I'm here."
Ibrahimović made good on his promise and ended up calling the Queensland product himself.
"He just said, really don't fear anyone. I'm here for a reason, so just go enjoy," Herrington said.
Dreams do come true
Herrington's meteoric rise means he has not yet played for Australia in his home state.
Something the former Roar product hopes to do in the Socceroos' friendlies against Brazil later this month, in Townsville and Brisbane.
"It'd be a dream come true to play for the Socceroos in Brisbane," he said.
"Something that I've always wanted to do, and to play in front of hopefully a packed-out Suncorp would be a dream, and in front of my family and friends would be awesome."
And he is happy to be a role model for others.
"Just trying to be an inspiration for all the young Australians that there is really a pathway to the Premier League," he said.
"I think a lot of young footballers in Australia like me wake up at all hours in the morning to watch the Premier League.
"So hopefully I can make them proud, make Australia proud.
"Just to keep working hard, enjoy the process, and to have big dreams because dreams do come true."

UK has not done enough to prepare for shocks to food supplies, says watchdog
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:02 UTC
15:00:02 KST

The climate crisis, disease and cyber-attacks pose growing risks to the UK’s food supplies and the government needs to act to make the system more resilient, according to the public spending watchdog.
The National Audit Office (NAO) is urging the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) to work more closely with households, communities and businesses to ensure the flow of crucial food into the country can withstand supply shocks that are becoming increasingly common and severe.
Its latest report found Defra – the department responsible for security of food supply – had taken some steps to better prepare for future shocks, but said it had not done enough in recent years to get citizens and industry to plan for possible emergencies.
Britain relies on overseas imports for more than a third of its food, most of it entering through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway – making supplies particularly vulnerable to potential disruption.
The NAO’s report comes after months of warnings about the resilience of the UK’s food supply chain from experts who have told households to build up a stockpile of long-life items they could rely on in an emergency. Britons are less prepared for potential future catastrophic events than citizens of several other European countries, according to government research.
The supply chain has already come under pressure during the Covid-19 pandemic and after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, although businesses including the nation’s largest supermarkets managed to keep goods flowing, in most cases without the need for significant government assistance.
However, Defra is less confident about the private sector’s ability to withstand future shocks, such as extreme weather events, without greater government intervention.
Food industry businesses praised Defra’s engagement with them during the pandemic, but told the NAO it had communicated with them less frequently since. The report said the companies had limited input into the government’s plans for reacting to supply disruption, which could mean officials created proposals that would not work in practice.
Gareth Davies, the NAO’s head, said: “Recent disruptions have shown the resilience of the UK’s food supply chain, but risks are increasing in likelihood and severity.
“Defra should learn from approaches taken in other countries, and strengthen preparedness for emergencies by testing plans with local government and industry.”
The government has designated food as one of 13 critical national infrastructure sectors it considers essential for the proper functioning of the country.
However, food industry representatives have said that does not go far enough and have called on ministers to add the UK’s cold stores and food transport hubs to the critical list, which would ensure their power supplies would be maintained in the event of widespread outages.
The NAO report comes just a few months after the trade body for cold storage and logistics, the Cold Chain Federation, accused the government of “complacency” over national food storage and urged ministers to make potential disruption to the UK’s food system an “immediate national priority”.
The last national exercise testing Defra’s preparedness for catastrophic events that would severely disrupt the availability of food took place in 2023, but did not include most supply chain businesses, the NAO found.
In addition, local resilience forums indicated they lacked clarity from Defra on what would be expected from them in the event of disruption.

Save the Children aid for 1.5 million in need wiped out by Iran war oil shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:02 UTC
15:00:02 KST

The charity Save the Children has said the oil price shock unleashed by Donald Trump’s war on Iran is forcing it to “spend more to reach fewer children”.
The NGO analysed the increased costs of transport, fuel, food and medical supplies as a result of the Middle East conflict.
It calculated that the extra burden of delivering aid had already been $13m (£10m), which could instead have allowed it to reach an additional 1.5 million children.
Willem Zuidema, Save the Children’s global supply chain director, said: “The conflict in the Middle East is not only putting children at risk in the region but also globally, because every spike in fuel prices drives up the cost of every truck, every shipment, every box of supplies we deliver around the world. We are being forced to spend more to reach fewer children.”
Developing countries have tended to be hit hardest by the oil shock, which the International Energy Agency has called the largest disruption to supplies in history. Many governments have introduced restrictions on energy use.
Save the Children operates in about 110 countries, with a particular focus on safeguarding children’s rights. Its health and nutrition programmes reached more than 30 million children last year, including in hard-to-reach countries such as Afghanistan.
The charity said the additional costs of delivering aid were equivalent to 47 health clinics in Afghanistan operating for six months, or five 30-bed hospitals in Somalia operating for a year.
Before the conflict, the oil price was expected to be about $60 a barrel during 2026. After the US administration went to war with Iran, prompting Tehran to choke supplies though the strait of Hormuz, it surged above $100 a barrel.
Prices declined after the US-Iran ceasefire in the summer but have jumped back above $90 in recent days as hostilities have resumed. Recent US rhetoric about increasing economic sanctions on Iran has raised fears the conflict could continue indefinitely.
With the strait of Hormuz also an important conduit for fertiliser, the crisis has increased the prices of other commodities including food.
Zuidema said Save the Children had been working to source alternative supplies and transport routes in an attempt to keep costs under control.
“Despite the extreme challenges and rising costs, our teams are working around the clock to find alternative and cost-effective ways to deliver essential supplies and ensure we reach children where it is needed the most,” he said.
The higher price of providing aid is coinciding with declining global aid budgets. The Trump administration has gutted USAID, the country’s development agency, and the UK is among the other countries reducing spending.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which gathers authoritative data, found that global aid spending plunged by 23% in real terms last year.
Save the Children has previously criticised the UK government’s deep cuts to the overseas aid budget, with Moazzam Malik, its director, calling them a “tragedy”.
Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, who oversees aid spending, has been urged by charities and some Labour backbenchers to set out a path to fulfilling Gordon Brown’s promise to spend 0.7% of national income on aid.
Save the Children was set up in 1919 by two sisters, Eglantyne Jebb and Dorothy Buxton, who were horrified by the impact of a post-first world war export blockade on children in Berlin and Vienna.

‘It feels like Italy with the volume turned down’: readers’ favourite (smaller) city breaks in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:02 UTC
15:00:02 KST

Renaissance art without the crowds in Italy
Ferrara in Emilia-Romagna won me over precisely because it feels like Italy with the volume turned down. I stayed in a small family-run hotel near Via delle Volte, where mornings began with quiet cobbled streets and the smell of fresh pastries. The Palazzo dei Diamanti was almost empty when I visited, giving me space to enjoy its Renaissance art without crowds. Evenings meant cycling past terracotta walls to tiny trattorias serving pumpkin cappellacci, a traditional pasta dish. It’s a city that lets you slow down, breathe and enjoy its beauty.
John
One of Germany’s greenest cities
Next to flashy Munich or cool Berlin, Hanover in northern Germany has a reputation of being boring. It is totally undeserved: there are world-class museums, such as the modern art gallery Sprengel, one of the best-preserved baroque gardens in Europe – the Great Garden at Herrenhausen – impressive Victorian era architecture, 640 hectares (1,680 acres) of city forest (the Eilenriede, nearly double the size of New York’s Central Park) and a large artificial lake just south of the centre that you can travel on with a bus ticket (or hire a boat). Explore the city and its surroundings on more than 600 miles of cycle paths, find independent shops in the well-heeled art nouveau district of List or the multicultural Linden, and relax in a deck chair on Ballhofplatz with tea and cake at the Teestübchen.
Ulrike
The Algarve’s city of crafts
Bursting with Portuguese charm, Loulé is 10 miles inland from Faro, capital of the Algarve. The small city has a rich history of preserving traditional crafts, supported by Loulé Criativo, a network of community-driven artisans that keeps alive and celebrates the identity of Loulé and the Algarve. It includes the House of Weaving (Casa da Empreita) and the Watchmakers (Oficina do Relojoeiro) and Stringed Instrument Workshop (Oficina de Cordofones). In these vibrant spaces – where visitors can interact with artisans – the city’s heritage is preserved and passed down through generations. 
Sue
Unesco sites in northern France
Arras, 35 minutes on the train from Lille, has two Unesco world heritage sites: the belfry of the Hotel de Ville and the Vauban Citadel. Exploring the Boves, a 10th-century network of tunnels which played roles in the first and second world wars, is an amazing experience. Above are two magnificent large squares in the Flemish style with a wide variety of alfresco cafes, restaurants and indie shops. Arras also holds one of the biggest Christmas markets north of Paris, noted for its amazing range of international gourmet foods.
Bryan Boese
Artistry and cake in Sweden’s beautiful south
Malmö is easily accessible (being connected by bridge to Copenhagen) and very walkable. We enjoyed the free Malmö Konsthall arts centre with contemporary exhibitions and also the skateboard artistry in the square outside. The Western Harbour contains architectural gems, such as the twisted skyscraper Turning Turso, restaurants and swimming piers in a former industrial area. The cafe Hollandia offered classic Swedish cakes and a lovely atmosphere. The Disgusting Food Museum next door was an interesting cultural experience showing food considered to be delicacies in some countries, not so much in others. A sign shows the number of people who have thrown up (visit Hollandia first)!
Elisabeth
Brilliant beach and seafood in Sardinia
If you can tear yourself away from Poetto – surely one of the prettiest city beaches in Europe – you’ll find a lot more to love in Cagliari, capital of Sardinia. The huge indoor produce market is a riot of glistening seafood, local pecorino and sweet, nutty Sardinian treats. The town centre strides uphill from the port, with the elegant bulwark of Bastione St Remy delineating the ancient Castello district and serving up epic rooftop and coastal views. We missed the renowned archaeological museum, but that just gives us the perfect excuse to go back. Cagliari’s affordable seafood was a definite highlight, and Trattoria Lillicu’s chargrilled bream and calamari is another tempting reason to hurry back. 
Martha
Stained glass wonder in north-west Spain
In León, colours grab your attention and take away words. León cathedral completely wrongfooted me. This city seems to be under the British tourist radar. I thought I’d already seen stained glass that was worthy of heaven – this was another level. Coupled with this was how visitors were reacting. Everyone was using the free audio guide. No one was just marching round and ticking off the sights. People were learning and savouring the experience. The humble ninth-century San Isidoro church, one of the most important romanesque buildings in Spain, is a refreshing contrast. 
Deborah
Norway’s art nouveau gem
Ålesund is one of Norway’s most beautiful stops on an already spectacular western coast, despite having been devastated by fire in 1904. We reached the small, rebuilt art nouveau city via the breathtaking winding roads of the Trollstigen (the “Troll’s Path”) and had our first sighting from the top of the panoramic Aksla mountain viewpoint. Exactly 418 steps lead down to the historic centre where museums, cafes, restaurants and shops cluster around the Brosundet Canal in renovated warehouses and ornate buildings. Kayaking, a rib boat ride or a trip to the stunning Geirangerfjord? We couldn’t choose so did them all!
Teresa Stansby
The French city with a bit of everything
I spent five days in Saint-Malo this August. It has everything: a beautiful walled city with lots of history, a variety of beaches offering shifts in light and character throughout the day, a modernist tidal pool with a high diving platform. The city has so much pride, and the art inspired by its famous landmarks make for great souvenirs. My favourite thing, though? The wonderful cider at La Passage (on Instagram) with my sister. And despite the heat everywhere else, the temperature never got above 25C.
Sophie Amos
Winning tip: a watery Dutch master of a city
Leiden starts badly. The walk from the station is grim. Scruffy bars and vape shops. And then, suddenly, this watery Dutch gem reveals itself. Canals shoot off from a boat-filled basin, each one lined with grand brick mansions tapering to elegant finials under the sort of blue lowland skies that typify every good (and bad) Flemish painting. Dig deeper into its narrow traffic-free courtyards and squares with cafes spilling out light and chatter, much as they did when Rembrandt trudged to the school that still stands here, just round the corner from his first tutor’s studio. He’d find it mostly unchanged if he walked back. At Christmas, an ice rink spreads across the main canal, and the smell of warm wine, cloves and crepes hovers over the market stalls.
Bill Jones

====================================================================================================

Revealed: how companies ‘secretly’ use billions of litres of public water in drought-hit England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Less than 1% of businesses in England use more water than the daily needs of 10 million people, as millions of households face hosepipe bans and three-quarters of the country is in drought.
Businesses across England use 2.6bn litres a day from the public water supply, which includes potable and non-potable water provided by water companies. In total, businesses account for about 30% of public supply use, with two-thirds of their consumption in water-stressed areas, according to Mosl, the organisation that operates England’s business water market.
Tracking industrial water use appears difficult. Regulators say they are frustrated by a lack of data and “commercial secrecy”, and the water sector says it is prevented from planning effectively for growth industries.
The biggest users of the public water supply include oil refineries, chemical plants and paper mills, and some face no requirement to cut their consumption.
Mosl’s map of business water supply points, ranked by volume used, showed the site of ExxonMobil’s Esso refinery at Fawley, Southampton, as the largest user of public water supply. However, the site includes a number of other operators that also use the water, including waste, gas, chemicals and energy companies.
Mosl cited the refinery’s water use in written evidence to a House of Lords committee as an example of “the high volume of water wastage in industry that is not disincentivised by government or the regulatory framework”.
Mosl did not name the refinery but described its location, which was also visible on its map of supply points.
ExxonMobil disputed Mosl’s figures, saying its water use was commercially confidential. Mosl said it planned to ask the committee to redact parts of its evidence. During reporting, Mosl also removed a report and its supply point map from its website.
The refinery said the “vast majority” of the water it used came from the Solent strait for cooling, while “industrial water” was used for processes that could not easily be reduced without shutting down operating units. Potable water accounted for less than 1% of total consumption, it said.
Apart from refineries, other major users of the public water supply include paper mills and companies in the chemicals and soft drinks industries. But the overall picture of business water use is incomplete. One in 10 businesses are not metered, meaning their use is not measured or reported. Of those that are metered, only 11% have smart meters.
Despite Mosl collecting data on water taken from the public supply, it is not free to share all of it, even with government departments, according to Mosl’s chief executive, Sarah McMath.
McMath told the House of Lords committee that when the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) or the Environment Agency requested data, Mosl had to negotiate a bespoke agreement to share it.
Mosl was working with the water regulator, Ofwat, to change this, she said, so that data would be shared when it would benefit “the environment or society”.
A lack of data is already affecting national water planning. Gaps in local authority growth plans, combined with what the Environment Agency and Ofwat describe as “commercial secrecy, especially in the energy sector”, mean plans are often based on assumptions.
The Environment Agency and Ofwat are calling for mandatory reporting of current and projected water use across all sectors to improve water security.
A spokesperson for Mosl said: “Our data highlights both the opportunities and regulatory barriers to incentivising businesses to use less water. Rather than focusing on individual users – many of whom are actively seeking to reduce their water demand – we should focus on creating the right conditions to invest in water efficiency and increase water reuse where it is safe and practical.”
Water resources planning assumes business water consumption will fall by 9% by 2038 and 15% by 2050.
But the trade body Water UK argues the assumption is unrealistic as demand grows from new homes, as datacentres, hydrogen production and other developments. It wants water companies to be able to plan for projected demand rather than government reduction targets.
Companies are not required to report all their water use, and for some, the more water they use, the cheaper each unit becomes.
One operator told Mosl that a single UK datacentre uses 219m litres a year. It also has a tankered-water supply on standby if its mains connection fails, as well as its own borehole as a backup.
Businesses can also take water directly from rivers, lakes, aquifers and the sea via abstraction . This is regulated separately by the Environment Agency.
Some abstraction is invisible. Anyone can take up to 20,000 litres a day from a stream, borehole or spring without a licence or reporting it. The gap covers an estimated 850,000 people and organisations across England, mostly on farms and in rural areas.
Richard Benwell, the chief executive of the NGO coalition Wildlife and Countryside Link, said: “It’s surely an injustice that petrochemical and fossil fuel companies most responsible for the climate crisis are also draining … water supplies and drawing more water from our parched environment.
The water campaigner Feargal Sharkey said: “Yet again, regulatory ineptitude is allowed to triumph over the needs of people and the environment. While water supplies run dry, corporate bank accounts are flooded with the proceeds of corporate greed.”
Defra said the government was taking “decisive action to secure water supplies”, including planning to build nine reservoirs and investing in infrastructure.
A Water UK spokesperson said: “Supplies are increasingly at risk because England’s official forecasts for how much water the country needs rely on flawed assumptions. The water needed by fast-growing datacentres is explicitly excluded from the forecasts.
“At the same time, lower water bills have been prioritised over building a resilient system, meaning in some places water companies only have 2% of water spare to deal with increased demand.”
The Environment Agency said abstraction licences had strict conditions and were reviewed regularly, and that it was working towards the 9% reduction in business water use from the public supply.
Meanwhile, England’s water companies are losing about 2.2bn litres of water a day through leaking pipes.

Also in striking distance is the vast Stamford Park, which has a full-sized football pitch, basketball courts, ponds, playgrounds and woodland trails. Anti-national forces harming India's unity will face consequences: Adityanath
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Friday warned that anti-national and anti-social forces seeking to spread hatred or undermine India's unity would face consequences, invoking Lord Krishna's message on the occasion of Janmashtami.Addressing a gathering in Mathura, the birthplace of Lord Krishna, on the second day of his visit, Adityanath emphasised that His teachings and message remained equally relevant today.
"Wherever the forces of goodness exist, they will be protected under all circumstances. But wherever anti-national and anti-social forces raise their heads, create hatred in society or attempt to harm India's unity, integrity and faith, Lord Krishna had already said 5,000 years ago what their fate would be," PTI quoted the chief minister as saying.Yogi Adityanath also cited the Bhagavad Gita's teaching, "Paritranaya sadhunam, vinashaya cha dushkritam" (for the protection of the righteous and destruction of evil), stressing that it continued to guide society.The chief minister highlighted the Braj region's role in preserving its religious heritage and the memories of Lord Krishna despite repeated invasions and attempts by various groups to impose their faith on India.
"Many invasions took place and many people tried to impose their faith on India, but no one could erase the Sanatan faith," Yogi Adityanath said."Those who dared to erase Sanatan faith themselves disappeared into the dust, but the memories of Shri Krishna and Radha Rani, not only in Braj but across India, continue to inspire us today and provide an encouraging environment for future generations," he added.The chief minister welcomed devotees arriving in Mathura for Janmashtami and extended his greetings to the people of Uttar Pradesh on the festival marking the birth of Lord Krishna.Yogi Adityanath has been in Mathura since Thursday for Janmashtami celebrations and has been attending programmes ahead of the festival.

BERLIN, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Volkswagen approved a transformation plan Thursday that will cut another 50,000 jobs and halve its model portfolio by 2035.
The Supervisory Board of the Volkswagen Group unanimously approved the Executive Board's Future Plan 2030, which includes "a Group-wide workforce adjustment of approximately 50,000 positions" in addition to 50,000 job cuts already under way, the group said in a statement.
"By 2035, the Volkswagen Group will streamline its model portfolio by around 50 percent and reduce its offering complexity by around 75 percent," the statement said.
The company did not provide further details on the timing of the job cuts or how the cuts would be distributed across its brands and regions.
"This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group. We are taking responsibility for our entire workforce, for our partners and for industrial jobs worldwide," Oliver Blume, CEO of Volkswagen Group, was quoted as saying in the statement. ■

Interview: Customer-oriented approach vital in AI-driven economy, says Sberbank CFO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:58:59 CST
14:58:59 KST

by Xinhua writers Vladislava Chugueva, Zhang Chaoqun
MOSCOW, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Only companies that prioritize their customers' interests will survive and thrive amid the fundamental changes artificial intelligence (AI) has brought to the global economy, Sberbank Deputy Chairman and CFO Taras Skvortsov has said.
Over one billion people worldwide still lack access to formal bank accounts, and AI can effectively lower banks' service thresholds to reach these underserved groups, Skvortsov told Xinhua ahead of the ongoing Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
As Russia's largest bank, Sberbank plays a leading role in the country's AI research and application, translating its advances in AI into more accessible everyday services for customers, he said.
In Russia, social tax deductions for education, fitness and medical expenses have long been underused because of cumbersome procedures. Sberbank has simplified the process with one-click processing, allowing customers to have the bank apply for deductions on their behalf.
"Within the framework of our human-centric strategy, we asked ourselves whether we could streamline the entire process for users, allowing them to simply tick a box to authorize Sberbank to apply for tax deductions on their behalf," Skvortsov said, noting that the bank expects the service to attract 60 million to 70 million users annually.
The bank itself is also among the biggest beneficiaries of AI, he noted, saying that the technology is transforming the traditional financial cycle of data collection, reporting, analysis and decision-making by generating analysis and actionable solutions as soon as data is acquired.
Sberbank has stepped up AI investment, Skvortsov said, spending about 100 billion rubles (1.15 billion U.S. dollars) on AI research and development in 2024 and planning to invest 350 billion rubles by 2026, with a focus on its GigaChat model and applications in personalized financial services, credit risk assessment and operational cost reduction.
Earlier this year, Sberbank unveiled Russia's first optical computing processor for AI applications, designed to speed up AI model training and deployment while improving energy efficiency, helping address rising power demands from AI data centers, he added.
In an era of global economic uncertainty, institutional resilience hinges on adaptability and a human-centric philosophy, Skvortsov said. "We believe that in a decade, only enterprises embracing this people-oriented mindset will survive and thrive."
"Companies that fail to prioritize user interests will gradually lose competitiveness and fade from the market," he said. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Japan's household spending dropped 3.6 percent in inflation-adjusted real terms in July from a year earlier, the eighth straight monthly decline, government data showed Friday.
The reading marked the steepest fall since a 6.3 percent slide in January 2024, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications said.
Households of two or more people spent an average of 301,245 yen (around 1,926 U.S. dollars) in the reporting month.
By category, food and beverage spending declined 1.3 percent as inflation weighed on purchases, while cooler weather than the previous year also curbed beverage demand.

Outlays for energy and water bills tumbled 9.2 percent, a drop an official attributed largely to reduced air-conditioning use amid lower temperatures than the same month last year.
The household spending data serves as a key indicator of private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's gross domestic product.
The average monthly income of salaried households of at least two individuals fell by a real 3.8 percent to 689,476 yen, according to the ministry. ■

New Zealand records 3rd-warmest winter on record
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:58:33 CST
14:58:33 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand recorded its third-warmest winter on record in 2026, with a nationwide average temperature of 9.7 degrees Celsius, Earth Sciences New Zealand said Friday.
The temperature was 1.1 degrees Celsius above the 1991-2020 winter average, making it the third-warmest winter since the country's seven-station temperature series began in 1909, the agency said in a statement.
Exceptional warmth in June and a relatively warm winter throughout the South Island were the dominant features of the country's overall seasonal temperature, while temperatures were near average in parts of Northland, Auckland, Waikato, eastern Bay of Plenty and Gisborne on the North Island, it said.
Winter rainfall was above or well above normal in Southland, Otago, southern and inland Canterbury and the West Coast on the South Island, while large parts of the North Island recorded below-normal rainfall, the agency said.
Impactful heavy rainfall from July 5 to July 9 affected eastern parts of the country, with three local states of emergency declared, it noted.
The highest winter temperature was 26 degrees Celsius on June 20 at Bromley in Christchurch, the South Island's largest city. It was the country's second-highest winter temperature on record. The lowest was minus 13.5 degrees Celsius at Lake Tekapo on July 12.
El Niño conditions in the tropical Pacific strengthened considerably from mid-winter onward, the agency said, adding that sea surface temperatures around New Zealand were mostly near or above average, with marine heatwave conditions experienced around much of the South Island and Tasman Sea during July and August.
Scientists said El Niño typically brings stronger, more frequent southwesterly to northwesterly winds, resulting in drier conditions in eastern and northern areas of both islands and wetter conditions in the western and lower South Island. ■

2 trapped Nepal hydropower tunnel workers rescued 9 days after devastating floods
Kathmandu, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday as emergency teams continued an operation to reach others believed to be trapped inside, officials said.
The two men were rescued from the Trishuli 3A tunnel nine days after floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, devastated towns and swept away villages in Nepal on Aug. 26.
Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane posted about the second rescue on his Facebook page shortly after army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker's rescue.
CBS News' Ramy Inocencio reports that "there's renewed hope that we might be seeing more survivors come out — possibly dozens more — because rescuers have already heard more voices deeper in those tunnels."
Nepal Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told Inocencio in a text message that he's "thrilled" about the two rescues and is "hoping to see more survivors." He said it's unclear how many survivors there are, but with those voices being heard, there are more people alive waiting to be saved and the clock is ticking to get to them.
Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning, confirming that people were alive and enabling them to locate the two men, Neupane said.
Local television news channels showed images of the first rescued worker covered in mud and being carried from the site on a rescuer's shoulder. Officials said both men were in stable condition and were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.
When mechanical foreman Sanjay Shah was pulled out, he said "thank you," but he's been advised not to talk anymore because of his condition, CBS News' Inocencio says.
Amir Maharjan, brother of the other rescued worker, mechanical supervisor Kabir Maharjan, told The Associated Press he "can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to God." He said the family was on its way to the hospital to see him.
