Before global fame, Steve Irwin was a wildlife researcher with a tatty green backpack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:34:09 UTC
11:34:09 KST

In brief
- Steve Irwin's friends remember the passionate wildlife researcher behind the global icon.
- Twenty years after his death, his conservation legacy continues to inspire new generations.
Twenty years after Steve Irwin's sudden death, a man who wrestled crocodiles with him for a living still can't talk about it without choking up.
In 2006, while holidaying in France, Mark Read had just returned from a walk with his baby daughter when he found his wife sobbing outside an internet café.
"When I came back, she was sitting in the gutter crying," he recalls.
"She said: 'Steve ... '".
Two decades on, the memories of the man the world knew as the Crocodile Hunter still bring a lump to his throat.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"He's on the photograph on the wall in my lounge room," Read says.
"He's still very much part of us."
Read first met Irwin in 1997 on what can only be described as a very Steve Irwin kind of operation, a turtle rodeo in Queensland's Moreton Bay.
People were tearing around in small, fast boats in shallow water, hurling themselves overboard to wrestle the surprised critters to the surface in order to study their health, breeding status and growth rates.
From that chaotic first encounter, the pair went on to spend years working together on crocodile research across north Queensland.
Their collaboration helped launch a pioneering satellite‑tracking effort dubbed Crocs in Space, a partnership between the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service, Australia Zoo and the University of Queensland.
It used some of the first functional satellite transmitters ever fitted to estuarine crocodiles, revealing how far the big predators could roam and even how many found their way home after relocation.
Far from a caricature, Read remembers Irwin as an extraordinarily intelligent, relentlessly curious collaborator in the field.
Irwin carried a tatty green backpack everywhere he went.
Inside was an even tattier folder and notepad he constantly filled with sketches to capture techniques and ideas for future research.
"You saw all the hallmarks of an incredibly active mind," Read says.
"He was super interested in the science."
There were long, quiet hours that never made it to television — nights around campfires and early mornings when Irwin would wake Read for tea and conversations about crocodiles, wild places and how to get the public to care.
For a man with global reach and serious earning power, Irwin never changed, turning up to remote field trips in boots with holes patched up with gaffer tape.
"This is not a bloke who relaxed on his airs and graces," Read says.
"It most certainly wasn't about earning a heap of money and living a lavish lifestyle."
What struck Read was Irwin's visceral understanding of dangerous animals.
It was in the way he could read a crocodile's body language in a heartbeat or calmly scoop up a six‑foot coastal taipan snake from the grass, keep it unruffled, and then let it slide away as if it were the most natural thing in the world.
"He had this uncanny awareness working with crocodiles and snakes," Read says.
"He was so in tune with them."
He was, Read says, both a "proper stirrer" who loved teasing people in good humour and a deeply tender family man who "lived for his family".
When Steve and Terri Irwin's first daughter was born, they sent boxes of presents and an enormous floral arrangement to the family home.
When the Reads visited Australia Zoo with the baby, Irwin cried upon meeting her.
"He was such a family man. He lived for his family and epitomised that idea of Aussies being the salt of the earth."
It's this mixture of raw emotion, outrageous stunts and genuine care that has kept Irwin's memory alive long after dying from a stingray barb in waters off Port Douglas, North Queensland, on 4 September 2006.
'He inspired whole generations'
For people like Clancy Lester, Irwin has never been forgotten.
Growing up in country Victoria, the native bee researcher says he rarely watched movies or sitcoms on the family TV.
"I loved any nature documentary I could get my hands on," he tells AAP.
"I wasn't interested in watching TV or movies — it was just nature docs — so that's why Steve was always on."
Lester was five or six when Irwin died but the impact has endured.
Asked whether the Crocodile Hunter simply mirrored an existing obsession or lit the spark, he doesn't hesitate.
"Oh no, he absolutely got me interested," he says.
In primary school, when most of his classmates arrived at Book Week dressed as superheroes, Lester turned up in khaki as a tiny Crocodile Hunter.
Years later he completed a master's research project on native bees at the University of Melbourne, specialising in how Australia's pollinators interact with flowering plants.
In workshops, online posts and his Bees and Blossoms business he echoes Irwin's over‑the‑top enthusiasm to get people buzzing about pollinators and native plants.
"I definitely try and channel some of his enthusiasm for nature," Lester says.
"When someone has such a burning passion and is so extreme and just absolutely loves it to bits, it's infectious."
Long before algorithms and clickbait, it was Irwin's charm and love for the natural world that opened doors of wildlife fascination in viewers from Brisbane to New York.
Lester admits he uses Irwin's blueprint: be "a little bit extra", lean into enthusiasm and reach people who might never pick up a conservation report or tune into a science lecture.
"I don't think, I know that he inspired whole generations," he says.
From backpacker hostels overseas to university labs at home, Irwin remains shorthand for Australia itself.
"One of the first things people think of when you mention Australia is snakes and crocodiles and spiders and sharks - and then they go, and you've got the Crocodile Hunter on top," Lester says.
"He's like his own category."
Family carry the torch
Irwin's global recognition has been carried by widow Terri, daughter Bindi and son Robert.
They continue to run Australia Zoo and its wildlife hospital while fronting documentaries, talk shows and social media channels that reach millions.
For them, this anniversary is not just about a global wildlife warrior but a much‑missed family man who has been sadly absent from his children's lives longer than he was in them.
"You'll be my hero for my entire existence. I love you more than words can describe," Bindi wrote in one tribute, alongside a photo of Irwin in his trademark khaki, proudly hoisting his infant daughter.
Where Irwin once leapt into frame with a writhing crocodile, today's conservation influencers are just as likely to be found on TikTok or in classrooms, talking about bees, soil microbes or urban wetlands.
But the template — big‑hearted enthusiasm, simple language and an insistence that even "scary" animals deserve protection — is unmistakably his.
Read sees that clearly in Irwin's son.
"One of his most outstanding legacies is the bloke who comes on television pretty regularly now and just looks like him, sounds like him, has the same mindset as him," he says.
"He's unashamedly using whatever weapons he has in his arsenal to promote conservation."
He believes Irwin would be "super proud" of his family and of what Australia Zoo has become, and still out there pushing hard for wildlife and wild places.
"If we want to change people's behaviours, change their mindset about why conserving species and habitats is important, you've got to give them messages that resonate with their value system," Read says.
"Steve could do that better than anyone."

Ukraine Optimistic On Russia Sanctions Bill As House Vote Window Narrows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:31:35 UTC
11:31:35 KST

WASHINGTON -- Ukraine's top sanctions official says he remains optimistic about prospects for a sweeping Russia sanctions bill in the US Congress despite growing uncertainty over when the House of Representatives will take it up, as lawmakers face a sharply shortened legislative calendar ahead of the November midterm elections.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's sanctions commissioner, spent this week in Washington meeting lawmakers and congressional staff as Kyiv presses Congress to advance the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
The legislation passed the Senate on August 7 by an overwhelming 86-11 vote, reflecting rare bipartisan agreement. The bill would give the president additional authority to impose punitive tariffs on countries that continue buying Russian fossil fuels. It also includes provisions targeting Iran, which Vlasiuk said is engaged in close military-industrial cooperation with Moscow.
But the measure faces a more complicated path in the House, where some Democrats have expressed reservations about provisions that would give President Donald Trump additional authority to impose tariffs.
Republican leaders announced on September 3 that the final two weeks of the pre-election House session are canceled, severely curtailing what had been a full legislative calendar for September.
House members are expected to leave Washington no later than September 17 and not return until mid-November. The House will reconvene for one additional week of business after next week's Labor Day break.
The compressed calendar has increased pressure on supporters of the sanctions legislation. Senior Republican aides told RFE/RL that the bill remains a GOP priority, provided Democrats "get their ducks in a row."
Democratic aides, in response to RFE/RL inquiries, expressed cautious optimism about the measure, underscoring uncertainty over whether Speaker Mike Johnson will bring it to the floor.
Vlasiuk: 'Good Chance'
Vlasiuk said he held roughly 20 meetings with lawmakers and congressional staff during his Washington visit, including discussions with members of both parties.
He said the Ukrainian delegation encountered broad support for increasing pressure on Russia and that no lawmaker told him outright they would oppose the legislation.
"Everyone agreed that it was necessary to increase pressure on Russia," Vlasiuk said at a briefing at the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington. "No one said that he definitely would not support this bill."
He described Ukraine as "quite optimistic" about the level of support for the legislation, including among Democrats.
One potentially important route would be for the House to consider the bill under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure generally used for legislation expected to command broad support. Vlasiuk said that was among the realistic scenarios for moving the bill forward.
"I think that there is really good chance that this bill will be brought onto the floor," he said.
Vlasiuk has previously identified the week after next as Kyiv's preferred window for a House vote. With the House calendar now compressed, that period could provide one of the last opportunities for a vote before lawmakers leave Washington.
Asked by RFE/RL whether the momentum surrounding the bill was still there, Vlasiuk pointed to what he characterized as continued bipartisan backing for Ukraine.
"There is a lot of support for Ukraine on the Hill," he said, adding that Kyiv has been "very vocal" in stressing the urgency of passing the bill. "At the same time, well, I mean, let's wait and see," Vlasiuk said.
Democrats Wary Of Trump Powers
The principal obstacle is not broad disagreement over confronting Russia, according to Thomas Melia, a former senior State Department official and Senate Foreign Relations Committee deputy staff director who is currently with the Free Russia Foundation.
In an interview with RFE/RL, Melia explained that Democratic leaders have several reasons for hesitating. One is that the legislation is not strictly necessary for the administration to impose sanctions, he said. Trump already possesses significant authority to sanction Russian individuals and entities.
The bill's principal value, in Melia's assessment, is therefore partly political and symbolic: Its bipartisan backing would demonstrate congressional resolve to increase pressure on Moscow.
But Melia said the House Democratic leadership was not sufficiently involved in negotiating the version that ultimately emerged from the Senate.
That concern is particularly relevant to Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who has expressed general support for tougher pressure on Russia but has raised concerns about provisions of the legislation.
There is also a substantive concern: The final version of the legislation gives the president additional tariff authority. Melia said that has created hesitation among Democrats who are wary of giving Trump another instrument that could be used broadly against US trading partners.
Melia also emphasized another change from the bill’s earlier form: The final version makes the sanctions optional rather than mandatory.
That distinction matters, he said, because the original legislation's political force came in part from its mandatory sanctions provisions and overwhelming bipartisan support in the Senate.
After the death of Senator Lindsey Graham, the administration backed a version of the legislation but sought changes that made sanctions nonmandatory and added tariff authority, Melia said.
The result, in his view, is a weaker measure than the original. Melia said the final version nevertheless retains substantial political significance because of the broad bipartisan support that surrounded the tougher proposal.
Kyiv Backs Tariffs
Vlasiuk defended the tariff provisions, arguing they could make sanctions substantially more effective. "This is a powerful instrument which will allow to amplify the effect of the sanctions," he said.
He argued that tariffs and sanctions can have similar economic effects but differ in their ability to be circumvented.
"Sanctions can be adapted, sanctions can be evaded. Tariffs cannot be adapted or evaded," Vlasiuk said.
He also rejected concerns that countries could be arbitrarily targeted under the bill, saying the legislation establishes criteria based on purchases of Russian fossil fuels.
In particular, he pointed to China and India, which Ukraine considers central to Russia's continued ability to sell its energy exports.
Vlasiuk said the pressure could represent "a huge blow" to Russia's ability to finance its war against Ukraine.
Ukraine also supports the bill's inclusion of Iran, he said, citing Tehran's close military cooperation with Moscow.
"Everyone understands how close cooperation is between the military-industrial complex of these countries," Vlasiuk said. "Therefore, Iran is very well-deserved."
House Vote Window Narrows
The political stakes are heightened by the House's decision to cancel its final two weeks of pre-election legislative work.
The chamber is expected to depart Washington no later than September 17, although Republican leaders have said members could be recalled if the Senate advances a party-line budget reconciliation package. That scenario is not currently expected.
Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska, a Republican who has supported the sanctions effort, described the lack of congressional action as a serious failure.
"This is a real shame. It passed 86-11 in the Senate," Bacon said. "Congressional inaction on Russia's invasion of Ukraine and on Putin’s crimes is a real failure. The history books will not be kind."
For Kyiv, the urgency is not simply legislative.
Vlasiuk warned that Ukraine faces another difficult winter after months of Russian missile and drone attacks. He said 160 people had been killed in missile and drone strikes in recent months.
"We have to increase the pressure over Russia to make them change their plans, to make them really negotiate," he said.
He argued that passing the sanctions bill now would have two effects: It could eventually increase economic pressure on Russia, while immediately sending a political signal to both Ukraine and the Russian government.
There is, he said, an element of inertia in sanctions policy. Even after legislation passes, implementing measures can take days, and producing a significant effect on Russia’s economy can take weeks.
"But at the same time, the very fact of passing this sanction bill," Vlasiuk said, would send a "strong signal of support to Ukrainian people" and a "really strong signal to Russian government."

India’s national space agency launched a rocket Friday carrying an Earth-imaging satellite, successfully placing it into orbit.
“Mission Success! GSLV-F17 has successfully accomplished its mission, placing EOS-05 into the intended orbit,” the Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) announced in a post on the US social media platform X.

Boost for EVs: Chinese carmaker Chery to begin testing solid-state batteries next year
Chairman says it plans to invest US$1.49 billion in the new battery technology over the next two years
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Daniel Renin Shanghai
Chery Automobile, China’s largest car exporter by deliveries, will begin testing its solid-state batteries next year, aiming to spearhead commercialisation of a technology likely to further spur the electrification of the global automotive industry.
Yin Tongyue, the chairman of the state-owned carmaker, which is based in central China’s Anhui province, said on Thursday that it would invest 10 billion yuan (US$1.49 billion) in the new battery technology over the next two years, with 1,200 engineers to be deployed in the hunt for innovative breakthroughs.
“Multiple [battery] technology plans are being laid out,” he told the World Power Battery Conference in Yibin, Sichuan province, the National Business Daily reported. “We will not install them in our vehicles unless they prove to be absolutely safe.”
He said the solid-state batteries to be tested next year would have an energy density of 400 watt-hours per kilogram, double that of the batteries used in existing electric vehicles (EVs).
Solid-state batteries, which use a solid electrolyte to conduct ions between electrodes, are widely seen as a superior alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries, which rely on liquid or gel-based materials. Analysts said the technology promised higher energy density, improved safety and longer driving range.
But no solid-state batteries have been installed in mass-produced EVs.

Five more Ukrainians return from occupied territories
The “Bring Kids Back UA” initiative reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
As part of the Ukrainian President’s “Bring Kids Back UA” initiative, the Helping to Leave team worked together to successfully return Natalia, Katya, and Maria (names changed for security reasons) to territory controlled by Ukraine.
Natalia and Katya are sisters from a large family. Their older brothers had left the temporarily occupied territory earlier, so the girls and their mother eventually decided to leave as well and turned to Helping to Leave for assistance. The team helped the family organize their route and accompanied them during their departure. With the assistance of the Coordination Headquarters, the sisters received permits to return to Ukraine and, together with their mother, successfully crossed the border.
Today, the family is in territory controlled by Ukraine and is reunited with their older brothers. The girls plan to continue their lives here.
Maria left a part of the Luhansk region occupied by Russia back in 2014. There, she managed to complete only one grade under the Ukrainian curriculum before being forced to study under the Russian one. Maria also reached out to Helping to Leave. The team helped plan her route, and with the assistance of the Coordination Headquarters, she received a return permit and was able to travel to territory controlled by Ukraine.
Maria is now back in Ukraine. She plans to finish 11th grade and then work and build her future here.
Also, as part of the President of Ukraine’s “Bring Kids Back UA” initiative, thanks to the efforts of the Compass of Dreams NGO team, two more young people were successfully returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Eighteen-year-old Kyrylo (name changed for security reasons) had been living under occupation since 2014, when he was still a child. His family supported his desire to live and study in a free Ukraine. Therefore, even before reaching the age of majority, he enrolled remotely in a Ukrainian institution of higher education. The team at the “Compass of Dreams” NGO helped Kyrylo obtain the necessary documents and arranged his departure. Just one week after turning 18, he was able to leave the temporarily occupied territory and return to free Ukraine.
Seventeen-year-old Maria (name changed for security reasons) was still a child when Russia occupied her hometown in 2022. The occupiers quickly closed Ukrainian schools, but she refused to attend a Russian school and, despite the risks, secretly continued her Ukrainian education online. Maria and her parents were pressured to obtain Russian passports, but the family refused. The pressure intensified when Russian soldiers came to their home, ostensibly to “get to know them.” Despite this, Maria remotely earned a Ukrainian high school diploma and enrolled in college under Quota-2. The young woman reached out to the NGO “Compass of Dreams” for help several months before her departure. After careful preparation, Maria, along with her grandmother, was able to leave the temporarily occupied territory. She is now in Chernivtsi and will begin her freshman year and a new life in a free Ukraine this September.
As reported by Ukrinform, at the end of August, 23 Ukrainians returned home from the temporarily occupied territories—including elderly people, citizens with limited mobility, Ukrainians with health issues, and families with children.

Pacific summit backs concerns over China missile test despite Nauru dissent
- Pacific Island leaders expressed concern over China’s July missile test, urging transparency and advance warnings for such tests in the region.
- Nauru dissented from the consensus, reflecting its recent diplomatic ties with China amid regional disagreements.
- China dismissed claims of threats, accusing Palau of exaggeration and opposing Taiwan’s participation in the summit, which caused tensions among members.
AI generated
SYDNEY – Pacific Island leaders expressed concern about China’s Pacific missile test at their annual summit, though Nauru formally dissented, in a meeting largely overshadowed by Beijing’s objections to Taiwan’s presence.
Summit host and Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr said on Sept 3 that China’s intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test in July, Beijing’s first known launch in the Pacific since September 2024, passed over several island nations without adequate warning.
“Leaders called on all states undertaking ICBM testing to ensure transparency and reassurance, including through the provision of advance notification of a test at least 24 hours in accordance with international practice,” he said at a media briefing at the conclusion of the Pacific Islands Forum.
“I might note that the Republic of Nauru has dissented,” he added, reading from a prepared statement.
Nauru, which has a history of switching diplomatic recognition between Beijing and Taipei, re-established diplomatic ties with China in 2024.
China’s Foreign Ministry, in response to the statement, said the country is committed to peaceful development and pursues a defensive national defence policy, adding that it has never engaged in military expansion.
“China is willing to work with South Pacific countries to contribute to safeguarding peace, stability, development and prosperity in the region,” ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a regular press conference.
Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who attended the summit with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, said on Sept 4 it was “perfectly reasonable for the vast majority of Pacific countries to express a view and for one or two to say that they have a different view”.
“Unanimity is not necessary to express very strong views on behalf of the vast majority of the Pacific island states, which was very clear,” Bowen told ABC Radio.
Beijing accuses Palau of ‘hype’ over missile test
The consensus came after a meeting of the 18-member grouping’s foreign ministers in August failed to agree on a statement condemning the test, despite public and private expressions of concern from several leaders about the region’s militarisation.
Palau, one of three Pacific island nations that maintain official diplomatic ties with Taiwan, had pushed the group to formally condemn the missile test.
Beijing pushed back on Sept 3, accusing Palau of stirring “hype” over the missile test and warning that its attempts to influence fellow Pacific island nations were “malicious and will not succeed”.
The summit was further strained by China’s objections to Taiwan’s participation, with Beijing arguing the island was not qualified to attend. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory – a position Taiwan firmly rejects.
Proceedings were also overshadowed by the absence of five Pacific leaders, who sent low-ranking ministers in their place.
The next Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ summit will be hosted by New Zealand in 2027. REUTERS

Musk super PAC wades into US midterms with $800,000 for Republicans in close races
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:21:19 UTC
11:21:19 KST

Elon Musk’s super PAC wades into US midterms with more than $1m for Republicans in close races
NEW YORK – SpaceX founder Elon Musk has spent more than US$800,000 (S$1 million) in recent days on over a dozen key congressional races through his super Political Action Committee (PAC), funding direct-mail and other campaign materials for Republican candidates who face close races in the midterm elections.
Musk’s America PAC, which has been sitting on a US$50 million war chest funded by the world’s richest man, reported its first spending for the 2026 election in a filing late on Sept 2, with a focus on races in Texas and other battleground states.
The PAC expects to play a major role in Republican voter turnout efforts, with spending on door knockers, digital advertising and direct-mail campaigns ahead of the Nov 3 election, Reuters reported in July. It has a funding target of up to US$120 million, according to The New York Times.
A spokesperson for America PAC declined to comment on Sept 3. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The PAC spent the most money in Texas, where Musk’s SpaceX is headquartered with multiple rocket and Starlink facilities.
Texas Attorney-General Ken Paxton has received a US$247,595 boost from Musk since Aug 20 for his Senate race against Democrat James Talarico, who has been narrowly leading in public opinion polls since mid-April according to election tracker Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin.
US Senator Susan Collins, a Maine Republican and the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee which controls federal spending, was the next biggest beneficiary with US$170,224 going towards her campaign, the filing shows. She is in a closely watched race against Democrat Troy Jackson.
In Ohio, where Republican Senator Jon Husted faces a tough battle to keep his seat against former senator Sherrod Brown, America PAC has printed US$105,675 in materials.
Like Collins, Husted sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee which controls the funding for some of Musk’s biggest government contracts at SpaceX.
The PAC’s filing showed Musk also boosted the campaign of Senator Dan Sullivan, an Alaska Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
That committee oversees the Pentagon and many of the projects that Musk’s space, satellite and artificial intelligence companies provide to the federal government.
In US House races, Musk’s PAC boosted several sitting members of the Armed Services, Foreign Affairs and Homeland Security committees as well as other committees that may touch on or oversee the work of his companies.
They include Republican Representatives Scott Perry and Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania, Tom Kean of New Jersey, Jennifer Kiggans of Virginia, Mike Lawler of New York and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin.
All of the spending disclosed on the night of Sept 2 was for “printing”, suggesting that it was used for direct-mail, postcards, door hangers, canvassing literature, yard signs and the like.
The spending has drawn criticism from Democrats, including US Representative Chris Pappas, who is favoured in polls to win next week’s Democratic primary for the New Hampshire Senate race.
If victorious, he would face former Republican Senator John Sununu, who is running for his old seat.
Musk’s PAC spent more than US$90,000 on materials opposing Pappas, who has been highly critical of Musk’s past work running the Department of Government Efficiency.
“MAGA Republicans like Elon Musk are trying to buy this Senate seat for John Sununu because they know he would be a rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s toxic agenda,” Rachel Petri, Pappas’ campaign manager, said in a statement to Reuters.
Sununu’s office did not return a request for comment.
A spokesman for US Representative Ryan Mackenzie said the campaign has not talked with any super PACs, including Musk’s, about coordinated campaign spending.
Spokesman Arnaud Armstrong said Mackenzie was a champion for government reform “leading the charge to crack down on congressional stock trading, taking on large corporations and holding big tech accountable”.
A spokesperson for Husted declined to comment while representatives for the other Republican candidates did not immediately return requests for comment. REUTERS

VLADIVOSTOK, September 4. /TASS/. Russian Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilyov earlier said that the project was in the final stages of preparations for the construction phase.

====================================================================================================

‘They’ll be finding bodies next year’: a renowned forensic scientist on Nepal’s ‘extreme challenges’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:02:42 UTC
11:02:42 KST

The bodies of some of those killed in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster may never be found, and some of those that are may never be identified, a world-renowned forensic scientist says.
Prof Richard Bassed, the head of forensic medicine at Melbourne’s Monash University, spent three months in Thailand after the 2004 Boxing Day tsunami and also helped to identify victims of Victoria’s catastrophic Black Saturday bushfires in 2009.
Now he has watched as authorities in Nepal and Tibet struggle to find and identify the dead amid the agonies of the living after last week’s devastating flash flood. More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead, with more than 5,000 missing.
The difficult terrain, and inadequate communications and resources, would all hamper efforts, Bassed says.
“They could be washed anywhere, buried under mud. I imagine there’s a number they’ll never find. I imagine they’ll be finding bodies next year.”
Authorities are still finding bodies from the 2011 Japanese tsunami, he says.
The bodies from the 2004 tsunami were relatively easy to recover, but it still took a year to identify 5,000 people, he says.
“And there were still some we couldn’t identify.”
Asked how he copes with the horror of death on such a scale, he says he has “never found it long-term traumatising”.
“Occasionally you’ll see something that’ll hit close to home. For me, it’s kids,” he says.
“And the randomness. The randomness of a tsunami, the randomness of this massive flood. That gets to you.
“But mostly you have your clinical face on, you do the best you can and know you’re doing it to help people.”
Authorities will use rapidly improving DNA techniques to try to identify the victims. This week Nepali police urged relatives of missing tourists to provide “a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the police hospital in Kathmandu.
But authorities in Nepal and Tibet face “extreme challenges”, Bassed says.
They include the danger of more mudslides, the complexity of co-ordinating across international borders and the likelihood of local mortuaries and other infrastructure being overwhelmed by the number of bodies.
The mix of nations and religions also brings issues of different cultural beliefs around how and whether people should be buried.
The International Committee of the Red Cross and other international bodies have published Management of dead bodies after disasters: A field manual for First Responders to help people deal with bodies in a “proper and dignified way”, including by taking down details that will later help experts identify the remains.
First responders – often locals who are not forensic experts – are trained to follow those guidelines, tagging bodies in the hope they will later be matched to a missing person.
They give each body a unique code (for example the name of the place, the name of the team and a number). They will also take photos of the body and any distinguishing features such as gold teeth, clothing and tattoos, including that code in the image.
Then they place the body in a body bag and organise its “orderly temporary storage”, again marked with the body code.
In Nepal, morgues are filling up and mass burials are taking place, as authorities collect DNA samples.
Bassed says most of the missing Australians would have dental records, which could help to identify them, but in Nepal many matches will be made using DNA or pictures, as fingerprints will often no longer be usable.
Work is under way to use AI and facial recognition technology to identify victims after disasters, but it’s controversial – Ukraine used Clearview AI software after the Russian invasion in 2022, just as the company was fined millions of dollars for collecting images of people in the UK and elsewhere without consent. Widespread use is also limited by access to the technology.
Bassed says researchers have also worked to devise an algorithm that could use passport or driver’s licence photos to identify someone.
“But it’s really complex, and it depends how they look, the trauma,” he says.
Another possibility is CT scanning, which can get a serial number from joint replacements, for example.
“But trying to get this technology to the places it’s needed in the middle of a disaster … you need running water, you need electricity … you could put CT scanners into helicopters, but all this costs an awful lot of money.”

Friedrich Merz will lose Sunday’s regional election — whatever the result
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

Friedrich Merz will lose Sunday’s regional election — whatever the result
An outright win for the far right in Saxony-Anhalt will hurt Merz. But things will also be messy if his party has to form coalitions with left-wingers to box out the AfD.
Friedrich Merz during final press conference after two-day retreat of the federal government coalition cabinet at Schloss Neuhardenberg. | Michele Tantussi/Getty Images
MAGDEBURG, Germany — For Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Sunday’s election in eastern Germany offers no good outcomes — only varying degrees of political humiliation.
The Alternative for Germany, or AfD, is expected to win decisively in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, finishing well ahead of Merz’s conservatives, according to pre-election polls. This result would show, in the clearest terms, the degree to which the far right has strengthened and surpassed mainstream parties in broad swaths of the country.
That humiliation would be even worse for Merz if the AfD wins enough votes to secure an outright parliamentary majority and govern the state alone. At least from the perspective of Germany’s mainstream parties, it would give him an ignominious place in the country’s postwar history as the national leader who presided over the far-right’s first rise to real governing power since World War II.
Advertisement
But the other likely outcomes offer little relief for Merz.
If the AfD falls short of a governing majority in the state — an outcome that appears increasingly likely based on the latest polling — Merz’s second-place Christian Democratic Union will face a series of untenable choices as it tries to cobble together a coalition with left-wing parties. Any such alliance would likely be doomed from the outset, while remaining dependent on far-left or far-right support to pass legislation.
Concerns are also mounting that the AfD may be preparing for this scenario by challenging the outcome of Sunday’s election. The party has already issued press releases casting doubt on mail-in ballots, while its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, has voiced similar concerns on social media.
Whatever the result on Sunday, the election could set off a chain of events for Merz — already a historically weak leader — that could ultimately lead to his downfall, and it’s unclear whether the chancellor has a coherent strategy for dealing with the fallout.
In the lead-up to the vote, Merz almost seemed to be in a state of denial.
“I’m not speculating today about what will happen the day after [the election],” Merz said in a television interview last Sunday. “We’ll assess the situation in light of the election results, and we’ll do everything we can to prevent Saxony-Anhalt from falling into the hands of the radicals.”
Advertisement
Billboards and election posters featuring election campaign ads for various parties are pictured in Magdeburg. | Ronny Hartmann/AFP via Getty Images
But the chancellor comes into the election in Saxony-Anhalt — and two more elections on Sept. 20 — in a precarious position. Already the least popular chancellor on record after 16 months in office, Merz’s fellow conservatives have been quietly debating what would be a remarkable scenario by German standards: replacing the chancellor — a so-called Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap.
“Given the dissatisfaction, the poll numbers and the fact that there are additional elections coming up next year … the pressure for fundamental change will naturally increase,” said Julian Schache, a CDU politician from Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt’s capital. “I could certainly imagine that some will push for Friedrich Merz to step down. But whether that’s the solution remains to be seen.
Already, conservative politicians in eastern Germany don’t want Merz on the campaign trail. In the rare appearances he’s made in the region earlier, he was booed. Angry voters yelled “Pinocchio” and “warmongerer” during a visit this week, after which a planned press statement was canceled.
Scenario 1 — AfD wins power
If the AfD can win enough votes to govern alone in Saxony-Anhalt, it would in some respects be a simpler, easier outcome for Merz’s conservatives.
Some CDU politicians in the state see notable advantages that would give conservatives the benefit of what the AfD has long enjoyed — the ability to attack the government from the comfort of the opposition bench. Conservatives believe an AfD stint in government could well turn into a debacle that would demystify the far right — allowing for a later resurgence of the CDU.
“On the day [Siegmund] becomes premier, he’s finished,” said Alexander Räuscher, a CDU lawmaker from Saxony-Anhalt, referring to the AfD’s lead candidate in the race. “That’s my speculation. He’ll fail as state premier. He won’t be able to fulfill all the promises he’s made.”
Advertisement
But this outcome is still fraught with major risks that could speed Merz’s downfall, because the political pressure on Merz and his conservatives is likely only to further rise after the Saxony-Anhalt election.
The AfD is expected to win a regional election in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and is even polling strongly in the left-leaning bastion of Berlin ahead of votes later this month; four additional state elections are set for next year.
CDU lawmakers fear a major loss in Saxony-Anhalt would snowball into further big defeats. It could also lead to open conflict in the party about whether to maintain Merz’s “firewall” around the AfD — the promise not to govern with the far right — which some conservatives believe has only strengthened the AfD by forcing them to govern with left-wing parties.
Supporters gather at the AfD election campaign launch event ahead of Saxony-Anhalt state elections. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images
There are already some signs of open dissent with Merz’s vow not to formally cooperate with the far right, especially in the East.
“Anyone who still talks about firewalls hasn’t recognized the signs of the times,” Michael Kretschmer, the CDU premier of the eastern state of Saxony, said in July.
Scenario 2 — Conservatives forced into minority government supported by the far left
If the AfD fails to win an absolute majority, it will force the CDU to attempt to govern in some form with the remaining parties — likely all of them on the political left, including the far-left Die Linke, or The Left party.
Advertisement
But Merz’s CDU has ruled out any formal cooperation not only with the AfD, but also with Die Linke — which, according to polls, is set to come in third place. As a result, the CDU would likely form a minority government with the center-left Social Democratic Party, set to come in fourth place, and also potentially the Greens.
But given the election math, there would be no clear way out of working with Die Linke in some form, at least while excluding cooperation with the AfD. This would make the CDU dependent on Die Linke’s support to elect its premier and pass legislation.
There’s some precedent for this arrangement. In the eastern states of Thuringia and Saxony, the CDU leads minority governments with formalized support from Die Linke. The far-left party has said it will support a similar arrangement in Saxony-Anhalt, but would demand a price.
An election poster by the state of Saxony-Anhalt reading “We have a choice” and “Your Vote for Democracy and Diversity.” | Ronny Hartmann/AFP via Getty Images
But internal CDU resistance to such a constellation is growing. A local CDU group already rejected any governing coalition that could survive only with the “goodwill, toleration or explicit consent” of the Die Linke.
“A model that gives the Left a de facto veto over the entire work of a center-right government is unacceptable,” the paper says.
Ultimately, these politicians contend that governing alongside left-wing parties is actively strengthening the AfD, handing it ammunition to portray conservatives as leftists in disguise.
Advertisement
Such a scenario could leave the CDU fighting, again, over the tactical wisdom of the firewall — and further weaken the party politically.
It would leave Saxony-Anhalt virtually ungovernable. More consequentially for national politics, it could fuel the kind of frustration within the CDU that ultimately brings about Merz’s downfall.

Ukraine, Poland explore joint FIFA World Cup bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

The FIFA World Cup Trophy is displayed during the FIFA World Cup 2026 Official Draw at the John F. Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. | Pool photo by Mandel Ngan/Getty Images
Ukraine and Poland are weighing up a joint bid to host the biggest sporting event on the planet: the men’s FIFA World Cup.
Kyiv’s sports minister Matvii Bidnyi told POLITICO that Ukraine, which is currently fending off the Kremlin’s yearslong full-scale invasion, would like to host with Poland in the next open World Cup slot. Poland is discussing the prospect, according to an official briefed by the Warsaw government.
“The nearest open date for the World Cup is somewhere in the 2040s … so we need to plan for this perspective right now,” said Bidnyi, as he confirmed his country was interested in exploring a joint-hosting bid. Spain, Portugal and Morocco are hosting in 2030, and Saudi Arabia is the lone host in 2034.
Advertisement
Ukraine already has experience organizing a major tournament with Poland, Bidnyi added, pointing to the men’s Euro 2012 football championship. “It would be very logical to repeat this successful case,” he said, noting that such a bid could also “invite investors’ attention.”
Any proposal would unfold in a dramatically different context from Euro 2012. Russia’s assault has left Ukraine with reconstruction and recovery needs estimated at nearly $588 billion over the next decade — almost three times the country’s projected nominal GDP for 2025 — according to an assessment by the Ukrainian government, the World Bank Group, the European Commission and the United Nations.
Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin’s onslaught also shows no signs of abating, as Russian forces push to occupy Ukraine and bombard major cities across the country almost every night. Addressing the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 1, Assembly President Annalena Baerbock said there was “no safe space left” in the country and that civilian casualties during the first half of 2026 were 114 percent higher than during the same period in 2024.
The Donbas Arena offers a glimpse into the infrastructure challenges Ukraine would face in hosting another major tournament. The futuristic stadium in Donetsk staged five Euro 2012 matches, but in 2014 Russian-backed separatists seized control of parts of the region and fighting broke out between them and the Ukrainian army. FC Shakhtar Donetsk, the domestic club that played in the stadium, was forced to leave the city and shelling later damaged the arena. The club has never been able to return and now plays its home games in western Ukraine.
The politics behind the cup
The World Cup is frequently staged with political tensions as a backdrop. Russia itself hosted in 2018, years after Putin annexed Crimea and instigated the war in eastern Ukraine. Some Western politicians called on FIFA to strip Russia of its hosting rights, but the tournament went ahead as planned, offering Moscow an opportunity to project an image of normalcy and prestige amid continued criticism of its belligerent foreign policy.
Artists perform during the opening ceremony ahead of the 2026 World Cup. | Alfredo Estrella/AFP via Getty Images
Pressed on whether the Polish-Ukrainian idea reflected live discussions or a longer-term postwar ambition, Bidnyi said, “We will work on it … we continue to be the country who is directed on the biggest sports achievements. It’s part of our national culture, and we want to develop it despite all these difficulties.”
Any formal push, he noted, would need to originate with the sports community or football federations themselves. “We’re interested in it, but … it starts from the initiatives of sports community or sports federation. So we will see,” he said.
The idea was also raised in conversations on the sidelines of this year’s Ukraine Recovery Conference in Gdańsk, according to the official briefed by the Polish government, who was granted anonymity to talk about private discussions. The country’s sports ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
Fragile friendship
Poland and Ukraine’s wartime partnership has become strained, as a dispute over historical memory spills into a broader political row.
Tensions flared in June after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy renamed a military unit after the “Heroes of the UPA,” a nationalist force that fought for Ukrainian independence but also carried out massacres of Polish civilians during World War II.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki responded by stripping Zelenskyy of Poland’s highest state honor and threatening to block Ukraine’s path to EU membership unless Kyiv issued an apology. Prime Minister Donald Tusk sought to defuse the dispute, warning politicians on both sides against turning it into a “strategic mistake” that could benefit Russia.
Advertisement
An August poll found that 46 percent of Poles now view relations with Ukraine negatively — the highest share on record.
Vasyl Mokan, a member of Ukraine’s parliament and deputy chair of its Committee on Youth and Sports, said the committee had not received official information confirming that discussions over a possible bid had taken place — though he called the proposal “both compelling and full of potential.”
“A joint FIFA World Cup bid by Ukraine and Poland would be much more than a major sporting event,” he said. “It would serve as a powerful symbol of European solidarity with Ukraine.”
An end to the war, a just and lasting peace, and credible long-term security guarantees would be essential prerequisites for hosting matches in Ukraine, Mokan said.
“Without these conditions, it would be premature to speak about hosting a FIFA World Cup in Ukraine,” he said — adding that if Ukraine aspires to co-host the tournament one day, “preparations must begin now through consistent long-term planning.”
Any candidacy would still hinge on security conditions, infrastructure development and FIFA’s formal bidding process.

UN to vote on adopting new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:00:54 UTC
11:00:54 KST

The UN general assembly will vote on Friday on a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.
Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said the resolution was sponsored by Togo and backed by countries including the African Union’s 54 other member states. He did not specify the total number.
“This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality,” he said.
UN resolutions are non-enforceable but if the vote passes, it could lead to an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology, given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.
The layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later it remains the global standard.
Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.
“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.
Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.
Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This, they say, has reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.
One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.
Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign is promoting the use of the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.
Some analysts agree too. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.
He added: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”
Togolese authorities hope the vote will go the same way as another African Union-backed decision at the UN this year. In March a Ghana-sponsored resolution to describe the slave trade as “gravest crime against humanity” passed, with 123 states voting in favour. Three states voted no and 52 abstained.
Ghana’s success has given supporters of the map cause to believe in a favourable outcome. Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.
Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say, why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”
He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

President Javier Milei has said that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the Falkland Islands, pointing to Washington's readiness to review its neutrality on his country's territorial dispute with Britain.
"There are winds of change in the world that are favourable to our claim," Milei said in a nationally televised address on Thursday about the South Atlantic archipelago, a British territory.
Britain and Argentina fought a war over the islands in 1982.
Control of the islands, referred to by Argentines as Las Malvinas, remains a highly emotive issue in Argentina and periodically leads to tensions with Britain.
Argentina players held up a banner saying "The Falklands are Argentine" after beating England 2-1 in the World Cup semi-final earlier this year.
The fate of the islands has hit headlines again in recent days, with US President Donald Trump threatening to wade into the dispute and a British-Israeli oil project near the islands causing anger in Argentina.
Push back
Flanked by cabinet members, Milei assured Argentina would not "stand idly by" and announced tougher sanctions on firms linked to Falklands oil projects.
On Tuesday, Argentine Falklands War veterans and environmental lawyers filed a lawsuit to halt the project promoted by the British company Rockhopper and the Israeli company Navitas in waters north of the islands.
Milei said the project violated a United Nations resolution calling on both sides to desist from unilateral actions in the Falklands while the dispute is ongoing.
"We will not allow it," he said.
"If we allow it, we will be creating an incentive for the British government to deepen the occupation of the islands and the exploitation of our resources."
His address comes as his approval ratings plummet, just over a year before he seeks re-election.
Polls show only around 34 percent of Argentines supporting his actions.
The Falkland Islands have a population of 3,000 to 3,600 people. In a 2013 referendum, over 90 percent voted in favour of remaining an overseas UK territory.

Germany’s far-right moment hastens EU’s push for €2T budget deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Germany’s far-right moment hastens EU’s push for €2T budget deal
With the AfD on course to win the Saxony-Anhalt state election, the need to secure an agreement on Brussels’ spending power is more pressing than ever.
Young neo-Nazis with German flags, including one young man with a t-shirt that reads: "Germania", wait to be allowed by police to resume their demonstration march on April 26, 2025 in Berlin, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The prospect of the far right running a German state for the first time since 1945 will provide the clearest warning yet to EU governments about the urgency of striking a deal on the bloc’s next seven-year budget.
Sunday’s regional election in Saxony-Anhalt is giving European diplomats cause to sound the alarm over how disagreements between countries will only get worse next year. With 2027 set to see votes in France, Spain, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia and Slovakia, the prospect of other Euroskeptic voices sweeping to power — with a mandate to make the EU less expensive and less powerful — is focusing minds on getting a deal on the budget before the end of the year, four diplomats and officials told POLITICO.
With its mix of nationalism and anti-migration rhetoric, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is on course to be within a few seats of winning an absolute parliamentary majority in the east German state on Sunday. While that won’t directly change the country’s national leadership, votes in other countries next year might.
Advertisement
“With four of the five largest EU member states voting in parliamentary or presidential elections, it will be more difficult to reach an agreement, especially if we look at the rise of anti-European populism,” said Siegfried Mureșan, the Parliament’s lead lawmaker on the budget. “Everyone understands the obvious negative consequences of a delayed adoption and entry into force of the MFF [the Multiannual Financial Framework, the seven-year budget].”
Negotiations on the budget — which must be agreed by all 27 governments — have been deadlocked for months. Neither of the two main groups of countries, those that want the EU to have more to spend and those that want it to have less, has seen an advantage in giving ground so far. European Council President António Costa is currently touring capitals in an effort to narrow differences.
“Saxony-Anhalt could really define the fall,” said one of those diplomats involved in the talks. “It will make it clear that it is crucial to get agreement this year. If we don’t get it in December, it can’t be February or March, that will be too close to the French election.”
Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), attends an AfD-sponsored outing of Simson motorcycle enthusiasts ahead of upcoming state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on July 26, 2026 in Weissenfels, Germany. The AfD is currently leading in polls in state elections scheduled for September 6 by such a wide margin that it could possibly hold a majority in the state parliament. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images
Brussels is spooked by the prospect of France’s far-right veteran Marine Le Pen winning the country’s presidential election, scheduled to start on April 18, and following through on her campaign pledge to halve France’s contribution to the EU budget, the diplomats and EU officials said.
Macron’s challenge
But while at the European level that adds urgency for France to get a deal before the election, domestic pressures make it more complicated.
Macron, whose far-right opponents are pushing for massive reductions in the country’s own EU contributions, is under pressure to get a deal that won’t worsen Paris’ national economic woes. He is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, known as “own resources,” as a way to pay for the bloc’s priorities without capitals being stuck with the bill themselves. France wants to give Brussels the power to put levies on U.S. digital giants, foreign polluters and online gambling.
“Any agreement without own resources will be a no-go for France,” said an EU official. “We get it.”
Advertisement
The disagreements got another airing at a meeting of European ministers which kicked off on Thursday in Ireland, which holds the six-month rotating presidency of the Council of the EU. Germany is leading a group of countries that want the EU budget to be smaller than that proposed by the European Commission, but any cuts will hit the very areas Brussels most wants to strengthen — competitiveness, defense and security — EU Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin told reporters on the sidelines of the meeting.
Those top priorities could “become the first victims of cuts,” he said.
The budget will be discussed at a summit of EU leaders on Oct. 15, where Ireland will present an updated negotiating position. An additional summit is expected to be held Nov. 26-27, two officials confirmed, to advance the talks and a final, potentially very long, meeting will take place in December, where leaders will be persuaded not to leave without striking a deal, they said.
‘Difficult choices’
Countries are still split on the scale of the budget, with a handful of wealthier countries led by Germany pushing for hundreds of billions of euros to be shaved off the seven-year spending plan. Others, including Romania, Poland and other net recipients of EU funds, want to maintain the size of the pot. Meanwhile, the EU’s frontier countries have launched a push for more funding to deal with Russia’s hybrid threats and shore up their economies.
“The next EU budget will inevitably involve difficult choices. There will never be enough money for every priority,” Estonian Prime Minister Kirsten Michal said following a meeting with Costa last week. “But the choice should be clear: Europe cannot ask its eastern members to carry a growing security burden while funding priorities as if the world had not changed.”
The deadlock, while profound, looks likely to be resolved by a flurry of talks for the rest of this year, those involved in the negotiations said. “Everybody seems to be aware of and committed to the end-of-year deadline,” said one of the officials. Costa’s “key message has been we need to get this deal over the line by then because of the context.”
Advertisement
Asked whether elections — including in Saxony-Anhalt — were creating a sense of urgency in budget talks, Ireland’s Europe Minister Thomas Byrne, who is steering the negotiations on behalf of the EU presidency country, said Dublin had a simple agenda: “To get it done by the end of the year in order that the legislation can be passed next year.”
Another diplomat, from a country that wants to see the budget to be smaller than that the Commission proposed, put it more bluntly: “If you want to do it, you have to do it within the next three months. After that, maybe the party is over for all of us.”

Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella struggle to stay on the same page

11:00:00 KST

PARIS — Jordan Bardella spent months preparing to replace Marine Le Pen as France’s far-right presidential candidate. Now he has a different challenge: falling back in line behind her.
In just a few days, the two leaders of the National Rally have struck competing notes on sensitive issues, from pensions and the high-profile departure of a top adviser to a long-standing proposal by Le Pen to ban hijabs.
Once seen as his party’s most likely candidate, the 30-year-old member of the European Parliament had to step aside in early July after a court shortened Le Pen’s sentence for embezzlement of EU funds, allowing her to run.
Advertisement
In positioning himself for a possible campaign, Bardella had tried to soften the National Rally’s image, especially on the economy, in an attempt to appeal to more moderate voters the party will likely need to win next year’s presidential election.
Le Pen is leading the polls in a crowded field, making it likely she will win the first round of the French election and advance to the two-candidate runoff — a feat she has accomplished twice before, only to lose to French President Emmanuel Macron.
Tensions between the two have bubbled just below the surface in the weeks since Le Pen reasserted herself as the party’s presidential standard-bearer.
On the day after the July verdict, Bardella stood stern-faced beside his mentor as she sought to cast their relationship as a partnership, with Le Pen as the candidate for France’s highest office and her protégé as her pick for prime minister, a much less powerful role.
Bardella did not attend a presidential debate last week in which Le Pen doubled down on a campaign promise to roll back a key element of Macron’s pension reform and allow workers to retire at 62.
He had openly questioned that policy earlier this year as part of his campaign to cast himself as a fiscally responsible leader.
Advertisement
As Le Pen outlined her economic agenda at the debate, news broke that François Durvye, one of her key economic advisers and a leading advocate of fiscal discipline, was leaving the campaign.
The former financier left after he had reportedly pushed Bardella to rebel and run instead of Le Pen. He also made clear privately and publicly that he did not feel able to defend the party’s positions on the economy.
Pressed by reporters at a campaign event, Bardella described the departure as Durvye’s “personal decision” — seemingly contradicting Le Pen, who said on the sidelines of the debate that it had been “her wish.”
Jean-Philippe Tanguy is pictured in the National Assembly in Paris on July 6, 2026. | Julien de Rosa/AFP via Getty Images
Tensions were also on display this week after one of Le Pen’s top lieutenants, MP Jean-Philippe Tanguy, said that wearing the hijab in public would become a fineable offense if she took office, a controversial measure rivals say is unconstitutional.
The day after, Bardella appeared to downplay the proposal, saying instead it would be up to French voters to decide via a proposed referendum, which Le Pen later said would include a series of measures that would “fight Islamist ideology.”
National Rally officials have sought to downplay the disagreements between the two leaders.
Advertisement
“There was an internal debate, and the conclusion was the proposed hijab ban,” said Laurent Jacobelli, a member of Parliament and a spokesperson for the National Rally. “It was settled with everyone’s agreement, Jordan included.”
“There was agreement on the ban itself,” Jacobelli added. “What got debated was the how … There were no tensions.”
Alexandre Loubet, a member of Parliament for the National Rally, acknowledged that the party was still discussing the details of some elements of the platform.
“There are still many things that need deciding,” Loubet told POLITICO at an agricultural fair where Bardella was making an appearance Saturday.
Loubet acknowledged the party was still working out the numbers to pay for the cost of rolling back Macron’s reform. Le Pen has promised to present a plan this fall to cut some €125 billion in spending.
Bardella, Loubet said, will be “her first support … in the media, on the field, to broaden the [future] majority.”
Advertisement
Not everyone at the fair was convinced. “Bardella would have been a better candidate,” said Kaelig Le Bris, a 41-year-old garbage collector who had come to see him.
Le Bris said he was a fan of Le Pen but “a guy like him at the helm of the country, that would have been something.”
During his appearance at the fair, Bardella repeatedly batted down reporters’ questions about the disagreements between him and Le Pen.
“I will campaign whatever happens,” he said. “Alleged hurt feelings don’t matter.”

It’s the first time a living person has appeared on U.S. currency since 1866, when Spencer Clark, who headed the National Currency Bureau, put his own face on a note in what can only be described as a ballsy move — the 19th-century equivalent of those TV adverts featuring the owner of the company.

Meloni beats Berlusconi’s record as prime minister. Here’s what she wants to do next.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Meloni beats Berlusconi’s record as prime minister. Here’s what she wants to do next.
Meloni now holds the record for the longest unbroken leadership of an Italian government. But she still has a long way to go to define her own political era.
ROME — One date has always loomed large in Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s political calendar: Friday, Sept. 4.
As she gathers with her allies for a jamboree in the southern port city of Bari, Meloni will overtake Silvio Berlusconi’s record for the longest unbroken stretch running a government in the history of the Italian Republic: 1,412 days.
The big question — with a general election due next year — is how far Meloni’s right-wing dominance of Italy’s politics will endure. She still has a long way to go to rival Berlusconi’s total of 3,340 days in charge across all his mandates.
Advertisement
Berlusconi’s extraordinary endurance rested on his ability to survive electoral defeats, collapsed governments, criminal trials and repeated predictions of his political death. His wealth, television empire and a party constructed around himself gave him resources independent of his popularity at any particular moment.
Meloni lacks those tycoon-style advantages, but she is still only 49 years old, tops the polls and is planning an electoral reform that could make it easier for her to keep her grip on power. Nearly four years after taking office, she towers over her coalition partners without an obvious challenger on the right.
Italo Bocchino, a former conservative parliamentarian and prominent Meloni supporter, predicted her era “will last 30 years” — even if some of those years are in opposition.
Her appeal, he argued, lies in her unfiltered authenticity: She complains in dialect about high heels and needing the toilet at international summits and press conferences, embraces her “fishwife” nickname and is notorious for eye-rolls that betray what she is thinking.
“She is sincere, she is transparent as glass,” he said. Her image as a petite blonde woman, Bocchino argued, also made a leader from Italy’s post-fascist right appear less threatening to wary voters.
On the other side of the political spectrum, Laura Boldrini, a center-left Democratic Party MP and former speaker of the lower house, insisted Meloni had not yet earned the comparison with Berlusconi.
Advertisement
“I don’t think she will last a long time because she has failed,” she said. “I think the results are very modest and very disappointing for those who supported her and voted for her.”
Meloni’s opponents accuse her of failing to revive the country’s stagnant economy and low wages and of wasting money on futile efforts to reduce migration. Critics say she focused her efforts on measures intended to cement her power, such as electoral reform and a failed shakeup of the judiciary, while failing to tackle a cost of living crisis.
Boldrini argued that the rise of former General Roberto Vannacci as a force on the far right also showed that disillusioned right-wing voters were already looking elsewhere.
Silvio Berlusconi at the Italy-France Summit on April 26, 2011 in Rome, Italy. | Giorgio Cosulich/Getty Images
“The right-wing coalition has a big problem called Vannacci: a fascist, racist, misogynist, who is collecting a lot of resentment from those who have been disappointed by Meloni’s government. They say they won’t run together but I think they will or they won’t win,” she said.
More credible than Silvio
On the international stage, Meloni has established far more credibility than her predecessor Berlusconi.
While Berlusconi cultivated allies across the political spectrum, from Russia’s Vladimir Putin to Britain’s Tony Blair, his gaffes, Bunga Bunga parties and sex scandals frequently made him an object of ridicule abroad. Meloni is regarded as a pragmatist at European summits and has built strong relationships with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Advertisement
Berlusconi, by contrast, had a bumpy relationship with then German Chancellor Angela Merkel.
Meloni has also proved successful in pulling the EU closer to positions she has advocated on migration, trade deals, industry and green policy. Four years of political stability under her leadership have themselves increased Italy’s weight abroad, analysts argue.
That influence is now being tested, however, as Germany, Ireland and several other European countries press Italy to take back asylum seekers who first entered the EU there under the bloc’s new migration rules, reopening an old fault line between Italy and northern European governments.
Lorenzo Pregliasco, a political analyst and pollster, said voters continue to give Meloni credit for her stewardship of the government and her handling of international affairs. “She is seen as fit to be prime minister in a way other party leaders maybe are not.”
Roberto D’Alimonte, a political scientist who has compared Meloni to Merkel, said: “She has become the center of gravity for the right,” adding that “there is no alternative leader in that coalition.”
But whether that dominance can survive a more uncertain political landscape is only beginning to be tested.
Advertisement
Much of the vote of her party, Brothers of Italy, comes from volatile center-right voters who have previously moved between parties.
Meloni also faces growing economic headwinds. The economy is forecast to enter recession later this year and Italy is on course to overtake Greece as Europe’s most indebted country. With energy prices high and pressure mounting to increase defense spending, she has little room for generous handouts to shore up support in her final pre-election budget this autumn.
Friedrich Merz, Donald Trump, Antonio Costa and Meloni at a work lunch as part of the G7 summit, in Evian, France, on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Christian Hartmann/AFP via Getty Images
Her coalition partners have meanwhile lost ground to Vannacci’s new force, leaving a united left potentially competitive if it can agree on a program and candidate before the election. Meloni may ultimately be forced to bring an unruly Vannacci inside the tent.
Next stop: the presidency?
For Pregliasco, Meloni has yet to have the overarching impact of Berlusconi, who created the modern center-right coalition in 1994 and helped reshape Italian politics around his highly personalized leadership.
Meloni has so far inherited and dominated that architecture rather than creating her own.
“I wouldn’t consider her as defining a figure as Berlusconi,” Pregliasco said.
Advertisement
That could yet change. Meloni’s majority is pursuing an electoral reform that would replace single-member constituencies with proportional representation and award a bonus to the winning coalition, potentially giving her a more commanding majority if the center-right wins again. That approach closely echoes Berlusconi’s 2005 reform, which also combined proportional representation with a majority bonus.
A second term with a reinforced parliamentary majority could strengthen her hand in the 2029 election of the president of the Republic and could allow her to revive her stalled plans for the direct election of the prime minister.
Neither would be straightforward: constitutional reform remains politically hazardous, while the president is elected by secret ballot. But success would give Meloni the opportunity to leave a more lasting institutional mark by reshaping the political system herself.
Her ambitions may also not end with a long tenure as premier.
Nicola Procaccini, a senior politician from Brothers of Italy who has known Meloni since their time in youth politics, said she could ultimately climb to the venerated role of president.
He explained that after three decades in public life, Italians know both her strengths and flaws. “She is not a leader by chance,” he said. “Everyone knows what to expect from her.”
Advertisement
Paradoxically, Berlusconi’s death in 2023 made Meloni’s task easier by removing a potentially troublesome figure with pro-Russian sympathies who was deeply reluctant to play second fiddle to a much younger woman from her coalition.
Procaccini sees Meloni remaining a political force for decades, although he laughed at the idea that she would want another 20 or 30 years in the prime minister’s office.
The job, performed with her level of intensity, was “grueling,” he said.
But as Meloni’s followers prepare to toast her success in Bari, Boldrini was unimpressed by the record itself.
“Longevity is not a value per se,” she cautioned. “You have to implement policies that improve people’s lives, make reforms and make a difference. And this hasn’t happened.”
