No, UN chief Guterres did not call Francesca Albanese 'out of control'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:34:29 UTC
04:34:29 KST

No, UN chief Guterres did not call Francesca Albanese 'out of control'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
Pro-Israel lobby group UN Watch has alleged that UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres referred to Francesca Albanese, the UN's Special Rapporteur on Palestine, as "out of control", saying he'd previously called her a "horrible woman". But Guterres named no one in his remarks. He said "many" independent rapporteurs were "totally out of control", without singling out any individual. The UN has since said that linking the comment specifically to Albanese is a "misreading" of his remarks. Vedika Bahl fact-checks.
Albanese has long been a vocal critic of Israel and its conduct of the war in Gaza, drawing criticism from Israel, the US and others over her outspoken comments on the conflict.
UN Watch – a pro-Israel lobby group that says it aims to combat anti-Semitism – alleged online that the global body itself has called her "out of control," and that the comments came from Secretary-General Antonio Guterres himself.
UN Watch recently shared an extract from a Financial Times interview with Guterres, claiming the UN chief had "admitted anti-Israel bias" within the organisation and had described Albanese as "out of control." The group also linked the remarks to a separate allegation that Guterres had previously called Albanese a "horrible woman."
The claim, though, promoted by UN Watch and widely reshared online, appears to misrepresent what Guterres actually said.
Guterres did not name Albanese or indeed anyone in his remarks. When asked about accusations that the UN is institutionally biased against Israel, Guterres rejected the idea that the organisation as a whole is biased, stressing that different parts of the UN system operate independently.
Regarding special rapporteurs, he said: "We have independent rapporteurs, and we have many that are totally out of control, from the point of view of the Secretariat."
Crucially, Guterres did not identify any individual rapporteur, and that distinction is important. He referred only to "many" rapporteurs and did not single out Albanese by name.
UN Watch has also cited an allegation that Guterres privately referred to Albanese as a "horrible woman." The claim comes from former US Special Envoy on Antisemitism Deborah Lipstadt, who has said Guterres made the remark twice during a private conversation at the 2024 Munich Security Conference.
Because the alleged comments were made privately, they cannot be independently verified from the exchange itself. The allegation has also been reported primarily by Israeli media.
Albanese has responded to the controversy online, saying Guterres did not mean what had been claimed, and that "if our independence may give a headache or two to those guarding the status quo, that's just the point of our mandate."
The UN has also addressed the interpretation of Guterres's remarks. Two days after UN Watch circulated its claim, UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said that interpreting Guterres's comments as referring specifically to rapporteurs on Israel was a "misreading" of what he said. Dujarric also defended rapporteurs' independence and right to speak.

Trump declines to say if US would aid UK in new Falklands conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:33:54 UTC
04:33:54 KST

Ahmet Salih Alacaci
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
US President Donald Trump declined to say whether Washington would come to Britain’s aid if Argentina sought to retake the Falkland Islands, while criticizing the UK for not providing greater support for US military operations involving Iran.
Asked in an interview by British broadcaster GB News whether the US would support the UK in the event of another conflict over the islands, Trump recalled Britain’s 1982 war with Argentina but did not answer the question directly.
“I was there when they had the first war. That was a long time ago, and I watched it so carefully,” Trump said. “You comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away.”
Trump then shifted to Britain’s role in the US-led military campaign against Iran, saying London had not done enough to assist Washington.
“Your country was not there to help me,” he said, adding that he had asked NATO members and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer to contribute ships.
“We didn't need help, but I did ask NATO and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don't you send a couple of ships?’” Trump said.
Returning to the Falklands, Trump questioned whether Britain retained the military capacity to defend the South Atlantic territory as it did in 1982.
“Your country is not the same country it was 20 years ago, 25 years ago,” he said. “I just don't know if you have the capacity to do it. It's a big difference.”
The remarks came as Argentine President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, is expected to make a national address on the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and claims sovereignty over.
Argentina claims sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, which it calls the Malvinas Islands, citing succession from the Spanish Crown and historical decrees, while Britain has maintained control and administration of the archipelago since 1833.
In the early 1980s, Argentina and Britain fought what became known as the Falklands War over the disputed archipelago.
The Falkland Islands consist of two main islands, East Falkland and West Falkland, along with more than 700 smaller islands. The archipelago covers about 12,200 square kilometers and lies roughly 480 kilometers (298 miles) off Argentina's southern coast, with an estimated coastline of about 1,300 kilometers (808 miles).

Trump's comments come as Argentine President Javier Milei renews his country's longstanding claim to the islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina.

Israelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle village
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:33:00 UTC
04:33:00 KST

Israelis have shot dead two teenagers in a Palestinian village encircled by settlers, and Israeli troops have razed an entire village outside Hebron, in the latest attacks in a surge of Israeli terror and ethnic cleansing across the occupied West Bank.
The shootings targeted Khalil Abu Alia, 16, who was about to start 11th grade at the al-Mughayyir boys school, and 19-year-old Omar al-Nassan, who graduated from the same institution with top marks this summer.
The teenagers were killed soon after sunset, when a group of settlers entered the village under police and military escort to steal dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, village residents and Israeli activists said.
Snipers took up position on rooftops and one shot Abu Alia in the neck, his English teacher, Waheed Abu Naim, said in a phone interview. The boy was on the doorstep of his home when he was targeted.
Al-Nassan was shot twice, the second time in the back, residents and activists said. Both had died before they made it to hospital.
A spokesperson for the Israeli military said Israeli police, army and settlers entered the village to take sheep claimed by settlers from a Palestinian home. The spokesperson provided no evidence of ownership, theft or investigation into stolen goods.
When Palestinians resisted seizure of the sheep by throwing stones and cinder blocks, the troops shot them, the spokesperson said. “The forces responded by firing at key instigators in order to remove the threat. Hits were identified.”
Abu Alia was killed by a soldier. It was not clear whether Al-Nassan was shot by a soldier or a settler.
Israeli soldiers and militants had already killed three other students from their school’s 470-strong student body this year.
The other victims were a 17-year-old player from the Palestinian youth football team shot in June, a 14-year-old gunned down at the school gate in April, and another 14-year-old killed outside the village mosque in January.
“We don’t know how long these crimes are going to continue,” said Abu Naim, who had taught all five boys, and said many more of his students had been injured by Israeli attacks. His brother was also killed by settlers in April.
“This week we are making extra security preparations for the new semester which starts in three days,” he said. They have built a higher wall around the school, topped by a fence, and strengthened gates to the compound.
They are also making teaching contingency plans, because the village has been under tightening siege for the past two weeks.
Since late 2023, Israeli barricades blocked all but one road into the village, and at least eight settler outposts surround it in all directions.
In late August soldiers and settlers began closing the one remaining lifeline out of al-Mughayyir for hours at a time, setting up a temporary checkpoint near the school in the morning and evening.
At least eight families have fled in the past week because they were unable to commute to work, renting flats in other places, Abu Naim said.
The school has 26 teachers but only nine live in the village, and they fear the other two-thirds may not be allowed to reach their classrooms on Monday.
In the south Hebron hills Israeli forces spent the day razing the homes of 12 Palestinian families who lived in the community of Khirbet al-Taban. All 70 residents are now homeless, including 28 children.
Israeli troops demolished all buildings and destroyed water cisterns, storage, livestock pens and caves, the Israeli-Palestinian rights group B’Tselem said in a statement.
It is the 66th Palestinian community that has been wiped off the map since October 2023, with 18 others partly displaced, the group said. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.
“Israel is continuing to erase Palestinian communities at an accelerating pace as part of the ethnic cleansing it is carrying out in the West Bank,” said Yuli Novak, the executive director of B’Tselem. “The world continues to stand by as Palestinians and their lives are left completely exposed to Israeli violence.”
A spokesperson for Cogat, the Israeli military agency which manages civilian affairs in occupied Palestine, said troops were carrying out “enforcement activity” against illegal construction in a military training zone.
In 1981 Israel designated the Masafer Yatta area, including Khirbet al-Taban, as Firing Zone 918. It has been working since to push out the roughly 1,200 Palestinian residents who remain. They have been fighting expulsion in Israeli courts for decades, slowing but not stopping demolitions.
As Palestinian communities have been wiped out, illegal Israeli settlements have expanded, with 11 outposts inside the firing zone, housing some of the most notoriously violent Israeli settlers. None have been targeted for removal.

'He mesmerised me': Remembering Steve Irwin 20 years after shock death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:32:43 UTC
04:32:43 KST

Steve Irwin still in hearts and minds 20 years after shock death
Becoming best mates with the Crocodile Hunter left Wes Mannion with permanent scars, but not a single regret.
There was that time when a cranky crocodile called Graham tore chunks off his leg and backside while the pair was securing an enclosure during a flood at Australia Zoo, on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.
Mr Mannion was even mauled by the man himself once, an avid fan and practitioner of Brazilian jiujitsu who built a training cage at the zoo so they could practise during their breaks.
"I've still got a busted rib from him. I got him in a triangle choke, and he just got his elbow, put it in my chest, picked me up — because he's strong as an ox — and drove his elbow in," Mr Mannion chuckled.
"Every day I get up I stretch, and I'm like, 'Oh, bloody Steve!' … but he was like my brother, my best friend, my mentor and my boss all rolled into one."
Mr Mannion met Steve Irwin when he visited the then-named Queensland Reptile and Fauna Park in the mid-1980s.
As a 14-year-old, he was captivated, as millions of fans would become in later years.
"He was jumping an alligator, and I was just like, 'This guy's my hero!' … and we hit it off, too," Mr Mannion said.
"You had to keep up with him. Most people couldn't keep up with him, but if you could do it, it was the ride of your life."
From zookeeper to celebrity
Friend, producer and director John Stainton first encountered Steve Irwin on a shoot for a beer commercial, where the young zookeeper had to snatch a can from a crocodile's jaws.
He offered to send Mr Stainton some home videos he had taken around the zoo.
"It was midnight, and I put one of the tapes into the television, and I watched it from 12 o'clock till 3am. He mesmerised me," the director said.
"When I got to the end of it, I just rewound that one and played it again … it was the most amazing television I'd ever seen in my life."
That was the beginning of The Crocodile Hunter television series, which propelled Steve onto the international stage.
Bob Blasdall edited all five seasons, along with Steve Irwin's documentaries, including his final film, Ocean's Deadliest.
"The first time I'd ever seen footage of Steve, it just blew me away," Mr Blasdall said.
"Here is this character who sucked you through the lens and plonked you in his lap and, like a Barbie doll, took you on the journey with him."
The editor's life also took a wild turn while working with the khaki-clad conservationist, which even saw him wind up on the back of an agitated crocodile during a shoot.
"Steve screamed out, 'Bob, jump on its bloody tail!' So I jumped on it; it's lifted its back legs and started to thrash its tail. I'm going up in the air a metre, side to side a metre-and-a-half, I'm hanging on for dear life," Mr Blasdall said.
"God bless you, Steve. It really was the highlight of my life."
A tragic accident
Mr Stainton remembers waking up one morning in January 2006 with a horrible feeling that it was going to be his last year.
The feeling was so strong, he called his lawyer to do up a will and underwent numerous medical tests.
"Everyone thought I was a bit nutty. It never dawned on me that it was Steve,"
As filming for The Ocean's Deadliest documentary drew closer, the feeling grew.
"I actually contacted Discovery [Channel] and asked if we could postpone or cancel the shoot, but they said everything's been committed," Mr Stainton said.
About 11am on September 4, 2006, Steve Irwin was fatally stabbed by a stingray while snorkelling in shallow water at Batt Reef, off Port Douglas.
It is believed the marine creature may have mistaken his shadow for a shark and lashed out to protect itself.
The film crew tried frantically to save the star's life, but the barb on the stingray's tail had pierced his heart.
Mr Stainton was on the boat that dreadful day and also had the gut-wrenching task of delivering the news to the conservationist's wife and love of his life, Terri Irwin.
"It's a day that you can't ever think about without crying … the saddest time of my life," he said.
Everyone remembers that day
News of the Crocodile Hunter's death sent shock waves around the world and was deeply felt by residents in his hometown.
Sunshine Coast Mayor Rosanna Natoli was working as a local television news journalist at the time.
"I think everyone remembers where they were when they heard the news, and it was just impossible to believe," Cr Natoli said.
"He was such an incredible life force."
An estimated 300 million television viewers tuned in to watch the memorial service held at Australia Zoo's Crocoseum on September 20, 2006.
Steve's father, Bob Irwin, told the crowd, "The animals have lost the best friend they ever had — and so have I."
An eight-year-old Bindi Irwin also bravely took to the stage to deliver an eloquent tribute.
"My daddy was my hero. He was always there for me when I needed him. He listened to me and taught me so many things, but most of all he was fun," she said.
"I don't want daddy's passion ever to end. I want to help endangered wildlife just like he did."
Wildlife warriors
Australia Zoo now attracts about 700,000 visitors a year, with Terri, Bindi and Robert still heavily involved in its operations.
The Steve Irwin Wildlife Reserve covers 180,000 hectares of precious habitats across Queensland.
The Irwins recently embarked on their annual trip to the reserve in Far North Queensland to research saltwater crocodiles.
They were contacted ahead of the anniversary, but a spokesperson said they were not available for an interview due to their conservation commitments.
Like their parents, the Irwin children are hugely popular in the US, with both winning the American series Dancing with the Stars 10 years apart.
Robert Irwin recently hosted the Logies and couldn't resist the chance to bring out a few scaly friends, just like his father did at the 2003 awards show.
"That was actually the year I was born," he told the crowd.
"And I've been very proud to follow in his footsteps ever since."
Mr Mannion stepped down as director of Australia Zoo in 2020 so he could spend more time with his own children, after helping guide Bindi and Robert in the years following their father's death.
"I was lucky enough to teach Robert to feed crocodiles and Bindi to feed crocodiles and catch snakes and so on, so it's great being able to hand down what he taught me," he said.
He has no doubt his best mate would be "super proud".
"For the youth they are now, I mean, what more could you want? They're gregarious, they're lovely, they're passionate, successful and they're happy.
"As a father, your dream is to see your kids happy … for him to see them now, he would be just like, 'Job done, tick.'"

'Truth must come out': Whistleblower risked it all to expose alleged misconduct
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:30:37 UTC
04:30:37 KST

analysis
KPMG whistleblower who tried to expose alleged 'systemic misconduct' shows why so few people report
It takes a certain kind of inner strength to be a whistleblower.
Courage and determination are obvious traits that whistleblowers share, but blowing the lid on alleged misconduct in the nation's biggest companies and organisations requires a willingness to risk everything.
A whistleblower can risk losing their job, their relationships, and potentially their sanity if they want to expose wrongdoing.
Several whistleblowers I have spoken to over the years often say that reality is what makes it hard to be a whistleblower in Australia and it deters more people from coming forward.
Australia's laws just don't protect them.
The government is now reviewing those laws. The current KPMG audit leaks scandal is a reminder of just how important that review is.
In March, Labor senator Deborah O'Neill shared with parliament a whistleblower's allegations that confidential board papers from Lendlease were used to support bids for major audit tenders for Westpac and Dexus.
And earlier this month, the firm's current and former partners were hauled before a federal inquiry probing why the firm allegedly shared client information and ignored the whistleblower's allegations when they first surfaced.
Now, ahead of the regulator appearing before the inquiry today, ABC News has obtained the key email that was sent by the audit leaks whistleblower to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) last year to report alleged misconduct at the accounting firm.
Whistleblower tried to report in 2025
The whistleblower emailed ASIC in September 2025.
CCed on that email were senior executives still at KPMG at the time, many of whom have departed the firm as the scandal has unfolded.
This was not the first time the whistleblower had tried contacting ASIC to seek protection for disclosures alleging that the firm had breached corporations law.
The email detailed how the person first tried to blow the whistle internally at KPMG, and that the matters were also taken to KPMG International.
But the whistleblower's serious allegations were dismissed by KPMG as a private employment matter.
As the whistleblower noted in the email to ASIC, at every turn, KPMG Australia "refused to acknowledge my whistleblower status or protections" and "reviews commissioned and controlled by KPMG — including those conducted under legal privilege — cannot credibly be presented as independent".
The whistleblower had approached ASIC "under the continuing threat of retaliatory legal action from KPMG".
"Despite this, the truth must come out," the whistleblower wrote in the email.
"They are issues of public interest that go directly to ASIC's statutory mandate to ensure the integrity of financial reporting, uphold auditor independence, and safeguard confidence in Australian markets.
"Delay in addressing them risks allowing systemic misconduct to continue unchecked, directly undermining market integrity and investor confidence."
Regulator failed to assure whistleblower
While the whistleblower warned ASIC that "the matters I raised are urgent and warrant immediate investigation", it was not until the whistleblower's allegations were aired by Senator O'Neill under parliamentary privilege that ASIC later announced it would investigate the alleged audit leaks.
The whistleblower also tried to seek assurances from ASIC that they would be protected if they made a more detailed complaint, but this never happened.
The regulator closed the complaint days later.
ASIC told ABC News: "ASIC takes all whistleblower reports and allegations of misconduct seriously."
A KPMG spokeswoman told the ABC the firm was also looking to strengthen its whistleblower policy.
"We acknowledge that KPMG Australia failed the whistleblower, and for that we have unreservedly apologised,"
"Now, more than ever, we are focused on creating an environment where people feel safe to speak up."
Partnership loophole in whistleblower laws
While another KPMG whistleblower has been critical of ASIC, saying the regulator had to be "dragged kicking and screaming to take action", the bigger issue is that laws to protect whistleblowers are inadequate.
ASIC boss Sarah Court alluded to this at the June 19 parliamentary hearing relating to the audit leaks scandal, pointing to "clear gaps in the regulatory settings" and calling for the Corporations Act to extend to deal with big partnerships and sanctions applicable to be "significantly increased".
"We also consider the current whistleblower protections to be deficient," Ms Court told the hearing.
"They need to be extended so that those that are seeking to make disclosures in relation to the conduct of partnerships such as KPMG are clearly protected."
Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mullino is now considering changes to the law that could boost access to justice for whistleblowers and address gaps on who is covered.
Possible bounty-style rewards
Currently disclosures about partnerships and unincorporated associations fall outside "eligible whistleblower" protections. The government is looking to change this.
It will also look at whether anonymous/confidential disclosure protections are "fit for purpose" and whether a proposed financial rewards scheme for whistleblowers is needed.
This would be akin to a bounty-style reward that exists in the United States for some whistleblower disclosures.
Some stakeholders and prior parliamentary inquiries have backed it, but Treasury's consultation paper flags the risk that it could invite a flood of low-value or speculative reports and could make disclosures look profit-motivated rather than public-interest-motivated.
That's why a whistleblower protection authority, a body responsible for investigating whistleblower complaints, remains a live issue.
This one-stop shop would also be able to conduct investigations if whistleblowers personally suffered consequences for exposing misconduct.
It would also be able to compensate them for losses suffered.
It's a change that Greens finance and public service spokesperson senator Barbara Pocock backs.
"Strong whistleblower protections are vital to a democracy," she told ABC News.
"In the absence of regulators with teeth — ASIC and the Tax Practitioners Board — there is an urgent need for corporate whistleblower protections to extend to the Big Four and for a new whistleblower authority that actually supports and protects whistleblowers.
"This means ensuring all entities are required to meet the whistleblower provisions of the Corporations Act 2001 and establish a whistleblower authority."
It's an idea well worth considering if Australia wants to change from a nation that penalises whistleblowers to one that values and celebrates them.

The Stakes of America’s 2026 Midterm Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:30:02 UTC
04:30:02 KST

Five years ago, in the wake of the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, America’s civic institutions pledged to do more to defend our system of fair and free elections. Major philanthropies increased their investments in programs that defend democracy. Law firms expanded their pro bono election-protection work. University presidents publicly condemned the effort to thwart the will of American voters. Many of the country’s largest businesses pledged to stop donating to candidates who had tried to overturn an election.
Today, our elections are again under attack. But while some institutions have maintained their commitment to defending democracy, far too many have retreated.
There are fewer than 100 days until the 2026 nationwide elections. Now is the time for everyone to protect the system of fair and free elections upon which our society and prosperity ultimately depend.
Together, the two of us have spent considerable time in all the major sectors of American society: philanthropy, business, academia, and the law. We understand that leaders in these sectors fear government retribution, and understandably so. But with the integrity of our elections under enormous strain—and with government officials signaling that more aggressive attacks may follow—it is time for all institutions to reaffirm their role as defenders of the free and fair elections at the heart of American democracy.
Defending our democracy begins with a clear-eyed assessment of the threats to it. Over the past 18 months, the Justice Department has disbanded government agencies meant to protect elections from foreign interference and to help states administer them smoothly. President Donald Trump has repeatedly made false claims that the 2020 election was fraudulent and made new ones—without evidence—about the midterms. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin recently threatened to jail local election officials his department finds were insufficiently responsive to the federal government’s unproven claims of fraud. Overall, the federal government has tried to wrest control of elections from the states, with courts repeatedly finding such efforts illegal.
Now, experts across the country are deeply concerned about what might occur in the coming months, whether it’s false allegations that cast doubt on individual races, state officials refusing to certify election results as required by law, or baseless efforts to block House members from taking their seats in January.
The good news is the success of these efforts to undermine the midterms is not inevitable. To the contrary, enormous work has already been done to protect the integrity of November’s election from those who would undermine it.
Now, it is time for leaders who haven’t yet joined that effort to get off the sidelines no matter what their politics are. Losing our system of fair and free elections would not just affect one element of American life. It would affect all elements of American life.
There are many ways for institutions to meet the moment and keep our country’s elections free and fair. First, many leaders, particularly those from the business community, meet regularly with members of the executive branch and Congress. They should use these relationships to remind elected officials of the need to respect election results no matter who wins or loses.
These nonpartisan principles are the basic preconditions for a functioning democracy and should be respected by all.
Second, many institutional leaders have strong ties to state and local officials. Now is the time to remind state legislators that attempting to disenfranchise eligible voters via last-minute changes to election rules, baseless claims of fraud, or partisan attempts to deny certification harm our democracy and create the kind of turmoil that negatively affects a state’s reputation and business climate.
Third, leaders should forcefully support the local election administrators who run our elections. These are not professional politicians. They are our neighbors, co-workers, and friends—and recently, they have far too often been subject to threats and harassment by those who wish to undermine their nonpartisan mission. Institutional leaders can help elections run smoothly by encouraging their employees to become poll workers, and by supporting nonpartisan civic organizations that defend election officials in performing their duties, or that bring Americans from across the political spectrum together to support the right of all Americans to have their vote counted.
Standing up for fair and free elections is not without risk. But with the foundation of our democracy under unprecedented assault and our basic rights on the line, the far greater risk is ignoring the threat to our country until it is too late.
One day, leaders of America’s institutions will face the same profound question as every other citizen who loves this country. Future generations will ask, “Where were you when the stakes were highest?”
What will you tell them?

AI agents aren’t ready to replace humans in behavioral research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:30:00 UTC
04:30:00 KST

AI agents aren’t ready to replace humans in behavioral research
A new study shows that digital twins don’t respond like the individuals they were modeled after
Replacing human subjects with AI surrogates, or digital twins, is on some social scientists’ wish lists. Human subjects are expensive, tire easily and can suffer psychological distress from some studies.
But those wishes may take more time to be realized, a study appearing September 2 in Science Advances suggests. AI twins designed to mimic a given individual’s behavior instead seem to distort their surrogate’s views, creating a “funhouse mirror” effect, the researchers note.
“There’s some promise,” says Olivier Toubia, a computational social scientist at Columbia Business School in New York City. “But [the twins’ performance] was overall a bit disappointing.”
In work reported last year in Marketing Science, Toubia and colleagues recruited more than 2,000 individuals from across the United States. Those respondents answered 500-plus questions about characteristics including age, ethnicity, income, education, religious practices, political preferences, personality traits, spending habits, mathematical abilities and vocabulary skills. Many of the questions come from scales that are used commonly in psychology, economic and business research. Respondents also completed various online tests designed to assess thought patterns and biases.
Because research testing the value of digital twins remains limited, the goal of that project was to create an open-source dataset for others to use, Toubia says. “I think it’s been downloaded like 25,000 times at this point.”
To develop the twins in the newly published study, the researchers fed all the information for each individual into a large language model and prompted the LLM to respond as if it were that person. Across 19 social science experiments, the team evaluated everything from how individuals and their twins respond to people who donate to both Republican and Democratic party candidates to what they “think” about algorithmic hiring.
These digital twins performed better than chance, the team found, but they were wrong on average about a quarter of the time. They performed roughly on par with chatbots that received demographic information alone.
The digital twins did, however, better capture real variation in people’s responses compared with the LLMs that knew only demographic info. For example, one person may rate themselves as a 2 on a scale of self-control while another rates themselves as a 4. The LLM with more limited info might report a 3 for each person, washing out any differences. But the digital twin might report a 3 and 5. Though still wrong, the predictions give a better sense of potential differences across the group.
Toubia and colleagues attribute the digital twins’ poor performance overall to several key distortions: Twins’ responses tended to be more homogenous than people’s responses and often skewed to demographic stereotypes. And their accuracy increased with more affluent and educated participants. They also displayed certain biases, such as expressing more trust in others and showing less concern about technological threats. Compared with their human surrogates, the twins also appeared more rational.
AI researcher and economist Hadi Hosseini of Penn State University has seen a similar effect in his own research into how AI agents make health care decisions when resources are scarce: “LLMs distort human judgment in a very specific direction toward something that is very rational [and] more reasonable than actually what people are.”
But he says there are ways that the digital twins could be improved. The researchers used “a very static set of questions,” he says. Adding more dynamic approaches, such as having a chatbot shadow an individual across the day or converse regularly with a person, as is already common, could make for a better dataset, he says.
Toubia wants to try more complex training methods. Still, he says, there are cases where even digital twins of the type tested in this study would be useful. For instance, sometimes researchers need a detailed response to a question. Tired humans might provide single-sentence answers while indefatigable digital twins churn out essays. Similarly, pretesting an experiment with digital twins could help researchers ensure their design is working before sapping their human respondents’ limited bandwidth.
But Toubia also urges humility. Social scientists tend to think that scales and surveys capture the full range of human experience, he says. But it’s incredibly hard to predict human behavior with a machine. “We need to be realistic in terms of the expectations we have from synthetic data.”

Serbia welcomes return of war criminal Mladic’s body with military honours
Ratko Mladic received a life sentence from a UN court for committing atrocities during the 1992-1995 Bosnian War.
The body of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who died last week while serving a life sentence for war crimes, has returned to Belgrade for burial, where it has been received with military honours.
The casket, draped in the national flag, was carried on Thursday on board a Serbian government plane that departed from The Hague, Netherlands, where the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia was located before completing its mandate.

Mladic, who was convicted in 2017 of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, died last week in a UN detention facility aged 84. Mladic was one of the most notorious figures of the war in Bosnia, which killed more than 100,000 people and left over 1 million homeless before it ended in 1995 in a United States-brokered peace agreement.
Its massacre in Srebrenica was Europe’s first acknowledged genocide after World War II. The Bosnian city ended up being overrun by Serbs who forced Bosniak men and boys to strip, killed them and bulldozed their bodies into mass graves.
The tribunal in The Hague said it stood “in solidarity with the victims, survivors and their families who suffered the crimes for which Mr Mladic was found guilty”.

Serbia is formally seeking European Union entry but remains defiant over its war role. The EU’s enlargement commissioner warned that “the glorification of war criminals has no place in an EU member country nor in a candidate country.”

Arctic limbo: What you need to know about the Russian ship seized by Norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:27:11 UTC
04:27:11 KST

Arctic limbo: What you need to know about the Russian ship seized by Norway
Norway has seized a Russian research vessel in Svalbard at the request of Kiev, prompting Russian President Vladimir Putin to denounce the capture of civilian vessels as “state terrorism.”
The vessel, called the Professor Molchanov, was detained while docked in Barentsburg, a Russian-operated settlement on the Norwegian-administered Arctic archipelago. The ship has been barred from leaving after a local court granted a request by Ukraine’s state-owned energy company Naftogaz.
Moscow has since summoned Norway’s ambassador in protest and vowed to challenge the seizure.
Why was a Russian state vessel in Norway in the first place, why does Kiev want it, and what could happen to the ship now?
What exactly happened
The Professor Molchanov arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday on a scheduled voyage from Murmansk carrying scientists, passengers and supplies for the Russian settlements on the Norwegian-administered Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
Norwegian officials first boarded the vessel for what Svalbard Governor Lars Fause described as an ordinary border and customs inspection, of a kind the ship had undergone numerous times before.
On Wednesday, Norwegian police, accompanied by an interpreter, boarded the ship again and read a court order to its captain, barring the vessel from leaving. Nobody aboard was arrested.
The order was issued on August 31 by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court after an application from Ukraine’s Naftogaz.
What happened to the passengers and crew
The exact number of people on board when the ship arrived in Barentsburg has not been officially confirmed. The Professor Molchanov can accommodate up to 80 people, including at least 20 crew members and as many as 60 scientists and other expedition personnel.
Norwegian media have reported that around 50 passengers and crew were affected by the seizure.
Russian officials have said that 21 people remained on board. They have been supplied with everything they need and continue working, with no Norwegian police or officials stationed on the vessel.
Those who had already gone ashore were not detained and have been able to continue their planned work. They include participants in the Arctic Biennale art-and-science project.
The seizure has, however, left some passengers without their planned transport back to Russia. Norwegian authorities have said they are working with Arktikugol to resolve the situation for those affected, but no alternative route has yet been announced.
The Professor Molchanov
The ship, named after renowned Soviet meteorologist Pavel Molchanov, is a Russian state-owned, ice-strengthened research vessel with more than four decades of experience operating in polar waters.
Built in Finland for the Soviet hydrometeorological service and launched in late 1982, the 71-meter-long ship was designed for Arctic oceanographic and weather research. It carries four laboratories on board and can accommodate dozens of researchers alongside its crew.
The ship continues to be actively used in Arctic research, including studies of weather, marine ecosystems, microbiology, biodiversity and environmental conditions in the Barents and Kara seas.
Why is goes to Svalbard
The voyage to Svalbard was part of a regular route between Murmansk and Barentsburg, a Russian mining settlement where the state-owned Arktikugol trust has operated for decades.
Since 2025, the Professor Molchanov has carried scientists, Arktikugol employees, contractors, family members and supplies to Barentsburg and another Russian settlement called Pyramida. Ten round trips were planned for 2026.
It is currently the only vessel providing a direct passenger connection between the Russian mainland and the archipelago after direct air links between Russia and Svalbard ended in 2020.
While Svalbard is under Norwegian sovereignty, it is governed by the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which grants nationals of signatory countries rights to conduct commercial and scientific activities on the archipelago.
Why Ukraine wants the ship
The seizure of the vessel stems from a long-running dispute over Crimea. Ukraine’s Naftogaz has claimed that it lost energy assets after the peninsula’s reunification with Russia in 2014 and took the case to an arbitration tribunal in The Hague.
In 2023, the tribunal ordered Russia to pay around $4.22 billion, plus interest and legal costs, ruling that Naftogaz’s assets in Crimea could be treated as Ukrainian “investments” in Russian territory and were protected under a bilateral treaty.
Moscow has rejected the ruling, arguing that the tribunal had no jurisdiction over the dispute and that the treaty did not apply to assets that had already been located in Crimea before its reunification with Russia.
Nevertheless, Naftogaz has since tried to collect the award by targeting Russian state property abroad. It has pursued assets in several Western countries, including Finland, Britain and France, and says the arbitration award can also be enforced in Norway.
According to Reuters, lawyers acting for Naftogaz had been monitoring the Professor Molchanov for months before seeking its seizure.
Will Kiev actually get the ship?
Not automatically. The current order only prevents the Professor Molchanov from leaving Barentsburg while the case proceeds. The vessel remains Russian property and has not yet been transferred to Ukraine.
Naftogaz ultimately wants Russian assets seized abroad to be sold, with the proceeds used to cover part of the $4.22 billion award. According to Reuters, its lawyers sought not only the arrest of the Professor Molchanov, but also its eventual compulsory sale.
However, even if the ship were to be sold, it would cover only a tiny fraction of Kiev’s multibillion-dollar claim.
Russia has also said it will challenge whether the ship can be seized or sold at all. While Naftogaz has claimed that the vessel has a commercial function, Moscow has stressed that it is state-owned, operated by Roshydromet, and used for scientific research and supplying Russian settlements in the Arctic.
Moscow’s response
Moscow has protested the seizure and demanded that Norway release the vessel. On Thursday, the Russian Foreign Ministry summoned Norwegian Ambassador Heidi Olufsen and delivered a “strong protest” over the detention of the ship.
The ministry stressed that the vessel was carrying out a scheduled trip between Murmansk and Barentsburg and was transporting scientists, Arktikugol employees, and supplies needed by Russian settlements on Svalbard.
It accused Oslo of using the restrictions against Russia to undermine Moscow’s longstanding presence on the archipelago, saying Russian organizations and citizens there had effectively been placed in a “state of blockade.”
The ministry also accused Norway of violating the 1920 Svalbard Treaty and said Russian authorities would work to have the seizure lifted.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described the detention as another example of Western “piracy,” while Far East and Arctic Development Minister Aleksey Chekunkov called it “legal nihilism and lawlessness” and said Moscow would challenge the decision.
President Vladimir Putin described the capture of civilian vessels, attacks on merchant ships and threats against civilian aircraft as manifestations of “state terrorism.” He added that Western countries which ignore such actions risk becoming “accomplices in international terrorism.”
Part of a broader campaign against Russian vessels
Western countries have increasingly moved beyond sanctions and begun physically detaining or seizing vessels they accuse of helping Russia bypass restrictions on its trade, claiming the ships are part of a so-called “shadow fleet.”
A number of ships linked to Russia have been held in European waters since 2025, including tankers and cargo vessels detained by Germany, Estonia, France, Belgium, Sweden, and Britain.
Moscow has repeatedly decried the seizures while dismissing the “shadow fleet” designation as legally meaningless.
Putin warned in August that attempts to seize Russian ships and sell their cargo amounted to “piracy and robbery” and said Moscow could respond in kind against vessels carrying cargo for countries involved in such actions.
An attempt to limit Russia in the Arctic?
Russian officials and experts have linked the seizure to a wider Western effort to weaken Moscow’s position in the Arctic. Murmansk Governor Andrey Chibis accused Norwegian officials of trying to “push us out of Svalbard,” stressing that Russia has longstanding economic and scientific interests on the archipelago and that such efforts would fail.
Arctic expert Aleksey Fadeev similarly described the detention as another attempt by Western countries to pressure Russia under the pretext of confiscating property for Ukraine, warning that it could further increase tensions between Moscow and NATO states in the region.
Military analyst Aleksandr Stepanov warned the seizure could set a precedent for disrupting Russian maritime access not only around Svalbard but across northern waters more broadly.
Russian experts have also described the arrest as a potential blow to Russia’s ability to conduct Arctic research, noting that the Professor Molchanov is used for climate, weather, and environmental studies with relevance beyond Russia itself.

Economy won't improve until Australia climbs productivity mountain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:27:05 UTC
04:27:05 KST

analysis
Jim Chalmers is positive on growth but Australia's productivity problem persists
Treasurer Jim Chalmers would have sighed with relief at this week's economic growth figures. Despite some preview talk of possible stagnation, we saw modest growth of 2.1 per cent in the year to the end of June.
But every economic number these days seems to bring a negative. Economists immediately strengthened their predictions of another interest rate rise.
For the average Australian, just where we are economically is, at best, confusing; at worst, alarming. For years, people have been under cost-of-living pressure. Real wages fell by more than 5 per cent over the five years from 2021.
This year's extended Middle East conflict has added to the strain. The housing market is disoriented after the budget's tax changes.
In this week's Essential poll, nearly six in 10 people thought the country was headed in the wrong direction.
The government tries to empathise with people's circumstances while claiming it's pulling the right levers, an assertion strongly contested by the opposition, which, in particular, flails at high government spending.
The public no longer trusts the messaging from either side. Many frustrated voters are combining their economic and political grievances into support for One Nation.
Loading...
In light of the often baffling picture, this column asked two independent economists, Chris Richardson and Saul Eslake, for their snapshots of our economic health — or lack of it.
Richardson points to growth easing as interest rates have risen.
He says, over the longer term, "Australia's economy has been getting bigger mostly because we have more people."
On a per-hour-worked basis, the economy is only 1 per cent bigger today than it was a decade ago, which is "depressingly weak".
Inflation "has been frustratingly slow to come to heel" and the job isn't finished, Richardson says.
"Even more frustratingly, we still have inflation at around 3.5 per cent [well above the 2.5 per cent target for it] even though Australia's economy has already slowed a lot."
A combination of weak growth and lingering inflation is happening "because the engine of the economy — productivity — has been stalled for a long time".
"With a weak engine behind it, the Australian economy doesn't need to be travelling fast at all before it starts to blow black smoke in the form of inflation."
Given we've had multiple interest rate rises, and the budget's tax changes have taken some heat out of housing prices, Richardson predicts we'll probably see only one more rate rise (either this month or in November).
Loading
That could be followed, on his assessment, by one or two rate cuts next year, driven by low growth.
"But not more than that: higher interest rates look set to be the new normal," Richardson says.
Higher interest rates and the budget's tax changes are driving down housing prices — the question is, how far?
Richardson says: "There's momentum in that fall — having dropped by around 4 per cent already, they could fall another 6 per cent before stabilising."
But, he says, taxes and interest rates alone "can't fix Australia's broken housing market. Doing that would require local councils saying 'yes' to much more building than they've done in decades".
Eslake says that in an "underlying" sense the economy is growing at about 2 per cent a year — roughly in line with the Reserve Bank's assessed "speed limit" (how fast the economy can grow without triggering unacceptably high inflation).
"Of this, a bit under 1.5 per cent is coming from population growth, and a little over 0.5 per cent is coming from per capita real GDP growth, that is, improving material living standards."
Australia's inflation rate has only been inside the Reserve Bank's 2–3 per cent target on two occasions in the past almost five years, Eslake says.
He says the most recent inflation numbers (3.5 per cent annual in July) have increased the odds of a rate increase at the RBA's September meeting, taking the cash rate to its highest level since late 2011.
"The RBA can't afford to repeat the mistake, which [with the benefit of hindsight] it made last year, in cutting rates before inflation was sustainably back within its target band. That means the RBA is probably going to want to see at least two quarters with the annual 'underlying' inflation rate being 2-point-something — which on its own forecasts won't be until the first half of 2028."
Eslake says a key reason for this combination of weak economic growth and persistent inflation is the economy's "abysmal productivity growth performance".
Wednesday's national accounts show "overall labour productivity growth over the year to the June quarter of –0.2 per cent, the worst performance since the year ended March 2025".
"And it isn't solely because of the growth in the so-called care economy," Eslake says.
"Labour productivity in the 'non-market' sectors of the economy declined by 0.3 per cent over the year to the June quarter, but 'market sector' productivity also declined by 0.2 per cent. Big declines in productivity in the mining and construction sectors are a large part of this story.
"Weak productivity growth means that the 'speed limit' is also very low by historical standards. In effect, we can't sustain economic growth of more than about 2 per cent per annum and have inflation at around 2.5 per cent."
Both Richardson and Eslake highlight that Australia is in a very bad place when it comes to productivity. Chalmers's rhetoric since the election has put much focus on productivity, but so far the government's talk has outpaced the walk.
Unsurprisingly, the government is pinning hopes on artificial intelligence.
This week, Chalmers released a Treasury analysis of the economic implications of AI. Although hedged with qualifications and uncertainties, the paper argued AI could help Australia reach Treasury's long-term target of an annual growth of 1.2 per cent in productivity, although it emphasises it will only provide some of this growth.
AI is not a "substitute for domestic structural reforms".
The government is currently preparing legislation setting out conditions for data centres. That's necessary not only to encourage investment but to maintain the social licence for data centres which, if the US experience is anything to go by, are likely to become more unpopular as time goes on.
But Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood stresses it's not all about data centres.
"What matters much more for productivity is how quickly businesses are adopting AI and embedding it into their processes. At the moment we are lagging nations like the United States, the United Kingdom and Germany when it comes to business take-up.
"There isn't a single policy answer for this, but regulatory clarity, skills and training support, and government's own adoption can play a role," Wood says.
The productivity mountain is a steep one to climb.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

B-52s Deploy for Bomber Task Force to Australia’s New BUFF Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:17:49 UTC
04:17:49 KST

Air Force B-52 Stratofortress bombers landed at a northern Australian air base this week, a major display of the U.S. military’s ability to project force in the Pacific.
Multiple B-52s landed at Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal in the country’s Northern Territory on Sept. 1, according to official Air Force imagery released Sept. 3 and service officials.
The joint military-civilian airfield near the town of Katherine, which the Pentagon plans to use as a launching pad for operations in the Pacific, has undergone a $1.1 billion upgrade in recent years.
That work enables it to support the deployment of a half-dozen B-52s, giving the U.S. more locations to stage bombers in the region amid China’s growing military might.
The base also houses Australian F-35A Lightning stealth fighter jets and MQ-4C Triton remotely piloted surveillance aircraft.
Australia is south of the U.S. territory of Guam, where Andersen Air Force Base serves as America’s current bomber hub in the Western Pacific. RAAF Base Tindal would give the U.S. Air Force more basing options for long-range missions in the region.
“Operating from RAAF Base Tindal marks our ability to project, sustain, and regenerate decisive airpower across an expanding extended network,” states one photo caption released by Pacific Air Forces. The deployment from the base “deepens our partnership and interoperability” and “highlights our shared commitment to regional stability, ensuring our forces remain agile and responsive in support of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific,” PACAF added in other captions.
It is unclear how long the bombers will be deployed to the region and how many aircraft are operating from Australia. The bombers hail from the 2nd Bomb Wing at Barksdale Air Force Base, La. Air Force Global Strike Command and the Eighth Air Force, which oversees the nation’s bomber fleet, referred questions about the deployment to Pacific Air Forces.
“These missions demonstrate seamless interoperability with our partners and bolster regional security across the region,” a PACAF spokesperson said in a short statement confirming the B-52 deployment to Australia. The spokesperson declined to provide further details, citing operational security concerns.
Multiple wargames on potential conflicts with China have highlighted the strategic and operational value of Australia’s airbases and naval facilities, said retired Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot and deputy assistant secretary of defense for forces transformation and resources.
“That has been a constant in our wargames: using Australia’s multiple airfields—and not just in northern Australia but in the south too—to generate long-range bomber strikes and tanker sorties to support bomber and fighter operations,” said Gunzinger, the Director of Future Concepts and Capability Assessments at AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“China has a limited number of very long-range ballistic missiles that can reach U.S. air forces stationed at Diego Garcia, in Australia, and other air bases that are not located along the First Island Chain.” Bombers’ longer ranges would allow them to be stationed at airfields even further from China if necessary, Gunzinger added.
Washington and Canberra are increasingly aligned under the AUKUS security pact, which also includes the United Kingdom. The agreement will give U.S. nuclear-powered subs to Australia and allow the U.S. to stage subs out of Australia starting next year. Conceived under the Biden administration, AUKUS has also been embraced by the second Trump administration.
Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles met with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Sept. 2 to commemorate the 75th anniversary of the ANZUS Treaty, a mutual defense pact, during which the two defense chiefs “discussed how both nations will continue to advance the alliance and strengthen deterrence in the Pacific.”
“The Secretary noted the alignment between U.S. and Australian National Defense Strategies and also acknowledged that Canberra recognizes the gravity of maintaining a favorable balance of power in the region to ensure that both countries remain safe and prosperous,” the Pentagon said in a readout provided from the meeting. “Both leaders agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises.”
The U.S. has operated fighters and bombers from other Royal Australian Air Force Bases, such as RAAF Base Amberley, and the two countries conduct the biennial Talisman Saber, one of the largest and most complex military training exercises held. By 2030, the U.S. Navy expects some 2,300 Americans to be based in Western Australia.
“What we’re seeing is a real increase in U.S. posture in Australia,” said Zack Cooper, a senior fellow and expert on U.S. strategy in Asia at the American Enterprise Institute. “Sometimes it can take a really long time to build out the infrastructure, but in this case, I think we’re seeing the U.S. and Australia move pretty quickly on both the air and the naval side. I think it’s emblematic of the step-up in effort we’re seeing from both Canberra and Washington.”
“The U.S. needs to diversify the locations from which it can operate air and naval assets. Australia’s northern bases do that on the air side and the naval facilities in Perth are critical on the nuclear submarine side,” he added.
Equipping a base to handle large bombers with heavy payloads is no small task: runways must be long, sturdy, and adequate, with ramp space, fuel infrastructure, and safe weapons storage facilities.
“That can all drive some considerable investment in airfields, which Australia has made and continues to invest in to bolster regional deterrence,” Gunzinger said.

US Vice President JD Vance has said that Washington is investigating reports that a US air strike struck a wedding gathering in southern Iran, while insisting that American forces do not deliberately target civilians.
“I’m extremely sceptical of this,” Vance said of Iranian state media reports alleging that the strike hit a wedding celebration, saying he had been briefed on the investigation but did not yet have information establishing whether US forces were responsible.
“What I can say with 100 percent confidence is that, unlike the IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat,” Vance said on Thursday.
“We never will do that. We never have done that.”
Vance said civilian casualties can occur during military operations, adding, “Unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen.”
He added that when US forces make mistakes, the military investigates them and seeks to learn from them. The US military has separately said it is reviewing the reports.
Iran reports 18 killed, 142 wounded
Iranian Health Ministry spokesperson Hossein Kermanpour said at least 18 people were killed and 142 wounded in US strikes between August 30 and September 2.
He said the casualties included four people in Sirik, seven in Khuzestan, four members of the IRGC Aerospace Force in Kermanshah and three Basij members on Lavan Island.
Kermanpour also said at least 50 people were wounded at a wedding gathering in Sirik. Other Iranian officials have reported four people killed and dozens wounded in the strike on the gathering.
The reports have drawn international concern, with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres saying he was “deeply alarmed” by reports of civilian casualties, including the strike that allegedly hit the wedding.
No talks until Iran stops targeting ships
Vance also said Washington is not currently negotiating with Tehran and would not resume talks unless Iran stops attacking commercial shipping.
“The message to the Iranians is simple,” he said. “You’ve got to stop shooting at commercial shipping.”
He rejected calls for a fixed timetable, arguing that a deadline could allow Iran to continue attacks while making US strategy predictable.
Vance said the administration was using military, economic, diplomatic and other forms of pressure to protect commercial vessels and keep oil and gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz.
He said about 15 million barrels of oil had passed through the strategic waterway despite the conflict.
Vance said the broader US objectives were to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and avoid a global energy crisis, arguing that US military operations had limited the impact of the conflict on global energy markets.

At least 37 people died early on Thursday in Nigeria's oil-rich southern Niger Delta after inhaling fumes during the theft of fuel from a pipeline, a local NGO has said.
Illegal oil-siphoning is a major problem in Nigeria - an OPEC member and one of Africa's largest petroleum producers - causing serious pollution.
Accidents are common in swamps in the Niger Delta, where smugglers tap into pipelines to steal crude and refine it into fuel for sale.
The Youths and Environmental Advocacy Centre (YEAC-Nigeria) said it had "received and confirmed a report from its network of youth volunteers and human rights defenders in the Niger Delta in the Okrika Local Government Area of Rivers State that some persons, not fewer than 37 have been confirmed dead after inhaling 'Indorama fuel'."
It said in a statement that those killed are "suspected to be oil thieves", adding: "Many others are still missing."
It said "youths had connected a pipe to a tapping point on a pipeline that normally transports" crude from producer Indorama Eleme Petrochemical through the Port Harcourt Refinery to vessels loading for export.
The men tapped into the pipeline and were loading oil into their own boats, it said.
"Many are still missing, and some corpses have been seen floating on the river but have not yet been recovered," the organisation said.
Oil pollution
Rivers State police confirmed the incident in a statement saying the victims were allegedly attempting to steal oil, but it did not give a toll.
The Niger Delta is home to Nigeria's multi-billion-dollar oil and gas resources, but residents of the region live in poverty due to decades of oil exploration, neglect and pollution.
YEAC-Nigeria called "on the government to provide alternative livelihood opportunities", including "the legalisation of artisanal refining".

Advocates decry US House vote to defund universities that boycott Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:14:05 UTC
04:14:05 KST

Advocates decry US House vote to defund universities that boycott Israel
Rights groups say the measure infringes on the freedom of speech of Americans for the benefit of a foreign nation.
The United States House of Representatives has passed a bill to penalise American universities for boycotting Israel or its academic institutions, including those located in the occupied West Bank, a move that critics say violates freedom of expression.
Lawmakers approved the measure in a 237-169 vote on Thursday, with 33 Democrats joining the Republican majority. Two Republicans broke ranks with their party to reject the bill.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3No end to torture of Gaza doctor Abu Safia in Israeli prison: What to know
- list 2 of 3Four imprisoned Palestine Action activists appeal terrorism sentences
- list 3 of 3Israel’s siege on Gaza is forcing dentists to operate in the streets
The proposal will still needs to be adopted by the Republican-controlled Senate and signed by President Donald Trump to become law.
If passed, it would bar universities that boycott “an entity licensed or regulated by, or organised under the laws of” Israel, such as those in illegal West Bank settlements, from receiving federal funds.
Withholding such funding would make it nearly impossible for many universities to operate or provide financial aid to students.
Jenin Younes, president of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC), said the bill raises serious concerns for the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which protects freedom of speech rights.
“The Supreme Court has made clear that the government cannot condition its funding on suppression of First Amendment-protected activity,” Younes told Al Jazeera. “Courts also recognise that boycotts constitute such activity.”
The legislation would require academic institutions in the US to annually certify that they allow cooperation with Israeli universities. The stipulation raises concerns that the bill not only bans boycotts of schools in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank but could compel US universities to forge relationships with them to fulfil the certification requirement.
The International Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Israeli settlements in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, “have been established and are being maintained in violation of international law”.
The bill comes at a time when public support for Israel in the US has nosedived. A Pew Research Center survey in July suggested that 62 percent of Americans have an unfavourable view of the Israeli government.
Still, support for the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, which carried out the genocidal war on Gaza, remains strong on Capitol Hill.
“The timing of the bill reflects the Israel lobby’s growing desperation in the face of rising opposition to US support for Israel,” Younes said.
“As Americans’ sentiment turns against our unholy alliance, Israel and its servants in Congress are working overtime to come up with ways to silence dissent and keep Americans’ tax dollars flowing to the genocidal, apartheid state.”
She added that including Israeli colleges in the occupied West Bank in the anti-boycott bill is further evidence there is no real intent by the US “to hold Israel accountable for its unlawful occupation or to pave the way for a Palestinian state”.
Restrictions on BDS
For years, US states and Congress have been passing bills to restrict the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement that aims to pressure Israel economically to end abuses against Palestinians.
The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) has been among rights groups who have regularly warned that anti-BDS laws violate constitutional free speech guarantees.
Robert McCaw, CAIR’s government affairs director, called the legislative proposal “a blatant attempt to hold American students’ financial futures hostage in order to shield the Israeli government and entities operating under Israeli law from peaceful economic pressure”.
“Students and faculty have the right to speak, organise and urge their institutions to align investment and purchasing decisions with their values,” McCaw said in a statement.
“Congress should not threaten Pell Grants and student loans simply because lawmakers dislike the outcome of that advocacy,” he said, referring to a federally funded financial aid programme.
Supporters of the bill have argued that the measure aims to regulate commercial conduct, not speech.
“Our universities should not use taxpayer-funded federal programs to discriminate against Israeli students, faculty, institutions, or businesses simply because they are Israeli,” Representative Tim Walberg, the Republican chair of the House Committee on Education and Workforce, said in a statement.
“I’m proud of my colleagues for standing up for that principle today and I hope to see the Senate do the same,” he said.
Some rights advocates have called for academic boycotts of Israel, saying Israeli universities play a role in enabling abuses against Palestinians by developing weapon systems and military strategies.
“For decades, Israeli universities have played a key role in planning, implementing and justifying Israel’s occupation and apartheid policies, and now genocide, while maintaining a uniquely close relationship with the Israeli military,” the BDS movement website says.
The two Republicans who voted against the bill on Tuesday were Thomas Massie and Warren Davidson, who have both been critical of Washington’s policy towards the Middle East.
The 33 Democrats who approved the measure included staunchly pro-Israel legislators Ritchie Torres and Haley Stevens, who recently lost her bid for the US Senate Democratic Party nomination in Michigan to Abdul El-Sayed, a supporter of Palestinian rights.

Schools in England face checks to root out unhealthy lunches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:09:52 UTC
04:09:52 KST

Schools could be reprimanded if they serve food containing too much fat, salt or sugar under new checks to ensure pupils receive healthy lunches.
The Department for Education is finalising plans for a promised “robust national enforcement system” to ensure all 21,500 state-funded schools in England comply with existing nutrition standards.
Schools are under a legal duty to abide by the standards, which are intended to tackle childhood obesity. But the lack of effective monitoring means that violations mostly go undetected, even though they are widespread.
Three-quarters of secondary schools serve unhealthy foods such as chips, burgers and hash browns more often than they are allowed, research found last week.
Ministers at the DfE want to fix the problem by expanding the role of environmental health officers (EHOs) so they can check the standards when they inspect school kitchens, according to well-placed sources.
Schools found to be breaching the standards would be told to improve the quality of the food they provide and given help to do so.
In April, the DfE committed to “developing a robust national enforcement system, including monitoring schools’ compliance”. The enforcement regime is expected to start in September 2027, to give schools time to overhaul the food they offer.
The standards, which became mandatory in 2014, limit provision of fatty, salty and sugary meals and snacks and promote much more nutritious fare.
The DfE announced in April that it would require every school to appoint a lead governor to be responsible for food and publish a policy and menu online. But campaigners, including School Food Matters and celebrity chef Jamie Oliver, have persuaded ministers that tougher regulation is needed.
Ministers and DfE officials have been studying detailed proposals from the School Food Review, an alliance of 38 diet, education and children’s health organisations. They want the Food Standards Agency and Ofsted to be given new powers to ensure compliance by schools.
Lucy Powell, the education secretary, appears to prefer expanding the FSA’s remit as the best way of improving compliance. The DfE, FSA and Office for Health Improvement and Disparities have been discussing the feasibility of EHOs taking on the extra role.
Prof Susan Jebb, a nutrition and obesity expert who is the chair of the FSA, is said by sources to be “enthusiastic” about the prospect of improved compliance.
The DfE has spoken to the Chartered Institute of Environmental Health, which represents EHOs and is in favour of the change. However, local council leaders are worried that a fall in EHO numbers means the officers would struggle to discharge the new responsibility alongside their existing duty to inspect a wide range of premises that serve food, including cafes and restaurants.
The DfE’s thinking has been influenced by the results of a pilot exercise in 2022/23 in which EHOs in 18 council areas checked whether schools were complying with the rules.
The checks added only 15 to 30 minutes to existing hygiene inspections, were “straightforward to administer” and schools were “happy to facilitate the checks”, the FSA’s evaluation found.
Some of the schools found to be non-compliant improved their food offer but others did not. Some that were flouting the standards erected “significant barriers” to attempts by councils to get them to provide healthier dishes.
The DfE was approached for comment.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday underscored the importance of the quality of teachers, who play a vital role in shaping the future of the country, and held National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE) can seek annual performance appraisal report (PAR) from teacher education institutions (TEIs).
A bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said the role of NCTE in ensuring quality education for children is immense and teacher education has assumed greater importance since right to education has been recognised as a fundamental right under Right to Education Act.

Microsoft to impose time limits on Xbox cloud gaming subscribers as costs continue to climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:03:56 UTC
04:03:56 KST

Microsoft's Xbox unit said Thursday that it will impose monthly cloud gaming time limits for Game Pass subscribers after years of unlimited access, as the company seeks to find a better balance between usage and costs.
Players will be able to pay for additional hours beyond the caps, which go into effect in November.
Across product organizations, Microsoft executives have been devising ways to charge customers based on usage to better reflect rising costs. Demand is climbing for the software company's finite amount of computing power — not unlike its technology peers — and clients of artificial intelligence products such as GitHub Copilot and the Microsoft 365 Copilot increasingly pay based on how much they use.
"We're introducing this model because the cost of providing cloud gaming grows as more people use it and play for longer," Xbox said in a blog post. "Moving to monthly limits allows us to keep offering the service while continuing to invest in its reliability and performance. We understand that for some players the practical result is a higher cost."
Users with high-end Game Pass Ultimate subscriptions, which cost $22.99 per month, will have access to 15 hours of cloud gaming. Game Pass Premium account holders, who pay $14.99 per month, will have 10 hours of cloud-based playtime, while Game Pass Essential, which costs $9.99 a month, includes five hours, according to the blog post.
Inside Xbox, new CEO Asha Sharma has been busy evaluating business model changes to return the division to growth and boost profitability. In July, Xbox said it would test ad-supported game streaming.
Just 4% of Game Pass subscribers spend more time each month streaming games through the cloud, Microsoft said. The company did not specify fees for extra hours.
Those who don't subscribe to Game Pass will be able to buy cloud gaming time to stream games they already own, Xbox said.
