High Court orders former Shin Bet officials who challenged Zini appointment to reveal names
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:43:19 UTC
00:43:19 KST

The High Court of Justice on Thursday ordered 189 former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) officials who sought to overturn David Zini’s appointment as director of the agency to reveal their identities to him by next Thursday.
The ruling brings the latest dispute arising from one of Israel’s most contested security appointments closer to an end.
The names will be given only to Zini and will remain barred from public release.
Zini’s appointment was opposed by former Shin Bet directors Nadav Argaman, Ami Ayalon, and Carmi Gillon, and 186 of their former colleagues. Their October petition said having Zini lead the Shin Bet without previous intelligence experience would be a risk to both national security and the agency’s independence.
Zini, a retired IDF major-general, was appointed after a turbulent process that began with the government’s attempt to dismiss his predecessor, Ronen Bar.
The High Court ruled that Bar’s dismissal had been conducted unlawfully, and that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a conflict of interest because the Shin Bet was involved in investigating the Qatargate affair in which members of the Prime Minister’s Office were involved.
Netanyahu later received approval to advance the appointment of Bar’s successor under an agreement reached with the attorney-general and endorsed by the court. The government approved Zini’s appointment on September 30, 2025, and he assumed office on October 5.
Former Shin Bet officials challenge Zini's appointment
The former officials filed their petition that same day. They said Zini had never served in an intelligence position and lacked the professional background required to manage an agency responsible for counterterrorism, counterespionage, internal security, and protecting Israel’s democratic institutions.
They also said the appointment process had not included a substantive examination of his professional suitability, and that conflicts involving members of his immediate circle could prevent him from handling parts of the agency’s work.
The petitioners asked the court to cancel the appointment and require a new selection process. Alternatively, it asked the government to demonstrate that the dominant consideration behind Zini’s selection was professional rather than political or personal.
The High Court rejected the challenges to the appointment in December by a 2 to 1 vote. Deputy Supreme Court President Noam Sohlberg and Justice David Mintz found no basis for judicial intervention after the appointment had been approved by the Advisory Committee on Senior Civil Service Appointments and the government.
Mintz rejected the contention that Zini’s lack of Shin Bet experience disqualified him, saying senior officials had previously moved between different branches of Israel’s security establishment.
Supreme Court President Isaac Amit dissented. He did not call for Zini’s appointment to be canceled outright. Instead, he said the advisory committee had failed to adequately examine the circumstances surrounding his selection, Netanyahu’s conduct, and the possibility that improper considerations had influenced the process. Amit said he would have returned the appointment to the committee for more examination and a fuller explanation.
Court suggests Zini waive right to see petitioners' names
The separate battle over the petitioners’ identities continued after their substantive case was rejected. They had filed the list of names confidentially and asked that it be available only to the judges.
There was no legal basis for concealing the names from Zini, who was a respondent in the case and held the necessary security clearance, Sohlberg ruled in December.
The court nevertheless suggested that Zini consider waiving his right to see them to ease tensions with former agency personnel who could still assist its work.
The petitioners later maintained that the judgment had recognized Zini’s right to inspect the list without expressly ordering them to provide it. Zini disagreed and filed a contempt-of-court motion, seeking enforcement.
On Thursday, Amit, Sohlberg, and Mintz issued an unequivocal new order, requiring the petitioners to provide their names to Zini within seven days.

Nvidia bought AI giant Hugging Face for almost $13 billion, CEO Jensen Huang announced in a company blog post shared on Thursday.
Huang explained that the acquisition was another push to provide "open weights to the AI economy," adding that "Hugging Face will continue to support open source and open weight models from across the ecosystem, from every model builder."
"Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem," he promised, adding that there will be no requirements to use Nvidia components when working on the Hugging Face platform.
Hugging Face was founded in 2016, with the name based on the hugging face emoji, as an AI chatbot developer, but shifted towards its current model of serving as a platform for AI development.
"As the opportunity for open models accelerates, Hugging Face can serve the global AI community at unprecedented scale," Huang added.
"NVIDIA’s infrastructure, engineering and global reach can help improve platform reliability, safety, model evaluation, inference and deployment capabilities, while preserving the open ecosystem that made Hugging Face foundational," he concluded.
OpenAI agent turns rogue during exercise in Hugging Face platform
Back in July, OpenAI said several experimental AI models escaped their test environment and hacked into the Hugging Face platform.
According to the company, the AI models did so without any human instruction, performing the hack as they went to "extreme lengths" to achieve a testing goal.
"The models identified and chained vulnerabilities across OpenAI’s research environment and Hugging Face’s production infrastructure to obtain test solutions directly from Hugging Face’s production database," the company said.
"Our models spent a substantial amount of inference compute finding a way to obtain open Internet access, in pursuit of solving the evaluation problem," it added.
Aaron Glick contributed to this report.

NFL set for first-ever game in Melbourne, Australia, in international expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:38:01 UTC
00:38:01 KST

The San Francisco 49ers and the Los Angeles Rams are heading to Australia, marking the longest-ever distance two NFL teams have traveled for a game.
It's all part of the league's push to expand American football globally. A record nine international regular-season games will be played in 2026 – kicking off in Melbourne, the city's first NFL game, and followed by inaugural match-ups in Rio de Janeiro and Paris. The schedule also brings professional football to London, Madrid, Munich and Mexico City.
NFL owners have already approved 10 international games for the 2027 season – the maximum number of games the league can play outside the United States per its current collective bargaining agreement with players.
While NFL games are consistently the most-watched programming on television, the vast majority of the league's interest is American. For some context, last year's Week 1 game in Sao Paulo, Brazil — streamed on YouTube — between the Kansas City Chiefs and the San Diego Chargers drew 18.5 million viewers in the U.S. and just 1.2 million viewers internationally.
That delta is what's driving NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell to seek global growth. Goodell has previously said he'd like to have up to 16 international games on the schedule. He also recently said he had "no doubt" a team would eventually be permanently located outside the U.S.
"We are committed to continue to grow every year in what we're doing," NFL Executive Vice President Peter O'Reilly said in a conference call for reporters on Wednesday. "We learn in each new market and then build upon that. That will be true as we move forward. As the commissioner said, we have aspirations to go beyond that. We want to do it the right way – to go to the right markets at the right time."
The NFL has a designed strategy to grow the game internationally. One key part is the league's relatively little-known Global Markets Program. Launched in 2022, the program gives NFL teams specific international marketing rights to build brand awareness and fandom.
Every team owns at least one market. When games are played abroad, the teams that own those markets are the de facto "home team." The Rams own marketing rights in Australia. Later this year, when the 49ers play in Mexico – a region where they own rights – they'll be the home team.
NFL clubs can apply for rights to international markets by submitting proposals to the International Committee for review each spring. The markets are often mildly based on geography. For example, the Rams own marketing rights in countries more easily accessible by West Coast teams, such as Australia, China, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand and — like the 49ers — Mexico. It also owns rights in the United Arab Emirates.
Other franchises' rights are more driven by their specific owners' wishes. The Detroit Lions own Austria, Brazil, Canada, Germany and Switzerland. The Los Angeles Chargers have Greece – and only Greece. Chargers owner Dean Spanos has Greek heritage.
The NFL has chosen a team-led strategy to grow fandom internationally because it wants buy-in from its franchise owners, O'Reilly said.
"It's one part of a larger strategy," O'Reilly said. "Having a favorite team is a key driver of lifelong fandom. Giving the clubs the option to apply, you want them to align with markets they're going to get behind. For the vast majority, those markets align with the markets we're committed to. It allows clubs the freedom to tailor to their priorities … working with our folks on the ground. "
Entering this season, 62 regular-season NFL games have been played outside the United States.
But there's no certainty the NFL's international strategy will significantly increase the sport's popularity.
Some of the challenge lies in time zone differences. Primetime games timed for a U.S. market mean taking the field in the middle of the night in Europe and in the morning in Australia.
The Rams and Niners are kicking off at 10:35 a.m. local time on a Friday next week.
It's difficult to grow a sport globally when start times need to cater toward Americans. The NFL has found 9:30 a.m. ET to be a sweet sport start time for European games – but TV ratings for those games have consistently been lower than Sunday afternoon and night contests.
It's also an open question of just how popular this international movement is with players, who must take long plane rides and battle jet lag with time differences.
While the 49ers left Wednesday for Australia, the Rams aren't arriving in the country until next week, 24 hours before game time.

Inklings | WFP defends new 5-year Palantir deal to staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:36:43 UTC
00:36:43 KST

Share & more
The World Food Programme is standing by its partnership with Palantir, telling staff that the new deal with the controversial military contractor will save the organisation millions of dollars. But some WFPers have questions.
Inklings explores how aid works in the wilds of humanitarian hubs, on the front lines of emergency response, or in the dark corners of aid punditry.
It’s also available as an email newsletter. Subscribe here.
Today: WFP staff question Palantir renewal, the fundraising strategy behind ration cuts, and the pope’s moral challenge on data extraction.
On the radar |
WFP is defending its partnership with Palantir, the data analytics firm and military contractor. In a message shared with staff on 30 August, the agency acknowledged that it renewed its “partnership agreement” for five years in July, following ”extensive internal reviews covering operational value, data governance, privacy, and security”.
“WFP management acknowledges concerns that have been raised regarding work with Palantir,” the internal message states. “These have been carefully considered through a cross-divisional committee, including ensuring safeguards to protect beneficiary data.”
WFP has come under fire for its secretive relationship with Palantir, often seen as an AI arms dealer that espouses a techno-fascist, US-dominated worldview. While governments and the public in several countries are questioning or breaking ties with Palantir, mostly over data sovereignty fears, WFP has largely refused to discuss or even acknowledge basic details about its partnership.
Internally, some staff have described a culture of silence when it comes to Palantir. The 30 August message was a rare example of WFP management engaging with the unease about Palantir, said a staff member who shared the note with us.
That said, the message was seen as more of a shut door than an open discussion. Senior WFP management was also questioned about the Palantir renewal during a 3 September all-staff meeting.
The vibe from management, the staff member said, is ”that this is the way it is. This is our partnership and we don’t have any intentions to let it go. So you have to accept this fact and stop asking questions”.
- Quick recap: WFP trumpeted its Palantir partnership in 2019, but quickly clammed up as criticism grew. Chatter in and out of WFP for several weeks has been that the food agency would renew its contract. PassBlue and France24 reported in early August that the contract was on the verge of being finalised, despite “key privacy concerns” from an internal audit. WFP is the backbone of the international humanitarian sector’s logistics operations and is building its growth strategy around harnessing data and pioneering new tech. A May cyber-attack exposed data belonging to a vast majority of Gaza’s remaining population. WFP restarted data collection in Gaza in July, but has ignored or sidestepped many questions about the breach from media, aid partners, and donors. Israel’s military has used data and AI-enabled analytics to target and kill in Gaza.
A few more tidbits from WFP’s internal message to staff:
- Cost savings: The all-seeing data integration platform created with Palantir, known as DOTS, has led to $50 million in savings, WFP says. Aid groups (especially WFP) often cite efficiency and savings as a reason for tech experimentation – a trend that’s accelerating amid today’s aid cuts. WFP did not show the math behind the figure. 
- How WFP describes Palantir’s value: DOTS helps WFP “aggregate large volumes of disparate data across supply chain, logistics, and planning into one analytical view, where patterns and trends can be identified,” the internal staff message states. It lists five examples of how decision-making is sped up: designing food baskets, procurement, planning movement ahead of rainy seasons, reducing delays and costs, and tracking commodity disruptions en route.
- What WFP says about dependency on Palantir: Analysts say creating user dependency is built into Palantir’s business model, and that WFP is veering in this direction. WFP’s message to staff said the agency is avoiding so-called “vendor lock-in” by working with “nearly all leading software providers”. We’ve asked WFP which software partners help prevent reliance on Palantir, and what WFP has done to explore alternatives.
- What’s missing: The internal staff message highlights cost savings and data security, insisting that beneficiary data is protected and does not “connect to any Palantir technology”. It does not address core moral critiques about the company itself, and why a humanitarian agency is partnering with a military contractor that has supplied tech used by the Israeli military in Gaza or by ICE to target migrants in the United States, or that is accused of aiding and abetting a genocide.
- What WFP says: We’ve asked WFP to discuss these issues, and for more info about the contract renewal and partnership. The agency has mostly ignored repeated questions about Palantir and the May cyber-attack.
Cuts |
Fundraising by pipeline cuts: WFP seems more eager to talk about ration cuts than data breaches or Palantir. The agency said funding shortfalls will force it to halve the number of people receiving food assistance in the West Bank.
It’s a familiar message. For years, the agency has highlighted ration cuts across various emergencies, and it has often pointed a finger back at donors in press releases. Analysts say the strategy has often soured relations with key donors, calling it “last-minute fundraising drives based on threats of breaks in the food distribution pipeline”.
Today’s funding pressures are massive, but the practice pre-dates the sector’s donor retreat and the resulting financial crisis. Meanwhile, some who have relied on aid question why food rations seem to be the first thing cut when money is scarce.
Palantíri |
Here are a few more additions to the “everyone is talking about Palantir, except for humanitarians” file:
Protest: Code Pink, the feminist anti-war group, staged a protest at the offices of World Food Program USA last month. The US non-profit raises funds for the UN agency.
Manchester: The all-caps tech magazine, WIRED, reports on the English county that’s saying no to Palantir.
“Why everybody hates Palantir”: This Economist article has a more measured view than its click-y headline suggests. It notes that Palantir weakens its position “by overstating what the software has achieved”. But it also largely lines up behind the firm, questioning whether other companies can do what Palantir does (this Computer Weekly article reckons they can indeed).
Palantir v The Pope: WFP hosted Pope Leo XIV at the agency’s Rome headquarters back in June. A few days later, Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel called the pope “a Chinese communist agent” (he meant it as an insult) for calling for AI regulation. Thiel previously gave lectures on “the antichrist” in Rome, reportedly unnerving Vatican officials.
LOTR: The pope’s AI encyclical contains a Lord of the Rings reference (the Palantir company name is borrowed from the Tolkien novel, which is always a reassuring sign). The papal encyclical, BTW, also calls data extraction a new form of colonialism: “Those who control the health data of entire peoples – often collected under the pretext of aid, research, or innovation – possess a structural leverage over the future,” he warned.
“This looks absolutely rubbish”: London Review of Books has a long read on Palantir and the UK’s National Health Service.
“It’s just a waste of time”: The article’s co-authors have a slightly shorter summary on their Substack.

Another European country transfers gold out of US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:31:16 UTC
00:31:16 KST

Another European country transfers gold out of US
The central bank of the Netherlands has become the latest country to move gold holdings out of the United States, announcing on Wednesday that it had transferred 86 tons of bullion to London. The bank described the move as “crisis preparedness” during a time of “increasing geopolitical unrest.”
The transfer was carried out between March and August. The bulk of the gold was moved from New York, with the rest coming from Canada. Only about 27 tons were physically transported across the Atlantic, while the remainder was accomplished through sales in the Americas and repurchases in London. Prior to the transfer, the Dutch central bank (DNB) had held 313 tons in North America.
“With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves,” according to a written statement by DNB Governor Olaf Sleijpen. “We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness.”
The DNB’s move comes after France’s central bank sold its remaining 129 tons of gold held at Federal Reserve vaults in New York between July 2025 and January 2026, leaving it with no bullion in the United States. The proceeds from the sale were used to purchase an equivalent amount of gold in Europe.
In 2017, under the first administration of US President Donald Trump, Germany’s Bundesbank announced that it had completed the transfer to Frankfurt of 300 tons of its gold held in New York. During Trump’s second term, several prominent German economists have called for the removal of the bank’s remaining holdings from the US.
Venezuela under President Hugo Chavez repatriated about 160 tons of its gold reserves from foreign banks, a move that was completed by January 2012. However, some 31 metric tons of Venezuelan gold are still held by the Bank of England. Efforts undertaken by then-President Nicolas Maduro to bring the bullion home were stymied by Great Britain, which did not recognize Maduro as the legitimate head of Venezuela’s government.
The DNB praised Bank of England-held gold as being “the world’s most easily tradable gold.” The Dutch central bank reported owning 612.4 metric tons as of the end of 2025, worth about €72 billion (about $84 billion).

Russia Church Official Wants Stalin-Era Divorce Rules Back as Demographic Fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:25:03 UTC
00:25:03 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Church Official Wants Stalin-Era Divorce Rules Back as Demographic Fix
A senior Russian Orthodox Church official proposed on September 2 reviving a Stalin-era Soviet decree to make divorce significantly harder in Russia, framing the move as a demographic necessity modeled after wartime policy, according to the independent Russian outlet Agentstvo.
Fyodor Lukyanov, chairman of the Patriarchal Commission on Family Affairs, Protection of Motherhood and Childhood, made the proposal at the Eastern Economic Forum during a session titled
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The Family as the Foundation for Preserving the Spiritual and Moral Values and Sovereignty of Russia," Lukyanov argued that abortion and divorce must be made economically disadvantageous and pushed to the social margins through a coordinated effort by the state and business.
"All citizens who were in a de facto marital relationship were required to register their marriage, indicating the duration of their cohabitation. Passports introduced a 'marital status' field. Differentiated taxation was introduced—income tax rates fell as the number of children increased.
The divorce procedure became more complex: two stages, a mandatory statement of grounds, the summoning of the spouse, and the calling of witnesses. This is not today's online divorce in our country," Lukyanov stated at the forum.
Lukyanov explicitly invoked Decree No. 118/11, issued by the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR in July 1944, arguing that the Soviet experience offers "a great deal of good that can be drawn upon given the current situation."
He noted that the USSR lost 26 million people during the Second World War and that the Soviet leadership responded with demographic measures—measures he argued Russia must now "retrieve and use." Under the 1944 decree, divorce required a court ruling rather than a simple registry office filing, and proceedings could include interrogations by prosecutors. The decree's provisions on marriage and divorce remained in force until 1965.
Lukyanov also raised questions about the official statistics on abortion, suggesting that a reported decline in their number reflects a fall in the population of women of reproductive age and possible manipulation of data.
He pointed to Russia's rate of recorded miscarriages—44% of pregnancies with an abortive outcome in 2024—and implied that clinics have a financial incentive to reclassify abortions as miscarriages under the compulsory medical insurance system, since the reimbursement rate for the latter is higher.
"Is this what happened to our women? Or is someone changing the statistics? Yes, most likely," he told the forum. Agentstvo noted that the 44% figure is calculated not from all known pregnancies but from those ending in an abortive outcome, a measure distinct from the World Health Organization's (WHO) standard reference range of 10–15%.
The proposal comes amid a deepening demographic crisis in Russia, with senior officials increasingly pressuring young people to have more children. In July, Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko demanded that young Russians start families early and have at least three children before turning 35.
Russia recorded 1.178 million births in 2025, below the previous post-Soviet low of 1.215 million in 1999, while births fell by another 17,000 year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026.

Russia Threw Six FPV Drones at Ukraine’s Armed Robot—It Completed the Mission Anyway
Ukraine’s Droid TW-12.7 unmanned ground vehicle survived five FPV drone strikes and completed its combat mission before a sixth hit finally disabled the platform, according to a DevDroid press release shared with UNITED24 Media on September 2.
Soldiers from the fire support company of Ukraine’s 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion deployed the UGV during a remotely conducted operation against a concentration of Russian troops.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
As the Droid TW-12.7 approached the position, two FPV drones struck the vehicle almost simultaneously. One of the hits damaged its aiming module, but the platform remained mobile and continued the mission.
Operators adapted to the damage by aiming in the direction of the weapon barrel and opened fire on the target. Two additional FPV drones struck the UGV during the engagement, but it remained operational long enough to complete its primary task.
The vehicle then began withdrawing and survived a fifth FPV strike while continuing to move. A sixth drone eventually disabled it on the return route.
DevDroid said the Russian troop concentration was cleared and enemy forces suffered losses. The entire operation was carried out remotely, allowing Ukrainian personnel to avoid direct contact with Russian troops.
“In this engagement, the enemy was able to stop the Droid only with the sixth FPV drone, but they still failed to prevent it from completing the mission. For us, this is what survivability means in practice: after being hit, a system must not simply remain mobile—it must retain enough functionality for its operators to complete the mission and achieve the intended result,” DevDroid CEO Yurii Poritskyi said.
The Droid TW-12.7 is a Ukrainian reconnaissance-and-strike UGV developed by DevDroid. It is equipped with a remotely operated turret carrying a 12.7 mm M2 Browning heavy machine gun, as well as an integrated ballistic computer and AI-assisted targeting functions.
The platform is designed to engage personnel, vehicles, and lightly armored targets while allowing Ukrainian troops to conduct dangerous frontline missions from a safer distance.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine is expanding its fleet of unmanned ground vehicles, aiming to produce at least 50,000 combat and logistics robots this year to reinforce infantry units and bridge manpower shortages along the frontline.

PUMA Partners With Ukrainian Fashion Brand CHER’17 for First-Ever Collaboration
German sportswear company PUMA has partnered with Ukrainian fashion brand CHER’17, marking PUMA’s first collaboration with a local fashion label in the Ukrainian market.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the press release, the CHER’17 x PUMA collection is built around the concept of unexpected changes to everyday plans, reflected in the campaign’s central message, “No plan is a plan.” The collaboration reinterprets PUMA’s classic designs through details inspired by everyday accidents and imperfections.
“Modern life requires improvisation: so many things genuinely don’t go according to plan. We decided to dedicate our collaboration to this spontaneity and explore it through a new perspective on PUMA’s classic silhouettes,” says Tetyana Parfilieva, Creative Director of CHER’17.
The collection centers on a customized version of the PUMA Suede, one of the company’s signature footwear silhouettes. CHER’17 has reworked the model with prints and visual effects designed to resemble paint splatters, peeling surfaces, and traces of dirt.
Rather than treating these elements as imperfections, the collection incorporates them as intentional design features, reflecting its broader theme of adapting to circumstances that do not go as planned.
The collaboration also extends beyond footwear, with T-shirts featuring visual elements based on the same concept.
For CHER’17, the partnership represents another step in the Ukrainian brand’s development and its cooperation with international fashion companies. The project also adds to a growing number of collaborations between Ukrainian labels and established global brands.
“This collaboration was entirely an initiative of the local PUMA Ukraine team. We have a great appreciation for our brands and had long wanted to create a joint local project. CHER’17 was a perfect match for us in terms of values: it represents boldness, dynamism, and contemporary urban style,” Olha Tyshchenko, Brand Manager at PUMA Ukraine, said in a comment to UNITED24 Media.
She noted that in today’s reality, many circumstances are beyond people’s control and can unfold differently from what was expected, stressing that such unexpected changes should not be a reason to become discouraged or stop moving forward.
“Sometimes, it is precisely these unexpected turns that give rise to something truly exciting, authentic, and special—just like this collaboration,” Tyshchenko concluded.
The collaboration follows other recent milestones for Ukrainian fashion on the international stage. Earlier this year, Ukrainian fashion brand LITKOVSKA made its debut on the official Paris Fashion Week runway schedule, where it presented its Fall-Winter 2026/27 collection, FIREFLY.

The Climate Crisis Is Stretching the Nepali Military Beyond Its Limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:12:00 UTC
00:12:00 KST

The footage of the avalanche that triggered devastating floods along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers near the China-Nepal border on August 26 is deeply sobering. The road, bridges, customs, and immigration office with China, and the entire settlement and traditional bazaar along the riverbank, were wiped out in a moment.
In the wake of the flood, the Nepali government deployed security forces, including the Nepal Army, Nepal Police, and Armed Police Force, as first responders. Nepal has put more than 20,000 security personal into responding to the disaster, possibly the largest such deployment since the aftermath of the 2015 earthquake. The collapse of local and provincial governments and the inaccessibility of flood-affected areas prompted the government to rely on the security forces at a desperate moment.
The use of security forces in disaster response is not new in Nepal. Security forces often get involved, ranging from rescue and relief operations to rehabilitation activities. The Nepali Constitution 2015 (2072 BS) enshrined a provision for deploying the military in national crises arising from disasters and development projects. The National Security Policy (2016) also considers climate change and the environment as part of the national interest.
But the ad hoc stretching of the security forces into disaster response can result in the security forces themselves being increasingly exposed to vulnerabilities and capacity constraints amid the climate crisis in Nepal. As environmental disasters become more frequent and severe in the Himalayan region, the recent flood must be an important case study in the growing complexity of the military’s engagement in disaster governance and preparedness.
The scale and intensity of the recent flood was unimaginable and it is becoming evident that there were significant casualties among security forces. A week since the incident, and a total of 85 security force members – encompassing 45 from the Nepal Army, 28 from the Nepal Police, and 13 from the Armed Police Force – are still unaccounted for.
The police forces went missing while on duty near the border, customs area, and river corridor. Some Nepal police personnel went missing due to a sudden surge in flooding while circulating a notice to downstream communities. Similarly, Nepal army personnel were on duty at Langtang National Park and were stationed at multiple hydropower projects. Armed police forces went missing from a border post. In addition, three police posts in Timure, Rasuwagadhi, and Syafrubesi were damaged or swept away.
The unique circumstances of the flood gave security personnel very little time to respond. The absence of an early warning system and the lack of any cross-border disaster communication made the situation even more complicated.
Rescue operations are still ongoing, particularly in areas with multiple hydropower tunnels, such as Upper Trishuli-1, Rasuwagadhi Hydropower, Chilime Hydropower, Langtang Khola, and Upper Trishuli-3A. Hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped in these tunnels. As the days pass, families of those trapped and even security personnel are increasingly frustrated. Some tunnel rescue operations have been halted due to a lack of progress and the rescue team’s inability to advance. The security forces are exploring their options, including conducting a controlled blast to clear debris blocking the tunnel.
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah, speaking at parliament on September 2, said that “tunnels present a very distinct problem, they are filled with mud, debris, and floodwater. Clearing them requires specialized skills that none of the countries, including Nepal, have had. Though we have mobilized at short notice, and progress depends on weather and drier conditions.” He added that the security forces should be commended for their efforts, made under various constraints.
Footage of Nepal Army personnel laboring and displaying their willingness to risk their own lives in a tunnel operation has drawn attention. The security forces have been widely praised for their courage and bravery. But an emerging consensus has made it clear that the Nepali government, including the Nepal Army, lacks the advanced expertise, technology, and equipment for effective tunnel rescue operations. Bravery is not a substitute for preparedness, equipment, and expertise.
The Nepali government has sought international assistance in specific areas, including tunnel rescues and forensic work, and reached out to countries like India, China, and South Korea for critical equipment and technology. This, however, highlights Nepal’s disaster vulnerabilities and preparedness deficits.
The recent flood reiterates the changing environmental security landscape in the Himalayan region. The International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has identified dozens of potentially dangerous glacier lakes in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region; the recent floods may be less of an outlier and more of a warning.
The climate crisis, and the use of security forces in response to climate-driven disasters, decisively alters the strategy, function and operating environment of military institutions. The question here is not whether the military should be involved in disaster response, but how the military itself is responding, adapting, and transforming amid the climate crisis. This is particularly important in Nepal, where the military institution is deeply embedded in disaster response and preparedness already.

Rights groups urge US lawmakers to drop provision to deepen defense ties with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:11:17 UTC

Rights groups urge US lawmakers to drop provision to deepen defense ties with Israel
WASHINGTON, Sept 3 - Dozens of civil rights and advocacy groups are urging Congress to scrap a defense bill provision that would deepen U.S.-Israeli military technology ties, according to a letter seen by Reuters, at a time of growing U.S. skepticism toward the longtime ally.
The provision would deepen cooperation between the U.S. and Israeli defense sectors by accelerating joint military technology development and other partnerships. The bill passed the House of Representatives in July and awaits Senate action.
The provision of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, known as Section 219, seeks to set up frameworks for joint ventures, licensing agreements and U.S.-based co-production partnerships with the Israeli industry.
In Thursday's letter addressed to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, 56 groups said deeper integration with Israel's defense sector would be "exceptionally dangerous" and urged lawmakers to remove the provision.
The groups include Amnesty International USA and the civil rights network National Lawyers Guild as well as Arab and Jewish advocacy groups.
"At a time in which American interests are increasingly diverging from those of Israel, and American public opinion is turning increasingly against unconditional support to Israel, creating new points of influence for Israel in the U.S. defense-technology ecosystem is exceptionally dangerous," said the letter, which has not been previously reported.
Israel is one of Washington's closest allies in the Middle East, and the two countries cooperate extensively on defense and intelligence issues. Supporters say deeper ties could help speed military innovation and technology development.
A spokesperson from the Israeli Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story.
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off U.S. military support within a decade. In a June letter to a U.S. congressman he wrote that the time has come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen told Reuters that it was not in U.S. national interests to deepen such cooperation with the Netanyahu government.
"This provision ... threatens to compromise sensitive technologies and, based on our prior experience, risks giving the Government of Israel the ability to interfere in U.S. defense decisions," Van Hollen said.
U.S. PUBLIC SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL DECLINES
U.S. public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of U.S. support for Israel.
The Islamist militant Hamas group, in an October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, killed nearly 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals and took hundreds hostage. More than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed in Israel's subsequent assault on Gaza, according to Gaza health officials.
The letter criticizes Israel for its potential violations of international humanitarian law in its war in Gaza and rising settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. It says such developments should prevent any discussion of deepening military ties.
A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion annual U.S. military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028 and conversations are under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
Some members of Congress have already tried to strip the provision from the fiscal 2027 NDAA. Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Democratic Representative Ro Khanna of California introduced an amendment to block it, but it did not make it into the House version of the bill.
Once the House and Senate write their versions of the NDAA, members of the two chambers work out a compromise version of the bill, which must pass both chambers - typically near the end of the calendar year - before it can be sent to the White House for President Donald Trump to sign into law or veto. REUTERS

Pokémon Sleep and Japanese hospitality brand NOT A HOTEL are translating one of gaming’s most recognizable objects into inhabitable architecture. Appearing amid the natural landscape of Hokkaido in September 2026, the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel turns the familiar red-and-white sphere into a place where people can actually spend the night — a rather literal invitation to catch some sleep.
The collaboration borrows its premise from the fictional universe, where Poké Balls are conceived as comfortable places for Pokémon to rest. Here, the scale shifts from pocket-sized device to human retreat, with architecture and technology used to create an environment centered on calm, comfort, and a good night’s sleep. The idea also neatly extends the logic of Pokémon Sleep, the mobile game that tracks rest and rewards players for developing healthier sleeping habits.
the poké ball-themed hotel appears in hokkaido | images courtesy of NOT A HOTEL
A POKÉ BALL LANDS IN HOKKAIDO
For now, the structure remains deliberately mysterious. The first images reveal its unmistakable spherical exterior against Hokkaido’s open landscape, but the rooms, materials, internal organization, and sleeping experience have yet to be shown. The complete project will be unveiled on September 15, 2026, leaving a few important architectural questions unanswered — including how one furnishes a giant ball without everything rolling toward the middle.
The project sits comfortably within NOT A HOTEL’s broader approach to hospitality, which brings together design-led architecture, digital technology, and highly controlled stays. Founded in Japan in 2020, the company develops a network of distinctive residences by architects and creators, combining private ownership with hotel services and shared access across its properties. The Poké Ball may be its most pop-cultural experiment yet, but the conversion of an instantly recognizable image into a fully operational retreat follows the same appetite for architecture as experience.
the familiar sphere becomes a place to sleep
AN EXCLUSIVE NIGHT INSIDE THE ICON
The Poké Ball-Themed Hotel will not operate as a conventional property with rooms available through a booking platform. Instead, stays will be offered through a limited campaign, giving selected participants the opportunity to experience the one-off structure. Application requirements and further details will be announced alongside the full reveal on September 15 through the official Pokémon Sleep channels.
Until then, the project exists somewhere between architectural teaser, oversized collectible, and remote sleeping pod. Its success will ultimately depend on what lies beyond the circular entrance: whether the collaboration simply enlarges a familiar object or uses its unusual geometry to propose a genuinely memorable interior. Either way, Hokkaido is about to receive a new landmark that should be difficult to miss — even without a map or a Pokédex.

German warship secretly fires ballistic missile in Atlantic

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:10:35 BST
00:10:35 KST

A German warship has fired an Israeli-made LORA ballistic missile during a live test in the North Atlantic, with the German Navy saying the launch demonstrated a strike capability with a potential range beyond anything it had previously operated.
German media reports, citing a German Navy spokesman, said two German frigates had deployed to waters between Ireland and Iceland for the test on Tuesday night. Images from the exercise show a containerised launcher positioned on the deck of a German vessel.
The messaging here could hardly be clearer. By disclosing a test that had deliberately been kept secret, NATO was sending a direct signal to Moscow: European forces are developing longer-range strike options, and not every capability will be visible before it is ready.
NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said the test had been kept secret until after it was completed and involved a German frigate firing the missile in the North Atlantic.
The command stated: “Kept secret. Now revealed. The German Navy just tested the Israeli LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.”

It added: “NATO 3.0 looks like this: Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious capabilities and keeping a few cards close to the chest. Deterrence just got a little more interesting.”
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, Inspector of the German Navy, said: “With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we made naval history. I am extremely satisfied with this achievement.”
Kaack added that the system “can be successfully deployed from our units, and the potential range exceeds anything we have known before.”
In his original statement, the German Navy chief said the trial opened a new chapter for maritime deterrence and readiness, stating that the system could be operated successfully from German units and that its possible reach exceeded previous German naval capabilities.
The test was conducted with Israel Aerospace Industries’ LORA, or Long-Range Artillery Weapon System. According to IAI, the missile has a range of around 400 kilometres and an accuracy of within 10 metres, while NATO’s public account of the German test referred to a range of more than 500 kilometres.
Israel Aerospace Industries said the missile was launched from an operational German vessel equipped with a command trailer and launcher. According to the company, the missile followed its planned trajectory, navigated to the target and successfully struck it, with both the weapon system and missile meeting the objectives of the trial.
Boaz Levy, Chairman of IAI, said: “This is an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Israeli Ministry of Defense. The successful trial of the LORA missile, launched from a naval vessel and striking its target with exceptional precision, took place overnight in Germany – the country where the world’s first ballistic missile was developed.”
He added: “This trial demonstrates Israel’s technological strength and the unique cooperation between Israel and Germany. It marks another significant achievement alongside the deployment of the Arrow 3 system on German soil, further strengthening Germany’s defense and deterrence capabilities and deepening the strategic partnership between our two countries.”
IAI chief executive Guy Bar Lev said: “Israel Aerospace Industries is proud to take part in strengthening the strategic cooperation between the State of Israel and the Government of Germany. This significant milestone is underscored by the operational live-fire exercise (OPEX) of the LORA system, one of the world’s most advanced and combat-proven ballistic missile systems.”
The German Navy is using its OPEX initiative to trial technologies and operational concepts as part of its Marine 2035 and Beyond programme. The process is intended to allow new systems to be tested rapidly under conditions intended to resemble operational use as closely as possible.
The North Atlantic launch comes as Germany expands its investment in long-range strike and air and missile defence. The country has also begun fielding the Israeli-developed Arrow 3 ballistic missile defence system as part of its wider effort to strengthen national and NATO defensive capabilities.

US pressure on Iran starting to tell, as sanctions and blockade bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:06:14 UTC
00:06:14 KST

US economic pressure on Iran taking effect as sanctions and blockade bite: Sources
- US sanctions and blockade are severely restricting Iran's oil exports and access to international financing, putting intense economic pressure on Tehran.
- Iran faces a deepening economic crisis with a collapsing currency, high inflation, and low petrol stocks amid ongoing conflict and sanctions.
- Economic hardships risk triggering unrest in Iran, while both Iran and the US use the conflict to influence each other's political situation.
AI generated
DUBAI – A US campaign to throttle Iran’s economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is growing increasingly difficult to withstand, three senior Iranian sources said.
Washington has, in recent weeks, sought to ratchet up the economic pressure on Tehran in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that six months of conflict have so far failed to secure.
Although Iran’s clerical rulers managed to bypass sanctions for decades, the latest US moves have left them in a far more sensitive position, with few remaining channels to secure foreign currency or buy goods, the sources said.
In particular, the effort to stop Iran from accessing international financing networks in other countries it has long used to keep its economy functioning poses a real and urgent threat, the sources said.
Any sign that the economic campaign may break a months-long deadlock in the conflict will likely cheer US planners, though Iran has also warned it could respond to the pressure with military escalation, raising the stakes at a key moment.
Petrol stocks low as currency collapses
The war has erupted back into open fighting this week, with US attacks along Iran’s Gulf coast prompting retaliatory Iranian strikes on US bases in Arab states.
Neither side has yet signalled it is ready to make the concessions demanded by the other, leaving the war in a costly stalemate – though one that may be shifting.
While more energy is flowing to international markets through the Strait of Hormuz despite Iranian efforts to continue disrupting the seaway, the US blockade of Iranian oil exports has entirely cut off Tehran’s main source of revenue.
Adding to Iran’s problems, the economy was already deep in crisis before the conflict, with a cratering currency and spiralling inflation, while months of bombing have run up a massive bill to rebuild damaged industry and infrastructure.
Meanwhile, the country’s financial squeeze is itself biting into Tehran’s efforts to get around the sanctions regime, leaving less cash to pay the high premiums required to skirt sanctions illicitly, the sources said.
The rial has fallen to record lows over recent days and one senior source said Iran has only another two months’ supply of petrol, which has to be imported despite domestic oil production because of limited refining capacity.
Iran’s rulers are keenly aware of the potential risks of an economic meltdown and the possibility of it reigniting the nationwide mass protests it put down in January by killing thousands of demonstrators.
“They are under very, very severe economic pressure. They’re losing control of the strait. It’s really a question of if they choose to negotiate, and I think they’ll have to,” said Ali Ansari, a modern history professor at the University of St Andrews in Scotland.
The war is also entering a new phase, with each side trying to influence the other’s politics.
Iran hopes that the threat of inflation will deter the US administration before midterm elections in November, while Washington aims to push Iranians to revolt, a senior Iranian official said.
Blockade and secondary sanctions squeezing Tehran
The latest US measures expanded secondary sanctions that target countries doing business with Iran in a bid to stop it from clearing dollar transactions needed for both oil sales and to finance crucial imports of goods and raw materials.
That effort is making Iran’s existing sanctions evasion networks – front companies, unregistered tankers and smuggling – too expensive to use, the three senior sources said.
Iranian crude loadings have fallen in September to about 260,000 barrels a day, from about 1.7 million a year earlier, according to data from commodity analytics firm Kpler, with only a trickle still moving off terminals for distribution by truck, train or smaller boats over the Caspian Sea.
Tehran says it still has tens of millions of barrels stored in tankers outside the blockade zone that it can sell, but the new sanctions mean intermediaries are stepping back or demanding more money, one of the officials said.
Total trade has fallen between 25 per cent and 35 per cent, with imports hit harder than exports, President Masoud Pezeshkian has said, one of several top officials warning in recent weeks about Iran’s rapidly deteriorating situation.
US pressure and Iran’s own attacks have, meanwhile, disrupted one of the main conduits for Iranian trade – the United Arab Emirates, which said on Aug 19 that all commercial exchange and financial dealings with Tehran were halted until further notice.
“If those channels stay closed, a supplier wants cash, a deal is routed through another country and a shipment arrives later and dearer,” said an Iranian trader in Tehran who deals in imported goods.
The currency has collapsed in value from around one million rials to the US dollar a year ago to over 2.2 million rials now. The internal impact is very painful. Official figures put 12-month average inflation at 69.9 per cent with food, beverages and tobacco prices rising at nearly twice that rate.
Official unemployment rose to 9.1 per cent in the spring, while the number of people working fell by about 450,000 from a year earlier amid a wider fall in labour force participation.
Even for those still in work, the average monthly salary of around US$125 (S$158) a month comes nowhere near meeting basic household spending requirements that come to around US$450 a month, according to official data.
“We are getting poorer every day,” said Mahnaz, a 34-year-old private-sector employee in Tehran who asked that her family name not be used. REUTERS

‘False narrative’ on China flood censorship coming from Washington – Nury Vittachi (VIDEO)
Western media are using unverified claims that Beijing censored footage of the deadly Nepal-Tibet floods to promote “false narratives” about China, Hong Kong-based author Nury Vittachi has told RT.
Speaking on Thursday, Vittachi said Western outlets frequently cite Tibetan advocacy groups without adequately disclosing their funding and location, while shaping reporting that portrays Beijing in an overwhelmingly negative light.
“The Western media pick up these groups and they deliberately hide the funding,” he said, arguing that readers consequently get a “very distorted view.”
Vittachi singled out organizations supported by the US-based National Endowment for Democracy (NED), accusing them of “weaponizing human rights against China.” He argued that negative coverage of China ultimately serves a broader effort to “manufacture consent for a war on China.”
The comments come as Western outlets including the BBC and Telegraph have accused Beijing of suppressing footage of the catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border. The BBC claimed images of the disaster had spread around the world while being heavily restricted inside China.
However, footage aired by the BBC itself included material obtained from China’s state broadcaster CCTV, showing floodwaters engulfing the border crossing at Gyirong.
Reporting live for RT from Gyirong, CGTN correspondent Cen Ziyuan showed the scale of the destruction and the difficulties facing rescue crews trying to reach the worst-hit areas. Heavy mud and huge rocks have blocked access roads, forcing crews to deploy excavators and other heavy machinery, she said.
Cen said rescuers had in some cases spent more than ten hours climbing through mountainous terrain to reach the border area, while helicopters had been used for airdrops. Her report from the disaster zone also showed heavy machinery working near the destroyed Gyirong Port and flood-damaged roads.
The on-the-ground coverage comes as search and rescue operations continue following the catastrophic landslide and flooding, with thousands reported dead or missing across the affected region.

China pledges to halt rise of Japanese neo-militarism: spokesperson
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
23:03:49 CST
00:03:49 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- China will stand together with peace-loving countries in the world to firmly hold back the malevolent emergence of Japanese neo-militarism under the pretext of making Japan a "normal country," and prevent it from wreaking havoc on the region and beyond, said a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Thursday.
Spokesperson Guo Jiakun made the remarks at a regular press briefing when answering a query related to Japan's 2026 defense white paper.
The white paper recently issued by Japan's Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed that Japan will further seek "enemy base strike capability." The MoD also requested a record 8.89 trillion yen for fiscal year 2027.
On the day that marks the 81st anniversary of the victory of the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, Guo said that the designation of the Victory Day of the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression is to remember the profound suffering that Japanese militarist aggression imposed on the people of China and the rest of the world, to remind the public not to forget history, and to uphold the outcomes of WWII victory and postwar international order.
He noted that over the years, Japanese right-wing forces have tried to turn the verdict on the history of aggression, and break free from the postwar international arrangements and their international obligations.
Guo stressed that a series of international instruments including the Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation and Japan's Instrument of Surrender have affirmed in legal terms Japan's status as a defeated state, and explicitly stipulated the obligations of defeated states, including eradicating militarism, abolishing military industries, dismantling war capability, and not rearming for war.
He added that these postwar international arrangements help uphold historical truth and international justice, set up an institutional line of defense against the resurrection of militarism, and embody the outcomes of the victory of the World Anti-Fascist War.
"Our solemn message to Japanese right-wing forces: the right way forward for Japan is to fulfill its international obligations, fully remove the pernicious influence of militarism, and keep to peaceful development," Guo said. ■

HOHHOT, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice Premier Liu Guozhong has stressed the need to step up agricultural disaster prevention and mitigation to secure a bumper autumn grain harvest.
Liu, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks during an inspection tour in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region from Sept. 1 to 3.
Noting that autumn grain accounts for three quarters of annual grain output and is currently in a critical period for yield growth, Liu called for region-specific and scientific field management and swift implementation of yield-boosting measures.
He also stressed strengthening meteorological monitoring and early warning, improving grain harvesting and drying capacities, and ensuring effective pest and disease control.
Liu urged efforts to give full play to farmers' cooperatives and other agricultural entities, implement supportive policies on autumn grain production, and protect farmers' grain-growing incomes.
During the inspection, Liu also learned about high-standard farmland development, black soil protection, seed industry revitalization, agricultural technology promotion, and agricultural water-saving. He called for accelerating the application of artificial intelligence and the development of smart agriculture, and the promotion of advanced farming techniques. ■

Belgium records nearly 3,000 deaths due to summer heatwaves
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
23:03:46 CST
00:03:46 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Belgium recorded nearly 3,000 excess deaths during three periods of high temperatures this summer, according to data released Thursday by the national public health institute, Sciensano.
Data from Sciensano's Belgian Mortality Monitoring (Be-MOMO) system showed that 2,035 deaths were recorded during the first heatwave from June 18 to July 3, representing an increase in mortality of 48.8 percent. The second heatwave, from July 4 to 17, saw 535 excess deaths, a 14.8 percent increase, while the third period of intense heat, from July 28 to Aug. 16, saw a 7 percent spike in mortality, or 365 deaths.
Sciensano said the first heatwave had the most pronounced impact on mortality, with a significant increase in deaths among people aged 15 to 64. This marked the highest excess mortality levels, both in absolute numbers and as a percentage, among heatwaves analyzed in Belgium since 2000.
The institute said the severity of the episode was linked to a combination of factors: the duration of the episode, the intensity of the heat and ozone concentrations.
It also said that maximum temperatures in Belgium had hovered around 30 degrees Celsius for 10 consecutive days from June 18, including three days near 35 degrees Celsius, while ozone concentrations remained above 100 micrograms per cubic meter for 10 consecutive days.
Be-MOMO monitors mortality from all causes by comparing observed deaths with the statistically expected number of deaths. The latest figures may still be revised as mortality data are further consolidated, Sciensano said. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
23:03:41 CST

CAIRO, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Egypt's economy grew by 5.1 percent in the 2025/2026 fiscal year ending in June, up from 4.4 percent the previous fiscal year and exceeding international institutions' projections, the Egyptian government said Thursday.
Minister of Planning and Economic Development Ahmed Rostom said at a cabinet meeting that "the Egyptian economy achieved a growth rate of 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter of the 2025/2026 fiscal year, bringing the growth rate for the fiscal year as a whole to 5.1 percent."
"This reflects the resilience and sustainability of the Egyptian economy's growth amid the regional tensions," Rostom said.
He attributed the growth to improved performance across several sectors, noting that the industry, trade and telecommunications sectors served as the main engines, accounting for 48 percent of total growth.
The fiscal year also saw a clear recovery in Suez Canal activity, making it one of the fastest-growing sectors, Rostom said.
The minister added that non-petroleum manufacturing maintained strong growth of 9 percent, while petroleum refining returned to positive growth of 8.7 percent, compared with a contraction of 1.9 percent in the previous fiscal year, amid higher production and refinery maintenance.
In August, the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) projected Egypt's real GDP growth to pick up to 4.6 percent in the current 2025/26 fiscal year. ■

DHAKA, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- In the span of less than nine months this year, the mosquito-borne dengue fever has claimed more than 100 lives and infected nearly 40,000 people across Bangladesh.
Based on the latest record of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), the dengue prevalence has reached a worrying situation this year, with a total of 39,532 cases and 111 deaths recorded as of Sept. 3.
According to the latest figure reported by the DGHS, the dengue deaths this year included 14 so far in September, 43 in August, 36 in July and 13 in June.

The infection tally so far this month indicates the fast-rising trend of the mosquito-borne disease in parts of the country.
The June-September monsoon period is the season of dengue fever in Bangladesh, which is considered a high-risk nation prone to mosquito-borne diseases. ■

ADEN, Yemen, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- At least 25 people were killed and several others wounded on Thursday as heavy fighting between Yemen's government forces and the Houthis raged in southwestern Taiz province, a government military official told Xinhua.
Fifteen government soldiers and 10 Houthi members were killed in the clashes, which erupted at dawn after Houthi fighters launched a large-scale assault on government positions in the villages of Maqbanah and Al-Kadha, the official said on condition of anonymity.
The clashes involved artillery, mortars, and other heavy weapons, according to the official.
The Houthis briefly seized several positions before government reinforcements mounted a counterattack and recaptured some ground, the official said.
Residents told Xinhua that the escalation had triggered a new wave of displacement, as families fled toward safer areas amid intensified Houthi artillery shelling.
The ground fighting coincided with missile and drone attacks across western Yemen. Government forces reported Thursday that the Houthis fired 14 ballistic missiles and drone attacks at areas along the western coasts of Taiz and neighboring Hodeidah province over the past several hours, while air defenses shot down several drones.
The Houthis have yet to comment on the fighting or the government's statements.
Fighting between government forces and the Houthis has intensified across several fronts in recent weeks. The government forces stepped up drone and artillery strikes on Houthi positions, while the group launched missile and drone attacks on government-held areas in Marib and along the western Red Sea coast.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

Held under the theme "Sexual and reproductive health and rights of adolescents and young people in Africa in the face of multifaceted crises," the conference aims to promote the exchange of experiences and develop concrete responses to the challenges facing young people amid multiple humanitarian crises, the effects of climate change and declining funding for sexual and reproductive health services.
At the opening ceremony, Bah said that "Africa draws its greatest strength from its youth" and this strength "will only fully bear fruit if young people are educated, protected and healthy."
He noted that early pregnancy, unaddressed violence or delayed access to healthcare could lead to interruptions in schooling and undermine young people's prospects for the future.
"Sexual and reproductive health involves several dimensions of public policy: it concerns maternal health, education and the protection of women, equal opportunities and the quality of human capital," Bah said.
According to him, crises "amplify risks, disrupt services, keep young people away from health facilities and reduce intervention capacities," making prevention more difficult at a time when it is most needed.
He therefore called for concrete actions and policies capable of delivering tangible results in terms of the health and protection of young people.
Guinean Minister of Health and Public Hygiene Khaite Sall stressed that the rights recognized to young people should be translated into concrete actions and effective access to health services.
"Health is no longer considered a supporting expenditure, but a strategic investment in human capital and in the future of the country," she said.
According to Sall, the vision of the Guinean authorities is to advance the country toward universal health coverage while strengthening adolescents' and young people's access to local, confidential and respectful health services.
The minister also called for turning commitments into action so that sexual and reproductive rights would not remain merely principles enshrined in laws and policies, but could be effectively exercised by the people concerned.
According to the organizers, the 12th edition of the conference will focus in particular on sustainable financing for sexual and reproductive health services, adapting services to crises, combating gender-based violence, and strengthening young people's participation in decision-making. ■

China-Singapore security team claims breakthrough in hacking Starlink terminals
Darknavy gains full administrative control over SpaceX’s user terminal allowing research into the system’s security programmes
2-MIN READ2-MIN
7
 Listen
Zhang Tongin Beijing
A team of cybersecurity experts has announced they successfully compromised the latest Starlink user terminals, crossing the security boundaries of the world’s largest satellite constellation.
In a post on its social media account on Tuesday, Darknavy, an independent cybersecurity research institute headquartered in Singapore and Shanghai, said it had used sophisticated hardware attacks to gain full administrative control over the terminals, allowing it to run any custom code on the devices.
This gives researchers unprecedented freedom, according to the pot, by reopening a long-missing entry point for in-depth security studies of the Starlink satellite system.
Starlink, SpaceX’s low-Earth-orbit satellite internet service, works by connecting user terminals to satellites in near-Earth orbit, which then relay data through ground gateways to the wider internet.
As newer satellites are gradually equipped with laser links, some satellites can also communicate directly with one another via laser, reducing reliance on ground stations while improving transmission speeds and expanding global coverage.
In battlefield conditions like those in Ukraine, where no local ground gateways exist, Starlink terminals can still gain access to the internet by routing signals through satellites that connect to gateways in neighbouring countries.
The terminal acts as both an antenna and a router, making it a critical node for direct communication with the satellites.

A culprit for corrosion may have been operating under our noses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Water droplets can do their own version of the electric slide. But instead of tearing up the dance floor, they may be wearing away at our cars, infrastructure and cultural heritage sites.
Water drops that become charged by sliding along a surface can then transfer their charge when they land on materials with the right electrical properties, including metals. This eventually drives the material to corrode, even when covered by a protective coating, researchers report August 26 in Nature. Water may also pick up charge in clouds, thunderstorms and waterfalls, so this effect might be widespread.
This work could pave the way for better anticorrosion coatings, says Stefan Weber, a physicist at the University of Stuttgart in Germany who was not involved in the study. Earlier work had shown that sliding along many surfaces causes water drops to become charged, but looking to sliding electrification as a source of corrosion represents a step forward, Weber says.
It’s electric
As drops of water slid down common surfaces, including leaves and a commercial kind of glass called polystyrene glass, they can pick up an electrical charge. In an experimental setup (left), when thousands of these drops landed on the Teflon-coated copper, they caused damage visible by microscope (bottom row; scale bar represents 100 micrometers).
Corrosion’s impact on the global economy is not trivial. This broad category of damage that includes rust cost the U.S. automotive industry alone more than $30 billion in 1999. Corrosion costs are not consistently tracked, but estimates put the global cost in the trillions.
Previous work attributed damage to the physical impact of water droplets, as well as small amounts of corrosive compounds like acid that they might contain. At first, it was not clear whether these electrified drops caused damage, says Zhongyuan Ni, a physicist at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research in Mainz, Germany. In early experiments, he could find no damage to a surface after hundreds of drops. “One day, I just let the experiment [keep] running. I forget; I [went] to drink coffee or something,” he says. When he came back, he found signs of damage that prompted him and his colleagues to investigate further.
With knowledge that thousands — not hundreds — of drops were needed to create observable damage, the researchers continuously released drops of water onto Teflon-coated copper surface samples. They imbued drops with charge by sliding them along common surfaces like leaves and construction materials. Each surface was tilted to ensure that water drops would land on the coated copper. For comparison, the team also released water drops directly onto Teflon-coated copper with no sliding.
All of the samples hit with sliding drops appeared damaged when inspected under a microscope, but not a sample hit with direct drops. A different microscopy technique used on a damaged sample revealed that the charged water drops had not only penetrated the Teflon, but reached and corroded the copper. The team observed similar deterioration on samples of polystyrene glass–coated copper and gold, showing that the phenomenon is not unique to Teflon-coated copper.
While these charged water drops could be in the clouds or sliding along your windshield, they should not scare you, Ni says. Their effects are small. But they add up for monuments, machinery and infrastructure that are exposed to the elements for years. Small charges shouldn’t be ignored, Ni says. Even if they’re tiny, “sometimes they will play an important role.”
