Unprecedented: the US deportees forcibly flown to a fourth country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

In late August, around 20 people were put on a flight in the US, shackled at the wrists, waist and ankles, and sent to Liberia as part of one of the largest third-country deportation arrangements of Donald Trump’s second term.
Although more than 23,000 people have been sent to 26 countries other than their own since last year, that day saw something that had not happened before: six people refused to get off the plane – and were instead taken to another country.
Four Cubans, one Brazilian and one Cameroonian refused to disembark in the Liberian capital Monrovia on 20 August; some of them were allegedly assaulted by ICE agents, who returned them to the plane and promised they would be taken back to the US.
A few hours later, however, they were dropped off in another African country: Equatorial Guinea, one of the world’s most repressive and corrupt regimes, where armed men took them to a former luxury hotel turned detention centre in the capital, Malabo, where they have been held ever since.
Meredyth Yoon, the litigation director at Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said: “It’s the first time I’ve heard of people being deported to a third country, refusing to disembark, and then being hastily deported on the same flight to a fourth country.”
The lawyer, who is in close contact with the group, said they were put on the flight without agreeing to, or even knowing they were being sent to Liberia, let alone Equatorial Guinea.
She said they are now being held in “horrific conditions of confinement”, unable to leave the hotel or even contact their families, watched by armed guards, with restricted access to food and no access to basic hygiene items or medical care.
Yoon said: “Their families are terrified, deeply concerned about their safety. They haven’t done anything wrong, and they’re being held against their will without knowing what will happen to them.”
Although deportation by the US to a fourth country appears to be unprecedented, nearly 60 other people, mostly Africans from other countries, have been deported directly to Equatorial Guinea since November.
The country remains far behind Mexico, the main destination for third-country deportees, which has received more than 19,000 people, but Equatorial Guinea has received more than any other country in Africa so far. The agreement with Liberia provides for the transfer of up to 1,200 people.
The flights to Equatorial Guinea are part of a deal secured by vice-president Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, known as Teodorín, the son of the dictator Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, the world’s longest-ruling head of state, who has been in power for nearly half a century.
Teodorín, who has faced criminal proceedings in other countries over money laundering and corruption, had been barred from entering the US. In France, he was tried in absentia and convicted of money laundering, embezzlement of public funds and corruption in 2017, with the conviction upheld by an appeals court in 2020.
Investigations by the US Senate and the Department of Justice (DoJ) concluded he used bribery and extortion to fund a wild spending spree in Equatorial Guinea, and he eventually reached a settlement to avoid trial.
However, the US state department granted him a one-month waiver so he could attend the UN general assembly in New York last year.
He then travelled to Washington and secured the third-country deportation deal, under which the US would pay his government $7.5m (£5.5m).
Tutu Alicante, founder and executive director of the Washington-based NGO EG Justice, said: “For Teodorín, as someone who is about to replace his father as president, having the US on his side is much more important than the money.”
Alicante has also been closely following the situation of about 30 deportees currently being held at the Bamy hotel, owned by Mbasogo’s family and which sits inside an isolated, walled compound heavily patrolled by armed soldiers.
“The conditions they’re being held in are inhumane,” said Alicante. “We’re talking about individuals who have not committed a crime in the US, and they’re locked up 24/7 in small rooms, and many have been deprived of food and water for considerably long periods.”
The Guardian exchanged text messages with one of the Cubans who arrived in late August, who said they were “very saddened” and “desperately hoping to draw attention to what is happening to us, in the hope that someone with the power to help will take pity on us”.
He soon stopped responding, however, because guards had confiscated all the phones to prevent the deportees from speaking to media outlets.
Among them is a man with a large ventral hernia who, after resisting landing in Liberia, was allegedly thrown down the aircraft steps by ICE agents. Last week, he told the Spanish newspaper El País he urgently needed reconstructive abdominal surgery but, when he was taken to a hospital in Malabo, was allegedly denied treatment because he had no documents.
“They cannot legally obtain a status there because Equatorial Guinea doesn’t have a legal framework for asylum, so they’re in this limbo,” said Alicante.
The deportees face two options: indefinite detention at the hotel or being sent back to their countries of origin, as has already happened to almost half of those who have arrived since November.
However, according to the monitoring project, Third Country Deportation Watch, many of these individuals had previously been granted withholding of removal by US immigration judges who found that they faced a real risk of persecution, torture or death in their home countries.
Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration is using third-country deportations as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries.
A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security said: “All of these illegal aliens were deported to a safe third country. We are applying the law as written.
“If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them, period. The Trump administration is utilising all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised.”
The governments of Equatorial Guinea and Liberia did not respond to requests for comment.
Last May, UN human rights experts urged Equatorial Guinea to stop sending US deportees back to their home countries, but, as the Guardian has learned, the practice has continued, with at least four Ethiopians sent back to Ethiopia last Wednesday.
“This is happening in Equatorial Guinea, in Eswatini, Sudan, Ghana, Liberia; in so many places where they are sending mostly innocent people who have not committed a crime in the US. This is unconscionable,” said Alicante.

AI Use in the Job Market Is Creating an Infinite Doom Loop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Jodi Beggs' résumé got dinged for being two pages long. She used her middle initial on one document but not another, which also cost her points. If she changed “percent” to the % sign, her score went up.
Beggs, a data scientist and job seeker, got this feedback from an online system that compares a job description with an applicant's materials to assess how well they match up. The most well known of these tools is Jobscan, though Beggs didn't say which one she tested.
“If my job is to please the robots,” Beggs says, “then even if I don't like AI-generated content, maybe the machines do.”
Jobscan and other apps like it work on the premise that hiring committees use AI to automatically rate and rank candidates in their applicant tracking system (ATS). Only the top 10 to 20 percent of applicants are considered. The bottom 80 might never see the light of day. That's the belief, anyway. To get on the short list, candidates must tailor the formatting of their CVs and cover letters and pack them with the right keywords to match what the ATS wants to see.
The problem is, this premise isn’t always correct. Automated ranking absolutely happens in some organizations, but in others, hiring is still managed personally by humans from start to finish.
The Curse of the Applicant Tracking System
At its most basic, an ATS collects job applications, helps hiring committees review them, and tracks applicants through the interviewing and hiring process. Some systems offer more, from onboarding management to automated AI screening interviews.
Daniel Chait, CEO of an ATS company called Greenhouse, says there's a lot of folklore about these tools, particularly from the job seeker side. No two ATSs are the same. The technology changes fast, so an AI tool inside an ATS might work one way today and a different way tomorrow. Whether an ATS uses AI at all depends on the exact product and which features a team pays for and uses.
Regardless, as long as applicants believe AI is involved, they'll still try to game it using their own AI.
To put the fate of your job search into the hands of a tool that says it can optimize for an ATS is a shaky proposition. One recruiter proved how even with atrocious Jobscan scores, she still got a dozen interviews and an offer. Consider, too, that Jobscan costs $30 to $50 per month. The company isn't exactly incentivized to get you off the job market.
Being in a low-fire, low-hire economy only makes matters worse. Job postings are scarce. Scams and ghost jobs are enough of a problem that some states are looking to write new laws to combat them.
Both job seekers and employers say they're experiencing a breakdown of trust. Candidates sink so much time into their search and hear nothing. Applying to jobs is a black box.
Some employers, meanwhile, say they receive hundreds of applications that look nearly identical. So they feed them into the AI rating system of their ATS to try and get some quick differentiation.
Chait says we're in an AI doom loop. “We've got this tragic situation where each side has a problem. They're using AI to solve their own problem, but in ways that make the problem worse. And so more AI use begets more AI use, to no one's benefit. The more it's happening, the worse it gets.”
Comparing Human Vetting to AI
I spoke with dozens of recruiters and HR managers, as well as small business owners who do their own hiring. Some admitted they use automated candidate ranking, and some were adamant that they do not. The division has nothing to do with the size of the organization or even the number of applicants received. It seems driven by philosophy and culture.
Kim Jones is vice president of human resources at Toshiba. “We have humans review every application,” she says. She doesn't mind applicants using AI to polish up their materials, but “it's not really going to help with getting through the ATS.” Culling applicants comes down to job requirements, salary expectations, and a few other factors, like whether the person would be a rehire.
Where she has seen unwanted AI usage is in the interviewing stage. “You hear the pause, maybe hear the typing, then they come up with a verbose answer,” Jones says.
Another company that relies more on humans than technology for hiring is Doist. It's a small, fully remote company that hires internationally, which means when they have an opening, they're flush with applications.
Nadia Vatalidis, head of people at the company, says her team experimented to see if ATS rankings could help. They took roles that had already been filled and fed in the job descriptions as well as all the applicant materials that they had saved from the hiring process. They wanted to know “what would happen if AI had to short-list the same batch of candidates and whether the folks we interviewed would show up in those same categories,” Vatalidis says. “In two instances that we tested, the person we hired wasn't in the short list.” She says there was overlap in who got an interview, but their new hires—people who were working out great after about six months—didn't make the cut.
Using AI Differently
When James Jacobsen started his job search five months ago, the amount of time he sank into searching and applying to jobs was equivalent to a full-time role. As a design professional, he knows AI can't match him when it comes to creativity, but he experiments with it heavily and knows it's a powerful tool for certain tasks. He used Claude and ChatGPT to polish up his application materials and make sure they were in line with the job description, but it wasn't moving the needle.
Instead of focusing only on his application materials, he started using Claude to streamline and track his job search from top to bottom. He instructed it to comb job listings, analyze descriptions, and log them. He devised an elaborate scoring system based on the type of work, seniority, and his salary requirements, which varied for in-person, hybrid, and remote roles. His AI assistant highlighted the top jobs he should apply to. When he rejected one, he added a note, so if the same position got reposted weeks later, his AI could immediately remind him why he wasn't interested. He spent less time searching to find more high-quality positions. He got a few bites but no offers.
He effectively built the opposite of an ATS—a tracking system for the job seeker.
He didn't stop there. Next, Jacobsen asked Claude and ChatGPT to critique his portfolio, resulting in a six-hour revamp. Two days later, he got a call from a prospective employer, but it still didn't result in an offer.
Chait says job candidates like Jacobsen are asking themselves how they can possibly put in more effort. “Doing more of the same isn't the answer,” he says.
“This is the first time I can remember when both sides are unhappy,” Chait says. “It's just not working.” For job seekers, “I'd say the answer is not just more spray-and-pray,” he says.
Spend time researching companies where you might want to work, Chait says, even if they aren't the first names that come to mind. Kim Jones of Toshiba mentioned that she almost never sees a cover letter anymore and says applicants stand out if they submit one. Networking is yet another underrated skill in today's job market.
Chait has one more message for job seekers, which is to remember: “It's not you; it’s the system, and it stinks.”

Malaysia declares emergency in Sarawak town as haze pollution level hits 521
Indonesian police have arrested 112 people suspected of starting the recent forest and peatland fires in 10 provinces on Sumatra and Borneo
The Air Pollutant Index in Serian, a small agricultural town of just under 90,000 near the border of Indonesia’s Kalimantan province, surged to 521 on Friday, according to Malaysia’s environment department. Sarawak’s much larger capital, Kuching, also showed a hazardous reading of 311.
Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar has consented to the declaration of an emergency in Serian, which would allow more effective measures to be taken, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement. It did not provide details but officials have said a reading above 500 could provide for non-essential work and outdoor activities to be halted. Schools are already shut if the index is above 200.
Haze is a recurring seasonal problem in Southeast Asia, where smoke from forest and peat fires in Indonesia can travel across national borders and affect neighbouring Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore.
Sarawak has been the worst-hit Malaysian state by the haze, with several areas having hazardous air levels in the past few days.
The haze this year has been particularly severe, with elevated fire activity in several provinces in Indonesia, including Kalimantan, and prolonged dry conditions contributing to worsening pollution across parts of Borneo.

India’s push to secure place in global chip supply has ‘secret weapon’: its people
Building up its pool of design talent can gain it a spot higher up in the value chain by turning ‘Make in India’ to ‘Engineer in India’
But observers say the country should set its sights even higher upstream on the value chain by mobilising its “secret weapon” – a talent pool that could realise its dream to turn “Make in India” into “Engineer in India”.
New Delhi earlier this week launched the second phase of its mission with a budget of US$13 billion to build an industrial ecosystem spanning chip design to manufacturing. The move on Monday comes as other countries in the region, such as Japan and Singapore, outline multibillion-dollar development plans for their semiconductor industries following chip shortages during the Covid-19 pandemic that exposed dependency on a handful of East Asian manufacturers.
Delhi has already approved 12 semiconductor manufacturing projects across six states. Three – Micron, Keynes Semicon and CG Semi – have started commercial production this year. They primarily handle assembly, testing and packaging rather than advanced wafer fabrication.

UK moves to secure critical minerals for defence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:14:26 BST
19:14:26 KST

The Ministry of Defence is working to reduce reliance on concentrated sources of critical minerals used by the defence sector, including through alternative suppliers, allied investment and domestic production, Defence Minister Luke Pollard has said.
Responding to a written parliamentary question, Pollard set out work under way to improve the resilience of critical raw material supply chains and reduce exposure to individual suppliers and higher-risk sources.
Pollard said: “The Department is addressing dependencies on concentrated sources of Critical Minerals likely to be affecting the defence sector by improving visibility and enhancing collaboration with industry and like-minded Allies (including NATO and Australia).”
He added: “Efforts focus on developing alternative sources of supply, investing in allied capacity, ensuring security of supply and promoting recycling and substitution to reduce reliance on single suppliers and high-risk geographies.”
The work forms part of the Government’s wider Vision 2035: UK Critical Mineral Strategy, with the MOD involved in implementing measures intended to strengthen access to materials required by defence and advanced industries.
Australia is one of the countries involved in that work, of course. Pollard said: “MOD is also playing an active role in implementing Vision 2035: UK Critical Mineral Strategy through this work, and on 10 June, signed a new Joint Statement of Intent with Australia on collaboration to secure critical minerals supply chains for Defence.”
The Government is also backing efforts to restore a domestic source of tungsten through the Hemerdon mine in Devon. Pollard said: “Furthermore, the UK Government is investing £71 million through the National Wealth Fund to restart Tungsten West’s Hemerdon mine in Devon, securing the ability to negotiate over the next 6 months for a domestic supply of tungsten, a strategically important mineral used in defence and advanced industries.”
Tungsten is used across a range of industrial and defence applications where high density, strength and resistance to heat are required. The Government’s investment in Hemerdon is intended to give the UK an opportunity to negotiate access to domestic production rather than relying entirely on overseas sources.
The MOD’s work also covers recycling and material substitution, alongside efforts to identify alternative suppliers and increase production capacity among allied countries. The department is working with NATO and Australia as part of that effort, while also seeking better visibility of where defence-related supply chains remain exposed to concentrated sources.
Pollard said the work reflected the growing importance of these materials to both the economy and national security, with early discussions identifying areas where countries face common supply risks.
He stated: “This recognises that critical minerals are essential to our modern economy and increasingly our national security, with initial exchanges identifying opportunities for closer collaboration on shared critical mineral supply risks.”

Argentina is not a credible power able to threaten Falklands
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:10:17 BST
19:10:17 KST

Argentina has spent the past two years rebuilding an air force it allowed to wither for a decade, and every time a new aircraft arrives the question surfaces again of whether the Falkland Islands are threatened by it.
The rebuild is real, the capability gap it addresses was actually genuine, but it does not amount to a force capable of operating against the islands.
At the centre of the programme sits the F-16, with Argentina having agreed in 2024 to buy 24 second-hand F-16AM/BM aircraft from Denmark for around $300 million, a deal the government of Javier Milei described as the country’s most important military acquisition in fifty years. The first six arrived at Río Cuarto in Córdoba on 5 December 2025, with the remainder due in batches of six each December through to 2028, and the fleet working up at the VI Air Brigade at Tandil.
Argentina, as readers will know, retired its last supersonic fighters in 2015 and spent nearly a decade without any aircraft capable of intercepting an intruder, which for a country of that size and coastline is an extraordinary gap, and the F-16 closes it while bringing Argentine aircrew into Western avionics, weapons and logistics standards for the first time in a generation.
Alongside the aircraft, Argentina has taken delivery of the first of a batch of American M1126 Stryker armoured vehicles for an army still operating TAM medium tanks and M113 carriers, and has signed with the Danish firm Terma for F-16 electronic warfare upgrades covering software, mission planning and ground support. The 2026 budget carries capital lines for hangars, ground support equipment and base protection systems at Tandil and Río Cuarto running through to 2028.
The navy has seen considerably less of this investment, with a surface fleet resting on German-designed MEKO 360 destroyers and MEKO 140 corvettes, most of which require extensive maintenance or mid-life work, while the service has been evaluating the retirement of its last S-2T Turbo Tracker anti-submarine aircraft and has operated without a functioning submarine force since the loss of the ARA San Juan in 2017.
The arithmetic
The nearest Argentine airfields sit roughly 300 nautical miles from the Falklands, which means an F-16 flying that distance, holding over the target area and returning would have very little fuel margin, and the tanker fleet behind it consists of a small number of ageing KC-130H Hercules rather than anything capable of sustaining a fighter campaign at that radius.
The same geography defined the 1982 campaign, of course, when Argentine Skyhawks and Daggers arrived over San Carlos with minutes of fuel remaining, attacked at low level because they had no other option, and lost heavily in the process. The aircraft available today are considerably better, though the distance between the mainland and the islands remains what it was.
Argentine defence spending sits at roughly 0.7 to 0.8 per cent of GDP, with the 2026 budget aiming to push the combined defence and internal security figure towards 2 per cent, though economic volatility has repeatedly disrupted procurement timelines. The armed forces number around 72,000 active personnel, and personnel costs consume the largest share of the budget, which is the usual pattern in a force that has been under-equipped for a long period.
What is on the islands
British Forces South Atlantic Islands is a permanent joint command established so that the circumstances of 1982, in which the islands were held by a small Royal Marines detachment and had to be retaken by a task force sailing 8,000 miles, cannot recur.
Four Typhoon FGR4 of 1435 Flight, as most readers will be aware, hold quick reaction alert round the clock covering the airspace over the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, supported by A400M and Voyager transport and tanker aircraft, which means British fighters operating in the area have the refuelling that Argentine ones lack.
Ground defence rests on a roulement infantry company, currently drawn from 5th Battalion The Rifles, working alongside the locally recruited Falkland Islands Defence Force, with Sky Sabre providing ground-based air defence and radar coverage from sites including Mount Byron. HMS Medway holds the South Atlantic Patrol Task, and RAF Mount Pleasant is a hardened airfield capable of accepting reinforcement direct from the United Kingdom.
The garrison exercises regularly, and Cape Upholder in early July combined live firing from mortars, snipers and machine guns with a section attack supported by simulated close air support from the Typhoons.
Seizing an airfield defended by fast jets, modern ground-based air defence and infantry, across 300 nautical miles of the South Atlantic, without air superiority, without meaningful tanker support and without any means of sustaining a lodgement once ashore, against a country that has demonstrated it will fight for the islands and now keeps a permanent garrison on them. Unlikely.
Argentine doctrine reflects as much, with the stated regional priority, described as the defence of the south, concerning presence in Patagonia, the policing of national waters and Antarctic logistics rather than anything directed at the islands. The Milei government has signalled no change in its Malvinas policy, which remains a diplomatic claim pursued annually at the United Nations rather than a military one.
Where the modernisation does matter, and it does, is over a longer horizon and across the wider region, because a country moving onto NATO-standard equipment, integrating with American logistics and rebuilding an air force from very little is a different security actor from one that had none of those things, and the British position in the South Atlantic rests on the garrison remaining credible rather than on Argentine weakness continuing indefinitely.
Islanders voted by 1,513 votes to three in the 2013 referendum to remain a British Overseas Territory, and the garrison maintained since 1982 has cost considerably less than the campaign that made it necessary.

Tanker captain arrested over cargo ship sinking off Istanbul, prosecutors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:13:21 UTC
19:13:21 KST

Search and resuce operations are ongoing with teams yet to reach the wreckage of the Tuğberk İmamoğlu or locate its voyage data recorder (VDR) or "black box."
The captain of an oil tanker that collided with a cargo ship and sank off Istanbul leaving 10 crew missing has been arrested along with his third-in-command on charges of negligent homicide, prosecutors said on Friday.
The pair were arrested by a court late on Thursday, a day after the pre-dawn collision in which the ALSU, an empty oil tanker, struck the Tuğberk İmamoğlu, a cargo vessel carrying rolled steel, in the Sea of Marmara near Istanbul.
The case is being handled by prosecutors in Silivri on the western outskirts of Istanbul province.
According to the prosecutors' statement, the Silvri court charged the pair with negligent homicide for failing to fulfil their navigational safety obligations and take the necessary measures to prevent the collision.
It said the captain, identified only as A.E., "failed to fulfil his duty of supervision and oversight of navigational safety" while the other suspect, M.E., "who served as the third captain and watch officer at the time of the incident, failed to take the necessary measures to prevent the collision in a timely and effective manner."
The court ordered four other suspects be granted conditional release, it said.
Officials said the damaged cargo ship sank "very quickly" in waters about 900 metres deep, some 18 nautical miles (33 kilometres) off Silivri, leaving all 10 crew members missing.
Rescuers have yet to reach the wreckage of the Tuğberk İmamoğlu or locate its voyage data recorder (VDR) or "black box."
According to a marine accident expert report prepared for prosecutors, a copy of which was seen by the AFP news agency on Thursday, there were multiple breaches of safety procedures aboard the tanker.
"The fundamental root cause...resulting in a catastrophe, was the deficiencies and failures on the bridge of the M/T ALSU," it said.
It said an inexperienced third officer was at the helm and there was no lookout on duty, describing it as "serious negligence."
"No helmsman or lookout was posted on the bridge and the officer, who had only recently joined the vessel and lacked experience, was left alone on watch," the report said.
It also pointed to shortcomings on the part of the cargo ship.
Search and rescue operations continued on Friday.
Prosecutors have started legal proceedings against nine of the ALSU's 10 crew members, excluding the cook, six of whom appeared in court on Thursday.
